Research notes: Chapter 62 · Reading guide: Guide, Chapter 62

Characters: Joachim Spitzer

Pillar 1 Not One Self

Pillar note: Pillar 1 Not One Self

The chapter opens with Mr. Spitzer uncertain whether he has ever slept, and this uncertainty is not incidental; it is constitutive. He cannot locate himself in time, in consciousness, or in identity. He is simultaneously:

  • Joachim Spitzer the musician, described as "dead musician and author of the music of the spheres"
  • Joachim Spitzer the lawyer, "Harvard graduate magna cum laude and attorney at law, retired"
  • The conductor of a water orchestra he has never assembled
  • The gargoyle "spouting water music from his mouth"
  • The pack rat's counterpart, existing in an exchange economy of stolen and returned objects
  • His brother's echo, wearing "his brother's milky blue stone ring", writing with both left and right hands as two different selves

The most explicit statement of plural selfhood comes near the end: "he was Mr. Spitzer now — there were not two. There was one. There was one who had gone over to the many". This is not resolution into unity but collapse of distinction: the plural self not reconciled but acknowledged as irreducibly multiple. His brother is not a separate person but a layer of himself, a sediment (see Pillar 8) pressing up through his identity.

The will itself, written by his left hand and witnessed by his right hand, is the legal document of a plural self attempting to notarize its own multiplicity. The absurdity is philosophical: you cannot witness yourself because there is no stable self to do the witnessing.

Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

Pillar note: Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

The chapter's entire architecture is built on the impossibility of distinguishing illusion from reality. Mr. Spitzer's dream sequence at the opening does not end; it bleeds into his waking actions. He writes his will "by the pale light of the old oil chimney lamp... still burning in the sunlight", where night's light and day's light fuse. There is no clean boundary between sleeping and waking, between dream river and real river.

The dream itself performs this: "But perhaps all these rivers were one great river of reality burning from light to darkness, darkness to light, water to freezing, ice to star". The word "reality" appears here inside the dream: reality is not what the dream obscures but what the dream is. The larger cave, more carefully lit.

The most devastating instance of this pillar is the violinist of the Philadelphia Symphony, who spent twenty years creating the illusion of music where no music was, never touching the strings, missing them "by an infinitesimal distance." He was praised as the perfect example of musicianship. When he accidentally touched the strings, when he crossed into reality; he was dismissed. The system rewarded the construction of illusion and punished contact with the real. This is not satirical exaggeration. It is the chapter's central parable: the conductor could not tolerate reality breaking through the performance of reality.

Mr. Spitzer's own music participates in this: he describes compositions full of "sounds which never should be heard" and "ultimate mysteries unsolvable", music that is more real for being unplayable, because the playable is always already a reduction of what was intended.

Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

Pillar note: Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

Grief in this chapter is not an event. It is atmospheric. It does not attach to a single loss but permeates everything: the composition of music no one plays, the brother whose ring Mr. Spitzer wears, the cities under the frozen sand, the cancelled stamps of exploded monarchies, the dead clarinetist, the tubercular horn-blower.

The chapter's weather is consistently elegiac. Mr. Spitzer writes "aquatic nocturnes", "flooded pastorales", a "Pavanne for a Dead Lady", a "Pavanne for the Dead Polar Bear and the Entombed Butterfly", an "Elegy for a Frog Eating a Firefly", and, most tellingly, "his elegy for himself who was dead and entombed in this life as in a dark star".

He is writing elegies for things that have not yet finished dying, including himself. This is grief as permanent weather in its purest form: "death did not balance with life. Death was greater than life — as night was greater than day". There is no consolation offered, no stage of acceptance reached. The chapter ends not with resolution but with Mr. Spitzer crossing Louisburg Square, absent-minded, thinking he was in Philadelphia: geographically lost inside his own grief, unable to locate himself in the present because the past is so much heavier.

The pack rat exchange (musical scrap for musical scrap, pearl button for apple core) is the chapter's small, tender acknowledgment that even grief has its economies, its strange reciprocities. But crucially, the exchange never balances: "whoever had stolen away his life, his death had brought nothing, nothing in return".

Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

Pillar note: Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

Mr. Spitzer is constitutionally incapable of looking away. The chapter is structured as an act of radical witnessing, of the horn-blower destroying his lungs, of the suicidal clarinetist playing from the Gloucester rooftop, of the silent violinist on the Library steps, of his own dying.

His response to the horn-blower is the clearest enactment of this pillar. Reason would suggest: stop blowing, save your life. But Mr. Spitzer, recognizing that reason would be its own violence here, instead says: "Blow on, horn-blower, blow on! Blow moon and sun and stars before thee!". This is not irresponsibility. It is the witness refusing to impose resolution on another's irreducible situation. He stays in the room. He does not flinch from the blood-specked phlegm, the spurting horn, the numbered days.

The scene with the silent violinist is even more extraordinary. Mr. Spitzer watches for an extended duration, his eyes sometimes "rolled back completely in his head", in a state of total receptive attention. He does not intervene. He does not explain. He does not simplify what he sees into a category (beggar, madman, genius). He simply witnesses, and then cries "Bravo, bravo!", which is the only appropriate response to something witnessed fully: acknowledgment without reduction.

Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

Pillar note: Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

Mr. Spitzer has been writing his will for so long it is "already several volumes long". He has been composing music his entire life in "scraps and fragments". He keeps "this task for his leisure years" of arranging his musical phrases into one great symphony: leisure years that will never come, and he knows it.

The will is the perfect emblem of recursive construction: a legal document that attempts to conclude, to settle, to distribute, but which keeps growing, keeps returning to its beginning, keeps adding codicils and cautionary phrases. It is witnessed by the same hand that writes it. It is stamped with a notary's seal "of about the period of the turn of the century", already obsolete at the moment of use.

His music operates the same way: "his scraps of paper flying around him like leaves merely reminded him of something attempted". The building is never finished. He knows this. He builds anyway: writing on shirt cuffs, on black handkerchiefs, in pigeon holes and warped drawers. The recursive return is not defeat. It is the only honest form the work can take.

The pack rat is the chapter's figure for recursive construction in its most elemental form: taking and returning, building a nest from stolen materials, exchanging one thing for another in an endless economy of provisional making.

Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

Pillar note: Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

This pillar is perhaps the chapter's most explicit philosophical concern. Mr. Spitzer directly addresses it:

"for what great musical composition was ever played as its composer had written it, and had not many great composers written their works with visual patterns none could play"

The music that cannot be played is not failed music. It is the most honest music, because it refuses to pretend that what can be expressed equals what was intended. The gap between intention and execution is not a technical problem; it is the condition of all making.

The clarinetist who committed suicide leaving the note "I am out of tune. I have gone to join a greater orchestra" is the tragic version of this pillar: the musician who could not survive his own incompletion, who needed a perfection this world cannot provide. Mr. Spitzer mourns him but does not judge him. The greater orchestra the clarinetist sought is, in Radical Immanence terms, a fantasy of completion, and yet Mr. Spitzer finds in this fantasy something beautiful, something worth mourning.

The recording angel who has "lost all his feathers but one", keeping his last pen for his last note, is the most poignant image of ethical incompletion in the chapter. He cannot write everything. He must choose his last note carefully. This is not failure of the recording project. It is the integrity of the ongoing sentence refusing false conclusion.

Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Pillar note: Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Every musician in this chapter is marginal. The tubercular horn-blower destroying himself. The suicidal clarinetist. The silent violinist dismissed for touching the strings. Mr. Spitzer himself, "never seen in musical circles, never seen at a Pop concert in the Great Shell, never seen along the windy Esplanade", is the most marginal of all: a musician who has never had his music played, a lawyer who witnesses his own will, a man who cannot remember his own address.

But the chapter makes clear that these marginal figures are not exceptions to the musical world; they are its most truthful representatives. The violinist who never touched the strings was praised as the perfect example. When he accidentally produced reality, he was expelled. The margin is where the constructed nature of the center becomes visible.

Mr. Spitzer's sympathy "with all derelicts and particularly wandering musicians whose music could not be recognized or musicians who played upon unrecognizable instruments" is not charity. It is epistemological solidarity: the recognition that the unrecognized musician knows something about music that the recognized musician, safely inside the system, cannot access.

The man kicked out of the orchestra "knew more about music than any playing in an orchestra, for the player was under the powers of the despotic conductor and could play only his own part". Marginality grants a totality of perception that inclusion forecloses.

Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

Pillar note: Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

The chapter's prose style is itself sedimentary; each sentence deposits layer upon layer, never clearing away what came before. The cancelled postage stamps of "exploded monarchies", the "old Polish kings who had been deposed", Queen Victoria in her youth, the great Consort in his age, the Leaning Tower of Pisa, Brooklyn Bridge, the Greek drachma of the period of Theseus; these are not random accumulations. They are the sediment of history pressing up through the drawers of Mr. Spitzer's desk.

The cities are the most explicit expression of this pillar: "Nineveh and Tyre and Ur of the Chaldees and Carthage... cities under the frozen sand of the Great Gobi Desert". These are not metaphors for loss. They are layers beneath the present, still there, still pressing. Mr. Spitzer writes the street music of dead cities, not as elegy for what is gone but as acknowledgment of what is still present beneath.

His own memory performs this sedimentary logic: "he had known since memory began... that all his memories were not his own, that they came from an alien source". The past that accumulates in him is not only his past. It is the past of all those who deposited experience before he arrived: his brother, the musicians he has known, the cities under the sand. The image of the old roll-top desk with its warped "drawers he had not opened for years" is the chapter's domestic figure for sedimentary time: the past is literally there, in the drawers, waiting. Opening them does not retrieve a past that has gone. It surfaces a past that never left.

Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

Pillar note: Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

The prose style of this chapter is itself the argument. The sentences do not end; they accrete, qualify, contradict, revise. This is language performing its own constructedness, refusing the false closure of the period, the false authority of the declarative sentence.

Mr. Spitzer writes his will with "spidery signature so delicate that one should look at it through a magnifying glass or even a telescope": language so fine it requires magnification to be read, so personal it approaches illegibility. This is the opposite of legal language, which pretends to speak from nowhere, to apply universally. Mr. Spitzer's legal language names its own location: written by a dead man, witnessed by himself, sworn to by the Pledge of Allegiance instead of the usual oath.

The music itself functions as language in this chapter, but language that "should be influenced by the waves and the wind blowing the strings", language that cannot be separated from its material conditions. There is "no score, no sheet music but the swelling waves". The score is the world. The world is the score. This is language that has stopped pretending to be a neutral vehicle.

The silent violinist's "beautiful sign language" is the chapter's ideal of honest language: a language that makes no pretense of transparency, that is visibly, physically, located in the body of the one who speaks it.

Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

Pillar note: Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

Mr. Spitzer does not look to heaven. He looks at the bull's-eye lamp, the checkered oilcloth, the warped drawers, the pearl buttons, the pack rat's exchange. The sacred in this chapter is entirely immanent: located in ordinary objects, ordinary exchanges, ordinary failures.

The water music is the chapter's central image of immanent transcendence. It is not music that points toward heaven. It is music that "should be played only upon swelling water, rivers or lakes or oceans": music that points deeper into the material world, into the waves, the cordages, the ear shells, the wings of migratory butterflies.

The dying dolphin, the sea anemones, the firefly, the pack rat; these are the chapter's sacred figures. Not angels, not gods, but creatures at the edges of visibility, creatures whose existence is fragile and brief and therefore most fully present.

The recording angel is the chapter's one explicitly supernatural figure, but he is presented as exhausted, nearly featherless, keeping his last pen for his last note. He is not transcendent. He is immanently depleted, subject to the same economies of loss as everything else. Even the angel is inside the world, not above it.

The most beautiful statement of immanent transcendence in the chapter: "he would live as long as his music lived and breathed". Not in heaven. Not in memory. In the music itself, in the material vibration of the world.

Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

Pillar note: Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

This pillar is the chapter's deepest structure. Mr. Spitzer is explicitly described as constituted by what came before him and constituting what comes after:

"just as one man might be two bodies existing sequentially as in time, perhaps one existing when the other was dead, so also one man might be two bodies existing simultaneously as in space"

He is the crossing point of his brother's life and his own, of the dead musicians and the unborn listeners, of the music written and the music never played. His will (his "mortmain", his "dead hand") is the legal instrument of the crossing point: the dead reaching forward to constitute the conditions of the living.

The music he bequeaths "to the generations", "free as a cloud driven down the wind", is not a gift from a completed self to a future self. It is the structural obligation of the crossing point: the ancestors in the sediment, the carrying continuing.

The final image of the chapter (Mr. Spitzer crossing Louisburg Square, asking where he is, being told "Boston", murmuring "My God! I thought I was in Philadelphia") is the crossing point made comic and heartbreaking simultaneously. He does not know where he is because he is constituted by so many places, times, and selves that no single location can contain him. He is not lost. He is everywhere at once, which from the outside looks exactly like being lost.

Research notes: Chapter 60 · Reading guide: Guide, Chapter 60

Characters: Joachim Spitzer

Pillar 1 Not One Self

Pillar note: Pillar 1 Not One Self

The chapter opens with a foundational question that it never answers: is Mr. Spitzer a musician or a gambler? But crucially, the text does not treat this as a mystery to be solved. The question is posed and re-posed, and both identities are developed with equal weight, equal interiority, equal validity.

"If he was a musician as he thought... if he was a gambler, on the other hand, if he was not a musician but had merely deceived himself..."

The grammatical structure, the endless conditional "if", is itself the philosophical statement. The self is not one thing awaiting discovery. It is multiple possibilities held simultaneously, irresolvably. The musician and the gambler are not competing hypotheses. They are co-present selves, each generating its own world of imagery: the harpsichord and the ace of clubs, the fugue and the horse race, Mozart and the moose call.

Furthermore, Mr. Spitzer is persistently doubled against his dead brother, who appears as a kind of shadow self: the gambler to his musician, the wild duck caller to his harpsichordist. The brother is not separate from Mr. Spitzer; he is another layer of the same plural identity, the self that might have been, the self that was in another version of the same life.

"Sound shared the silence, but his dead brother could not have imagined the silence."

The self here is not singular and bounded. It is a field of overlapping, simultaneous, irresolvable identities. This is not presented as tragedy. It is presented as the condition of being.

Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

Pillar note: Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

The chapter is saturated with the question of whether Mr. Spitzer's perceptions are real or constructed. The moose encounter and the wild duck encounter are the central examples. In both cases, what begins as an accidental sound, a noise made without intention, is received as real by the animal, and then the animal's response makes the illusion real for Mr. Spitzer.

"Mr. Spitzer had seen the great antlers of four-foot spread and enormous tines looming like tree boughs through the blowing purple fog..."

The text notes explicitly: "as when the auditory hallucination ushers in the visual", a direct acknowledgment that perception constructs reality rather than simply receiving it. The moose is real because the call was made. The ducks are real because he called them. The line between illusion and reality is not a stable border but a threshold that is crossed by the act of attention itself.

The mandarin ducks are reconstructed entirely from fragments:

"he reconstructed from these fragments the memory, even as a dead man might build the world, providing that which had been missing"

This is Pillar 2 stated almost directly: reality is not found, it is built from fragments, and the builder is always partially dead, partially absent, always working from incomplete evidence. The comparison to a dead man building the world is one of the most precise articulations of constructivist ontology imaginable.

Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

Pillar note: Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

The elegiac tone is not incidental to this chapter; it is its climate. The word "elegy" appears explicitly:

he "had almost decided that it would be unnecessary to write his elegy now. For surely, his elegy was this wild duck’s horn."

But the grief here is not about any single loss. It accumulates across the chapter: the lost musical career, the dead brother, the forgotten fugues, the forgotten scores, the horse races on a dead man's shirt, the horses' heads on tombs, the marble eyeballs. Loss does not arrive and depart. It sediments.

The chapter's syntax enacts this. The sentences do not resolve. They extend. They absorb more and more material (the gambling, the music, the moose, the ducks, the obituary columns, the Stock Exchange) without arriving at a conclusion. Grief here is not an event but a grammatical condition, the condition of the sentence that cannot end because ending would mean a resolution that does not exist.

"had never read the obituary columns listing himself as one who had gone over to that death which levels all, leveling the jockey with the horse, leveling the greatest king as if he were some poor old tramp..."

Even death is absorbed into the accumulation rather than standing as a terminal point. Death levels, but it does not conclude. The grief continues past it.

Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

Pillar note: Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

The narrative stance of this chapter is precisely that of the Witness. The text does not judge Mr. Spitzer. It does not resolve his identity. It does not tell us whether he is deluded or perceptive, musician or gambler, sane or mad. It stays in the room with him through the full complexity of his experience.

The moose encounter could be read as comic. The duck encounter could be read as pathological. The text refuses both readings. It holds the experience in full seriousness:

"Perhaps he was a man already metamorphosed into wings — tremblingly, standing still — hearing those great wings roar past him, soaring, billowing, ebbing — not so much past him as through him..."

This is not mockery and not simple celebration. It is witness. The attention is complete and non-simplifying. The refusal to conclude: is he mad? is he mystical? is he a musician? is he a gambler?: is not evasion. It is the ethical act of the Witness: to see without flinching, without rushing toward resolution.

Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

Pillar note: Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

The chapter's structure is itself recursive. It returns again and again to the same questions (musician or gambler, music or track) each time with slightly different material, slightly different imagery, building not toward an answer but toward a richer, denser version of the question.

"Yet sometimes, being absent-minded because he was troubled by so many tremulous thoughts like an unfinished fugue running through his mind, like that music he had never written or could not even remember now, for he had forgotten many fugues, many antiphonies, many winding horns..."

The unfinished fugue is the perfect metaphor for recursive construction. A fugue returns to its subject, transforms it, develops it, but the fugue Mr. Spitzer carries is one he cannot remember and never completed. He builds it anyway, in the act of living, in the act of calling to animals he did not mean to call, in the act of reconstructing mandarin ducks from fragments of light. The building is provisional. It is never finished. That is not presented as failure.

Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

Pillar note: Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

The chapter is, formally, a single sentence, or something very close to one. The syntax refuses the period. It refuses conclusion. The demand for completion is resisted at every level: thematic, grammatical, philosophical.

"the music like a path dividing sound from chaos, sound being an intellectual thing, sound moving like the human spirit through heavens of imagined silence"

Music itself is defined here not as a completed thing but as a path: ongoing, directional, never arrived. The honest life, by this logic, is the ongoing sentence. The chapter does not end so much as pause, and even its final note, "his elegy was this wild duck's horn", is an identification of the elegy with something wild, migratory, and passing rather than with a fixed monument.

Unfinished Is Honest is also visible in the treatment of Mr. Spitzer's career. He is an authority on instruments he may never have played, a musician who may never have written music, a gambler who may never have won. The incompletion is not shameful. It is the honest record of a life lived in the conditional tense.

Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Pillar note: Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Mr. Spitzer is marginal in multiple registers simultaneously. He occupies no clear professional identity (musician? gambler?), no clear social position (he has never been "in the carriage trade", never sat "in a diamond horseshoe or a silk-lined stall" ), no clear perceptual status (hallucinator? mystic? ordinary man on a street?).

But crucially, his marginality is not presented as deficiency. It is presented as the site where the constructed nature of identity becomes most visible. Because he is neither fully musician nor fully gambler, the text can examine both categories from the outside, revealing them as constructions rather than natural kinds.

The dead brother functions similarly; he is marginal to life itself, existing only in Mr. Spitzer's reconstruction of him, and yet he is more vivid in some ways than the living. The marginal figure (the dead, the amateur, the man who calls moose in empty streets) is not the exception. He is the evidence that categories are made, not found.

Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

Pillar note: Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

This pillar may be the most structurally central to the chapter. Time here does not move forward. It accumulates. The chapter layers geological strata of reference: horse races, the dead brother's shirt, old Locomobiles circa 1912, the Pleiades, golden shekels and drachmas, the Stock Exchange, marble tombs, the El. These are not arranged chronologically. They press up through the text simultaneously, like sediment that has never settled.

"the hieroglyphics of old horse races his brother had worn upon his shirt front, the hunched dwarf jockeys, the horses' heads upon the tombs, the marble eyeballs in the marble clouds"

The movement from horse races to shirt fronts to tombs to marble is a movement through sedimentary time: the present race, the worn record of past races, the tomb that preserves the image of the horse, the marble that outlasts the flesh. The past is not behind Mr. Spitzer. It is beneath him, pressing up.

The dead brother is the most powerful expression of this. He is gone but not past. He is beneath the present, still generating meaning, still being reconstructed, still answering when Mr. Spitzer makes the duck call without knowing he has made it.

Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

Pillar note: Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

The prose of this chapter is hyper-aware of its own constructedness. The long conditional sentences ("if he was a musician... if he was a gambler...") do not pretend to speak from a neutral position of knowledge. They name their own uncertainty. They locate themselves inside the problem they are examining.

The lists (of currencies (shekels, talents, florins, drachmas), of newspaper sections (financial news, obituary columns, sporting page), of instruments (harpsichord, viola da gamba, lute, tortoise-shell violin)) are not neutral catalogues. They are constructions of a world, and their excess reveals the constructedness. No neutral observer would list golden shekels alongside Boston dollars. The list itself is a made thing, shaped by a particular consciousness located in a particular place.

"the music of the Stock Exchange like a long surf blowing now in his ears"

This metaphor, the Stock Exchange as surf, does not describe reality. It constructs a reality in which financial abstraction and natural force are the same phenomenon. Language here is not a vehicle. It is the event.

Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

Pillar note: Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

The sacred in this chapter lives entirely within the ordinary world, but it is a world that has been opened by attention. The mandarin ducks are the clearest example:

"beautiful Asiatics gleaming like the dappled light cast by a dying dolphin, ducks with crested heads and veiled gold eyes as near as pools or a thousand city lights and gold-tipped wings and pale filaments drifting and blue under-feathers streaming"

This is transcendent language, but it describes ducks on a city street. The transcendence is not upward, toward a beyond. It is inward and downward, into the full reality of the thing itself. The dying dolphin's dappled light is not a symbol of something else. It is the thing. The sacred lives in the specificity of the gold-tipped wings, the blue under-feathers, the veiled gold eyes.

Similarly, the moose in the purple fog is not a symbol. It is a moose. But it is a moose that has been called into being by an accidental call, and it arrives with the force of revelation. The immanent transcendence is not found by leaving the world. It is found by accidentally calling to it in an empty street and hearing it answer.

Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

Pillar note: Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

This pillar finds its most explicit expression in the lighthouse image near the chapter's end:

"he being like the burning of the lighthouse on the distant rock as the wild sea billowed around him, and they being like those poor birds of passage who, with their eyes blinded by the light, are dashed to pieces against a lighthouse looming through the fog, for they have mistaken the lighthouse for the light, the reflection of a star. They are dashed to pieces against a star."

Mr. Spitzer here is not a self moving through time. He is a crossing point: a fixed light around which the migratory, the living, the beautiful, the transient break themselves. He is constituted by what has accumulated in him (the dead brother, the forgotten fugues, the lost career, the sedimentary past) and he is constituting something for those who pass through him (the ducks reconstruct their flight path by him; the moose answers his call; the wild duck's horn becomes his elegy).

The obligation is not chosen. It is structural. He did not choose to be a lighthouse. He stood still, and the world organized itself around his stillness. The ancestors (the dead brother, the old gamblers, the marble horses) are in the sediment beneath him. The carrying continues in the form of an elegy that is not a written thing but a living sound: the wild duck's horn, still moving, still calling, still answering.

Chapter 79

← Chapter 78 · Wheel and Spokes Home · Chapter 80 →

Research notes: Chapter 79 · Reading guide: Guide, Chapter 79

Characters: Esther Longtree · Rosemary

Pillar 1 Not One Self

Pillar note: Pillar 1 Not One Self

Esther is constitutively multiple from the very first paragraph. She is described as simultaneously "weak and gentle" and "firm, muscular, wind-burned", a contradiction the narrative does not attempt to resolve. She is cloud-like and mulish. She is the child of her father's immensity and her mother's smallness, inheriting both and fitting neither.

More radically, the chapter establishes that Esther is not one person at all; she is at minimum three:

  • Herself, the living, kicking, cross-eyed woman
  • Rosemary, the stillborn shadow twin she may have killed in the womb
  • The go-between, the dark woman whose features she has inherited and whose identity bleeds into hers

"If the other was a shadow, it must have been the shadow of a little jackass, too, she had thought, finally, trying to make things clear."

The self here is not a unified subject who has a history; it is the intersection of multiple incomplete persons. Rosemary is not separate from Esther; she is the other face of the same impossible birth. The go-between is not merely Esther's biological father-figure; she is Esther's physical template, her inherited chin, her future face in death.

The prose enacts this plurality formally: the narrative voice shifts constantly between reported interiority, remembered speech, imagined reconstruction, and something closer to myth. The sentence never fully commits to a single perspective because Esther herself never fully coheres into one. This is not a problem the text is trying to solve. It is what the text is.

Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

Pillar note: Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

The chapter is saturated with the impossibility of distinguishing dream from fact, memory from construction. Esther's entire origin story is received knowledge: told to her by her uncle laughing until his face turned purple, by her mother in moments of rage or grief, glimpsed at age seven in a dying woman's room. She was not present at her own conception in any ordinary sense, yet:

"she had been present, the moth flying from the spoon as it passed between her parents, and she had seen the whole transaction with her little eyes before her eyes were blinded by the light, the unholy light."

This is not memory. It is mythological self-construction: the self retroactively installing itself into its own origin. The cave is not something Esther can exit. Her entire sense of who she is has been built from other people's accounts, other people's shame, other people's need.

The silver spoon itself operates as a kind of primary illusion-made-real: an instrument that should not be capable of transmitting life, yet does. The chapter does not treat this as metaphor for something more real underneath. The spoon is the reality. There is no deeper, truer account available. The construction is the thing.

"Not that she was plucked out of heavens, out of the empty air, out of the earth—but the conception was painful and different from that of others."

Reality here is specifically what has been made through effort, shame, and the intervention of a stranger, not what was found naturally. Illusion and reality do not oppose each other; they are the same substance worked differently.

Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

Pillar note: Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

The chapter does not present grief as an event Esther moves through. It presents grief as the climate of her existence, the atmospheric condition in which all other experience occurs.

Her birthday, which should be a celebration, is also the anniversary of Rosemary's death, the day her mother bakes two cakes or none. There is no day that is not also a mourning. The April blizzard that killed all the flowers on the day of her birth is not a symbol pointing toward resolution; it is the permanent weather of her world, the condition under which everything grows or fails to grow.

"Esther's death had been gradual and was not yet achieved, though she was trying, through birth, to die."

Grief here is not even separable from existence. Esther's life is described as a gradual dying. Her many stillbirths, the striated body "because of the many births which were the stillbirths", are not tragedies that interrupt her life. They are her life, the recurring form her experience takes.

The mother's grief for Rosemary is equally unresolved and unresolvable; it does not diminish over years but instead becomes the medium through which she relates to Esther, constantly reminding her of the missing twin. Grief accumulates in this text with geological patience. It does not conclude. It deposits.

Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

Pillar note: Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

The narrative stance of this chapter is one of sustained, unflinching witness. The prose does not rush toward judgment or resolution. It stays in the room (the cold kitchen, the old mule farm, the dying woman's bed of chicken feathers) and it looks.

The seven-year-old Esther at the deathbed of the go-between is the chapter's central image of witnessing:

"But Esther had seen, staring through shadows, the woman's features, so much like her own, the great, crooked nose, the dimpled chin, and had heard the woman's rasping, final voice."

The child does not understand what she sees. The narrative does not explain it tidily. What is witnessed is held in suspension: the dying woman's face as mirror, as father, as stranger, as self. The text refuses to collapse this into a single meaning.

The ethical weight of the chapter falls on this act of seeing without flinching. Esther's crossed eyes, mentioned repeatedly, are not simply a physical trait. They are the figure of a consciousness that cannot look at anything straight on because what is there is too multiple, too painful, too contradictory to be taken in directly,. The witness here is impaired, partial, necessarily oblique, and the text honors that obliqueness rather than correcting it.

Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

Pillar note: Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

The chapter is itself a recursive structure. Esther circles her origin story repeatedly, each time approaching it from a slightly different angle, adding detail, revising emphasis, returning to the kitchen, the spoon, the go-between, the alarm clock. The narrative does not progress linearly toward revelation. It spirals.

"Why worry now as to how she had been conceived, as if someone had only thought of her, for the work was done?"

And yet she does worry. She returns again and again. This is not neurosis; it is the recursive construction of a self that was never given stable ground to stand on. Each return adds a layer. The conception takes seven years in the story, and the narrative's own reconstruction of it takes the entire chapter, never quite arriving at a finished account.

The building is never finished. The chapter ends not with resolution but with Esther as a child in a meadow, chewing clover blossoms, hearing voices that are "her other selves and all of different ages": a return to plurality, to the ongoing, to the unfinished sentence of a life.

Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

Pillar note: Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

The chapter is formally incomplete in ways that feel intentional rather than accidental. Sentences trail into qualification. The go-between's story is never fully told. Rosemary's death is never confirmed with certainty; she is "stillborn" in some passages and in others seems to persist as a presence Esther searches for.

"there was one who still might testify, but one who was none of these and whose death was unknown by anyone, stranger, friend, cloud, angel."

The demand for a complete, coherent account of Esther's origins (who her real father was, whether Rosemary existed, what the agreement between the women really was) is never satisfied. The text treats this refusal to conclude as honesty rather than failure.

Esther's mother's body is the image of this ethics: too small to be completed, too rigid to open, requiring seven years of effort and a stranger's intervention to produce even the partial result that is Esther. The child born of incompletion is herself incomplete, and the text presents this not as tragedy requiring remedy but as the condition of all genuine existence.

Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Pillar note: Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Esther Longtree is marginal in every possible dimension simultaneously. She is:

  • Too large for her world (her parents' house, her mother's womb, the small men who surround her)
  • Born of an unconsummated marriage, conceived through a third party with a spoon
  • The survivor of a twin whose death she is blamed for
  • The inheritor of features from a woman who may have been her biological father
  • A woman of enormous reproductive life, she "who had spilled so many, as many as the autumn leaves", whose children are stillborn

"She, so natural, the child of the unnatural mating."

This paradox, the most natural person produced by the most unnatural means, is the chapter's central ontological claim. Esther does not exist at the margins despite being natural. She exists at the margins because she is natural, because she is too fully embodied, too present, too large for the categories available to her.

The go-between is similarly marginal: wearing men's shoes, a man's hat, a man's coat, smoking a black cigar, a foreigner who speaks with a strange accent, her gender unstable, her role between midwife and father and lover. She is not the exception to the social order. She is the evidence of what the social order requires and cannot acknowledge.

Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

Pillar note: Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

This pillar may be the most completely realized of all eleven in this chapter. The past does not recede for Esther; it is the ground she stands on, pressing up through everything.

The seven years of the conception are not behind her. They are in her body, in her dimpled chin inherited from the go-between, in her crossed eyes, in her crippled foot that reminds her mother of the sorrow of the conception. The April blizzard of her birth year is not a historical fact. It is the permanent weather described under Pillar 3; it has deposited itself into the present.

"The past does not recede. It accumulates beneath us, layer on layer."

The chapter enacts this structurally. The narrative does not move forward in time. It moves downward, drilling through layers of accumulated history: Esther's adult consciousness, her childhood memory of the seventh birthday, her mother's account of the conception, the seven years of nightly visits, the wedding night that never happened, the parents who were never truly mated. Each layer reveals an older layer beneath it. There is no bottom.

The grandfather clock ticking, the alarm clock set to ring: time in this chapter is not linear progression but rhythmic accumulation, the same hour returning, the same effort repeated, the same grief re-deposited.

Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

Pillar note: Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

The prose of this chapter is itself a demonstration of language's constructive power. It does not describe Esther from a neutral vantage point. It builds her out of contradictions, metaphors that undermine themselves, qualifications that proliferate until the sentence nearly collapses under its own weight.

"Esther Longtree was illusive—yes, she was—cloud-like, drifting, herself the weak and gentle even though, from the outward view, she might seem otherwise."

The narrative voice is never stable. It slides between Esther's interiority, reported speech, mythological register, and something like legal testimony. The phrase "as a matter of fact" appears multiple times, each time introducing something that is anything but a straightforward fact,.

The language of the chapter consistently names its own location; it knows it is constructing, not reporting. When the narrative says Esther "had been present" at her own conception, it does not pretend this is literally true. It acknowledges the construction while making it anyway. The language here is doing what Pillar 9 demands: it is honest about its own situatedness, its own partiality, its own role in making rather than finding.

Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

Pillar note: Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

There is no heaven in this chapter, or rather, heaven appears only as something "far away" that Esther's parents "dreamed of" rather than found. The sacred in this text is entirely immanent, located in the grey kitchen, the alarm clock, the pots of geraniums at the window, the smell of clover in Esther's hair.

Her father's tenderness (calling her Little Jackass, rubbing his cheek against hers, saying she smells like "larkspur and ragged robin and buttercups and shepherd's purse, like sunburned oats") is the closest thing to grace in the chapter. It is entirely ordinary, entirely bodily, entirely immanent. It does not point beyond itself.

The go-between, for all her ugliness and cruelty, carries something the narrative treats as sacred:

"yet could she not have been beautiful, beautiful inside with something never to be visible, never to be seen, never to be expressed?"

This is immanent transcendence precisely: the sacred as something inside the ordinary, pointing deeper into the immanent rather than upward and out. The go-between's beauty is not supernatural. It is buried in the material, in the dark hands, the barnyard smell, the patient nightly return across seven years of winter and summer.

Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

Pillar note: Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

This final pillar may be the chapter's deepest philosophical claim. Esther is not a self moving through time. She is where time crosses itself.

"You are constituted by what was deposited before you arrived, and you are constituting the ground the not-yet-born will stand on."

Esther did not choose her conception. She did not choose her parents, their incompatibility, the go-between, the seven years, the silver spoon, the April blizzard, the dead twin. All of this was deposited before she arrived. And yet she carries it, in her body, her chin, her crossed eyes, her crippled foot, her enormous reproductive life that keeps producing stillbirths, as if she is trying to pass the accumulated grief forward and cannot.

"She stood in eternity and leaned her head toward life that was on the other side of the fence."

This image is the crossing point made visible. Esther is not on one side or the other. She is the fence. She is constituted by the past (the policeman, the tiny mother, the dark woman, the dead Rosemary) and she is constituting the future through her own endless, failing, necessary attempts at birth.

The chapter ends with Esther as a child hearing "little voices speaking in the wind as if they were her other selves and all of different ages". This is the crossing point as lived experience: the self as the place where multiple times intersect, where the not-yet-born and the already-dead speak simultaneously through the same body.

The obligation is not chosen. It is structural. Esther carries what she was given. She cannot put it down. The carrying continues.

Chapter 81
