Characters: Esther Longtree

Pillar 1 Not One Self

Pillar note: Pillar 1 Not One Self

She had gotten "the fathers confused. Her mind was so crowded, crowded, crowded, a great city."

Esther is explicitly not one person. She is a woman who contains multitudes: multiple pregnancies, multiple fathers (the detective, the locksmith, the soap salesman, the wind, memory itself), multiple timelines running simultaneously. The chapter refuses to give us a stable, singular Esther. She is:

  • The accused and the innocent
  • The sleeping woman and the knowing woman
  • The mother of the stillborn and the woman who may never have conceived
  • The one who resisted and the one who was entirely passive

The text makes no attempt to resolve these contradictions because the contradictions are Esther. The jury would demand a single coherent self to prosecute. The text refuses to produce one. Her mind is described as "a great city", not a unified consciousness but a metropolis of simultaneous, irresolvable inhabitants.

Crucially, she herself acknowledges this multiplicity without distress: she did not know the truth, "really, for she did not know it". This is not confusion. This is the honest acknowledgment that selfhood is plural and irresolvable.

Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

Pillar note: Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

"She could say that her husband had been lost at sea... or that he was the captain of a Great Lakes steamer which had not touched shore for many years... She could say what she pleased, and no one would be astonished."

The chapter is saturated with the constructedness of reality. Esther understands, with extraordinary clarity, that narrative is not truth; it is performance for a particular audience. In Chicago, she could construct any story and it would become socially real. In her small town, the already-constructed story of who she is forecloses invention.

The detective himself embodies this pillar. He came in disguise (as a locksmith, a soap salesman, himself) demonstrating that identity is costume, that reality is what is performed convincingly. He "could change his personality and was partly wax and was partly human". The line between the wax figure and the human is not a line between illusion and reality. It is a line between two kinds of construction.

Most devastatingly, the entire legal proceeding that threatens Esther is a construction: a demand that she produce, as real, children whose ontological status is precisely what is in question. The jury will manufacture a verdict from evidence that cannot speak to what actually happened. Reality, here, is what the jury decides to see.

Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

Pillar note: Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

"Her head roared here with tiny voices of the stillborn. Every jewel emitted a tiny voice."

This is perhaps the pillar most completely embodied in this chapter. Esther does not grieve and recover. She is grief. It is not a stage she passes through. It is the climate she inhabits permanently.

The stillborn are everywhere, in jewels, in the leafless bushes where "little white hands which seemed to be clapping", in the cracked church bells that ring throughout the chapter. Grief does not resolve into acceptance. It accumulates:

"her head roared here with tiny voices of the stillborn"

she "had heard little voices, thin and clear, and the sobbing of a bird"

"along with the birth cry, there was murder, murder, murder, old murder, the autumn leaves falling where there had never been a spring of any year within remembrance"

Notice the temporal structure of that last passage: "where there had never been a spring of any year within remembrance." Grief here is not the loss of something that once existed. It is the permanent absence of what never arrived: the stillborn spring, the unborn children. This is grief beyond grief: mourning what was never present, which means it can never be resolved by acceptance of loss, because there is no discrete thing to accept losing.

The chapter ends not with resolution but with accumulation: "everything was so sad, and the sky bled in her dreams, and she had no menstrual period, and she was always pregnant". Always. The weather does not change.

Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

Pillar note: Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

"She had lain still, still as always, not crying out from the first moment until the last."

The ethical posture of the chapter is witnessing, but with a crucial, painful inversion. No one witnesses Esther properly. The detective sees a corpse when she is alive. The jury will see a criminal when she is innocent. The women at the courthouse will see a scandal when they are looking at themselves: "they were her pale reflection".

Esther herself, however, is a supreme witness. She witnesses:

  • Her own rapes with extraordinary, unflinching attention
  • The winter landscape in precise, almost clinical detail (the bird dung, the broken gooseberry bushes, the moss rosebud, the buzzard)
  • Her own interior states, including their contradictions

The text practices the pillar of Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act formally; it stays in the room with Esther's experience without rushing toward verdict or resolution. It refuses to tell us whether the children existed. It refuses to tell us whether she was truly raped or willing. It refuses to simplify, holding the complexity open across many pages.

The jury represents the failure of witnessing: the institutional demand to conclude rather than to see. The courthouse is where attention collapses into verdict.

Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

Pillar note: Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

"She had gone on only because of her hopes and her belief in life. If sometimes she was flattened out, giving birth to nothing, yet she soon swelled and was seen again to be pregnant."

Esther builds anyway. She conceives again. She writes letters again. She hopes again. Each pregnancy is a new construction built on the ruins of the last stillbirth. She knows, with terrible clarity, that it will likely end the same way, she had realized "at the beginning what the end would be, another stillborn", and she does it anyway.

This is not optimism. It is recursive construction: returning to the beginning with what was learned, building again, not because success is guaranteed but because building is the condition of being Esther. Her pregnancies are not metaphors for hope. They are hope: material, embodied, cyclical, provisional.

The chapter itself is recursively constructed. It circles back to the same events (the three encounters with the detective, the stillborn, the threatened trial) from different angles, adding detail and complexity each time, never arriving at a conclusion. The reader is placed inside a recursive structure. We are doing what Esther does.

Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

Pillar note: Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

"How could she say what the truth was, really, for she did not know it?"

The entire chapter is structured as an ongoing sentence that refuses to conclude. The trial has not happened yet. The children have not been produced or disproven. The pregnancies are neither confirmed nor denied by any external witness. Everything is held in suspension.

The demand for completion (the trial, the jury, the verdict) is presented as violence. It would force Esther to reduce the irresolvable complexity of her experience into a statement that can be judged. The jury would demand: are the children real or not? Did she murder them or not? But these questions, the text insists, cannot be answered without doing violence to what actually is.

Esther's incompletion is her integrity:

"She was her own mystery, dragging the stars behind her, and not explaining herself to anybody."

The birth veil "had perhaps never been lifted from her face"; she came into the world already veiled, already unfinished, and this is not a deficiency. It is her condition, and the text honors it.

Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Pillar note: Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

"There was nothing about her case in the law books, nothing, for no one like her had ever been brought to court before."

This is stated with almost programmatic clarity. Esther Longtree is the evidence that the categories don't hold. She exists at the edges of every system:

  • The legal system has no precedent for her
  • The medical system cannot confirm or deny her pregnancies
  • The social system cannot classify her (old maid? mother? murderess? victim?)
  • The sexual system cannot place her (was she raped? willing? asleep? dreaming?)

She is not the exception to the rule. She is the place where the rule's constructed nature becomes visible. The law cannot process her because she did not happen inside the law's categories. The jury cannot judge her because judgment requires stable categories of guilt and innocence, and Esther inhabits the space between them.

"She was innocent of having murdered those three children. But perhaps... they would find, in searching for those who were never born, the evidence of a hidden birth... and they would blame her, her, her alone."

The marginal person does not merely suffer the violence of misclassification. They reveal that classification is always already violent: that the categories were never adequate to experience.

Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

Pillar note: Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

"along with the birth cry, there was murder, murder, murder, old murder, the autumn leaves falling where there had never been a spring of any year within remembrance, the withered flowers, the dead birds killed by nothing, which she could not get rid of"

Time in this chapter does not move forward. It sediments. The three encounters with the detective (three winters, three different years) are not past events; they are layers pressing upward through everything Esther experiences in the present. The stillborn are not behind her. They are beneath her, still present in every jewel's tiny voice, every cracked church bell. The chapter's temporal structure enacts this. We are not given the events in sequence. We are given them as they exist in Esther's consciousness, which is to say, simultaneously, all pressing upward at once. The first rape and the current threatened trial and the letters she wrote and the stillborn she has carried are not a timeline. They are a stratigraphy.

Most powerfully:

"her heart had been murdered by her heart"

The past self murdered the present self. The wound is not historical. It is structural. It continues to press upward.

Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

Pillar note: Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

"She had answered the letters of a father who was not dying, and that had been the worst mistake of her life, putting it all into handwriting, signing her name, adding some postscripts, too, her numerous after-thoughts which she should have saved for some old preacher or jack-in-the-pulpit."

Language in this chapter is explicitly dangerous and constructive. When Esther wrote to the detective, she brought a reality into existence (a legal reality, a relational reality) that now threatens to destroy her. The letters are evidence. Handwriting is identity. Language, once committed to paper, becomes a world that can be used against you.

The text is also acutely aware of the language used to describe Esther. The women at the courthouse will call her "a crazy old mule in heat". This language does not describe her. It constructs a version of her that can be dismissed, institutionalized, laughed at. The chapter shows us language as the mechanism by which the marginal person is erased.

Meanwhile, the text's own language is deliberately unstable: shifting between clinical precision ("her cheeks covered with the droppings of winter birds") and lyrical abstraction ("a scarred, dead, cold, bald planet, casting her radiance beyond the fields of power"). The text names its own location as uncertain, as oscillating, refusing to speak from nowhere.

Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

Pillar note: Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

"she waxed, reddish in wind, and walked in veils of clouds, a scarred, dead, cold, bald planet, casting her radiance beyond the fields of power, and pregnant though no one else believed this"

The sacred in this chapter is entirely immanent; it lives in the grey winter meadow, in the bird dung on the cheeks, in the cracked church bells, in the moss rosebud laid between Esther's breasts. There is no transcendence that points outward to a beyond. There is only this world, made luminous by grief and persistence.

Esther herself becomes a figure of immanent transcendence. She is compared to the moon:

"Like the slow moon itself in vaultless heavens that were not nailed down by any lid when the stars which were a thousand golden keys opened no doors, for death had no boundaries, she waxed"

The moon is not transcendent. It is the most immanent of celestial bodies: the one we can see most clearly, the one that governs tides and cycles, the one that waxes and wanes in ordinary time. And yet it is radiant. The sacred is here, in the "trumpeting breasts enlarged and marked by the sting of bees", in the perpetual pregnancy, in the ordinary extraordinary fact of a woman who will not stop being alive.

The cracked church bells are perhaps the most precise image of immanent transcendence in the chapter. They ring throughout,,. They are broken. They are not the perfect bells of a cathedral pointing toward God. They are cracked, earthly, imperfect, and they ring anyway, and their sound structures Esther's entire experience of memory and loss. The sacred is in the crack.

Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

Pillar note: Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

"her family tree was barren because her father and her mother had been barren and had not mated... She was the only one that had had the courage, the anger to give birth, the only one that had caused an increase in the population, as far as she could see."

This is the most structurally profound pillar in relation to the chapter. Esther understands herself, with explicit clarity, as a crossing point. She stands at the intersection of a barren lineage and an impossible future. Her parents did not mate (in any meaningful sense). The detective's children are stillborn. And yet she continues to conceive, to carry, to attempt birth.

She is constituted by what was deposited before her (the barren parents, the absent mother-love, the murdered heart of her girlhood) and she is constituting the ground the not-yet-born will stand on, even if what is born is always already dead. The stillborn are not nothing. They are deposited. They press upward. They are in the sediment.

The obligation is not chosen:

"She had gone on only because of her hopes and her belief in life."

She did not decide to be the crossing point of barrenness and generation. She is that crossing point. The carrying continues not because she chose it but because it is structural to what she is.

And crucially: "her own childhood reproached her". The ancestor, her own past self, is in the sediment, pressing upward, making demands. This is the crossing point made visceral: the child she was accuses the woman she is, and the woman she is carries the children who will never be born, who will nevertheless constitute some future ground.

Synthesis

What this chapter achieves is something extraordinary: it makes a woman's reproductive body into a complete philosophical system. Esther Longtree's perpetual pregnancy is not a symbol of fertility or failure. It is the enactment of all eleven pillars simultaneously:

  • She is plural and irresolvable (Pillar 1)
  • She constructs reality through narrative (Pillar 2)
  • She lives inside permanent grief (Pillar 3)
  • She witnesses without flinching (Pillar 4)
  • She builds again after every stillbirth (Pillar 5)
  • She refuses the violence of completion (Pillar 6)
  • She is the evidence that categories fail (Pillar 7)
  • She carries all her pasts simultaneously (Pillar 8)
  • She knows language creates and destroys (Pillar 9)
  • She is sacred in her ordinary luminous grief (Pillar 10)
  • She is where time crosses itself (Pillar 11)

The jury that threatens her represents everything this philosophy opposes: the demand for a singular self, a completed narrative, a verdict, a resolution. The text refuses to deliver her to that jury. It keeps her, perpetually, in the winter meadow, staring at the sky, "sleeping with her eyes wide open": present, multiple, unresolved, and radiant.
wheel-chapter-24:
Chapter 24

← Chapter 23 · Wheel and Spokes Home · Chapter 25 →

Research notes: Chapter 24 · Reading guide: Guide, Chapter 24

Characters: Cousin Hannah · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh

Pillar 1 Not One Self

Pillar note: Pillar 1 Not One Self

"There was an Irish housemaid who would never open her mouth to speak if there was more than one person present... She spoke only to herself, and she was several fine ladies and a swarm of fly-catching warblers"

The servants are the most explicit demonstration of the plural self; each one has fractured into multiple simultaneous identities. But the mother is the central case. She is simultaneously a telephone exchange, a social hostess, a dying woman, a dreamer, and perhaps the only genuine unbeliever in her own dreams:

"My mother herself might be, of course, the only genuine unbeliever, as everyone recognized, for she was very clever. My mother placed her faith only in the unreal."

This is not madness in the clinical sense; it is the honest condition of selfhood made visible. The mother contains contradictions that cannot be resolved: she both believes and disbelieves, she is both the dreamer and the skeptic of her own dream. The narrator herself is plural; she is child, witness, questioner, and the one who cannot find a stable interlocutor:

"To whom should I have turned that sun-lit morning, asking those personal questions which burned like low fires in my mind"

Even Mr. Spitzer is plural; he is simultaneously a roundhouse, a ghost ship, a bumble bee, a busy signal. No character in this chapter occupies a single, stable identity. The pillar is not illustrated; it is structurally enacted through the prose's refusal to fix anyone in place.

Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

Pillar note: Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

This is perhaps the chapter's most explicit theme, but Young complicates it beyond simple statement. The servants' illusions are not contrasted with a stable reality; they are the operating reality of the household:

"In fact, just to hear the servants talk, anyone might have thought they were all real, my mother's opium dreams, especially when they were unreal."

That sentence performs the pillar. The qualifier "especially when they were unreal" collapses the distinction rather than reinforcing it. The illusions are most real precisely in their unreality, which means the category of "real" has been quietly dissolved.

The larger cave argument appears in the description of the house itself; it is not presented as a deviation from a normal world outside. There is no outside referenced. The house with its imaginary chandeliers and famous guests sleeping tier upon tier is simply the world as it is constituted. The narrator does not stand outside it looking in. She is inside it, asking her questions from within:

"My imagination wandered like a dark and formless cloud, seeking that certitude it might never have."

The certitude is not available because there is no position outside the constructed world from which to obtain it. The cave has no exit. There is only the quality of the lighting.

Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

Pillar note: Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

Grief in this chapter is not an event; it is the atmosphere. The bronze chrysanthemums are "the flowers for the dead" ; the fires are lit "to greet those guests who would never come" ; the telephone calls are placed to the dead who never answer:

"What of Uncle Ronald who was dead? What of Uncle Bernard who had died in Moscow while bringing a message to the czar?"

The mother does not grieve these losses in any sequential sense; she simply keeps calling. She keeps leaving messages. She keeps adding names to lists. Grief here is not a stage to be passed through but the very medium of her existence. She cannot stop calling because stopping would mean accepting the finality that her dreaming refuses.

The servants' grief is structural too; they polish shoes for guests who left no shoes, they wait on Wellington who is not there, they light fires for arrivals that will never come. The whole household is organized around the labor of perpetual anticipation and perpetual disappointment. This is grief as permanent weather; everyone lives inside it, and no one names it as grief because it has become simply the climate.

The narrator's grief is quieter but present in the question she cannot find anyone to answer:

"questions as to the secret purpose of life, questions as to love and marriage and reproduction and death"

These questions are not asked in hope of resolution. They burn "like low fires": persistent, low-level, ongoing. Not acute grief but chronic grief. The weather kind.

Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

Pillar note: Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

The narrator's position in this chapter is almost entirely that of the witness. She does not intervene in her mother's dreams, does not correct the servants, does not attempt to restore order. She watches, catalogs, and asks questions she knows may not be answerable:

"Then who, I wondered, should offer any contrast to these wild illusions and selfish or selfless deceptions"

The wondering is the practice. She does not conclude. She does not diagnose her mother as simply mad and move on. She stays in the room, metaphorically and literally, attending to the full complexity of what she sees.

The ethical weight of this witnessing is made explicit in the contrast with Mr. Spitzer, who evades:

"he whose powers of evasion were greater than even he could realize"

Evasion is the failure mode. The narrator refuses it, even when what she witnesses resists resolution. The description of the servants (detailed, patient, accumulative) is itself an act of witnessing. Each servant gets their particularity noted: the one who polishes shoes, the one who thinks he waits on Wellington, the one who lives in a forest of cuckoo clocks, the one who is Hannibal. None is dismissed. All are seen.

The refusal to simplify is the act. Young's prose enacts this at the sentence level; it never arrives at a clean summary of what the mother is or what the household means. It keeps adding, qualifying, circling.

Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

Pillar note: Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

The mother's endless list-making and planning is the clearest image of recursive construction:

"My mother would discuss endlessly with her absent social secretaries these invitations and arrangements"

She builds the guest list knowing (at some level, as the "only genuine unbeliever") that the guests will not come. She builds anyway. She returns to the lists, the telephone directory, the arrangements. Morning slips into afternoon into evening, and the building continues. It is never finished. That is not presented as tragedy; it is simply her mode of being.

The servants participate in the same recursive construction. They arrange the Renaissance chairs "very intimately for conversation" that will not happen. They polish the brass fire-dogs in preparation for fires that will greet no one. They return to these tasks. The tasks are never completed because completion is not the point. The building is the point.

Even the narrator's questioning is recursive; she circles the same questions about life and death and love without arriving at answers, and the chapter ends not with resolution but with her imagination wandering "like a dark and formless cloud", still seeking, still building toward a certitude that remains out of reach.

Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

Pillar note: Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

The chapter is formally incomplete; it does not conclude, it accumulates and then stops. This is not a failure of craft. It is an ethical stance toward the material.

The mother's telephone calls are the most poignant illustration:

"She had called the Bishop of Hippo, but he had always just stepped out, was always expected to return in an hour."

The Bishop of Hippo, Saint Augustine, has always just stepped out. The call is never completed. The connection is never made. And yet the mother keeps calling, keeps leaving messages. The incompletion is not failure; it is the honest condition of trying to reach across time and death.

The demand for completion is identified as its own kind of violence in the description of what happens to "the most simple and apparently sensible persons" who enter this employment:

"did they not seem to undergo, after an hour or a year or many years in this employment, a sea change, a transformation, to be other than themselves"

The implication is that the simple, sensible person, the one who demands completion and resolution, is the one who becomes most destabilized. The household's incompletion is not what damages people. The attempt to impose completion on it is.

Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Pillar note: Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Every character in this chapter is marginal: the opium-dreaming mother, the servants who have fractured into historical fantasies, the narrator who cannot find a stable interlocutor, Mr. Spitzer who evades his own memories. But the pillar's deepest application here is structural: the marginal characters are not exceptions to a normal world. They are the evidence of what the world actually is.

The valet who waits on Wellington, the gardener who believes he is Potiphar's spouse, the housemaid who is several fine ladies; these figures are not presented as deviations from sanity. They are presented as the most visible instances of something universal: the self's construction of its own reality.

"The most simple and apparently sensible persons, did they not seem to undergo... a sea change, a transformation, to be other than themselves, to reach for door knobs which were not door knobs, to open doors which were not doors"

The "most simple and apparently sensible" person is not immune. They undergo the same transformation, only more slowly. The marginal servant who thinks he waits on Wellington is not different in kind from anyone else; he is just further along a continuum that everyone is on. His marginality makes visible what is always already true.

The mad lady retouching her makeup in the second powder room (who may or may not exist, who may be a unicorn wearing a necklace) occupies the most marginal position in the chapter, and she is also the most haunting. Her existence cannot be confirmed or denied. She is the edge of the category "real person," and at that edge, the constructed nature of the category becomes fully visible.

Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

Pillar note: Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

This pillar is everywhere in the chapter's temporal structure. The past does not recede; it accumulates, presses upward, populates the present:

"there was a mad lady retouching her make-up each night in the second powder room... Who left, each night, dusty face powder streaking the dark mirrors of Venetian glass, dead rose petals upon a rain-washed marble stair?"

The dead rose petals are physical evidence of the past pressing into the present. The face powder on the mirrors is the sediment of previous nights. The past is not behind anyone in this household; it is beneath them, still active, still leaving traces.

The telephone directory is the most explicit image of sedimentary time:

"she, still wearing her garden hat, sat poring over the lists... some antiquated copy of the Boston or Philadelphia telephone directory, perhaps even of Amsterdam or London or Prague, circa 1905"

The 1905 directory is the sediment. The mother dials numbers from it as if the people listed there are still reachable. They are not behind her; they are beneath her, still pressing up. The calls that go unanswered are not failures of communication across distance. They are failures of communication across the accumulated layers of time. The servants who polish shoes left by imaginary guests, who arrange chairs for conversations that belong to previous centuries, are living inside sedimentary time. The past is not past. It is the ground they stand on and work within.

Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

Pillar note: Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

Young's prose is itself the argument here. The language of this chapter does not describe a pre-existing reality; it constructs the reality as it goes. Consider:

"she thought that Mr. Spitzer was a roundhouse of the trains which run no more, the broken trains, the trains of ruined sequences, the trains of vanished thoughts and dreams"

This is not metaphor in the conventional sense: a comparison between two separate things. It is language constituting what Mr. Spitzer is. He is the roundhouse, in the mother's dreaming world, and the mother's dreaming world is the world the chapter inhabits. The language does not point to a reality outside itself. It is the reality.

The mother's awareness that her telephone connects only to the servants' quarters is a moment of language's location becoming visible; she has been speaking as if she were calling across time and the world, but the line runs only to the next room. The pretense of speaking from nowhere (calling Athens, calling the Bishop of Hippo) is revealed as speaking from somewhere very particular (a bedroom in a large house, connected to servants who may or may not reply).

The servants' language is equally constructive, by discussing Wellington, they make Wellington present. By naming the old valet "Wellington," they constitute him as Wellington. Language here is not describing the social world of the household. It is making it.

Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

Pillar note: Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

The sacred in this chapter does not point outward to a beyond. It lives inside the ordinary: inside the bronze chrysanthemums, the polished fire-dogs, the dusty face powder on the Venetian mirrors.

"The servants moved about in the dimmed evening light, arranging flowers in crystal vases, flowers as big as human heads, the bronze-colored chrysanthemums which are the flowers for the dead, lighting fires in jeweled fireplaces to greet those guests who would never come."

This is a liturgical passage. The servants perform a ritual (flowers, fire, arrangement, preparation) for an arrival that will not come. The ritual does not become meaningless because the guests are absent. It becomes more sacred. The care lavished on an empty house, the attention given to guests who are dead or imaginary, is the sacred living inside the immanent.

The mother's endless party-planning is the same; she is not planning a party in any practical sense. She is performing devotion to a world she has constructed and believes in more than she believes in the "real" world. Mr. Spitzer's "euphemistic certainties that an ultimate Heaven should unite us all" are explicitly contrasted with this: his transcendence points outward, to a beyond. The mother's transcendence points deeper into the immanent world of her dreams, her guests, her chrysanthemums, her telephone calls.

"She should die in the midst of her dreams and not be awakened, never know when she died"

This is immanent transcendence as the ideal death, not a crossing into another world, but a deepening into this one until the boundary between dreaming and dying dissolves.

Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

Pillar note: Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

This is perhaps the most structurally embedded pillar in the chapter. The narrator is explicitly constituted by what was deposited before she arrived:

"The refractions of that drugged, dazzling atmosphere produced snow crystals with their faces half inclined toward my mother"

The narrator is a refraction of her mother's atmosphere. She did not choose this. It is structural. The mother's opium dreams, the servants' fantasies, the household's accumulated sediment: all of this is the ground the narrator stands on, and it was deposited before she could have consented to it.

The telephone calls to the dead relatives (Cousin Hannah, Cousin Wilbur who disappeared at sea, Uncle Ronald who was dead, Uncle Bernard who died in Moscow) are the ancestors in the sediment. The mother keeps calling them not because she expects them to answer but because the obligation to call is structural. They are in the ground. The carrying continues.

The narrator's final position in the chapter is that of someone who is constituted by all of this and is now, in the act of witnessing and narrating, constituting the ground that comes after:

"My imagination wandered like a dark and formless cloud, seeking that certitude it might never have."

She is the crossing point, where the mother's world of illusion crosses with Miss MacIntosh's world of practical reality, where the dead cross with the living, where the question crosses with the unanswerable. She does not resolve this. She carries it. That is the structural obligation of the crossing point. It is not chosen. It continues.
wheel-chapter-12:
Chapter 12

← Chapter 11 · Wheel and Spokes Home · Chapter 13 →

Research notes: Chapter 12 · Reading guide: Guide, Chapter 12

Characters: Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh

Pillar 1 Not One Self

Pillar note: Pillar 1 Not One Self

The chapter presents selfhood as irreducibly multiple. The narrator is simultaneously a child, a remembering adult, a dreamer, a rationalist, and a vessel for other people's histories. She occupies all of these positions at once without resolving them.

Most strikingly, Miss MacIntosh herself (the novel's great champion of singular, unambiguous selfhood) is revealed to embody duality against her will:

"She had not two faces, one to turn toward the world, one to turn toward heaven."

The insistence is too fierce to be neutral. The denial performs the very anxiety it is denying. And the narrator's mother entertains the suspicion that Mr. Spitzer is himself plural:

"...that sometimes, as in a protracted, wakeful dream, he imagined himself to be his dead brother."

The self here is not a stable unit but a site of occupation, by the dead, by dream, by inherited guilt. The narrator herself moves through the chapter in a state of radical self-multiplication: she is the child who bayed at the moon, the young woman walking in the garden of the blind, and the retrospective consciousness narrating both. These selves do not converge. They coexist.

Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

Pillar note: Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

The chapter refuses any stable ground between illusion and reality. The house is structured around this refusal: all clocks except the Big Ben alarm clock have been stopped, each at a different hour, creating a domestic architecture of frozen time. The one "real" clock, Old Reliable, is itself described in terms that emphasize its constructed nature: it has been deliberately stripped of ornament, of Tritons and cupids and rosebuds, as if realism requires active suppression of the imaginary.

The narrator's childhood visions (the rooster with golden spurs, the gentleman in snuff-colored velvet, the belief that she was the reincarnation of Chopin) are presented not as errors corrected by Miss MacIntosh's realism, but as one mode of apprehension among others, no more or less constructed than the "reliable" world Miss MacIntosh insists upon. Miss MacIntosh's reality is itself a construction, maintained by effort:

"...she was very stout-minded, carrying a stout umbrella, and she was a middle brow, and she was a Middle Westerner, and she was middle aged."

The repetition of "middle" is not accidental. Her reality is a deliberate positioning at the center, away from edges, which is itself a choice, a made thing. The cave is not escaped. It is only differently furnished.

Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

Pillar note: Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

Grief in this chapter is not an event. It is the atmosphere. The stopped clocks throughout the house mark not a single loss but a prolonged, hesitant withdrawal from the world:

"...each clock having been stopped at a different hour over that period of time when my mother, retiring from the world, had gone to bed, by slow degrees and not suddenly, as if she had hesitated a great deal."

The mother's retreat is not grief's resolution but its institutionalization. And the garden of the blind, planted by a long-dead grandfather for a blind wife, is grief made into landscape:

"Are there places which seem to breed their special sorrow, that sorrow which colors the atmosphere often with the most illusive colors like the memory of a nature already dead?"

The narrator asks whether the sorrow comes from her or from the world around her. The question is not answered. It cannot be answered, because grief here is not located in a subject. It is the climate itself. Even the narrator's moment of preternatural joy, her feeling that "life should answer the quest of the heart", is retrospectively framed as the last moment before a shattering vision. Joy is not grief's opposite. It is grief's prelude, grief's highest register.

Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

Pillar note: Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

The ethical posture of the narrating consciousness is precisely that of the Witness: she does not conclude, does not resolve, does not flinch away. The prose itself enacts this through its recursive, accumulating sentences that refuse to arrive.

The narrator explicitly frames her retrospective account as necessarily incomplete but not therefore false:

"The details must be told only through a veil of oblivion which is itself a medium of memory, for there is no forgetfulness even of the smallest thing. If it is hidden, it is revealed through its absence, the sense of the void."

This is the ethics of witnessing stated as epistemology. Absence is not nothing. The void is evidence. The narrator does not rush toward resolution; she stays in the room with the stopped clocks, with the wet flowers, with the gleaming eyes in the bushes, with the horror she is about to see but has not yet seen. The question she poses

"Could I have foreseen, should I have turned back? Should I have gone on?"

is left open. The witness does not answer. The witness stays.

Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

Pillar note: Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

The chapter is itself a recursive structure. The narrator is building, in prose, a memory of a night that was itself a threshold: a night whose meaning she is still constructing in the act of narration. She returns to Miss MacIntosh's teachings not to endorse or refute them but to re-examine them from a new angle, with new evidence.

The stopped clocks that "would suddenly start up, wheezing or musical, seeming to make this one last effort" are images of recursive construction: the stopped thing trying again, the abandoned building resuming. The narrator's own prose does the same; it circles back, qualifies, reopens. The chapter does not build toward a conclusion. It builds toward a threshold, and stops there:

"...my first vision of the wonders and glories of this planet...the first vision would also be the last."

The construction is interrupted. But the interruption is not failure. It is the condition under which the next construction begins.

Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

Pillar note: Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

The chapter's prose style is itself an argument for incompletion as integrity. Sentences extend across pages, subordinate clauses multiplying, qualifications folding back on qualifications. The narrator explicitly defends this:

"The details must always seem, in retrospect, blurred, and for this reason, that they were not, even then, fully realized."

To complete the account would be to falsify it. The demand for a concluded sentence, a clear narrative of what happened that night, would be, in the chapter's own terms, a violence against experience. Miss MacIntosh represents the concluded sentence:

"...her moral principles which distinguished sharply between right and wrong, her excellent, narrow mind."

The sharpness of the distinction is not a virtue here. It is a narrowness. The narrator's ongoing, unfinished sentence is the more honest form.

Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Pillar note: Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

The chapter's most powerful image of the marginal is the garden of the blind. It is a space designed for someone whose sensory experience placed her outside the norm of visual culture. The garden does not pretend to offer what vision offers. It offers texture, odor, the Braille of petals:

"...for the commingling of odorous blooms and the Braille texture of flowers, whorls, petals, clusters, stamens which should move under the moving, visionary finger-tips of his blind wife."

The blind woman is not the exception who proves the rule of sight. She is the evidence that vision is one mode of apprehension among many, that the world built for sighted people is a construction, not a given. The narrator, standing in this garden and closing her own eyes, becomes temporarily marginal herself, and finds, in that marginality, a richer contact with the world.

Miss MacIntosh's own marginality is also present: she is the plain spinster, the middle-everything, the one whose "face was not her fortune". She is marginal to the world of beauty, romance, and transcendence that surrounds her in this household. Her insistence on the ordinary is not innocent. It is the insistence of someone who has been excluded from the extraordinary and has made a philosophy of that exclusion.

Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

Pillar note: Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

The chapter is structured by sedimentary time. The present moment of the narration rests on layers that do not recede: the mother's withdrawal, the grandfather's garden, the blind grandmother's walks, Mr. Spitzer's dead brother, the narrator's own childhood madness. None of these are past in the sense of being finished. They are all pressing upward.

The stopped clocks are the novel's most precise image of this:

"All the other clocks in the house were like enchanted cages, each clock having been stopped at a different hour."

Time has not moved on in this house. It has accumulated. Each stopped clock marks a layer of sedimented loss. The house is a stratigraphic record. And when a stopped clock suddenly starts up again

"...a stopped clock would suddenly start up, wheezing or musical, seeming to make this one last effort."

it is the past breaking through the surface, the sediment erupting. The three bells, then the four bells, sounding in the midnight air: the layers speaking.

The grandmother's garden is another sedimentary formation. It was planted "long years ago" for a woman now dead, by a man now dead, and it persists (overgrown, matted, knotted) as a physical record of their lives and losses. The narrator stands in it without knowing its full history, but the history acts on her nonetheless.

Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

Pillar note: Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

The chapter is acutely self-conscious about language as a shaping force. The narrator's extended meditation on the body's organs (eyes, ears, tongue, nose, skin, hair) reads as a kind of anatomical catalogue, but it is also an examination of how naming constructs the named. To say "the eyeball was made to see with" is not to describe a neutral fact. It is to impose a teleology, a purposiveness, on biological matter.

Miss MacIntosh's language is the chapter's most explicit example of language constructing reality. Her phrases, "a place for everything," "no siree, sir," "stark, raving mad", are the verbal architecture of a particular, located worldview. They are the language of a Middle Western, middle-aged, middle-brow spinster, and they speak from that location while pretending to speak from nowhere, from common sense, from plain truth.

The narrator's own language, by contrast, names its own uncertainty:

"The details must be told only through a veil of oblivion which is itself a medium of memory."

This is language acknowledging its own constructedness, its own location in a particular consciousness at a particular moment of retrospection.

Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

Pillar note: Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

The chapter's most sustained passage of transcendence is entirely immanent; it is located in the body, in the senses, in the physical world:

"The eyeball was made to see with...The organ of sight was repeated as the spot on a peacock's tail, the eyes gleaming among the tail feathers, the hole through the needle, the center of a flower."

The sacred here is the pattern repeating itself through matter. The eye is everywhere, in the peacock's tail, in the needle's eye, in the flower's center. This is not transcendence outward to a beyond. It is transcendence inward, into the structure of the ordinary world.

The narrator's joy in the garden is of the same order:

"...my whole being filled with the inestimable beauty and goodness of life, when I felt that life should answer the quest of the heart."

This is not a religious vision in any conventional sense. It is a vision of the world as sufficient, as answering, as sacred in itself. And it is immediately shadowed by the knowledge that this first vision will also be the last, which does not negate the sacredness. It deepens it. The sacred is here, in this moment, in this body, in this wet garden, and it is mortal, and that is what makes it sacred.

Even Miss MacIntosh's God is immanent in a dark way:

"God had suffered due to this erroneous creation and had quite frankly been filled with the greatest remorse ever since the day of the beginning."

This is not a transcendent God above the fray. This is a God embedded in the mess of creation, suffering alongside it, unable to fix what has gone awry. The sacred is not above the ordinary world. It is inside it, suffering inside it.

Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

Pillar note: Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

The chapter's deepest structural logic is that of the Crossing Point. The narrator is not a self moving through time. She is where multiple times cross: her own childhood, her mother's withdrawal, her grandmother's blindness, her grandfather's garden, Mr. Spitzer's dead brother, Miss MacIntosh's unnamed old guilt.

"...to do her work of retribution for some old guilt not conceived by her."

Miss MacIntosh carries guilt she did not generate. She is a crossing point for something that preceded her. And the narrator, standing in the garden planted for a blind woman she never knew, is constituted by that woman's absence:

"I stood in the garden of the blind which had been created for one whose eyes were as missing."

The blind grandmother's way of being in the world (her circular path, her practical memory, her argument about the clouds with her coachman) has shaped the physical space in which the narrator stands and has shaped, through that space, the narrator's own moment of vision and loss. The obligation is not chosen. It is structural. The grandmother is in the sediment of the garden. The narrator is standing on her.

The chapter ends at a threshold: the narrator about to see something that will permanently alter her vision of the past and the future. She is the crossing point between the world she has known and the world she is about to know. She is constituting, in this moment, the ground on which her future self will stand. The carrying continues.
wheel-chapter-02:
Chapter 2

← Chapter 1 · Wheel and Spokes Home · Chapter 3 →

Research notes: Chapter 2 · Reading guide: Guide, Chapter 2

Characters: Joachim Spitzer · Mr. Chandelier

Pillar 1 Not One Self

Pillar note: Pillar 1 Not One Self

The mother is perhaps the most radical embodiment of the plural self in American fiction. She is simultaneously:

  • A living woman in a bed
  • A beautiful corpse on a marble sarcophagus
  • A rider on a white horse through endless surf
  • A dead woman who is walking
  • A hostess receiving distinguished guests
  • A patient in a charity ward

"she believed that she had died in her youth and was yet alive, that there were two selves, the dead, the living"

But the text refuses to resolve which self is primary. The living self is horizontal and still; the dead self is the one walking. This inversion is not metaphor; it is ontological insistence. The self is not one thing that appears multiple; it is genuinely, irresolvably multiple.

Mr. Spitzer enacts the plural self differently. He is haunted by his dead twin brother to such a degree that others, including the Egyptian, cannot distinguish between them. He is himself and the ghost of his brother simultaneously:

"he was not the man the Egyptian was looking for... he was his living brother, his face covered with apologies, that his brother was dead... that the brother he now beheld and thought he recognized was a perfect stranger to him"

The Egyptian's inability to tell the living from the dead twin is not comic confusion. It is Young's argument: the self is not singular enough to be clearly distinguished even from another self. The plural self bleeds across the boundary of death.

Even the narrator, the child, is constituted by these plural, unstable selves. The chapter begins "My mother" but the mother never stabilizes into a single person the narrator can reliably know. The child is formed by a self that cannot be known because it is not one.

Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

Pillar note: Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

This pillar is the chapter's structural spine. Young does not present illusion as the mother's problem: a symptom of opium addiction or madness to be corrected by reality. She presents it as the universal condition, with the mother simply more honest about it than others.

"she could not tell where the divide was between what was real and what was unreal, for the unreal things were real to her... and the real were unreal. The dreams begot the only realities"

The crucial move Young makes is to validate this epistemology rather than pathologize it. The mother's visions are described with the same lush, precise attention as any "real" event in the chapter. The Egyptian sailor who arrives from Alexandria turns out to be actually there: Mr. Spitzer finds him:

he "was greatly surprised, therefore, that there was, indeed, just as she had said, an Egyptian, a gold-headed fellow sitting in the morning room in the evening light"

This is Young's most elegant structural argument: the moment the reader has accepted that the mother's visions are hallucinations, one of them is confirmed as real. The text will not let the reader settle into the comfortable position of knowing which is which. The larger cave is more carefully lit, but it is still a cave.

The mother herself articulates Pillar 2 directly:

"The world was this deception played upon her, and it included Mr. Spitzer with his high silk hat... How did she know that they were not both dead"

The "deception" is not the mother's illness. It is existence itself. Reality is not found; it is made. And once made, it cannot be distinguished from illusion with any certainty.

Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

Pillar note: Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

The chapter is saturated with grief that does not move, does not resolve, does not arrive anywhere. It accumulates.

The mother grieves:

  • Her husband's disappearance in the Alps
  • The death of Mr. Spitzer's brother (whom she loved)
  • Her father's domination and death
  • Her own abandoned social life
  • The child she has forgotten she bore
  • Her own beauty, which she preserves precisely because it cannot be used

None of these griefs are processed. They are all simultaneously present, layered in her opium dreams like geological strata. The husband who fell into a snowbank on the Jungfrau or the Matterhorn or the Dolomites, she cannot remember which, is not mourned and moved past. He is still falling:

"he had fallen head first, disappearing under a bank of snow and granite, and was never found... and had been wearing a white rose on his coat lapel when last seen, so should be easily recognized"

The white rose on the lapel, the detail she retains, is grief's specific, irrational texture. Not the fact of his death but the white rose. This is how grief actually works: not as narrative arc but as the persistence of specific, sensory fragments that refuse to recede.

Mr. Spitzer's grief is equally permanent. His entire life was broken by his brother's death:

"his life had been broken by his brother's sudden and unexpected death, and he had thus practiced law in only the most desultory fashion... and he had written only silent music, that which, for many years now, no one else had ever heard"

The silent music is grief made structural. He composes; no one hears it. The grief does not end. It becomes the form of his existence: the shape his life takes around the absence.

And the climate of the chapter itself (the sea road, the shrouded bedroom, the wave-washed garden) is the weather of permanent grief. The house is not a home. It is a monument to everything that did not happen.

Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

Pillar note: Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

The narrator of this chapter is perhaps the most important figure in it, not because the narrator acts, but because the narrator stays in the room. The child who begins "My mother" and then proceeds to describe, with extraordinary precision and without flinching, the full reality of a mother who has forgotten the child exists.

This is the ethical stance of the Witness: to see fully, without rushing toward resolution. The narrator does not explain the mother. Does not excuse her. Does not condemn her. Does not simplify her. The narrator attends.

The prose itself enacts witnessing. Look at the density of observation:

"Heavily laden with jewels as a Greek corpse, my mother, she who had retired from the brutal world, whose eyes were shielded against the vulgar sunlight, slept for tideless years which were her vast excitement, surrounding herself with a world of dreams, visions, phantoms, her bedroom as filled with visitors as the Grand Central Station"

The comparison, "as a Greek corpse," "as filled with visitors as the Grand Central Station", is not judgment. It is seeing. The narrator holds two incompatible images (the ancient, jeweled dead; the modern, crowded transit hub) simultaneously, refusing to collapse them into a single stable meaning.

Mr. Spitzer also practices a form of witnessing, though imperfect. He comes every evening, uninvited, unwelcome, and stays:

"he came in the evenings down the ribboned sea road for that unwelcomed visit which his own sense of honor or habit had imposed"

He does not fix the mother. He does not cure her. He does not leave. He witnesses. The chapter presents this faithfulness, staying in the room when nothing can be resolved, as the central ethical act.

Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

Pillar note: Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

The mother's entire existence is recursive construction. She builds her world of dreams, knowing it is provisional, knowing it depends on the canary living, knowing the drugs will wear thin. And she builds it again every day.

"Her own mind had been all that was left to provide for her a better world, cities, mountains, dead faces, vague, clouded longings"

She does not build despite knowing the building is provisional. She builds because there is nothing else. The recursion is structural: the dreams create her, and she creates the dreams:

"She had not created the dreams, for they had created her, making her all she was and more than even she could realize"

This is recursive construction at its most radical: the builder and the building are mutually constitutive. There is no original self who then began to dream. The dreaming and the self arose together.

The canary system is perhaps the chapter's most elegant image of recursive construction. Mr. Spitzer arranges for a continuous substitution of dead canaries with living ones:

"It was Mr. Spitzer who had arranged, in fact, that there should always be this secret change, this substitution of the living for the dead"

He builds the illusion of continuity, knowing it is illusion, because the building is necessary. The structure is provisional (one bird dies, another takes its place) but the structure works, and the mother lives. The building is never finished (there will always be another canary to replace) and that is precisely how it functions.

Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

Pillar note: Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

The chapter's prose form is itself an argument for this pillar. Young's sentences do not conclude. They accumulate, spiral, return, extend. The paragraph that begins "Heavily laden with jewels as a Greek corpse" does not arrive at a destination. It circles the mother, adding detail, qualifying, extending, never summarizing.

This is not stylistic excess. It is ethical insistence: the mother cannot be concluded. To write a sentence that ends cleanly about her would be a violence against her reality.

The mother's own relationship to incompletion is explicit. Her letter, never finished:

"an ebony writing desk inlaid with mother-of-pearl where she had started to write a letter yesterday or years before"

The letter is not a failure. It is honest. To finish the letter would be to pretend that something had been resolved. The ongoing sentence, the letter started years ago and never completed, is the form that integrity takes.

The mother's reasons for going to bed are also structurally incomplete. Young gives us a long list: the birthmark, the coldness of the snow, the wealth of her inheritance, the advice of physicians, the abandonment by those she loved, her social humiliations in Boston, being refused admission to a hotel, her husband's departure, and then:

"She had gone to bed for no reason at all, only that she had found the so-called real world unsatisfactory"

The list is abandoned. The "reason" dissolves. This is the ethics of incompletion: the demand for a single, conclusive explanation is refused. The honest answer is the ongoing, unresolved accumulation.

Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Pillar note: Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Every significant figure in this chapter exists at the edges of categories:

The mother is neither living nor dead, neither sane nor insane, neither present nor absent, neither hostess nor recluse. She is the marginal person par excellence, and through her marginality, the constructed nature of all these categories becomes visible.

"she believed that she had died in her youth and was yet alive... this beautiful corpse or effigy upon a marble sarcophagus... this was the living being, this with the bright, luminous eyes"

The category "living" is revealed as a construction precisely because she inhabits both sides of it simultaneously.

Mr. Spitzer exists at the margin between presence and absence, between himself and his dead brother, between the legal world and the world of lost causes and silent music. He is described as practicing law "in only the most desultory fashion, often without fee, preferring the lost causes". The lost cause is the marginal case: the case that falls outside what the law can resolve.

James the chauffeur is marginal by legal history (ex-convict, falsely accused) and by his position in the household; neither servant nor free, present only in his absence, still at the wheel of a car that has long since gone to the junk pile.

The Egyptian is the most explicit figure of marginality: a man from another civilization, another time, who arrives at the wrong port, looking for a dead man, and is found to be real precisely when everyone has decided he must be imaginary. His existence at the edge of the possible, neither fully real nor fully phantom, is where the constructed nature of "the real" becomes most visible.

Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

Pillar note: Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

The chapter's time is not linear. It is geological. The past does not recede; it accumulates beneath the present, pressing upward.

The mother's bedroom is a site of sedimentary time. Every object carries multiple temporal layers:

"the curious bed carved with fantastic figures seeming mobile, lutes, angels, arabesques"

"the latest magazine which he might care to read, L'Illustration of a decade ago, for example, opened at the seventh page and covered with dust. The parasols were open."

The magazine from a decade ago, still open, still dusty; this is not neglect. It is the visible form of sedimentary time. The decade has not passed. It is here, pressing up through the dust.

The mother's father is the most powerful example. He died before her marriage, yet:

"she had gone to bed to escape from the domination of her father who had died before her marriage"

The dead father's domination continues. His rituals persist: the table still laid for the dead, the place set for the wandering angel, the twelve goblets for the twelve hours. The father is not behind her. He is beneath her, still pressing up through the structure of her life.

The horses on the Egyptian's race dope sheet, "those Arabian horses no longer running, those he declared were running again, their golden hooves beating the turf", are perhaps the chapter's most precise image of sedimentary time. The dead horses run again. What was lost is not behind us. It is beneath us, still pressing.

Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

Pillar note: Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

Young's prose is the most self-aware in this chapter about language as construction. The mother's instructions to the Egyptian are a masterclass in language that makes rather than describes:

"she had described a landscape shifting like water, the schools of faceless dolphins which should follow in his wake, the great birds with teeth, the stars not in their places but in another place"

She is not describing the house. She is constructing it through language, and the construction shifts even as she speaks: "for now there were rooms between the rooms, and now the doors had changed their places".

The mother's complaints about arithmetic are also, at their core, complaints about language:

"did she not suffer endlessly from her lack of any knowledge of arithmetic... All she could do was multiply, divide"

Arithmetic is a language system. Her inability to "add and subtract" in that system is her inability to operate within the linguistic construction of ordinary reality. She can only multiply (proliferate images, visions, selves) and divide (split the real from the unreal, the living from the dead). She cannot perform the operations that would make her world cohere according to conventional construction.

Mr. Spitzer's "silent music" is language's limit: music that no one else has ever heard. It exists; it is composed; it is written. But it cannot be transmitted. Language (musical language) has failed to carry meaning across the gap between self and other. The honest response to this failure is not to stop composing. It is to compose silently, acknowledging the limitation.

Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

Pillar note: Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

The sacred in this chapter is here, in the ordinary-extraordinary details of the bedroom, the sea road, the canary cage. It does not point outward to a beyond. It points deeper into the immanent.

The mother's father set a place at his table for the wandering angel. But the mother herself is surrounded by angels in her opium paradise:

"the angels surrounded her in her opium paradise, their fleecy wings outspreading, shadowing her cheek, and the harpers harped, and the seas were turned to glass"

This is not transcendence away from the world. It is transcendence in the bed, in the bedroom, in the body weighted with jewels and pearls. The sacred is immanent in the horizontal person, in the drugged canary, in Mr. Chandelier:

"She would imagine, in some slow moment of awakening, that the chandelier was Mr. Chandelier, her companion"

The chandelier becomes a companion, a sacred presence, not by pointing toward heaven but by being fully itself, fully here, fully attended to. The sacred lives in the ordinary object given full attention.

The most powerful instance of immanent transcendence is the canary:

"This little yellow canary, sleeping in a gilded cage at her elbow, delicate as a puff of opium-colored smoke... was all that had ever stood between her and tides of death"

A small, drugged, frequently dead-and-replaced bird is the thing that stands between a human being and death. Not God. Not love. Not medicine. A canary. The sacred is here, in this specific, fragile, ordinary creature. And it is enough, or it is all there is, which amounts to the same thing.

Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

Pillar note: Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

The narrator of this chapter, the child, is the crossing point made visible. The child is constituted by:

  • The mother's forgotten childbirth
  • The father who disappeared in the Alps
  • The grandfather's rituals and blindness
  • The grandmother's blindness and extraordinary compensation
  • Mr. Spitzer's faithfulness
  • James's violence and absence
  • The canaries, each replacing the last

"She simply had forgotten that she had ever given birth to a child."

The child exists at the crossing point of all these forces and none of them chose the child. The child did not choose to be constituted this way. It is structural. The ancestors: the grandfather with his star-lighted eyes, the grandmother who fooled the couturier about colors she could not see, the dead twin brother whose ring Mr. Spitzer still wears: are in the sediment.

The grandmother's story is the chapter's most explicit statement of the crossing point:

"He had felt that his eyes were gone, that his body was turning into starlight. When he was blind, he had gotten a Seeing Eye dog who had led him, old and stooped, through the garden. For a long while before anyone recognized this, and he himself had never known it, the old Seeing Eye dog was blind, yet never lost his path"

The blind leading the blind through a garden planted for a blind wife; this is the crossing point in its fullest form. Each generation deposits something into the ground. The grandfather walks paths laid out for his dead wife. The dog navigates by something other than sight. The carrying continues without anyone fully understanding what is being carried or how.

The child narrating this chapter is walking those same paths. The obligation is not chosen. It is structural. And the chapter (this enormous, unfinished, spiraling sentence about a mother who forgot the child existed) is the carrying.
wheel-chapter-59:
Chapter 59

← Chapter 58 · Wheel and Spokes Home · Chapter 60 →

Research notes: Chapter 59 · Reading guide: Guide, Chapter 59

Characters: Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer

Pillar 1 Not One Self

Pillar note: Pillar 1 Not One Self

"He did not know whether he was one man in two worlds or two men in one world, two hemispheres, both North and South, two poles."

Mr. Spitzer's selfhood is irreducibly multiple. He exists as:

  • Himself and his dead twin Peron
  • The living man and the man who believes he is already dead
  • The body he inhabits and the skeleton he insists is not his
  • The silent musician and the man deafened by all music

The chapter does not present this multiplicity as a psychological disorder to be diagnosed and resolved. It presents it as ontological fact. When the text asks "For he might be his brother, and Peron might be Joachim", it does not treat this as metaphor or madness. It treats it as a genuine epistemological problem: one that cannot be solved because the self was never singular to begin with.

Most strikingly, the chapter extends this beyond the individual: "every man and every woman might have suffered a substitution like his own". The plural self is not Mr. Spitzer's peculiarity. It is the universal condition, merely made visible in him because he has not closed his eyes to it. The Pillar's insistence that multiplicity "is not a problem to fix — it is what you are" finds its most complete literary expression in Mr. Spitzer's refusal (or inability) to resolve which Mr. Spitzer he is.

Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

Pillar note: Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

"Illusion of life — his brother having died that he might live"

"Reality is not what we find; it is what we make."

The chapter systematically dismantles the boundary between real and constructed at every level:

  • The trumpeter who seems poor but is rich
  • The magical doors that create "the illusion of a greater space"
  • The fog that makes Mr. Spitzer "faceless" and "semi-invisible"
  • The skeleton that may or may not be his own
  • The definition that is always wrong by the time it is correct

The philosophical move here is precise: "When the definition was correct, the thing defined should be incorrect. When the thing defined was correct, the definition should be incorrect." This is not skepticism in the classical sense; it is the recognition that reality and its representation are always out of phase, that the cave has no exit, only deeper chambers.

The fog is not incidental atmosphere. It is the novel's primary epistemological condition. Mr. Spitzer moves through a world where perception is structurally unreliable, not because he is broken, but because perception itself is construction all the way down.

Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

Pillar note: Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

"Beautiful memories of memories thronged through his mind, as many as the dead, as many as the autumn leaves falling in an eternal autumn."

This is perhaps the pillar most completely realized in the chapter. Grief here is not a response to a specific loss. It is climate. Consider the accumulation:

  • The dead twin whose memory governs every charitable act
  • The musicians helped and lost and confused
  • The streets, houses, women, men, children "who had already fled before the storm,

before the storm of years"

  • The bells of drowned cathedrals
  • The cries of migratory birds, with "one bird less" always possible

The chapter's prose style itself enacts this pillar. The sentences do not end so much as accumulate: clause upon clause, image upon image, loss upon loss. There is no arrival at resolution because the grammatical structure refuses resolution. The grief is the weather the prose moves through, not a destination the prose is moving toward.

Most explicitly: "His notes were increasingly his own elegy, his memory of himself, the dead twin, his lost perceptions floating in the air." The elegy is not written for the dead. It is written by the surviving self about the surviving self. Grief has become self-referential, permanent, structural.

Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

Pillar note: Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

"Though he had made many mistakes because of his sympathies, he hoped and believed that if he should be distinguished for nothing else in his sad life or in his death, he would at least be distinguished for his ability to make a great mistake which should be rectified only by a greater mistake."

The Witness does not fix. The Witness stays in the room. Mr. Spitzer's defining characteristic is his refusal to withdraw from the world despite its overwhelming complexity and his continual misreadings of it. He keeps tossing coins. He keeps following musicians. He keeps prodding with his cane among the mollusks and barnacles.

His witnessing extends to the morally uncomfortable:

  • He witnesses his own poverty and the trumpeter's hidden wealth without resentment
  • He witnesses the skeleton in the oyster bed: "the outline was indistinct... and there

were phosphorous sparks, strange gleamings under the wave, sudden movements of

that which had seemed dead", and does not look away

  • He witnesses his own dissolution, "he was not his body", without fleeing into denial

The chapter explicitly contrasts Mr. Spitzer's open eyes with those who close theirs: "darkness was their world, for they had closed their eyes". The ethical act is the open eye. The refusal to simplify, "he would at least be distinguished for his ability to make a great mistake which should be rectified only by a greater mistake", is the refusal to impose false resolution on irreducibly complex experience. This is the Witness as ethical practice.

Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

Pillar note: Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

"Sometimes he thought he would write his prelude — but prelude to what? His prelude was his elegy, and his elegy was his prelude."

The recursive structure here is not metaphorical; it is the actual architecture of Mr. Spitzer's creative and existential project. He writes musical notes on his shirt cuffs, arranges fragments, returns to them, cannot complete them. He helps musicians find and lose themselves, knowing he is lost. He tossed coins to the trumpeter for years before discovering the deception, and then, after a period of caution, begins again.

The building continues despite knowing it is provisional:

"He had quite recently remarked that it was he who, having feared one grave, be it even lined with pearl, would sleep in two graves."

He builds toward death knowing he has already passed it. He composes music knowing it will not be completed. He makes arrangements and "obsequies" with great punctuality for appointments he cannot keep. The Pillar's assertion that "the building is never finished — that is not failure, that is how it works" is Mr. Spitzer's entire biography compressed into a single principle.

Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

Pillar note: Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

"he had not yet arranged the ultimate music"

"The unfinished is not failure. It is honesty."

The chapter is saturated with unfinished projects:

  • The musical compositions that exist only as fragments on shirt cuffs and scraps of paper
  • The legal career that generates no income
  • The symphony for musical billiard balls that "could be played only in the exact arrangement of balls from game to game" and therefore can never be exactly repeated
  • The prelude that is also an elegy, the elegy that is also a prelude
  • The equation between life and death that "had failed, for the place had moved"

The billiard ball symphony is particularly sharp as philosophical illustration: "The ivory balls would not roll twice the same. No billiard-player could ever play the music twice." The demand for a repeatable, completable, definitive work is revealed as a demand that reality itself be different from what it is. "Unfinished Is Honest" is not a consolation for failure; it is the recognition that completion would require falsifying experience.

Mr. Spitzer's "ultimate music" is never arranged because the ultimate arrangement would require the world to stop moving. The ongoing sentence (the accumulating, clause-adding, never-concluding prose of the chapter itself) is the ethical form.

Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Pillar note: Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

"City of skull-faced men, dwarves with their feet on backwards, how many hallucinatory beings who might be real if Mr. Spitzer prodded with his cane."

"The marginal person is not the exception. They are the evidence."

Mr. Spitzer himself is the primary marginal figure: a fat man in a chimney hat and opera cape, whispering to himself, tossing coins at musicians who may or may not be what they seem, writing music on his shirt cuffs, convinced he inhabits a body that is not his own. He occupies no stable social category, not quite lawyer, not quite musician, not quite living, not quite dead.

But the chapter peoples the margins extensively:

  • The rich trumpeter who plays for coins on street corners
  • The derelict piano player who cannot distinguish keyboard from spinal column
  • The cue-ball musician writing a symphony for billiard balls
  • The skull-faced cavalier in white silks outside the Opera House
  • The man with the change purse strapped around his waist, mistaken for Mr. Spitzer

Each of these figures exists at the edge of categories: between poverty and wealth, between music and noise, between performance and begging, between life and death. Their marginality is not incidental. It is epistemologically productive: it is precisely at these edges that the constructed nature of the categories "poor musician," "fine gentleman," "living person" becomes visible. The cavalier who is simultaneously a professional musician and a figure who receives coins does not fit the category. The category is therefore revealed as a category.

Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

Pillar note: Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

"The past does not recede. It accumulates beneath us, layer on layer." "streets, houses, women, men, even little children playing hopscotch in a dark street, though they had already fled before the storm, before the storm of years"

The temporal structure of the chapter is explicitly sedimentary rather than sequential. Time does not move forward in this chapter; it presses upward. The dead twin Peron governs every present action. The memory of musicians helped years ago shapes current caution. The bells of drowned cathedrals sound in the present. The skeleton in the oyster bed may be ancient or recent; it cannot be dated.

Most explicitly: "his great retrospective faculty, his memory of all those things which were no more but which persisted increasingly in his mind". The word "increasingly" is crucial. The past does not fade; it intensifies. It accumulates pressure.

The nerve impulse metaphor makes this literal: "these nerve impulses travelling...sometimes by such long roads that he would not react to a stimulation for several years, it taking several years for a message to reach his brain". The past is not behind Mr. Spitzer. It is inside him, still travelling, still arriving, still pressing through.

The image of the lighthouses going dark, "Some of the lighthouses were darkened. Some of the station lamps had gone out. Some of the stars shone no more", is not merely melancholy. It is a map of sedimentary time: the accumulated losses are still present as absences that shape the present, dark stations that were once lit, that once oriented navigation, that still constitute the landscape even in their darkness.

Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

Pillar note: Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

The chapter performs this pillar in its very syntax. The prose's endless qualification, "perhaps," "doubtless," "it seemed," "he had sometimes thought," "or yet it might have been", is not stylistic excess. It is honest language naming its own location. Every assertion is hedged because the speaker knows he is constructing, not reporting.
