The definitional problem is made explicit: "When the definition was correct, the thing defined should be incorrect. When the thing defined was correct, the definition should be incorrect." Language chases reality and always arrives a moment late, having shaped a target that has already moved.

The music Mr. Spitzer cannot write is itself a language problem: "he had not yet arranged the ultimate music" because the ultimate arrangement would require a language adequate to experience, and no such language exists. His notes on shirt cuffs, "fragments of notes... half notes, the quarter notes, the eighth notes", are honest language: partial, located, aware of their own incompleteness.

Even the chapter's title, "Chapter 59", participates in this. The chapter is one node in an enormous, famously unfinishable novel. The language of the chapter knows it is embedded in a structure too large to conclude.

Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

Pillar note: Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

"The darkness was his illumination."

This pillar is perhaps the most theologically precise in its application to the chapter. Mr. Spitzer does not seek transcendence upward or outward. He finds the sacred downward and inward:

  • In the darkness rather than the light: "finding the darkness his only light"
  • In the bells of drowned cathedrals rather than standing ones
  • In the skeleton in the oyster bed rather than the living body
  • In the music he cannot complete rather than the music performed in concert halls
  • In the coin for Charon carried alongside ordinary coins

The sacred in this chapter is consistently located in:

  1. Threshold states: between life and death, between music and silence, between self and other 2. Marginal figures: the derelict musician, the blind sheep dog, the skull-faced cavalier 3. Ordinary materials: shirt cuffs, coins, fog, oyster shells, barnacles

"There were gleamings seen by night which were never seen by day — fish fins, fish eyes, iridescences, stars." The transcendent is not elsewhere. It is what becomes visible when you stop looking for the sunlit world and accept the luminous dark.

The white rose Mr. Spitzer wears, "the body mystical as the white rose he wore", is sacred not as symbol of an elsewhere but as immanent presence: the body itself, mystical, here, now, dying, gleaming.

Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

Pillar note: Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

"his brother having died that he might live"

This is the pillar that most completely illuminates the twin structure of the chapter. Mr. Spitzer is not a self moving through time. He is the crossing point between Peron and Joachim, between the dead and the living, between the past that deposited him and the future he is constituting.

The chapter makes this structural:

  • He carries Peron's habits (writing on shirt cuffs) without having chosen them
  • He acts in "his faithless brother's persistent memory": the dead brother's will operating through the living body
  • He is constituted by losses he did not choose: "doubtless long ago at a time when he

had not been conscious of his suffering"

The Pillar's language, "constituted by what was deposited before you arrived, and constituting the ground the not-yet-born will stand on", maps precisely onto: "he had tried to make a symbolic equation between life and death... but he had failed, for the place had moved". The crossing point cannot be fixed because it is always moving. Mr. Spitzer is the movement, not the point.

Most profoundly: "Perhaps though he was dead, he had begotten himself." This is the Crossing Point in its most compressed form. The self that exists now was constituted by a death that preceded it. The obligation is not chosen; it is structural. He carries the dead. The carrying continues.
wheel-chapter-71:
Chapter 71

← Chapter 70 · Wheel and Spokes Home · Chapter 72 →

Research notes: Chapter 71 · Reading guide: Guide, Chapter 71

Characters: Tabitha

Pillar 1 Not One Self

Pillar note: Pillar 1 Not One Self

The narrator is never singular. She wears her dead mother's clothes, "the black velvet which had been her abandoned shroud", her mother's lace collar, her mother's pearls. She is not dressed as herself. She is dressed as a sediment of persons. The mother's voice continues inside her mind as an active presence, not a memory: "Those real pearls, my sleeping mother had always said, could not be lost or stolen or sold". The mother is simultaneously dead, sleeping, and speaking.

The doctor, Dr. O'Leary, is perhaps the chapter's most explicit figure of the plural self. He is simultaneously a Yale-trained physician, a man in second childhood, a grieving brother calling for Sarah, a deliverer of imaginary babies, and a naked figure wandering a barren countryside. He cannot be resolved into one person. When the narrator stands in his room, she notes that even his clothes hang there without him: the self and its social costume are separated, the costume remaining while the person has vanished into some other version of himself.

Even the landlady, whose speech has collapsed into a private linguistic system, "she rid the elephants," "her husbane," "clombed the stars", is a plural self in the most radical sense: a person whose interior language no longer maps onto shared language, who therefore exists in a kind of sovereign but unreachable interiority. She is simultaneously present and inaccessible.

The widow on the stairs is split literally down the face: "the high red lighted only one cheek — the other was ashen". The self, here, is visually incomplete, half-constructed, half-absent.

Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

Pillar note: Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

The chapter systematically refuses to let us know what is real. Was the hangman there at all: "Had I dreamed the hangman?". Is Sarah real? The widow insists she is not: "there was no Sarah, none at all". But the narrator heard her. The doctor's patients are described as imaginary, yet their shoes are on the floor. The pregnant man is described as "a real, pregnant man": the insistence on the word real is itself suspicious, a construction trying to assert its own status.

The narrator's mother entertained a thief who, when he left, could not be certain whether he had "dreamed all those great, crystal-lighted rooms". The house may have been a dream. The thief may have been a dream. The Revolution he was going to finance, which could not be named with an exact sum or exact date, is the dream of all dreams: a transformation that cannot be located in time or money.

Most crucially: "The grey light came from the mind if not from the sky". The chapter does not decide. It offers both possibilities with equal weight. The cave is everywhere. The larger cave is more carefully lit.

Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

Pillar note: Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

The entire chapter is saturated with unresolved, accumulating grief. The hangman's grief is the most explicit: his wife Marie hanged herself from a sleety peach tree while pregnant, and he had known where she was going and had searched instead for his hanging clothes and his Jew's harp. His grief is not guilt resolved into acceptance. It is guilt compounded, by habit, by the mandrake children springing from the gallows, by his own children playing at hanging when he is away. His grief has become his entire cosmology.

The narrator's grief for her mother is not past tense. The mother's pearls, clothes, voice, and stories are present tense throughout. The grief is the climate of the narration; it is the atmosphere in which all observation occurs.

The landlady's grief for her dead dog is folded into grief for her fallen-away husband, which is folded into grief for the priest who no longer comes, which is folded into the grief of the small dancer whose castaway clothes Tabitha now wears. These griefs do not form a sequence. They exist simultaneously, layered, each one pressing on the others.

The widow upstairs grieves a husband who "died before he ever came to bed": grief for what never happened, for the unlived life, which is perhaps the most irresolvable grief of all.

Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

Pillar note: Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

The narrator's primary activity in this chapter is witnessing. She does not fix anything. She does not conclude anything. She moves through the hotel (the hangman's story, the doctor's room, the widow's rage, the landlady's speech) and she looks. She reads the books on the shelf. She studies the mateless shoes. She reads the calendar that stopped twenty years ago. She notes the cracked mirror, the thermometer she crushes underfoot, the wet sponge her hand brushes against.

The witnessing is not passive. It is ethically active. When the widow delivers her antisemitic, racist tirade, the narrator does not argue, does not fix, does not editorialize at length. She records it. The refusal to simplify, to either endorse or dismiss, is the act. The reader is left holding the ugliness without a frame that neutralizes it.

The chapter ends with Tabitha, the mute chambermaid, washing one stone in the pale spring air. The narrator witnesses this without interpretation. Tabitha looks up and says "Good-morning", and the chapter ends. No conclusion. No meaning assigned. The witness stays in the room, and the room is enough.

Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

Pillar note: Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

The narrator is explicitly on a quest; she has come "to pick wild flowers, the first white flowers of spring", she has come "to find" something, she has traveled far. But the quest keeps folding back on itself. She enters the doctor's room looking for something and finds only evidence of other searches. The doctor's room is itself a recursive construction: prescription blanks, old magazines, instruments for birth, books from every era, a calendar stopped at a different time.

The mother's story of the pearls is the chapter's most explicit image of recursive construction: every time the string breaks and pearls are lost, the faithful James returns more pearls than were lost, "The more often she lost the pearls...the more pearls there were". The building is never finished. Loss generates more material. You return with more than you started with, though the original string is broken.

The hangman's recursive construction is darker: he has hanged men all his life, perfecting a craft, only to find the craft "unperfected", the mandrake children rising from the gallows, the habit of preparation persisting even as his wife hanged herself. He builds the same structure over and over, and it keeps producing what he did not intend.

Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

Pillar note: Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

The chapter's formal structure enacts this pillar directly. Sentences run for half a page. Parenthetical clauses open and never quite close. The landlady's speech is perhaps the most radical example: her syntax has become genuinely incompletable, not from stupidity but from a kind of excess of reality pressing through damaged language. She is not failing to complete her sentences. She is being honest about a world that does not complete.

The doctor's life is structurally incomplete. His diploma hangs on the wall. His instruments are laid out. His practice continues, but his patients are imaginary, his telephone does not exist, his calendar stopped twenty years ago. He is a physician who cannot complete the act of medicine. And yet the narrator does not judge this as failure. She asks: "how many of us, if we expressed our inner lives, would not express disorder?".

The quest for the white flower, the stated reason for the journey, is never completed in this chapter. The flower is described as "far away, the landscape of a dream which should not be dreamed in the Wabash country". The incompletion is the honest report.

Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Pillar note: Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Every character in this chapter is marginal. The hangman is professionally marginal: society's necessary executioner who must be kept at a distance from society. The mad doctor delivers imaginary babies in a barren countryside. The pregnant man, "a real, pregnant man", violates the categorical boundary of biological sex. Tabitha is mute, described as "too crazy to be on relief", wearing another woman's castaway clothes, performing labor that is noticed only in its absence.

The landlady's aphasia places her at the margin of language itself; she exists in the gap between private meaning and shared communication. She is not outside the community; she runs the hotel. But she runs it from a position of linguistic marginality that makes her simultaneously central and unreachable.

The narrator herself is marginal: a woman traveling alone, accused of being a "tramp girl" by the widow, wearing a dead woman's clothes, carrying pearls that are worth no more than fakes in the current market. She belongs nowhere in this landscape. Her marginality is precisely what allows her to witness it all.

The widow's bigotry is, under this pillar, particularly revealing: her rage against Jews, Catholics, Black people, Roosevelt, her insistence on categorical purity, is the reaction to the ontology of the marginal. She senses that the categories are constructed and responds with violence against that perception, doubling down on the lines. Her hysteria is the evidence that the lines are not holding.

Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

Pillar note: Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

This is perhaps the pillar most thoroughly embodied in the chapter's texture. The doctor's room is a geological cross-section of time: Mary Pickford on a calendar from twenty years ago, books from every era, instruments from different periods of medicine, shoes from "every era and every land". Time has not passed in this room. It has accumulated.

The narrator's mother's estate (the sea-blackened house with gold towers, the rose garden, the marble statues) is described as gone and simultaneously present: "though the world renamed and the house was gone" it enters the hotel room, "included" in the space of sleeplessness and memory. The house does not recede. It presses up through the floor of the present.

The hangman's wife Marie is cut down, dead, but her children play at hanging in the orchard, and the hangman fears to return home not because of Marie but because of what her children might be doing now: the past's action continuing in the present through the bodies of the living.

The dogs' graveyard in the hotel backyard, wooden crosses made from missing fence palings, is a perfect image of sedimentary time: the dead are beneath the yard, the fence is incomplete because of them, the living space is shaped by the accumulated dead.

Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

Pillar note: Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

The chapter is acutely self-aware about language as construction. The Jew's harp is noted to be "not Jewish": the name constructs an association that the object does not bear. The hangman plays it before every hanging: an instrument named for an othered group, used in the ritual of state killing. The chapter notices this without belaboring it.

The landlady's speech is the chapter's most extended meditation on language as construction. Her private language, "clombed," "husbane," "agone," "axed," "combed", is not random. It is a consistent system, internally coherent, shaped by her particular history and body. It constructs a reality that is partially shared and partially sovereign. When she says "there was martial happiness", she may mean marital, or she may mean something more precise than either word captures.

The narrator notes that the mother's pearls "in the present market, would bring no more than cultivated pearls". The word real has lost its market value. The language of authenticity has been devalued by the language of the market. What counts as real is determined by what counts as economically real.

The widow's language constructs a world in which racial and religious categories are ontologically fixed, "the dirty Jew," "the Negroes," "mulattoes", a world in which the constructed nature of categories is violently refused. Her language does not describe the world. It attempts to enforce it.

Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

Pillar note: Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

The chapter's sacred moments are all embedded in the most degraded ordinary. The hangman's Jew's harp music before a hanging: music as the thin membrane between the ordinary and the transcendent, played in the moment before death. The mother's pearls that multiply when lost: an infinity discovered not in heaven but in arithmetic, in the faithful servant's hands, in the broken string.

The doctor's room, for all its squalor, contains "lurid illustrations" that "fluttered into a golden light": diseased kidneys and enlarged hearts illuminated as if sacred. The instruments of birth laid out on the dresser (forceps, bellows, wooden arm) are described with a reverence usually reserved for altar objects.

Tabitha washing one stone in the pale spring air; this is the chapter's final and most concentrated image of immanent transcendence. A mute woman, called crazy, wearing dead people's clothes, performing the most menial labor, washing one round stone that caught the sunlight. The sunlight on the stone. The attention given to one stone. The sacred is here, in this, not elsewhere.

The narrator's quest for the white flower, "the first white flower of spring, the last white winter flower", is a quest for immanent transcendence: not a flower that symbolizes something beyond itself, but a flower that is the crossing point of winter and spring, death and life, in its own ordinary flowering.

Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

Pillar note: Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

The narrator is explicitly constituted by what was deposited before she arrived. She wears her mother's clothes, her mother's pearls, her mother's stories. She carries the memory of a house that no longer exists. She is traveling through Indiana looking for something her mother's world contained: a white flower, a beauty "such as I had seen once and lost". She is not a self moving through time. She is the place where her mother's time and her own time cross.

The hangman is a crossing point of the state's violence and his own domestic grief: the professional habit of preparing for a hanging crossed with the knowledge that his wife was hanging herself in the orchard. He could not separate the two. The preparation ritual crossed both events simultaneously.

The doctor is the crossing point of Yale medicine and rural Indiana madness, of the living and the imaginary, of the competent young man in the photograph and the old man screaming for his dead sister. His room is the physical space where these times cross: the diploma above the pillow where two heads have left their indentations.

Tabitha is perhaps the most structurally significant crossing point: she is the only character who is described as genuinely present in the chapter's final image. She is mute; she cannot construct language. She wears the clothes of a dead dancer. She tends the mad doctor. She washes one stone. She is the ground on which all the chapter's accumulated grief, plurality, and incompletion finally rests. When she says "Good-morning", the chapter's last words, it is not a greeting. It is an acknowledgment. The crossing continues.

Chapter 50

Research notes: Chapter 50 · Reading guide: Guide, Chapter 50

Characters: Joachim Spitzer

Pillar 1 Not One Self

Pillar note: Pillar 1 Not One Self

"he had seen how one may be two or one may be many, many even in his dying"

Mr. Spitzer is constitutively multiple. The chapter never resolves him into a single, stable identity. He is simultaneously:

  • The living man and his own ghost
  • The dreamer and the one who cannot dream
  • The man who has already died and the man still walking
  • The lawyer without a brief, the doctor without patients: defined by absences that are themselves identities

The most devastating articulation comes here:

"what he feared most was doubtless not that one should be two—he feared that one should be one"

This is a direct inversion of conventional anxiety. Most philosophical traditions treat multiplicity as the problem and unity as the solution. Mr. Spitzer fears the opposite: unity is the death. To be collapsed into singularity (to have dream and reality, living and dead, fuse without remainder) is the true annihilation. The plural self is not his disorder. It is his survival strategy, his ontological condition, and ultimately his only form of grace.

The chapter also presents him as plural across time: "the same in his end as in his beginning" is offered not as comfort but as one possibility among several, immediately undermined by its opposite. He cannot determine whether he has changed or remained the same because both are simultaneously true. The self is not a continuous thread but a set of overlapping, irresolvable versions.

Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

Pillar note: Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

"one chair might be only the dream, and one might be real, and one might collapse if he touched it. One might suddenly fly away with many tinkling bells."

The two golden chairs in the clouds (Cassiopeia's Chair, the dream chair, the real chair) constitute one of the chapter's central images. But Young never resolves which is which. The epistemological problem is not presented as solvable. Mr. Spitzer dares not touch the strings of the constellation Lyre "for fear he might touch only upon the imaginary strings".

The crucial move here is that illusion is not positioned as secondary or degraded. The dream chair is as present, as weighted, as consequential as the real one. Young's prose enacts this by giving equal syntactic weight to both:

"One might be only the shadowed part of life."

Note: only the shadowed part, and yet the shadowed part is what fills the chapter. The light exists only as something that casts shadow. There is no sunlit world outside the cave. The opium lady, the invalid, the suffragette: all live entirely inside constructed realities, and the chapter treats these constructions not as pathologies but as the primary mode of human existence.

The line "Or was there only the dream, and had nothing ever been real?" is not answered. In the framework of Radical Immanence, it need not be. The question itself is the territory.

Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

Pillar note: Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

This pillar may be the one most completely embodied by the chapter's texture. Grief here is not an event or a response. It is the climate of Mr. Spitzer's consciousness.

"how often Mr. Spitzer had lamented as the wind whirred around his cape, this universe tacking like the wild white snow bird away from central fires"

The grief is not located. It has no object named, no single loss identified. It is atmospheric: the wind, the fog, the vanished moons, the stars that have followed "an old bellwether to his grave". The accumulation of images of dissolution (snowflakes, fading stars, dried-up streams, broken hourglasses) does not build toward catharsis. Each image simply adds to the sediment of loss.

The suffragette captain who "long ago had paused in a broken melody and would not take up her music in this life" is a figure of grief so total it has become structural; she stopped mid-sentence and never resumed. Mr. Spitzer's grief is the same: it does not resolve into mourning and recovery. It is the condition under which all his perception operates.

Most tellingly:

he "might live to mourn for her as for himself"

He mourns himself. This is grief without even the consolation of a distinct lost object. The griever and the grieved are the same person. This is grief as permanent weather in its most radical form; there is no outside of it, no position from which to observe it as something that happened and passed.

Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

Pillar note: Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

Mr. Spitzer is above all a witness: to others, to himself, to the moment of dying. But Young's treatment of witnessing is complex and troubling in ways that deepen the pillar rather than simply illustrate it.

"was thus a man continually checking, rechecking, altering his impressions which altered of themselves, making little notes to mark his journeys back and forth"

This is witnessing as practice, as discipline: the "making little notes" is the act of attention rendered literal. He does not rush toward resolution. He checks, rechecks, alters, and crucially, the impressions alter of themselves, meaning the act of witnessing is not passive recording but active, destabilizing participation.

His ethical stance toward the invalid lady is witnessing in its most sustained form:

"she had always lived by such indirections and evasions that she would never know when he was gone"

He stays in the room. He keeps returning, punctually "by his broken watch or by the shadow on a moondial in a flooded garden". The broken watch and the flooded moondial are instruments of witnessing that are themselves unreliable, and yet he uses them. The witness does not require perfect instruments. The witness requires presence and refusal to simplify.

The chapter also shows the cost of witnessing. Mr. Spitzer is frightened:

"He was frightened of loud noises. He was frightened of causing disturbances."

The witness is not heroic. The witness is terrified of his own impact on what he observes. This is the ethics of witnessing taken to its logical extreme: the observer so aware of the observer effect that he tries to breathe softly enough not to start an avalanche.

Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

Pillar note: Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

"many changes prepared for greater changes, for by many small changes he saw what greater change would be, and many confusions prepared for greater confusions"

The chapter is itself a recursive construction. The prose returns again and again to the same images (the golden chairs, the fog, the stars, the tide, the mirrors) but each return is slightly altered, slightly further along in dissolution. This is not repetition. It is building with what was learned from the previous pass.

Mr. Spitzer's life is described as a series of provisional structures:

"many assumptions once taken for certain had become uncertain, and many premises had been abandoned"

This is not presented as failure or tragedy but as the natural rhythm of a conscious life. The abandoned premise was not wasted; it prepared the ground for the next construction. The building is never finished. The chapter enacts this by refusing closure even as it approaches death. The final images of the chapter are not resolutions but new openings: the suffragette's unfinished melody, the nocturne he writes for her, the continuing question of what the firefly is.

The recursive structure also appears in Mr. Spitzer's relationship to the opium lady. He returns visit after visit, and each visit is both the same (she may not know he has been gone) and different (he has changed "imperceptibly from point to point"). The relationship is a loop that is also a spiral: returning to the same place but at a different elevation each time.

Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

Pillar note: Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

This pillar is perhaps most explicitly theorized in the chapter's central statement of Mr. Spitzer's condition:

"died wholly who had lived partially, who had lived not as the star but as the day's firefly lost in the sunlight streaked with the dead iris"

Living partially is not a failure; it is the honest mode. The star that burns completely and visibly is actually less truthful than the firefly lost in daylight: the firefly's invisibility is its integrity. It does not pretend to more luminosity than it has.

The chapter is full of unfinished things presented without apology:

  • The suffragette's broken melody
  • The calling cards piled up "as if he had come many times when he had not come": the record of visits that didn't happen, an incomplete archive
  • "his unuttered thoughts and his unrealized loves and his unfinished business, his

hope without foundation stone"

These are not catalogued as failures. They are catalogued as what a life is made of. The demand for completion (the finished melody, the realized love, the founded hope) is implicitly identified as a violence against the texture of actual experience.

Most powerfully:

"was but a moment's passage... was not the Holy Writ but was the mere flyleaf stuck between two passages or testaments"

The flyleaf. Not the text. Not the Old Testament, not the New. The blank page between them, which is also the page that holds them together. Mr. Spitzer is the ethics of incompletion made flesh: the connective tissue between things that never itself gets read.

Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Pillar note: Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Mr. Spitzer inhabits every margin simultaneously. He is:

  • Possibly already dead, possibly still living
  • Neither the dream nor the reality but the space between them
  • "stuck between the millstone above him and the millstone below him"
  • "caught between the penumbra and the penumbra"
  • Neither of the water nor of the land

"Were there not places which were neither of the water nor of the land, neither of the land-locked water nor of the water-locked land, neither one nor the other, places which could not be defined?"

This is the ontology of the marginal stated as cosmology. The liminal zone is not an exception or an edge case. It is a category of place that exists throughout the world. Mr. Spitzer does not occupy the margin because he is unusual. He occupies the margin because the margin is where the constructed nature of all categories becomes visible.

The chapter's gallery of marginal figures reinforces this:

  • The opium lady: neither sane nor mad, neither awake nor asleep
  • The suffragette: neither living nor dead before her death, her name hyphenated, "the hyphen was more important than the two names it joined"
  • Mr. Spitzer himself: "was not the Holy Writ but was the mere flyleaf"

Each of these figures is evidence, as the pillar states, not exception. They reveal that all categories (life/death, real/dream, self/other) are constructions with permeable, inhabited edges.

Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

Pillar note: Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

The chapter's treatment of time is explicitly sedimentary. The past is not behind Mr. Spitzer; it is beneath him, pressing up:

"this life was extended perhaps only one mournful moment longer than he lived, many pebbles rolling in the dried-up streams shining with light"

The dried-up stream still has pebbles rolling in it: the memory of water moving the stones even after the water is gone. This is sedimentary time as physical metaphor: the past's pressure continuing to produce present effects even after the cause has departed.

Most explicitly:

"the whispers lost under the silence, the voices not noticed then"

The voices were deposited in the past and are now pressing up through the silence. They were not noticed then; they are being heard now, from below. This is the sedimentary model of time: what was laid down continues to exert force. The image of the shore is the chapter's master image of sedimentary time:

"this shore of broken hourglasses where was no hour"

The broken hourglasses are time's instruments, shattered and accumulated on the shore. Time does not flow through them anymore, but they are still there, still constituting the ground he walks on. The shore itself is made of what time deposited and then abandoned.

Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

Pillar note: Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

Young's prose in this chapter is one of the most radical enactments of language-as-construction in American literature. The sentences do not describe Mr. Spitzer's consciousness; they perform it. The syntax itself is the content.

Consider the characteristic sentence structure: long, recursive, self-interrupting, qualifying each clause with another clause that partially contradicts it:

"perhaps the fact that he was not himself, that he had changed imperceptibly from point to point, perhaps the fact that he had not changed and was ever the same man"

The language cannot settle. Each perhaps is not a rhetorical hedge but an ontological statement: this is a consciousness for which certainty is not available, and the language must be built to match. Language that pretended to declarative certainty here would be lying; it would be speaking from nowhere, as the pillar says, while actually speaking from a very particular place: the place of false authority.

The chapter also makes language's constructedness explicit thematically:

"no word, sign, mark, image in the silent flood"

Mr. Spitzer will leave no writing. He is "the writings of mutes for the ears of the dead": language that cannot be received, communication that is structurally incomplete. And yet the chapter is full of language, dense with it. The gap between the silence Mr. Spitzer will leave and the extraordinary verbosity of Young's prose describing that silence is itself a statement about language: language is what we use to point at what language cannot contain.

Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

Pillar note: Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

This is perhaps the pillar most beautifully realized in the chapter. Mr. Spitzer does not seek transcendence upward and outward. He finds (or rather, he is) transcendence folded into the ordinary and the dying.

"His little firefly was the soul of the dead. Perhaps his little firefly was all there was."

The firefly. Not the star, not the constellation, not the divine light: the firefly. Small, brief, organic, already dying. And yet: "perhaps his little firefly was all there was." This is immanent transcendence stated with absolute precision. The sacred is here, in the smallest and most fugitive thing, not despite its smallness but because of it.

The chapter repeatedly pulls transcendent imagery (stars, constellations, the Holy Writ, eternity) back into the immanent:

"There was no other star. There was no garden where the white peacocks screamed in a snow storm on any other star than this"

This is the theological statement of the chapter. There is no other star. The transcendence that exists is this transcendence: the peacocks screaming in the snowstorm on this star, this dying man with his firefly key, this moment. The chapter does not mourn the absence of a beyond. It insists on the sufficiency, the extraordinary sufficiency, of the here.

Even death is immanentized:

"this which he was living now—for when had he lived before his death?"

His afterlife is this life. The life after death is the life he is living now, after whatever death he has already passed through. Transcendence is not deferred to another world. It is located in the present moment of this one.

Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

Pillar note: Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

This pillar finds its most complete expression in the chapter's treatment of Mr. Spitzer's relationship to the dead and the not-yet-born:

"was not the Holy Writ but was the mere flyleaf stuck between two passages or testaments, the Old and the New"

He is the crossing point between what came before and what comes after. He does not move through time; he is the place where the Old Testament and the New Testament touch each other. He is the blank page that is also the hinge.

The structural obligation of the crossing point is present in his relationship to the suffragette:

"She had died before he knew, before he had come with his arrangements by which to deceive the chaos, before he had placed her with her head pointing North and her feet pointing South that she might sleep according to the turning of the earth"

He tries to orient the dead according to the earth's axis: to align the individual body with the planet's turning. This is the crossing point made ritual: the dead woman's body placed at the intersection of her individual death and the earth's structural movement. He is constituted by her (he learned from her) and he is constituting the ground of her remembrance.

Most explicitly:

"he was merely the dream of the dream or the reflection of the reflection"

He is not original. He is derived from what came before him, and he will be the origin of what comes after him, but as a reflection, not as a source. The ancestors are in the sediment. He is standing on them. The carrying continues, and he will become sediment for those who follow.

The chapter ends with him writing a nocturne for the suffragette. This is the crossing point's obligation fulfilled: he carries her forward into language, into music, into the not-yet. He does not choose this obligation. It is structural. She deposited herself in him; he deposits her in the work.
wheel-chapter-41:
Chapter 41

← Chapter 40 · Wheel and Spokes Home · Chapter 42 →

Research notes: Chapter 41 · Reading guide: Guide, Chapter 41

Characters: Cousin Hannah · Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer

Pillar 1 Not One Self

Pillar note: Pillar 1 Not One Self

The mother is explicitly fragmented throughout. She is described as having

"so many selves, such as the look-out in the crow's-nest, the negress in the belfry, the human barometer moaning whenever the wind shifted, the lady in the phaeton, the figurehead in the foam"

This is not metaphor deployed for color. It is ontological statement. The self here is not a unified consciousness narrating experience; it is a collection of partial selves, each operating semi-independently, each incomplete. The text explicitly names this condition:

"these fragmentations of partial selves, of splintered mirrors and partial images, vague and illusive thoughts seeming to have a being of their own, to act outside of her even when she was sleeping"

Crucially, the mother is contrasted with Cousin Hannah, who appears to possess a unified self: "that splendid unity of character which she herself had never achieved". But the text does not valorize Hannah's unity straightforwardly. The mother's fragmentation is presented with a kind of awed, melancholy pride. Hannah's singularity is admired but also slightly suspect: too clean, too resolved, perhaps a kind of violence against complexity.

Mr. Spitzer adds a third mode of selfhood: the twin without his twin, a self defined by absence, by being the lesser reflection of another. He is "not his identical brother" perpetually haunted by the shape of what he is not.

The chapter thus presents three models of selfhood: the radically plural (the mother), the apparently unified (Hannah), and the negatively defined (Spitzer). None is stable. None is complete.

Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

Pillar note: Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

The entire chapter operates inside a system where the distinction between the living and the dead has been dissolved as an organizing principle. The mother issues formal invitations to the dead:

"how cordial she would be now if Cousin Hannah should accept her formal invitation, her announcement that she would be at home, receiving at three minutes after three"

This is not presented as madness or delusion requiring correction. It is presented as a legitimate mode of social reality. The dead are more present, more vivid, more reliably communicative than the living:

"Cousin Hannah had always answered her, sometimes achieving communication in spite of unbelievable distances"

while Mr. Spitzer, physically present, produces only

"silence roaring like the ebony waves of the sea"

The text thus inverts the conventional hierarchy of real/illusory. The living man who sits in the room is less real, less present, less communicative than the dead woman who exists only in memory and imagination. Reality is not found; it is constructed by attention and desire. The mother's attention constitutes Hannah as real. Her inattention renders Spitzer ghostly.

The line

"Cousin Hannah should remain in mind, even like Queen Maud Mountains with her trailing cape of snow reaching five hundred miles"

makes this explicit: the dead woman has become geological, more permanent than the living, precisely because she exists now only as construction, as memory, as language, as the mother's ongoing act of making.

Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

Pillar note: Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

This is perhaps the pillar most completely embodied by the chapter's texture. Grief here is not an event with a trajectory. It is climate.

The prose itself enacts this. The sentences do not resolve. They accumulate, circle, return, add new layers without concluding. The mother's grief for Hannah is not moving toward acceptance or release. It is simply the condition in which she exists:

"my mother, through all the empty years, yearned for her as one might yearn for anyone who was no more, anyone who was less than water, less than fire, less than wind, anyone who was less than a thought, less than a dream repeating itself"

The diminishing series (less than water, less than fire, less than wind, less than a thought, less than a dream) does not arrive at zero. It arrives at an ongoing sentence that cannot end because ending would mean release, and release is not available.

Even Hannah's death is described in terms that refuse finality:

"now when she was dead, cold and petrified and rigid, now when she should have passed beyond the powers of insult"

The phrase "should have passed beyond" is telling. She should have, but hasn't. Death has not resolved her. It has intensified her presence, made her "more vivid in death than she had been in life".

Grief accumulates here rather than resolving. The mother's bed, from which she never rises, is the spatial emblem of this permanent weather. She lives inside grief the way one lives inside a climate.

Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

Pillar note: Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

The narrator's stance throughout is one of sustained, non-resolving attention. The prose refuses to simplify any of its figures. Cousin Hannah is simultaneously:

  • A heroic suffrage captain of genuine courage and vision
  • A possible card cheat
  • A woman who may have secretly yearned for marriage
  • A figure who showed "no compassion to the weak"
  • Someone who died clutching a faded rose, "forgotten"

Mr. Spitzer is simultaneously:

  • Pathetically limited, unable to tell "a heart from a spade"
  • Possibly correct in his assessment of Hannah as a cheat
  • A man of genuine if unexpressed knowledge: "his pride which gave him his

knowledge of that which he did not know"

  • A figure of real compassion, sheltering "dead men, poor creatures incomplete

and helpless"

The narrator does not adjudicate between these. The ethical act is the refusal to conclude. To stay in the room with all of it. The chapter's extraordinary length and syntactic complexity is not stylistic excess; it is the formal enactment of this witnessing stance. Every qualification, every subordinate clause, every returning spiral is the text refusing to simplify what it sees.

Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

Pillar note: Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

The chapter's structure is itself recursive. It begins with card games, spirals outward through Hannah's suffrage campaigns, Antarctica, Arabia, the Arctic, and returns again and again to the same domestic scene: the mother in bed, Mr. Spitzer present and absent, Hannah dead and vivid.

Each return arrives with new sediment. We know more about Hannah each time we circle back, but the knowledge does not resolve into a portrait; it deepens the mystery. The building of Hannah as a figure is explicitly provisional:

"Cousin Hannah's life had been well known, not shrouded in mystery"

stated with confidence, immediately followed by layers of speculation, qualification, and uncertainty that reveal how unknown she actually is.

The mother's imaginative construction of Hannah (inviting her to visit, imagining her in the spare rooms, planning the conversation) is presented as ongoing creative work, never finished, never successful, never abandoned:

"A light burned at the window against which the blind moth fluttered with jewels upon its wings"

The light is kept burning. The building continues. That it will never be completed, Hannah will never arrive, is not failure. It is the structure of the work.

Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

Pillar note: Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

The prose style is the most direct embodiment of this pillar. These are sentences that refuse to end. Consider the passage describing Hannah's qualities:

"with unflinching firmness, with undiminishing vigor even when her strength diminished, with dauntless and increasing spirit when her body faded, with heroic fortitude when she was faced with only gentleness and evasiveness, with that noble rigor of manner which was and perhaps is always the outgrowth of the resistance against quavering timidity, even one's own"

This sentence does not conclude so much as exhaust one angle of approach before the next clause begins. The demand for a concluded sentence (a clean subject, verb, object, period) would be a violence against the complexity of what is being described.

Hannah herself is described as "the ongoing sentence" in structural terms: her life was "seemingly only one course, grand but not simple" but the simplicity is immediately qualified, complicated, opened back up. Her apparent unity is itself shown to be a kind of ongoing construction, not a achieved resolution.

The mother's life, by contrast, is explicitly described as radically incomplete, "this fragmented ego", and this fragmentation is presented not as failure but as honesty about what a self actually is.

Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Pillar note: Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Every significant figure in this chapter occupies a marginal position:

  • The mother: bedridden, outside ordinary social time, conversing with the dead
  • Mr. Spitzer: the surviving twin, defined by his brother's absence, "amorphous" existing in the margins of his own life
  • Cousin Hannah: a woman who occupied public space in ways women were not meant to, who "crashed the gates" who rode through capitals, crossed forbidden frontiers, entered spaces guarded by "minotaurs and dragons and speaking

birds"

Hannah's marginality is the most developed. She is described as having crossed "so many boundary lines which had been forbidden during her life", and these are not only geographical. She crossed the boundary of gender performance, of acceptable female life, of domestic expectation. She is explicitly described as having "a pointed silver beard": a detail that places her outside conventional gender categories entirely.

The text presents her marginality not as exception or aberration but as evidence: evidence of what the categories are, where they are enforced, and what it costs to cross them. Her death clutching a faded rose, forgotten, in a bed, the most conventionally feminine of deaths, is the text's most devastating irony: the woman who escaped every boundary was finally contained by the ultimate one.

Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

Pillar note: Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

This pillar is perhaps the chapter's deepest structural principle. The past does not recede in this text. It presses upward.

Hannah is dead, but she is described in the present tense of active memory, more present than the living Spitzer. The mother's grief is not a memory of grief; it is current grief, still accumulating:

"his jealousy had been fed by every new disappointment"

The same is true of the mother's love for Hannah. Each new absence feeds it. Time does not move these figures away from their losses; it deposits new layers of loss on top of the original loss, making it heavier, more present, more geological.

The house itself is described as

"unchanging throughout the years because it was always changing, even through changelessness"

This is a precise description of sedimentary time: the house accumulates change without losing what was there before. The "beds of great kings who had migrated to other beds": the kings are gone but their beds remain, the impression of their bodies still somehow present in the mattresses.

The Antarctic imagery that recurs throughout, "great glacial mountains of snow and ice and lakes of ice", is also sedimentary imagery: ice as compressed time, layer upon layer of accumulated weather, the past literally frozen into the present landscape.

Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

Pillar note: Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

The prose here is self-consciously constructive. It does not pretend to transparent description. It builds Hannah through accumulation, qualification, metaphor, and revision, and in doing so, it makes visible the act of construction.

Consider how Hannah is described:

"she was still, my mother insisted, unforgettable even when she was forgotten"

This is language naming its own paradox, its own location. My mother insisted: the text marks the source, marks the subjectivity, refuses the pretense of objective description. Hannah's reality is explicitly the mother's construction: "my mother's continuing memory of her".

The passage about the mother's walk is particularly striking:

"she had walked in circles and semicircles, describing various elegant patterns in her most casual movements, measuring the distance from a blue brocade divan to a gilt and ivory chair as if this distance were a complicated problem in infinity"

The mother's movement through space is itself described as language: as "describing" patterns, as choreography, as inscription. Movement is writing. The body speaks. But it speaks in a language that "confus[es] persons with whom she had tried to carry on a polite conversation", because her language is not theirs, does not pretend to speak from nowhere, does not pretend to the neutral.

Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

Pillar note: Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

The sacred in this chapter is entirely immanent: located in the ordinary materials of the world, pointing deeper in rather than upward and out.

The house is described with a kind of reverence that is explicitly not supernatural:

"its crazy porches and balconies and chimneys and widow walks lighted like amphibian stars and intricate mother-of-pearl circular stairways, great wentletraps reaching to mother-of-pearl clouds, helmeted snails in salt pools, rain-drenched gardens and broken shells and furry buds"

The sacred is in the snails, the broken shells, the widow walks. The "wentletraps", a type of spiral shell, reaching to "mother-of-pearl clouds" is the chapter's most concentrated image of immanent transcendence: the shell (entirely earthly, biological, ordinary) reaching toward the sky, but the sky itself made of the same material as the shell. Transcendence is the ordinary world seen more deeply.

The light burning at the window, against which the moth with "jewels upon its wings" flutters, is another such image. The moth is not a symbol pointing elsewhere. It is the sacred: fragile, drawn to light it cannot reach, beautiful in its futility, entirely of this world.

Hannah's death (clutching a faded rose, forgotten) is presented with the same quality of immanent sacredness. The rose is not a symbol of eternal love. It is a faded rose, possibly imaginary, possibly brought by the mother in a dream she has forgotten. The sacred is here, in the fading, in the forgetting, in the not-knowing.

Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

Pillar note: Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

This is the pillar that gives the chapter its deepest structure. The mother, Hannah, and Spitzer are all crossing points: places where time crosses itself, where the deposited past presses up through the living present.

The mother is constituted by Hannah, by what Hannah was, what Hannah represented, what Hannah's life made possible and impossible. She is also constituted by the absent Peron (Hannah's twin's brother), by dead kings whose beds she inhabits, by all the "birds of passage" who have moved through the house.

The chapter's most explicit statement of this pillar:

"she having achieved emancipation, having escaped this wide-meshed net of years as a fish escapes from the fisherman's net or as the fisherman escapes from the boat"

Hannah has escaped, but into what? Not into a beyond. Into the sediment beneath the mother's present. She is now part of what the mother stands on. The obligation continues: the mother keeps the light burning, keeps the invitation open, keeps the memory alive, not out of choice but out of structural necessity. She is where Hannah's time crosses her time.

Spitzer embodies this pillar in its most painful form. He is the crossing point of his brother's life and his own: "not his identical brother" defined by what was deposited before he arrived (his brother's gambling debts, his brother's charisma, his brother's death), constituting nothing forward, apparently, but the "mournful, wild howling" of his continued presence.

The suffrage movement itself is described in these terms: Hannah as the crossing point of all the women who came before her and all who would come after:

"she had been this unconquerable, tumultuous suffrage captain... carrying her emblazoned suffrage message to the far corners of the earth"

She carried what was given to her and deposited it forward. The carrying continues, in the mother's memory, in this text, in the reader's encounter with it.
wheel-chapter-10:
Chapter 10

← Chapter 9 · Wheel and Spokes Home · Chapter 11 →

Research notes: Chapter 10 · Reading guide: Guide, Chapter 10

Characters: Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Solomon the Turtle

Pillar 1 Not One Self

Pillar note: Pillar 1 Not One Self

The chapter opens with the narrator unable to visualize her own marriage, "neither my lover nor his rough, frost-bearded cheek", and immediately displaces the self outward into speculation about other weddings, other brides, other bridegrooms. The self cannot hold its own image and so proliferates into others.

Mr. Spitzer is the chapter's most explicit embodiment of the plural self. He sleeps in twin beds, his own and his dead brother's, and is "sometimes disturbed by the baffled feeling that he was two bodies sleeping in two separate beds, that there were two heads on two striped pillows". He does not resolve this. He whistles in the dark and migrates from bed to bed. The plural self is not diagnosed here; it is simply inhabited.

The dream wedding then performs the ultimate dissolution: Mr. Spitzer becomes the bride, Miss MacIntosh becomes the bridegroom, the preacher cannot determine "who was woman and who was man and who was beast and who was bird". The narrator, observing, notes: "I could see quite clearly though I was not myself at all". The witness is present but the self behind the witness has dissolved. This is not presented as crisis. It is presented as the condition of perception itself.

The narrator's post-dream reflection compounds this: she feels she has wronged Miss MacIntosh through her own dreaming, as though the boundary between the dreaming self and its objects is permeable, as though imagining someone is already an act performed upon them. The self bleeds outward. Its multiplicity is not contained within the skull.

Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

Pillar note: Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

The chapter's central formal gesture is the dream that cannot be distinguished from waking. The narrator says: "I must have been dreaming when the wedding march started up" and then immediately: "it must be the continuation of my dream, as then I reasoned". The hedge, as then I reasoned, is crucial. It locates the reasoning inside the dream, which means the reasoning cannot adjudicate between dream and waking. The instrument of verification is itself contaminated.

When the narrator wakes, she performs a kind of inventory of the unreal: "The stars had not really fallen from the sky, and Mr. Spitzer had not married Miss MacIntosh, and I had not been the bridesmaid". But the triple negation reads less like reassurance than like a list of things that happened in a register that counts. The denial is too elaborate. It enacts the very persistence of what it denies.

The preacher's sermon deepens this. He moves without transition from wedding rites to burial rites, "the preacher had changed, even without the flicker of an eyelid, from the wedding rites to the rites for the burial of the dead", and "no one seemed amazed." The absence of amazement is the tell. In a world where illusion is primary, the collapse of categorical distinction between wedding and funeral is not a rupture. It is the baseline.

The cave here is not Plato's. There is no philosopher who has seen the sun. The preacher himself is lost: "May God forgive us, for we know not who or where we are". The larger cave is not more carefully lit. It is lit by snowflakes and a single missing candle, "There was no candle lighted", until suddenly the stars illuminate everything, at which point the narrator sees that the error was not the preacher's and not hers, but the dream's own, "the error of the dream which had begotten nothing and no marriage". Illusion generates its own internal error. There is no outside position from which to correct it.

Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

Pillar note: Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

The chapter's weather is literal and structural. The shapes of the dream wedding are "blurred by everlasting snow and ice as if the surface of the earth were some enormous, frosted wedding cake under the dark, blowing heavens". The frosted wedding cake is a collapsed image (celebration and burial, sweetness and cold, the festive and the permanent) and the word everlasting does the most work. This is not a storm that passes. It is the climate.

Mr. Spitzer is grief's primary figure. He has been waiting for his dead brother for the entirety of his existence. He wears clothes "of the style he had worn when his brother was alive". His clothes are a form of temporal arrest: grief worn on the body, grief as costume, grief as the refusal to let time move him forward. He told the narrator's mother that he "would be married to no one now but his brother worm who was under the ground". His grief has become his primary relationship. It is not a stage he is passing through. It is his permanent address.

The preacher's sermon accumulates grief without resolving it. The litany of the lost, "Where, my dearest heart, is Issachar? Where is Nepthalin? Where is Reuben who begot a horde? Where is Manasses? Where is Kansas? Where is Iowa?", is not a lament moving toward consolation. It is a list that keeps growing. Kansas and Iowa alongside the biblical patriarchs: the sacred and the ordinary are equally lost, equally unlocatable. Grief does not discriminate between the holy and the mundane. It takes everything.

The narrator's post-dream meditation on Miss MacIntosh touches grief obliquely but precisely: "What would it be like to be old and unloved? It was hard enough to be young and unloved as I was, to waste one's sweetness in the desert air, but at least, the future was mine, as then I thought, and she had no future". The phrase as then I thought performs the same function as as then I reasoned earlier; it marks the thought as already suspect, already past, already the kind of certainty that will not hold. The grief here is anticipatory: grief for Miss MacIntosh's unlived life, grief for the narrator's own unloved present, grief that accumulates across both of them in a single paragraph.

Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

Pillar note: Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

The narrator's position throughout is that of the witness who cannot fully see. She says: "Though I could clearly hear, I could not clearly see, for the shapes were blurred by everlasting snow and ice". This is the precise condition of the Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act pillar: present, attentive, unable to resolve. She does not leave. She does not stop looking. She stays in the room, or the dream, and reports what partial vision yields.

The ethical weight of witnessing appears most clearly in the narrator's guilt about her dream. She has seen Miss MacIntosh in an undignified position (as the bridegroom with a waxed mustache, as the object of the preacher's confused ceremony) and she feels this as a violation: "What had I done to Miss MacIntosh, and how must I blush when I saw her next, for suppose she guessed my forbidden thoughts, and they were written on my face as plain as day!". The witness is not neutral. Seeing is already an act. The act of imagination is already a form of doing. The narrator understands that attention is not passive.

The preacher is a dark mirror of the Witness. He sees everything and nothing. He addresses the congregation as "Dearly beloved" while being unable to identify the parties before him. He speaks with total authority and total confusion simultaneously. He is the anti-Witness: present, verbose, and fundamentally refusing to see what is actually in front of him. His failure throws the narrator's partial, honest, blurred witnessing into relief.

Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

Pillar note: Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

The chapter is structurally recursive. The narrator dreams a wedding, wakes, reflects on the dream, imagines Miss MacIntosh's future, circles back to Miss MacIntosh's stated opinions about marriage, circles back to the narrator's own loneliness, arrives at the impulse to go see Miss MacIntosh, and is stopped by the locked door. Nothing is concluded. The thought returns to its beginning with what it has learned, which is not resolution but a slightly different orientation toward the same unresolved material.

The preacher's sermon is itself a recursive construction. It begins as a wedding ceremony, becomes a funeral, incorporates elements of both simultaneously, and ends with "Amen, amen, amen. Strike up the music! On with the dance". The amen and the dance instruction are not contradictions resolved. They are contradictions held in the same breath, the building never finished, the ceremony that contains its own ending and beginning simultaneously.

Mr. Spitzer's migration between beds is a nightly recursion. He does not choose one bed and stay. He returns, night after night, to the problem of his brother's absence, building the same incomplete structure of grief and presence, knowing it is provisional, returning to the beginning.

Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

Pillar note: Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

The wedding that is also a funeral and also neither is the chapter's central image of the unfinished as honesty. The preacher's ceremony does not conclude. Miss MacIntosh "did not reply" when addressed. The marriage does not take place. The narrator reflects afterward: "there had been neither the wedding nor the funeral". The double negation is not a failure of the dream. It is the dream's most honest statement: that the categories themselves (wedding, funeral, beginning, ending) are constructions that the experience refuses to honor.

The birthday cake that is never cut is a small, domestic enactment of the same principle. The celebratory form exists. The completion of the celebration does not occur. The narrator is hungry. The incompletion is not symbolic only; it is physical, embodied, felt as an ache.

Miss MacIntosh's refusal of marriage is framed, by the narrator, as a kind of ethical position: she "had no illusions" and was "so clear as to her necessary limitations". The narrator reads Miss MacIntosh's self-assessment as a form of integrity: the refusal to complete a story (courtship, marriage, happiness) that the facts do not support. Miss MacIntosh is, in this reading, the practitioner of Unfinished Is Honest. She will not pretend to a conclusion the evidence does not warrant.

Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Pillar note: Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Every figure in this chapter is marginal. Mr. Spitzer is the surviving brother, the one who was not preferred, the one who inhabits his own life as a kind of remainder. Miss MacIntosh is the old maid, the woman past the zenith, the one "no man in his senses would think of looking at twice". The narrator is the young, unloved, hungry girl who cannot visualize her own future.

The preacher's inability to distinguish gender, asking Mr. Spitzer if he will take "this man to be your lawful wedded husband" and asking Miss MacIntosh if she will take "this woman", is not merely comic. It is the ceremony's revelation of its own categorical instability. The institution of marriage depends on the categories of man and woman being clear and fixed. The preacher's confusion does not corrupt the ceremony. It reveals what the ceremony was always doing: imposing clarity on what is fundamentally unclear.

The wedding guests are: the narrator (who is not herself), the turtle Solomon, the red geranium, and an old empty shoe. This is the most precise image in the chapter. The marginal witnesses to a marginal event are themselves objects at the edge of personhood: a reptile, a plant, a discarded object. They are the evidence that the category of witness is as constructed as the category of bride.

Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

Pillar note: Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

The chapter's temporal structure is layered rather than linear. The narrator moves through: present wakefulness, dream, waking reflection on the dream, memory of Miss MacIntosh's statements, anticipation of Miss MacIntosh's future, memory of Miss MacIntosh's recent complaints, projection of tomorrow's reformed behavior, and return to the present locked door. These are not sequential. They press upward simultaneously.

Mr. Spitzer's dead brother is the chapter's most explicit figure of sedimentary time. The brother is under the ground (literally, in the earth) but he presses upward through every detail of Mr. Spitzer's existence: the twin beds, the old-fashioned clothes, the rejection of all future relationships. The dead brother is not in the past. He is in the sediment beneath Mr. Spitzer's present, still constituting it.

The preacher's geographical litany performs sedimentary time: "He has gone from Newport to Mystic, from Wellfleet to Buzzards Bay, from Boston to Boston. He has gone to Gloucester". The accumulation of place names (each a layer of movement, of history, of loss) does not arrive anywhere. Boston to Boston: the journey that returns to its origin having changed nothing except that it has happened. The sediment of travel without destination.

Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

Pillar note: Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

The preacher's language is the chapter's most sustained meditation on language as construction. His ceremony begins with the formula of the wedding rite, "Dearly beloved," the preacher said, "according to the words of the old text", and immediately begins to deviate. The deviation is not random. It is the old text's suppressed content surfacing: the wedding rite contains a funeral because marriage is an institution that acknowledges mortality ("till Death do us part"), and the preacher simply lets that suppressed content rise.

His pronouns collapse: he addresses Mr. Spitzer as the one who will take "this man" as husband, addresses Miss MacIntosh as the one who will take "this woman" as wife. The pronoun system that organizes the ceremony, that makes the ceremony legible as a ceremony, fails. When the pronouns fail, the ceremony fails. Language was doing more structural work than the participants realized.

The narrator's own language is marked by its own location. The repeated "as then I thought" and "as then I reasoned" are a narrator speaking from a later position, flagging her own past certainties as provisional. The language names its own temporal location. It refuses to speak from nowhere.

The preacher's list of what marriage requires the renunciation of, "all earthly goods, titles, claims, demands, estates, effects, all corporeal and incorporeal hereditaments, spheres of influence, feelings of neglect, golden crowns and thrones, heirlooms, appurtenances", is language enacting its own excess. The legal formula proliferates past usefulness into absurdity, and in that proliferation reveals that the legal formula was always a construction, always an attempt to enumerate what cannot be fully enumerated.

Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

Pillar note: Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

The sacred in this chapter lives entirely within the ordinary and the broken. The preacher invokes God, St. Michael, all the holy angels, the Day of Judgment, golden thrones, jewels, stars burning like lamps, the sea turning to glass, and all of this transcendent apparatus is delivered in the same breath as the information that "a mighty hurricane is blowing in from the Canary Islands or Hebrides this night of nights". The transcendent and the meteorological are grammatically equivalent. Neither is more real than the other.

The moment of genuine illumination in the chapter is not divine. It is stellar and sudden: "Then suddenly, in perfect silence, the manifold skies were illuminated, pointed star by pointed star". The illumination comes from within the natural world, from the immanent sky, and what it reveals is not truth but correction of error, not revelation of the divine but clarification of the dream's own internal mistake. The sacred is here, doing the work of perception, not transcendence.

Miss MacIntosh's silver dollar watch and waxed mustache, the ordinary objects of her ordinary life, are what she carries into the ceremony. She brings no veil, no flowers. Her sacredness, if she has any, is in the silver dollar, the watch, the umbrella. The immanent objects are her regalia.

The narrator's first feeling of pity for Miss MacIntosh is described as "the first embryonic emotion": a biological metaphor for a moral development. The transcendence here is entirely interior, entirely developmental, entirely located in the body of the narrator's feeling. Poor old soul: the word soul appears once, casually, in a phrase that is almost dismissive, and in that casualness it does more work than the preacher's entire invocation of the divine.

Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

Pillar note: Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

The chapter's final image is the locked door. The narrator wants to go to Miss MacIntosh. She is stopped. She is where two impulses cross: the impulse toward connection and the law of the other's privacy. She is constituted by what has been deposited before her (her mother's opium dreams, Mr. Spitzer's grief, Miss MacIntosh's discipline, the whole sediment of the house) and she is constituting the ground of her own future understanding, the maturity she promises herself for tomorrow. The structural position of the narrator throughout is the Crossing Point made explicit. She is the child of a mother lost to illusion and a father absent from the text. She is being formed by Miss MacIntosh, who is herself formed by a history the narrator does not fully know. The narrator's dream does not belong only to her; it contains Mr. Spitzer's grief, Miss MacIntosh's self-assessment, the preacher's confusion, the turtle Solomon. She is where all of this crosses.

The preacher's sermon contains the most precise statement of the Crossing Point: "As it was in the beginning, is now, and ever shall be, world without end". This is the liturgical formula for continuity, for the crossing of past and present and future in a single moment. The preacher delivers it in the middle of a ceremony that cannot determine whether it is a wedding or a funeral, which means the formula applies equally to both: the beginning and the end are the same structure, and you are where they cross.

The narrator's final thought before the locked door is about "all those wall-eyed phantoms, necromancers, shades, whirling dervishes who had no place" and "the old rapists lurking in the grey or purple sea fog": the threats that are both real and unreal, specific and vague. She is warned against wandering. She stays. The staying is not safety. It is the structural position of the one who is constituted by what came before and is constituting what comes after, unable to move forward, unable to return, holding the crossing point in the dark.
wheel-chapter-55:
Chapter 55

← Chapter 54 · Wheel and Spokes Home · Chapter 56 →

Research notes: Chapter 55 · Reading guide: Guide, Chapter 55

Characters: Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer

Pillar 1 Not One Self

Pillar note: Pillar 1 Not One Self

"his mind did not now so easily differentiate between himself and his brother as in the past, there being now no thinker thinking Mr. Spitzer's thoughts"

Mr. Spitzer is constitutionally multiple. He and Peron are not merely two brothers; they are two simultaneous versions of a single being, divided by temperament (order vs. chaos, composer vs. gambler, introvert vs. extrovert) but sharing a body of patrimony, a house, a face, a comb swept up from the same waves. The plural self is not metaphor here; it is the literal condition of being a twin.

But the plurality deepens after Peron's death. Mr. Spitzer does not become singular; he becomes more fractured:

"After Peron's death, he had dreamed he was two brothers, and one was dead."

He cannot mourn cleanly because he cannot locate the boundary between himself and what he mourns. His retinal rivalry (each eye seeing a different image, the images refusing to fuse) is the somatic expression of the plural self. He sees double because he is double. The self is not one person. The chapter does not treat this as tragedy to be overcome. It treats it as the permanent condition of Mr. Spitzer's existence, as irreducible as his grief.

Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

Pillar note: Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

"The morning had never come. The morning had been the dream, and the night had been real."

Young's prose enacts this pillar rather than merely stating it. The chapter is saturated with mirages, hallucinations, counterfeit currencies, forged signatures, and false identities. Peron forges Joachim's name on checks. The bank teller insists there is only one brother. Mr. Spitzer finds himself in the wrong carriage, as the wrong passenger.

Most strikingly, the chapter offers this formulation:

"for all money was counterfeit even like the sun, moon, stars turned out at the great Mint"

This is not cynicism; it is ontological. The counterfeit is not the exception to the real; it is the condition of the real. Even the sun is manufactured. The cave has no outside. Mr. Spitzer's investments in sunken Roman galleys and Phoenician traders and kingdoms never marked on any map are not delusions of a failed man; they are the honest investments, the ones that acknowledge their own speculative nature, their dependence on contingencies that may never arrive. The conventional "secure" investments are the real illusions, pretending to stability in a world that has none.

Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

Pillar note: Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

This pillar may be the chapter's dominant key.

"He had already worn the black mourning cape, how often he must remember now. He had already mourned for the man he once had been, for he had foreseen the empty future."

Mr. Spitzer does not grieve in sequence. He grieves simultaneously and recursively, for his brother, for himself, for the music he never composed, for the life he might have led if his brother had died earlier, for the life his brother led and he did not. He leaves white roses or red roses at his brother's grave:

"a white rose or a red rose depending upon whether he mourned for himself or his brother"

The roses are interchangeable. The mourning is undifferentiated. Grief here is not a response to a specific loss; it is the climate of Mr. Spitzer's entire existence, the weather in which all his other experiences occur. His forehead is "seamed vertically by a line of grief" as a permanent topographical feature, not a temporary expression. The chapter offers no arc toward healing. It is, structurally, a long meditation on grief that does not move, and the prose formally enacts this through its recursive, digressive, non-advancing sentences that circle back endlessly on the same losses.

Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

Pillar note: Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

Young's narrative stance is itself an exercise in this pillar. The prose refuses to judge Mr. Spitzer, to pathologize him, to conclude about him. It stays in the room with his confusion, his double vision, his sleeping-while-waking, his inability to distinguish his own memories from his brother's experiences.

Mr. Spitzer himself practices a version of witnessing:

"he posed his questions in such a way as to receive only the most discursive replies and was also very discursive in his replies... he wished if possible his life to be this continuum"

He refuses resolution. He keeps the questions open. He does not want to "absolve himself completely from the responsibility for his own dark past": meaning he insists on staying in the ambiguity rather than achieving the clean verdict of either guilt or innocence. This is attention as ethics: refusing the simplification that would make things easier but less true.

The architectural design of the house (its twin rooms, its perfect symmetries, its maps and plumb lines) is also a form of witnessing: an attempt to see everything accurately, to leave nothing unaccounted for, to mark every boundary. That it fails does not invalidate the attempt. The witness does not guarantee clarity. The witness guarantees presence.

Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

Pillar note: Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

"he had made his map and marked his boundary lines before the discovery—had mapped out his entire life"

"Using compasses like those which had moved between two golden-footed stars, also moving, using slide rulers and quadrants and plumb-lines... he had drawn the intricate maps"

Mr. Spitzer builds obsessively and provisionally. The house with its twin gardens, twin portraits, twin staircases, twin chimney pieces is a structure built on the knowledge of its own incompleteness; it accounts for Peron's chaos by trying to contain it within symmetry, but symmetry is always already undermined by the "slight ripple in one which was not in the other".

His musical project is the purest expression of recursive construction:

"he would write the tenth symphony, that which had never been written... that he would begin with the tenth symphony—begin where others had ended—ended their lives."

He does not intend to build on what others completed. He intends to begin at the point of incompletion: to start where the building was abandoned. This is recursive construction as explicit program: return to the unfinished, work from there, knowing the work will itself remain unfinished. The music sheets remain empty. This is not failure. It is the structure of the project.

Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

Pillar note: Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

"The other great composers had written only their ninth symphonies—perhaps not even these—had never finished the tenth symphony, for they had died in the midst of it"
