The tenth symphony, the one that has never been written, is Mr. Spitzer's life work precisely because it cannot be completed. He does not choose an achievable goal and fail to reach it. He chooses the structurally unachievable as his ethical commitment. The demand for completion would be a violence against the truth of musical experience, which always points beyond itself.

His music is described as his tomb, his sarcophagus:

"his music was his tomb. He had wished to be his own sarcophagus."

The work is not separate from the life; it is the life, and like the life, it cannot be sealed. The attempt to "cement his roof before the tide" is the honest acknowledgment that the roof will not hold, that the tide will come, and that building anyway is the only integrity available.

His unfinished manuscripts, his empty music scrolls in every room, his silence that is "more beautiful than music"; these are not signs of failure. They are the honest record of a man who refused to falsify completion.

Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Pillar note: Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Mr. Spitzer inhabits multiple marginal categories simultaneously:

  • He is a twin: a person whose identity is structurally divided, never fully singular
  • He is a composer who cannot compose: an artist defined by the work he cannot make
  • He is a lawyer who never practices law: a professional identity held without exercise
  • He is a man who cannot be sure he is alive: suspended between sleep and waking, life and death
  • He invests in kingdoms that never existed, ships that have sunk, bonds of lost empires

"some cancelled postage stamps from kingdoms this world had never seen—republics never marked upon any map"

These marginal investments are not mistakes; they are the evidence. They reveal that all investments depend on contingencies, that all kingdoms are provisional, that the difference between the Republic of Lost Atlantis and the United States Treasury is a matter of duration, not ontology. Mr. Spitzer's marginal position makes visible what the conventional investor's position conceals.

His double vision (the near things seeming small, the far things seeming large, the proportions reversed) is a marginal epistemology that, rather than being corrected, reveals something true: that conventional perspective is also a construction, that the "normal" proportions are not natural but learned.

Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

Pillar note: Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

This pillar is perhaps most beautifully enacted in the chapter's relationship to the past.

"his memory was become like an Aeolian harp, a harp with many strings"

"The past does not recede. It accumulates beneath us."

For Mr. Spitzer, the past does not recede at all. His brother's laughter still sounds:

"he had heard his brother's mocking laughter then as now, for never would his brother's laughter depart from him"

His investments in sunken galleys and Phoenician traders are literally sedimentary; they exist beneath the water, beneath the ground, pressing upward, not yet reclaimed but not gone. His house, now demolished, is still present in his memory as he passes the street. The twin cupids still point their arrows in his mind even though the walls have been knocked down.

Most strikingly, the chapter's very prose style is sedimentary. Each sentence deposits the previous one beneath it rather than moving past it. The accumulation of clauses (clause upon clause, memory upon memory, loss upon loss) formally enacts the sedimentary model of time. You cannot read this chapter quickly because it will not let the past recede.

"He wandered, and the twin house was no more, and he only dreamed that he passed it now—only dreamed that it had once been real and true, stone by stone, glass by glass, bird by bird."

Stone by stone, glass by glass, bird by bird: the granular specificity of accumulation. The past is not a blur. It is a precise deposit.

Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

Pillar note: Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

Young's prose is one of the most radical enactments of this pillar in American literature. The chapter's sentences do not describe Mr. Spitzer's condition from outside; they perform it from inside. The recursive syntax, the endless qualification, the refusal to arrive at a period, the doubling and redoubling of images: all of this is language that names its own location as the consciousness of a man who cannot see one thing without seeing two.

"When he looked at one spot, his eyes saw two spots. When he looked at two spots, his eyes saw four spots."

This is not just description. The prose itself doubles. Every image in the chapter has its mirror: twin portraits, twin gardens, twin moons, twin brothers, twin graves. The language has built the reality it appears to describe.

The legal language scattered through the chapter ("party of the second part," "party of the first part", the law library titles like Authenticity of Will, Will of the Dead, Cases in Chancery) is language that pretends to speak from nowhere, to establish objective categories, to fix identity and ownership. Mr. Spitzer's inability to practice this language, his constant confusion about which party he is, his forgery of his own name; these expose the constructed nature of legal identity itself.

Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

Pillar note: Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

"Death was silence, though it was also figured like a state of mind, he believed, for there could be no state of mind which was not figured, wrought with its possibilities."

The sacred in this chapter is entirely immanent; it lives in the double vision, the sunken ships, the empty music scrolls, the white rose left at the grave. There is no heaven Mr. Spitzer appeals to, no transcendent resolution he awaits. His music, his "tomb," his "sarcophagus", is the closest thing to the sacred, and it exists in the silence between notes, in the echo that outlasts the sound:

"Silence was more beautiful than music, for the echo was more beautiful than the sound... Sound was life, echo of echo."

The sacred is the echo. The echo is immanent; it exists in the same physical space as the sound, it is made of the same air, it is the sound continuing into its own absence. This is not transcendence upward and out. This is transcendence deeper in.

His investments in the unreachable (sunken galleys, drowned moons, lost empires) are acts of immanent devotion. He worships what is here, beneath the water, beneath the ground, in the sediment. The czar's iron bell, Kolokol, that might ring in Moscow; this is not a fantasy of escape. It is an investment in the sacred possibility latent within the ordinary impossible.

Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

Pillar note: Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

"He was not omniscient—no heron's blue eye floated out of his forehead—or if so, his vision was in another sphere."

Mr. Spitzer is constituted by what was deposited before he arrived. His patrimony comes from sunken ships. His house was built according to plans that preceded his occupation of it. His musical ambition begins where Beethoven and others ended. He carries his brother's comb on the opposite side of his body: a structural symmetry he did not choose, only discovered.

And he is constituting the ground others will stand on, though he cannot know it. His music, unwritten, is still a presence in the culture, the tenth symphony that defines what has not yet been done. His empty scrolls are the negative space that shapes what comes after.

"He had gone on when he could not go on—that was the great thing, really, in Mr. Spitzer's life."

This is the crossing point's obligation stated plainly. The carrying continues not because it is chosen but because it is structural. Mr. Spitzer did not choose to be Peron's keeper, his alibi, his financial backstop, his mourner. He did not choose to be the survivor. The obligation was deposited in him by the fact of being a twin, by the accident of outliving, by the architecture of the house that divided space into two equal hemispheres neither brother could fully occupy alone.

The ancestors are in the sediment. The sunken ships are the patrimony. The carrying continues.
wheel-chapter-08:
Chapter 8

← Chapter 7 · Wheel and Spokes Home · Chapter 9 →

Research notes: Chapter 8 · Reading guide: Guide, Chapter 8

Characters: Beatrice Fitzgerald · Homer Capehorn · Justice O’Leary · Madge Capehorn · Moses Hunnecker

Pillar 1 Not One Self

Pillar note: Pillar 1 Not One Self

The narrative voice is fundamentally unstable throughout. The "I" who narrates is never clearly located; we have the narrator, Madge, Homer, the bus-driver, and the implied consciousness of Beatrice Fitzgerald, all speaking in and through each other, none of them sovereign.

The narrator says explicitly:

"it was not myself who sank or my life which I remembered. It was another, another's ultimate face, cold and unchanging, those features I did not recognize"

This is not metaphor for confusion; it is a structural statement about selfhood. The drowning self cannot locate its own life because the self was never singular to begin with. The narrator is sinking, but into someone else's experience, which is also somehow their own.

Madge and Homer perform this plurality differently. Madge speaks with aggressive certainty about identity; she insists on being known, on leaving the light on so that he cannot say he did not know. But her certainty is itself a performance of anxiety about selfhood's instability. Homer, by contrast, moves fluidly between registers (laundry, royalty, baseball, the Navy, the bar sinister) as if identity is simply a matter of which story you are currently telling. Neither of them is one person. They are assemblages of social memory, desire, and narrative.

The bus-driver may be the most explicitly plural self in the chapter. His long monologue shifts without transition between first person grievance, biblical quotation, medical anxiety, political commentary, and cosmic complaint. He is not one speaker. He is a site where multiple voices converge and argue with each other, unable to resolve into a single position.

Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

Pillar note: Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

The chapter establishes from its opening paragraph that the landscape itself is constructed, provisional, dreamlike:

"the rain-filled hollow was lighted up only in that way in which one might see a realm of visionary hypothesis or uncertain speculation"

This is not the narrator saying the scene resembled hypothesis. It is saying that the mode of visibility is itself hypothetical: that what can be seen is already a construction of the light that reveals it.

The village at the end enacts this directly:

"A spectral village was gliding by, seeming a conspiracy of illusion and not of brick or stone or wood"

And the closing meditation confirms it:

"To come to a village at night may be never to know it with that clarity which one realizes if he comes to that same village in the beautiful sunlight of day"

But this is not a promise of a clearer daylight reality. The chapter does not offer the sunlit village as correction to the night village. The night vision, "Cyclops, men whose heads do grow beneath their shoulders, dead souls, unsoluble mystery", is not a distortion of a truer scene. It is a different construction. The "larger cave more carefully lit" is exactly what the village in daylight would be. The text refuses to grant either version priority.

The old woman Beatrice is perhaps the most concentrated site of this pillar. She exists simultaneously as: royal lineage (the Fitzgerald bar sinister), common prostitute, devoted laundress, abandoned mother, nearly blind woman in a flooded yard. None of these versions cancels the others. She is the sum of competing constructions, and the text refuses to adjudicate between them.

Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

Pillar note: Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

The opening passage establishes grief not as event but as atmosphere:

"Yet there was only this greyness as if we had by-passed, long ago, the spring of the year, and now the bus plowed on through darkness and whirling waters toward no known season or toward one season which should be all seasons."

One season which should be all seasons. This is grief as climate. Not the grief of a specific loss, but the grief of a world in which loss is the structural condition. Spring has not failed to arrive; it has been bypassed permanently. The bus is not traveling toward resolution. It is traveling through a permanent weather system.

The narrator's interior experience deepens this:

"my head was heavy with the grief unexpressed"

Unexpressed, not unresolved, not unprocessed, but unexpressed. The grief is not moving through stages. It is accumulating, pressing, finding no adequate language. The drowning metaphor that follows is not about dying; it is about the weight of accumulated grief pulling the self under while the self watches someone else's face in the water.

The bus-driver's monologue is grief's most extended expression in the chapter. His litany of the dead ("old Josh is dead, gone to join old Rudolph", "Where's Moses Hunnecker, the old bus-driver, now?", the baby thrown into the winter grass) is not eulogy. It is accumulation without resolution. He does not mourn any of them specifically. He catalogs them. Grief as permanent weather means you do not grieve each loss separately. You live inside the cumulative condition of loss.

Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

Pillar note: Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

The narrator's ethical position throughout is precisely that of the Witness: present, attentive, refusing to conclude.

"Three, five, ten minutes passing—who could tell, and where was I that I should hear these voices, see these faces?"

This question, where was I, is not disorientation. It is the Witness's honest acknowledgment of their own uncertain location. The Witness does not claim a stable vantage point. They stay in the room anyway.

The narrator does not intervene in the argument between Madge and Homer about Beatrice. They do not correct either version. They hold both. When the bus-driver delivers his sprawling, self-contradicting monologue, the narrator does not summarize or evaluate it. They transcribe it in its full incoherence, which is the act of witnessing.

The most concentrated instance is the description of Beatrice's flooded yard:

"A white chamber pot in the midst of the yellow flood, clumps of old rags, broom handles, twisted bedsprings, tin tubs, a soggy mattress laid upon the drumming waters, barrels, empty chicken crates, a broken rocking chair, wreckage."

This is a list. It does not interpret. It does not soften. It does not rush toward meaning. It sees fully, catalogs completely, and stops. The Witness stays in the room with the wreckage.

Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

Pillar note: Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

The journey itself is recursive. The bus is traveling toward a village the narrator has already dreamed of:

"that obscure village I had dreamed of, the beautiful life toward which I had travelled, that land of promise through eternity"

The narrator is not discovering the village. They are returning to a construction they have already made, now testing it against the actual arrival. And the actual arrival is the spectral, coffin-like row of houses, which both is and is not the dreamed village. The building is never finished. The dream and the reality are both provisional.

The bus-driver's monologue is structurally recursive; he circles back repeatedly to old Doc, to the question of mortality, to the question of who killed whom, each time with slightly different emphasis, never arriving at a conclusion. He is building an argument that keeps returning to its own beginning:

You "understand, old Doc would be all right if the world was."

This is the recursive builder's honest statement. The construction would work if the conditions were different. But the conditions are what they are, and so you return to the beginning and try again.

Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

Pillar note: Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

The chapter's syntax enacts this pillar before the content does. Young's sentences accumulate, extend, qualify, and refuse to close. Consider:

"there where the trees would blossom and where no flower would fade, there where the children would dance, where the young would not grow old, where the old would never die, for time should cease."

This is not a sentence that arrives. It is a sentence that continues arriving, each clause adding another layer of the impossible promise, never landing because the promised land is itself a construction that cannot be completed.

The bus-driver's monologue is the most sustained performance of ethical incompletion. He never finishes a thought. He interrupts himself with questions, qualifications, biblical passages, sudden shifts of subject. This is not stylistic disorder; it is the honest form of a mind that refuses to conclude prematurely:

"You understand, he means well. It kind of makes your heart give to see a doctor going like that."

The bus-driver has been savaging old Doc for pages. Then suddenly: it kind of makes your heart give. He does not resolve the contradiction. He holds it. The incomplete ethical position, neither pure condemnation nor pure sympathy, is the honest one.

The story of Beatrice is never concluded. We never know what the bus-driver does inside. We never know whose son young Doc really is. We never know what happened to Josh. The text does not withhold these conclusions as a narrative device. It withholds them because conclusion would be violence against the experience; it would falsify the irreducible complexity of these lives.

Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Pillar note: Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Beatrice Fitzgerald is the chapter's central marginal figure, and she is handled with the full weight this pillar demands.

She exists at every edge simultaneously: the edge of visibility (nearly blind, turns out the light), the edge of respectability (laundress or prostitute, depending on who is speaking), the edge of genealogy (royal blood or bastard line, but crucially, Homer points out these are the same thing: "It's the bar sinister. It's the bastard line"), the edge of the living (in a flooded yard that looks like the end of the world, yet someone had survived).

Homer's instinct toward her is the ontologically correct one:

"She's clean. She brings my mother's laundry... In winter, she pulls the clean clothes in a wicker basket on a little red sled over the snow... Her face turns blue. They say she's royal, that there's blue blood in her."

The blue face and the blue blood are the same blue. The marginal person does not become visible by being brought to the center. They are the evidence that the center's categories are constructed. Beatrice's one eye (lost to a child's arrow, accepted "as if it were a hailstone that fell out of a cloud") is the mark of the marginal person's relationship to violence: absorbed, unnamed, not made into narrative.

The graveyard at the crossroads is itself a marginal space; neither the village nor the open road, neither the living nor the dead, the place where the road divides. The bus stops here, at the margin, before it can reach either destination.

Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

Pillar note: Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

The chapter's geological metaphor appears in its very first paragraph:

"here to where the cape of the glacier had reached, inching like a crystal sea, leaving, when it had passed, this rich soil which was to be populated by wild swans and wild geese, wild herons and cranes and kingfishers and chimney swallows, horny-tongued woodpeckers and marsh butterflies."

The glacier is gone, but it is beneath everything: the soil itself is the glacier's deposit. The living world (swans, geese, butterflies) stands on the sediment of what passed. This is not metaphor for the chapter's concerns. It is the chapter's structural principle stated directly at the outset.

The tombstones at the graveyard:

"Stonecipher, Longtree, Thistlewaite, Chesterfield, Dalton, Grebe, Thomas, Whitehill, and there were other names in the darkness and names effaced by erosion"

The names effaced by erosion are still there. They are not gone; they are illegible, which is different. The past does not recede. It becomes harder to read. It is still pressing up.

The bus-driver's litany of the dead performs this directly. He does not say old Josh used to live here. He says old Josh is dead, gone to join old Rudolph, as if the dead are somewhere specific, a location you can join. The dead accumulate in a place. They are not behind us. They are below us.

Homer's memory of Beatrice pulling the red sled is sedimentary; it is a layer deposited in childhood that is now pressing up through the present argument. The sled belongs to the son who went to sea. The son belongs to old Doc who doesn't know he's a father. Old Doc belongs to the influenza epidemic and the Armistice. Each layer presses on the one above it.

Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

Pillar note: Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

The bus-driver's monologue is the chapter's most extended meditation on language as construction, though it does not announce itself as such. He speaks in a torrent of idioms, biblical quotation, medical terminology, folk sayings, and sudden neologisms, and the effect is to make visible that none of these registers is neutral:

"Plaster, he says, plaster, plaster! What's that, vulnerability? What's that, a key and lock hospital? What's that, a bird mason?"

He is not confused. He is exposing the constructed nature of medical language by placing it next to its own absurdity. A key and lock hospital is not nonsense; it is the literal content of the metaphor plaster when you refuse to let the metaphor pass as transparent.

The biblical passage about Leviathan is placed in the bus-driver's mouth without introduction or attribution. It arrives as his language, which makes it strange; this ancient, formal, cosmological language suddenly speaking from a fat bus-driver on a flooded road. The juxtaposition makes visible that the biblical register is also a construction, also a location, also a somewhere-in-particular pretending to speak from nowhere.

Homer's explanation of the Fitzgerald name is a small masterpiece of language-as-construction:

"Everything that begins with Fitz is royal in this country. Fitzwater, Fitzsimmon, Fitzhugh, Fitzpatrick, Fitzgerald. I don't care what it is, just so it is Fitz. That was because of some woman that was never married to some old king but had a child by him. It's the bar sinister. It's the bastard line."

The prefix Fitz, which means son of in Norman French, carries inside it the entire history of illegitimacy normalized into aristocracy. The language itself contains the sedimented power structure. Homer names this without fully knowing he has named it. Language speaks from somewhere even when the speaker doesn't know where.

Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

Pillar note: Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

The chapter opens with a vision of the promised land, "that land of promise through eternity, there where the trees would blossom and where no flower would fade", and then immediately places the bus in a flooded yard full of wreckage. This is not irony. It is the chapter's central theological move: the sacred does not live in the promised land. It lives in the flooded yard.

The bus-driver's question:

"Was I not made,’ the bus-driver asked, ‘as man in all his glory to rule over the peacocks and the pelicans and the polar bears and the whole benighted universe?"

This is a genuine theological question asked by a fat man with rolling hips who has just come back from visiting a nearly blind woman in a house weighted down with stovepipe chimneys. The grandeur of the question is not diminished by its speaker. It is located by its speaker. The sacred is here, in this man, asking this question, on this road.

The closing vision of the village:

"old, amorphous shapes like those which creep through mist and fog, Cyclops, men whose heads do grow beneath their shoulders, dead souls, unsoluble mystery, that fleeting image, that dream within the dream"

This is not a failure of transcendence. This is where transcendence actually lives, in the unsoluble mystery, the dream within the dream, the village that is and is not what was promised. The grey bus, the permanent flood, the one-eyed woman, the dead men joining each other underground: this is the sacred in its actual location.

Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

Pillar note: Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

The narrator's drowning meditation is the most direct statement of this pillar in the chapter:

"I was sinking for the first, the second, the third time, though yet it was not myself who sank or my life which I remembered. It was another, another's ultimate face, cold and unchanging, those features I did not recognize, that face pillowed upon the oozy tides of time."

The narrator is where time crosses itself. They are sinking through someone else's life, remembering what they did not witness, constituted by what was deposited before they arrived. The face they see in the water is not their own; it is the face of what came before, pressing up through the sediment.

The Fitzgerald genealogy is a perfect structural image of the Crossing Point. Beatrice is the deposit of an unnamed king's illegitimate line. Her son is the deposit of old Doc's unknowing fatherhood. That son is now depositing postal cards from Gibraltar, Singapore, the China Sea: constituting the ground of Beatrice's continued existence, the proof that she was here, that she mattered, that the thread did not break.

The bus-driver says:

"But the thread never broke."

This is the Crossing Point's essential statement. The thread running from the glacier's deposit through the tombstone names through Beatrice's red sled through the son's Navy uniform through the postal cards; this thread is not chosen. It is structural. The carrying continues whether or not anyone decides to carry.

The closing image of the village, "a tall, humped man disappearing into the shadows", is the Crossing Point made visible: someone constituted by everything that preceded them, constituting the ground for what comes next, disappearing into the dark that is not absence but the next layer of sediment.

Chapter 65

← Chapter 64 · Wheel and Spokes Home · Chapter 66 →

Research notes: Chapter 65 · Reading guide: Guide, Chapter 65

Characters: John Knox MacIntosh · Lorena · Mercy MacIntosh · Miss MacIntosh · Mr. Titus Bonebreaker

Pillar 1 Not One Self

Pillar note: Pillar 1 Not One Self

"Yet one revelation seemed to lead to another — and Miss MacIntosh, little by little, seemed to take on many moods and many dimensions such as, in the previously well-ordered days of almost meaningless years, I had hardly guessed."

Miss MacIntosh is not one person. She is simultaneously:

  • The stern, practical nurse of the "previously well-ordered days"
  • The bald, wounded woman revealed in September's dying light
  • The young hopeful in black gloves walking Chicago's rain-soaked streets
  • The pin-setter in the bowling alley, staggering after surgery
  • The soprano singing Love Lifted Me to the blind
  • The would-be bride who was never a bride
  • The woman who walked into the ocean

None of these selves cancels the others. They are simultaneous and irresolvable, layered rather than sequential. The narrator's growing awareness of Miss MacIntosh's multiplicity is itself the chapter's central drama, not any external event, but the collapse of the illusion that a person is singular and legible.

The narrator explicitly names this: Miss MacIntosh becomes "a storm center of mirages", "perhaps being nothing in herself" while simultaneously being "a mirror to the dreams of others." The plural self is not a psychological curiosity here; it is the ontological condition of every person in the novel, made visible through Miss MacIntosh's stripped-bare literalness.

Mr. Bonebreaker, too, is plural in ways he cannot acknowledge: the failed royalty claimant, the Gospel salesman, the shoe-store clerk, the man who sleeps with his umbrella, the man who cracked heads in saloons, the man who ran from a bald woman into the hailstones. He is constituted by his contradictions: eating eggs while refusing meat, preaching the end of time while consulting a punctual watch, proposing marriage while perpetually deferring it. He cannot hold his own multiplicity, and this failure is precisely what destroys him as a moral actor in Miss MacIntosh's life.

Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

Pillar note: Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

This pillar runs through the chapter as its deepest structural principle.

"Perhaps she would be a mirror held up to a mirror when all images faded, when there was neither moon nor sun nor star nor cloud."

Young does not offer us a "real" Miss MacIntosh beneath the wigs. The wigs are not concealment of a true self; they are themselves constitutive. The black wig worn in memory of Lorena. The red wig worn in memory of Richard. The ashen wig worn at Niagara Falls in the attempt to remake herself entirely. Each wig is a constructed reality, and each is as real as any other. The bald head beneath is not more true; it is simply another layer, equally constructed, equally contingent.

The chapter's most philosophically charged moment on this point is the Niagara Falls passage:

"She changed from the dark to the fair... she was the changed person, wearing an ashen wig, for it was her decision to put the past entirely behind her."

This is not self-deception presented as failure. Young presents it with a kind of solemn respect. The construction of a new self through a new wig is not less real than the bald self it covers. The line between illusion and reality is, as the Pillar states, itself a construction.

Mr. Bonebreaker's entire existence dramatizes Pillar 2 from the other direction. He builds an elaborate reality (the imminent end of the world, his claim to the Swedish throne, Miss MacIntosh as a beautiful woman with flowing hair) and inhabits it with total conviction. His reality is more coherent than most, precisely because he has constructed it so completely. When the construction fails (the moment Miss MacIntosh removes her wig), he cannot integrate the new information. He runs. The cave he built was carefully lit, but it was still a cave, and he could not survive a larger one.

Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

Pillar note: Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

"My poor darling. When she was young and hopeful, she had scrupulously mended those black gloves for a sad occasion which she could not foresee."

This is the chapter's emotional center, and it is a perfect enactment of grief as climate rather than event. The grief does not arrive with Mr. Bonebreaker's flight. It was already present in the loss of the breast, in the childhood in What Cheer, in the brother Richard lost among the head-hunters. It accumulates across the chapter in layers: the pink envelope burned in the fireplace, the black gloves mended with white thread, the watch worn over the missing breast.

The chapter's most devastating grief-as-weather passage:

"Those black gloves she mended so patiently, with such great, ominous care, awkward but graceful, white thread zigzagging on black, were those very black gloves she must have worn when, with her head shining, bald as a lost planet, with her hands crossed over two major wounds, the breast, the side, she walked into the roaring ocean on a cold September morning."

The reader knows the end before the story arrives there. The grief is proleptic; it reaches backward from the ocean into every scene of mending, every patient domestic act. The gloves she mends for a future she cannot foresee are the gloves she wears to her death. This is grief as permanent weather in its most precise form: the loss was always already happening, and the honest life, Miss MacIntosh's life, did not pretend otherwise, even when it could not name what it knew.

The chapter refuses the stages of grief entirely. Miss MacIntosh does not move from wound to healing to acceptance. She moves from wound to work to ocean. The grief does not resolve. It accumulates until it becomes the sea itself.

Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

Pillar note: Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

The narrator (young, naive, hopeful by her own admission) is positioned throughout as witness:

"I felt as if it were I who was far away from reality now, not she, and might I never return to reality if this was what I found in recompense for all that had been lost."

The narrator's function in this chapter is not to intervene, explain, or resolve. She bends over Miss MacIntosh's bald head and sees prisms and flames. She listens to the history of Mr. Bonebreaker without flinching. She observes the gradual dissolution of Miss MacIntosh's person (the increasing informality, the wig removed, the breast exposed) without rushing toward conclusion.

"It seemed to me that all people might love her if they saw her as I saw her now in her essential loneliness and mystery stripped bare of all pretense."

This is the witness's credo. The narrator does not try to save Miss MacIntosh. She does not argue against the ocean. She stays in the room, attends fully, and refuses to simplify. The chapter's extraordinary length, its refusal to compress or summarize, is itself the act of witnessing. Young's prose enacts Pillar 4 formally: the refusal to rush toward resolution is built into the syntax, which spirals and recurses rather than proceeding.

The narrator's admission that she "scarcely listened to these sad prophecies of mortal woe" is not a failure of witnessing; it is its honest acknowledgment. The witness is not omniscient. She is present, imperfect, and continuing.

Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

Pillar note: Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

The chapter is structured recursively. Miss MacIntosh's history is not told linearly but returned to, circled, approached from different angles. The Chicago story is begun, interrupted, resumed. The Mr. Bonebreaker narrative loops back to What Cheer, forward to Buffalo, back to Chicago, forward to Niagara Falls, back to the blind musician, forward to the ocean.

"She had made her plans. As Mrs. Titus Bonebreaker, she had planned, she would be able to hold up her head among the women of What Cheer."

The plan is built knowing it will not be completed. Miss MacIntosh buys the mutilated crockery for the mission. She finds the abandoned poultry store. She imagines the hens and the rooster. She builds anyway. The building is never finished, Mr. Bonebreaker runs, but the building was not therefore meaningless. The crockery was purchased. The plans were real. The provisional construction is the only construction available, and Miss MacIntosh, for all her practicality, understands this.

The watch given as an engagement seal, worn for decades over the missing breast, is the most precise emblem of Pillar 5 in the chapter. It is the artifact of an unfinished building, carried forward into a life that continued being built anyway:

"Which for many, many years she had worn on her dress over the breastbone where the breast was missing — as if to equalize the unequal body."

She returns to the beginning with what she learned. The watch keeps time over the wound. The building continues.

Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

Pillar note: Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

Mr. Bonebreaker's marriage is "continually postponed", and this postponement is presented not as his failure of commitment but as a structural feature of his entire relationship to reality. He cannot complete because completion would require confronting what is actually there. His theology of the world's imminent end is itself a theology of incompletion elevated to cosmic principle: the world will end before anything needs to be finished.

Miss MacIntosh's life, by contrast, embodies incompletion as integrity. She never finishes the mission. She never marries. She never resolves her relationship to Mr. Bonebreaker, to her baldness, to her lost breast. But she mends the gloves. She darns the black cotton gloves. She sews on the seed pearl button. These are ongoing sentences, not concluded ones.

"God forgive me for this present vanity... and yet may I not hope what every woman hopes? There is surely a man somewhere in every woman's life."

This is incompletion at its most ethically precise. She sews on the button. She hopes. She knows the hope is probably futile. She sews on the button anyway. Unfinished Is Honest does not demand resolution; it demands the ongoing act, which is itself the integrity.

The chapter's own form embodies Pillar 6. It does not conclude. Miss MacIntosh walks into the ocean, but the prose does not treat this as resolution:

"The sun and the moon shone in the same pearly sky when she walked into the ocean. There was no direct light but only a diffusion of blowing light... At last, however, she was given to something."

"At last, however, she was given to something." This is not the language of completion. It is the language of a process that continues in a different register. The unfinished life does not become finished by ending.

Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Pillar note: Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Miss MacIntosh is the chapter's central evidence for this Pillar, and she is designed to be.

She is bald in a world where hair signifies femininity, desirability, and social legibility. She has one breast in a world that counts women by their bodies. She is unmarried by circumstance rather than choice. She is from What Cheer, Iowa: a place whose very name is ironic, whose horizons are "limited", where "seeing was believing" and Mr. Bonebreaker would have to be seen to be believed.

"She was born with some deficiencies, and she had acquired others, being mortal."

This sentence is devastating in its precision. The deficiencies are both congenital and accumulated. She is marginal by birth and by experience. And it is precisely this marginality that makes her the evidence: the place where the constructed nature of beauty, femininity, normalcy, and salvation becomes most visible.

Mr. Bonebreaker's Biblical quotations about baldness are the chapter's darkest irony: "Instead of well-set hair, there would be a baldness". He preaches baldness as apocalyptic punishment to a woman who is already bald, without knowing it. The marginal person is present in the center of the discourse that defines her as marginal, and the discourse cannot see her.

The blind musician passage extends this:

"She was born without her hair as they without their eyes, that she was a type of beauty which was vanquished before time began."

"A type of beauty which was vanquished before time began." This is Pillar 7 at its most philosophically acute. The marginal is not the exception to beauty; it is the evidence of beauty's constructed and violent nature. Miss MacIntosh's baldness is not a deviation from a norm. It is the norm's exposure.

Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

Pillar note: Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

The chapter's temporal structure is explicitly sedimentary. The past does not recede. It presses upward through everything.

The watch worn over the missing breast for "many, many years" is sedimentary time made wearable. The black umbrella: plucked by Mr. Bonebreaker from a dead man, left behind in his flight, carried by Miss MacIntosh for the rest of her life, turned inside out on the beach at her death: is an object that accumulates time in layers: the dead man's time, Mr. Bonebreaker's time, Miss MacIntosh's time, the ocean's time.

"Old church bells rang in memory, after all, like bells under water. She heard them."

This is Pillar 8 in its most lyrical form. The What Cheer childhood does not recede when Miss MacIntosh stands in the rain in Chicago listening to Mr. Bonebreaker. It rises. The bells ring from below. The past is beneath her, still pressing.

The chapter's narrative structure enacts this formally. The narrator moves between Miss MacIntosh's present dying and her past Chicago, not as flashback but as simultaneous layers. The bald woman mending gloves by the hurricane lamp and the young woman in the black wig staggering after surgery are not separated by time in the prose; they press against each other, the past beneath the present, still active.

"Perhaps the doctor knew. She had already gone back to her work in the bowling alley where, every evening, it was her duty to set ninepins up as the balls knocked against them and caused them to fall."

The ninepins fall and are set up again. This is sedimentary time as labor: the past is always falling, and the work is always setting it back up. The bowling alley is not merely a job. It is a cosmological image of how time works in this chapter.

Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

Pillar note: Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

Young's prose is the most direct enactment of Pillar 9 in the chapter. The language does not report reality; it constructs it in the act of speaking, and it names its own constructedness.

Mr. Bonebreaker speaks almost entirely in Biblical quotation, and the chapter is acutely aware of what this means:

"He spoke words more than necessary, as if he were in love with the sound of his rushing voice."

His language does not describe the world; it replaces it. He cannot see Miss MacIntosh's face because his language has already constructed a face for her: "her hair was as a flock of wild goats... her neck was a tower of ivory... her eyelids were the eyelids of morning". The Biblical language shapes what can be seen. It makes Miss MacIntosh invisible by making her too visible in the wrong register.

The narrator's language, by contrast, is explicitly self-aware of its own location:

"Perhaps I was confused now by my dreams of her even before she should leave me."

The narrator names her own constructedness as witness. She does not speak from nowhere. She speaks from the position of a young, naive, hopeful girl who is already dreaming the person she is trying to see. This is honest language in the Pillar 9 sense: it names its own location rather than pretending to neutrality.

The chapter's most formally interesting moment of language-as-construction is the Chamber of Commerce pamphlets mixed in with the Bible literature:

"See Chicago and live — for he had mixed up with his Bible literature some pamphlets of the Chamber of Commerce, and the messages were not the same."

They are not the same, but they are both constructions, both languages that shape what can be seen, both speaking from somewhere in particular. The juxtaposition is comic and devastating simultaneously. Language that promises salvation and language that promises new skyscrapers are both, in Young's hands, constructions that cannot deliver their goods.

Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

Pillar note: Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

The sacred in this chapter is entirely immanent. It lives in the ordinary objects, the domestic acts, the grey and salt-stained particulars of Miss MacIntosh's existence.

"She hemmed an old grey skirt, patched an old coat with many-colored patches, sewed on bone buttons, darned her long-fingered black cotton gloves."

This is the chapter's liturgy. The hemming and patching and darning are sacred acts, not because they point toward a beyond, but because they are fully present in the immanent world, performed with attention and care in the face of approaching death. The sacred here is the act of mending what will not last, of preparing for a winter that will not come, of sewing a seed pearl button onto gloves that will be worn into the ocean.

Miss MacIntosh's baldness is immanent transcendence made literal:

"Sometimes I saw a prism or a flame reflected there or a flame which seemed to gleam under her bald dome and sometimes the reflection of an eye gleaming as if at the world's top."

The sacred is visible in the bald head, not beyond it, not above it, but in it, as light in a physical surface. The narrator bends over the dome and sees the world reflected there. This is the sacred as depth within the immanent, not height above it.

Mr. Bonebreaker's religion, by contrast, is the chapter's counter-example: a transcendence that points entirely outward and upward, toward heavenly crowns and ivory gates and angels on cherubim. His God is always somewhere else, in the beginning, at the end, in the sky over Chicago. He cannot see the sacred in Miss MacIntosh's face because he is looking in the wrong direction.

The ocean into which Miss MacIntosh walks is the chapter's final image of immanent transcendence:

"At last, however, she was given to something."

Not to heaven. Not to God. To the ocean, which is here, which is immanent, which is the same water that ran under the frozen lake in Chicago, the same water that fell as rain around Mr. Bonebreaker's umbrella, the same water that is the first and last element of this world. The transcendence is entirely within the immanent. She is given to something that was always already here.

Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

Pillar note: Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

This is the Pillar that the chapter's final pages most directly enact, and it is where the analysis must end.

"I felt as if it were I who was far away from reality now, not she, and might I never return to reality if this was what I found in recompense for all that had been lost, this more beautiful than life or death, this which was death in the heart of life or life in the heart of death."

The narrator is constituted by Miss MacIntosh. She is where Miss MacIntosh's life crosses into the life of the next generation. She carries the watch, the umbrella, the history of Mr. Bonebreaker, the image of the bald head with its prisms and flames. She is the ground on which Miss MacIntosh's life continues to press upward.

The chapter's most explicit statement of Pillar 11:

"Her death might seem more difficult to her than her life had been, certainly... and perhaps in some ways she had already done so as I scarcely realized then, being young, naive, hopeful, and hopeful most when there was no reason for hope."

The narrator will carry Miss MacIntosh forward. The obligation is not chosen; it is structural. Miss MacIntosh deposited herself in the narrator's sediment before the narrator understood what was being deposited.

And Miss MacIntosh herself is a crossing point in the same sense. She carries What Cheer, Iowa, and John Knox MacIntosh, and Mercy MacIntosh who knew how to cut the umbilical cord in the snow, and the bald generations of dour Scots, and Mr. Bonebreaker's watch with his grandmother's snow-colored hair in the back compartment. She is constituted by what was deposited before she arrived. She carries the ancestors in her sediment. She walks into the ocean carrying all of it.

"The sun and the moon shone in the same pearly sky when she walked into the ocean. There was no direct light but only a diffusion of blowing light. There was no division between the turbulent water and the wild, wet sky."

No division. This is the Crossing Point as image: the place where the boundaries dissolve, where the self that was deposited and the self that will deposit meet in a single undivided light. The ancestors are in the sediment. The carrying continues. Miss MacIntosh walks into the water that was always already her element, and the narrator remains on the shore, carrying what was given.

Chapter 67

← Chapter 66 · Wheel and Spokes Home · Chapter 68 →

Research notes: Chapter 67 · Reading guide: Guide, Chapter 67

Characters: Justice O’Leary

Pillar 1 Not One Self

Pillar note: Pillar 1 Not One Self

The narrator observes that "probably half the conversation in America occurs in this manner": meaning addressed to someone who cannot hear, someone absent, someone who exists only in the speaker's interior. The bus-driver is not one person having one conversation. He is simultaneously:

  • A working man trying to park a bus
  • A grieving interlocutor addressing an absent friend
  • A moralist delivering judgment on life and death
  • A singer, a cursing man, a weeping man

The passengers mirror this plurality. The football player dreams "of a bride his wife might never know"; he is literally two selves, the married man and the man who dreams elsewhere. The pregnant girl laughs at misery she says is "nothing new to her", which means she carries a prior self who has already metabolized this scene. The narrator, exhausted, notes their heads "zooming with stars and flies and memories of distant places": the self dispersed across geography and time simultaneously.

Not One Self here is not a psychological observation. It is the structural condition of everyone in the bus. No one is singular. No one is present in only one sense.

Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

Pillar note: Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

The chapter's central formal device is the invisible automobile. The bus-driver wages a full, passionate, detailed argument with "an old Ford with black canvas curtains flapping" that is "invisible to me but not to the bus-driver". The narrator cannot see it. We cannot see it. The bus-driver sees it completely.

The chapter refuses to resolve this. It does not tell us the bus-driver is simply drunk and wrong. It does not confirm the car exists. The narrator notes: "Or did I merely dream of this?", implicating their own perception as equally constructed.

This is the Pillar in its most radical form: there is no sunlit world outside the cave. The bus-driver's reality and the narrator's reality are both constructions. The hearse is real. The milk truck is real. The invisible Ford may or may not be real. The chapter offers no arbiter. Reality is what is made, and different people in the same space are making different realities simultaneously.

The girl's image of the crazy house with mirrored walls is the chapter's own gloss on this pillar:

"The walls, when you got inside, were all glass, lined with mirrors like the floor and ceiling. You felt along the glass, but you did not know how to get out, which mirror was a door."

There is no exit to an unmediated real. There is only the ongoing negotiation with constructed surfaces.

Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

Pillar note: Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

The bus-driver's monologue is not simply comic. Beneath its absurdist surface runs a sustained lament. He grieves for:

  • Old Doc, who brought children into the world "when they had never had parents"
  • The rabbit-faced girlfriends whose "rabbit's womb never burst": lives unlived, pregnancies that never were
  • The one-horse shay that "ain't what she used to was": the decay of things once vital
  • The buzzards returning to Rush Creek at sundown, "the great grandfather of them all": death as cyclical, permanent, generational

The bus-driver does not move through grief toward resolution. He accumulates it. Each new complaint layers onto the last. He swings between cursing and singing, between threatening Doc and pledging to shed "every drop of his blood" for him. This is not the arc of mourning. This is grief as climate: the weather the bus-driver lives inside permanently. The pregnant girl's laughter is the same structure in a different register. She laughs at misery that is "nothing new to her". She is not beyond grief. She has learned to inhabit it. The laughter is not resolution. It is a form of permanent coexistence with loss.

Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

Pillar note: Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

The narrator's role in this chapter is almost entirely that of witness. They do not intervene, do not correct the bus-driver, do not get off the bus, do not explain the invisible car. They observe:

"I was the witness to a strange traffic problem."

This is a direct, almost programmatic statement of the Pillar. The narrator stays in the room. They are exhausted, "my head zooming with stars and flies", and yet they continue to attend. They notice the bus-driver's beard, his red spotted handkerchief, his voice buzzing "like some great bumble bee through the fog". They notice that "pretty soon, I was sure of it — a bird would fly out of the bus-driver's beard".

This last image is crucial. The narrator is not reporting facts. They are attending so fully that the surreal becomes visible. Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act in this Pillar is not a passive recorder. It is an active ethical stance: the refusal to simplify, the willingness to stay with the scene until its stranger truth emerges.

The narrator does not conclude what the bus-driver's monologue means. They do not diagnose him as drunk, delusional, or wise. They hold all possibilities simultaneously. That holding is the ethical act.

Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

Pillar note: Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

The bus-driver's argument is structurally recursive. He makes the same appeal to Doc repeatedly, each time with new evidence, new songs, new threats, new pledges of friendship, and each time he returns to the beginning:

"Move over, Doc." "Move your old ghost buggy out of here, Doc." "So move over, Doc, will yuh." "Be a good Boy Scout, Doc, and move over."

He builds the argument, it fails, he returns to the beginning with what he has learned (nothing, or everything), and builds again. The bus never parks. The building is never finished. This is not presented as failure: the chapter does not end with the bus successfully parked. It ends mid-sentence, mid-thought, mid-dream.

The narrator's own journey enacts this. They have "walked the streets of New York until my shoe soles were as thin as paper" (they have been building something, a life, a presence in the city) and now they are returning, on a bus, to a home that is "no home". They are back at the beginning. With worn soles. Ready to build again.

Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

Pillar note: Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

The chapter does not end. It stops. The boy is "still yawning". The bus has not parked. Old Doc has not moved. The narrator has not arrived anywhere. Jackie, whoever she is, has gone through "which door" nobody knows.

The demand for completion (for the bus to park, for the argument to resolve, for the passengers to disembark and begin their lives) is never met. And the chapter implicitly argues that this is honest. The concluded sentence would be a lie. The ongoing sentence, "The boy was still yawning", is the truth.

The girl's crazy house image reinforces this. You cannot find the door. The mirror that is a door looks like all the other mirrors. The staircase becomes a clothes chute. There is no completion available. Unfinished Is Honest here is not a resigned shrug. It is the chapter's formal argument: enacted in its own refusal to conclude.

Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Pillar note: Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Every figure in this chapter is marginal:

  • The pregnant girl with a bird on her hat: unmarried, it is implied, or at least displaced, traveling alone at night, arriving at no home
  • The football player dreaming of a woman who is not his wife
  • The narrator who has worn their shoe soles to paper walking a city of "paper dolls"
  • Old Doc: the grizzled country doctor who brought children into the world "when they had never had parents", now apparently dead or dying, his ghost buggy taking up space in a world that wants him to move
  • The bus-driver himself: long-haired, bearded, talking to invisible men, drinking from a bottle through Indiana night

These are not the people at the center of American life in the mid-twentieth century. They are the edges. And at the edges, the constructed nature of reality becomes most visible. The center of society tells a story of arrival, completion, home, family, resolution. These marginal figures reveal that the story is a construction. Nobody is arriving. Nobody has a home. Nobody's womb burst. The rabbit's womb never burst. The categories (home, family, life, death) are visible here as the fictions they are.

Old Doc himself is the most powerful instance. He brought life into the world. Now he is a ghost. The children he delivered shot at him with bean-shooters. The marginal figure who made the center possible is now an obstacle to be cursed and moved. His marginality is not incidental. It is evidence of how the center constructs itself by forgetting its origins.

Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

Pillar note: Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

The bus-driver's monologue is a geological cross-section of time. In a single speech he moves through:

  • The rabbit tests of past girlfriends
  • Old Doc's history of delivering children
  • The one-horse shay as emblem of a vanished era
  • The buzzards returning to Rush Creek: a cyclical, generational time
  • "Sweet Mary O’Grady,’ he was singing again, ‘down by the old mill stream": a song from another era, another self

The past does not recede for the bus-driver. It presses upward. The dead girlfriends, the unborn children, the dead doctor who will not move his ghost buggy; they are all present, all simultaneously active, all still pressing on the steering wheel.

The narrator's own sediment is visible in their exhaustion: "memories of distant places", shoe soles worn thin by a city that turned out to be "one-dimensional". The layers are there. They press up through the fatigue.

The hearse sitting next to the bus is the chapter's most literal image of this pillar. The vehicle of death is parked next to the vehicle of ordinary transit. Past and present, death and life, are parked side by side, equally real, equally obstructing passage.

Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

Pillar note: Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

The bus-driver's language is the chapter's most elaborate demonstration of this Pillar. He constructs Old Doc entirely through language. Doc has "elongated, nerveless hands". His buggy has "black canvas curtains flapping". His passengers are "heathen Chinee", then "naked birds", then "pigs", then "bastards", then "luna moths". The description shifts constantly because language is not reporting Doc; it is building him, and the building is unstable.

The narrator is acutely aware of this. They note that the city of New York seemed "one-dimensional": a city of "paper dolls". The language that built New York as a destination, a place of arrival and possibility, turned out to be flat. The paper city was a paper construction.

The girl's crazy house is also a language-construction: she builds it in words as she speaks it, and it becomes real enough that the boy responds to it, "Jackie found the door", as if it were a shared reality. Language has made a space both of them now inhabit.

The chapter's own language is self-consciously constructed. The narrator uses traffic-sign language, "steep incline," "slow turn," "crumbling gravel," "bridge ahead", to describe the logic of human relationships and sleep. The language of roads is being used to map something roads cannot map. The construction is visible. The narrator is not pretending to speak from nowhere.

Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

Pillar note: Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

The sacred in this chapter lives entirely in the ordinary and the degraded:

  • The bus-driver's beard, through which his voice buzzes "like some great bumble bee through the fog": a figure almost Biblical in its strangeness, a prophet in a Greyhound
  • The pregnant girl with the bird upon her hat: the bird as emblem of spirit, perched on the most ordinary domestic accessory, riding a night bus through Indiana
  • Old Doc's ghost buggy, a vehicle with "no head lights, no steering wheel, no motor, no license plates", a vehicle that should not be able to exist and yet is, somehow, blocking the way
  • The buzzards coming in to roost at sundown near Rush Creek: death as "the great grandfather of them all", something ancient, cyclical, present

The bus-driver's song, "I can't give you anything but love, baby", is perhaps the chapter's most concentrated image of The Sacred Is Here. It is a cheap popular song. It is sung by a drunk man draped across a steering wheel. And it is, in this context, genuinely sacred: the only honest statement available, the irreducible thing that survives when everything else (the motor, the license plates, the steering wheel, the rabbit's womb) has failed or vanished.

The grey bus, stalled in the Indiana night, surrounded by a milk truck leaking "a milkish fluid" and a hearse with "tissue-colored eyes"; this is where the sacred lives. Not in a church. Not in a resolution. Here, in this careening, exhausted, impossible scene.

Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

Pillar note: Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

This is perhaps the Pillar most fully embodied by the chapter's structure.

The narrator is explicitly constituted by what was deposited before they arrived. They carry New York in their worn shoe soles. They carry "memories of distant places". They are returning to "no home", which means they are constituted by a home that no longer exists, or never existed as imagined.

The pregnant girl is the chapter's most literal Crossing Point. She carries the not-yet-born. She is the place where past and future cross. She is traveling at night, arriving at no home, laughing at misery that is nothing new to her, and she carries, under her bird-hatted head, a new life that will stand on ground she is constituting right now, in this bus, in this night.

Old Doc is the crossing point of generations. He brought children into the world who shot at him with bean-shooters. He is the sediment the living stand on, and they have forgotten this, and he will not move, and the bus-driver loves him and curses him in the same breath, because you cannot move the ground you stand on, even when it is inconvenient, even when it is dead.

The bus-driver's closing argument is the Pillar stated plainly:

"The generations of buzzards do go on, honest to God. You haven't a chance."

This is not nihilism. It is the structural truth of the Crossing Point. The generations go on. The carrying continues. You have not a chance to stop it, to step outside it, to be singular and self-originating. You are where time crosses itself. The obligation is not chosen. It is structural.

Chapter 33

Research notes: Chapter 33 · Reading guide: Guide, Chapter 33

Characters: Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer

Pillar 1 Not One Self

Pillar note: Pillar 1 Not One Self

The chapter refuses to stabilize any single identity. My mother is simultaneously alive and reported dead, simultaneously a "famous beauty" and a forgotten recluse, simultaneously a bride and someone who "had never been married". She is married to a camel, a church steeple, a key, a keyhole, the wind, a flame. These are not metaphors for a single hidden truth. They are competing, simultaneous, irresolvable versions of selfhood.

Mr. Spitzer himself is doubled: perpetually shadowed by his brother Peron, seen walking on Benevolent Street, whose debts Mr. Spitzer inherits, whose watch he squints at to "detect a moment's falsehood". He is never quite one person either; he is himself plus the negative space of his brother.

Even the narrator exists only as a grammatical position, "my mother", never named, never located, present only as a relational axis. The self here is not a substance. It is a set of relations that keep shifting.

"She would often say that she was the kind of woman who could love only the man she had never married, perhaps the man she had not known, had not seen."

The self is constituted by its absences, its negations, its uncompleted relations. This is Not One Self not as pathology but as ontological condition.

Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

Pillar note: Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

This pillar is perhaps the chapter's central philosophical axis. Mr. Spitzer explicitly theorizes it:

"her conscious states were probably like the unconscious states of other people"

He does not say she is more deluded than others. He says the lamp-lighters, the factory workers at their time-clocks and wheels: they too can live only while they dream. They too were never quite awake. The opium is not the cause of unreality. It is merely the visible mechanism of a universal condition.

The Boston newspaper's error, reporting my mother as dead, is not treated as a simple mistake to correct. Mr. Spitzer reflects that "this Boston newspaper, though noted for its errors, would probably be right, having merely mistaken the time". The distinction between true and false collapses into a distinction between premature and eventual. The lie will become true. The truth was always provisional.

The wedding itself, that foundational event, dissolves under scrutiny: "her powers of ratiocination were not good", she cannot reconstruct it, she may have been married to Death, she cannot confirm the bridegroom's identity. There is no sunlit world outside the cave. The wedding, like all originary events, exists only as sedimented impression, partially retrieved, partially invented.

Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

Pillar note: Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

The chapter is saturated with grief, but it never moves. It does not arc toward resolution. It accumulates.

Mr. Spitzer carries "this diffused sense of woe, this sorrow which seemed to have no source in his own life". This is the precise phenomenology of grief as permanent weather: it is not attached to a specific loss, not traceable to an event, not curable by understanding its origin. It is climate. He inherited it, or it preceded him, or it is simply what it is to be a conscious being in this world.

My mother's grief is equally sourceless and total. She grieves the social seasons that never were, the garden parties attended by no one, the yacht meets with kings in canvas shrouds. She grieves not what she had and lost, but what was never recognized while it existed. This is grief without even the consolation of having been real.

The wedding music is described as "a vast overture which was never quite completed, an eternal prelude to nothing". Grief here is not the aftermath of something. It is the condition of living in a world where completion never arrives.

Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

Pillar note: Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

Mr. Spitzer is the chapter's primary ethical figure, and his ethics are precisely those of the Witness. He does not fix. He does not conclude. He stays in the room.

He chooses not to correct the newspaper's error about my mother's death. He chooses not to correct her wedding memories. He chooses not to intervene in her opium-sustained illusions. This is not passivity born of indifference; it is a principled refusal to simplify, a recognition that correction would be its own violence:

"What should she do with accuracy, and why should it confine her? Who was he to correct these surface impressions or differentiate between black and white, green and yellow and red? Who was he to say that a thing was different from what it seemed? How would he know?"

His witnessing extends to the physical: when my mother speaks to a human-sized blackbird and says to open the door, Mr. Spitzer gets up and opens the door. He does not argue. He does not diagnose. He acts within her reality. This is attention as practice, taken to its logical conclusion; he enters the world as she perceives it rather than demanding she enter his.

Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

Pillar note: Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

Mr. Spitzer's harp music is the chapter's clearest emblem of recursive construction:

"he was writing harp music which should be the exact imitation of the wind playing through the strings and cables of a bridge... and his music should be finished only with the dying wind"

The composition can only be completed by something outside itself, the wind's death, which means it is structurally unfinishable. He returns to it, measures it, studies "the velocity of wind over bridges, the tonnage of wind pressure against cables", accumulating data toward a work that recedes as he approaches. He builds anyway. The building is never finished. That is not failure. That is how it works.

Similarly, my mother recursively reconstructs her wedding: returning to it, finding different details each time, arriving at different bridegrooms. The reconstruction is the event. There is no original beneath the reconstructions to recover.

Mr. Spitzer also mails himself a letter he never receives: a perfect image of recursive construction: the self attempting to communicate with itself across time, the message marked with the sender's own return address, containing blank paper. The content is nothing. The act of sending and waiting is everything.

Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

Pillar note: Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

The chapter is formally and thematically committed to incompletion. Sentences extend across pages. The wedding is never reconstructed. The music is never finished. The letter is never delivered. The dead letter office holds the message indefinitely.

Mr. Spitzer explicitly defends incompletion as the honest condition:

"there were many more important errors to rectify"

meaning: the completed correction of any single error would be a false closure that obscures the larger incompleteness of all knowledge. He allows things to take their course "for they ultimately would", not because he is resigned, but because he understands that forcing resolution is its own distortion.

My mother's memory is described as "always quite beautifully inaccurate", and Mr. Spitzer's modifier beautifully is philosophically precise. The inaccuracy is not ugly failure. It is the honest shape of a consciousness that refuses to falsify experience by completing it prematurely.

Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Pillar note: Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Every figure in this chapter exists at the margins of recognized social reality. My mother is reported dead while alive. She entertains "ambassadors to vanished courts and kings of vanished realms": people whose social categories no longer exist, who are marginal not by personal failure but by historical obsolescence.

Mr. Spitzer is marginal by disposition: furtive, avoiding strangers, carrying his brother's debts to creditors he cannot identify. He exists in the gap between himself and his brother, between the living and the dead, between the correctable and the uncorrectable.

The figures at my mother's wedding (king penguins, melancholy seals, tinkling duchesses) are at the edge of the human, the edge of the real, the edge of the socially legible. They are the evidence that the categories of the real are constructed, that the center is maintained only by constant suppression of the marginal.

The human-sized blackbird is perhaps the chapter's most concentrated image of this pillar: a figure that is simultaneously person and animal, that participates in conventional social exchange (opening doors), that exists at the categorical boundary where the constructed nature of "the human" becomes most visible.

Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

Pillar note: Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

This pillar is enacted in the chapter's very texture. The past does not recede. It presses upward through every sentence.

My mother's wedding, possibly decades past, is more present than the present moment. The social seasons that never were accumulate beneath her current despair. Mr. Spitzer carries his brother's financial debts and his mother's emotional debts and his own unlived life simultaneously, all pressing upward at once.

The newspaper's error about my mother's death is treated as a temporal rather than factual mistake: "having merely mistaken the time". This is sedimentary time precisely: the past and future are not separate from the present but are layers of the same geological formation. The death is real; it is simply not yet.

Mr. Spitzer's walk down Benevolent Street the evening after reading about his brother retraces his brother's steps; he moves through space that is already layered with another's passage. The street is not neutral. It is sediment. His black cape whirling "like the sobbing of the rain upon the river Styx" marks him as a figure who moves through multiple temporal layers simultaneously: the living world and the underworld occupying the same geography.

Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

Pillar note: Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

The chapter is acutely self-conscious about language's constructive power. The newspaper's error does not merely describe my mother as dead; it constitutes a social reality in which she is dead, one that Mr. Spitzer must decide whether to correct or allow to stand. Language here is not reporting on a pre-existing fact. It is creating a social fact.

My mother's wedding vows, whatever they were, constructed a marriage that she simultaneously insists never happened. The language of the ceremony did or did not create the marriage, but the uncertainty is not resolvable by appeal to what "really" occurred, because what really occurred is itself a construction of memory and narration.

The passage about her wedding music, "many reverberations, many keys and strings and wandering echoes", describes language itself: echoes of echoes, meaning that has lost its origin, signification that continues after the signifying event has dissolved. The text performs what it describes.

Mr. Spitzer's blank letter is the purest image of language as construction: he mails himself a message containing nothing, marked with his own address, and waits for it. The envelope, the address, the postal system, all the apparatus of linguistic communication, surround an absence. The construction is complete. The content is void. This is language naming its own location: I am the structure that surrounds what cannot be said.

Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

Pillar note: Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

The sacred in this chapter is entirely immanent; it does not point outward to a beyond but inward and downward into the thickness of ordinary experience.

My mother's opium visions are not escapes from reality. They are intensifications of the immanent: the world made more itself, more saturated, more present. Mr. Spitzer recognizes this:

"hers was a greater freedom, a greater aura of improbable possibility than if she had ever closed a door or written finis to a deathless dream"

The sacred here is the deathless dream, not a transcendent realm but the ordinary world experienced without the violence of closure.

The wedding music ("ethereal", vast, never completed) is sacred not because it points to God but because it points deeper into experience, into the wind, into the harp strings, into the cables of bridges. Mr. Spitzer's harp composition is a sacred project precisely because it seeks to imitate this world (the wind on this bridge, the pressure of these cables) with perfect fidelity. The sacred is the ordinary world more fully attended to.

Even grief is sacred here. The "diffused sense of woe" that Mr. Spitzer carries is not a problem to solve but a form of contact with the weight of existence: the immanent transcendence of being a conscious creature in a world where everything is always already passing.

Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

Pillar note: Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

This is perhaps the pillar most structurally present in the chapter's deepest architecture. The narrator exists only as "my mother": constituted entirely by the sediment deposited before their arrival, speaking from within a structure they did not choose.

Mr. Spitzer is explicitly a crossing point: he carries his brother's debts, his mother's unlived life, his own unfinished music, the dead letter addressed to himself. He is where time crosses itself: the living man who has attended his own funeral, who walks the streets of Boston as if haunting them, who squints at his dead brother's watch to detect falsehood in the present moment.

My mother's wedding, that founding event, is the crossing point of multiple times: the remembered past, the misremembered past, the imagined past, the present moment of remembering, the future death already reported. All of these cross in the single act of her trying to reconstruct what happened.

The chapter ends with Mr. Spitzer opening a door that is already open: a perfect image of the Crossing Point. He acts in response to a reality he cannot perceive, constituting the ground of someone else's experience, carrying forward an obligation that is not chosen but structural. The ancestors are in the sediment. The carrying continues. He opens the door.

Chapter 58

Research notes: Chapter 58 · Reading guide: Guide, Chapter 58

Characters: Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer

Pillar 1 Not One Self

Pillar note: Pillar 1 Not One Self

Mr. Spitzer is never singular. He is simultaneously the musician who cannot play, the mourner who cannot stop mourning, the observer who cannot simply observe, the critic who cannot separate admiration from pity. The chapter explicitly states:

"For probably Mr. Spitzer was so constituted that his admiration would always be his pity — and his pity, his admiration."

This is not psychological ambivalence in the ordinary sense. It is ontological plurality: the self as a site where contradictory orientations coexist without resolution. He is the catcher and the pitcher, the musician and the audience, the living and the possibly dead. The old violinist himself multiplies across the chapter's famous catalogue of transformations (violinist, baseball player, tennis player, shepherd, judge, king, conductor) demonstrating that identity is not a stable property but a function of which instrument, which wand, which stance one happens to hold at a given moment:

"Ah, what miracles could be achieved with a simple wand! What forms of being might evolve."

Not One Self is not presented as a crisis to be resolved. It is presented as the fundamental condition of existence. The self is whatever crossing of roles and memories happens to be activated in a given moment. Mr. Spitzer contains his dead brother Peron, the old violinist, all the old sportsmen, the recording angel, the loggerhead turtle, the walking concert program. He is, structurally, a crowd.

Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

Pillar note: Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

The entire encounter is built on layers of unreality that are treated with complete seriousness. The violinist plays an imaginary violin with an imaginary bow producing imaginary sound. Mr. Spitzer, who may himself be beyond ordinary hearing, responds to this non-sound with genuine emotion:

"it was the most beautiful music he had never heard, making his heart shake in the great silence as the tears came stinging to his eyes"

The music is more beautiful because it is not heard. The chapter explicitly argues that hearing would diminish it:

"something which would be less beautiful if heard by living ears, for it would lose in the hearing"

This is not a paradox the text tries to escape. It is its central thesis. The constructed, the imagined, the illusory is not a degraded version of the real; it is the primary form of the real.
