Characters: Lorena · Miss MacIntosh · Mr. Titus Bonebreaker · Old Friday

Pillar 1 Not One Self

Pillar note: Pillar 1 Not One Self

Miss MacIntosh presents herself as the embodiment of radical singularity ("absolutely normal," she insists, "just like other people") and yet she is constitutively multiple and irresolvable. She is simultaneously:

  • A nursemaid who dresses as a whaler
  • A socialist who haunts the Stock Exchange
  • A bald woman who wears a red wig
  • A woman without ovaries who obsesses over recipes
  • A woman without a breast who lectures on household arts
  • A woman who preaches common sense while drowning herself at dawn

The narrator notes that she "took on every color except my own", which is itself a description of the plural self: the child narrator has no fixed self either, only a reflective surface absorbing Miss MacIntosh's multiplicities. But Miss MacIntosh herself is the deeper demonstration: she cannot be resolved into a single coherent person because she is not one. Her bald head under the red wig is not a secret hidden from her true self. It is one layer of a self that is all layers simultaneously.

The Arctic explorer, who sits beside her at the Stock Exchange, mirrors this plurality back at her. He is a Great Dane, a Greater Dog, a man who killed twin sisters with an arrow, a man with a wooden leg who has "eaten his dead master", a man whose eyes cannot close. He is not one thing either. Their encounter is not between two unified persons but between two unresolvable multiplicities who briefly orbit each other.

Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

Pillar note: Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

The entire epistemological structure of the chapter rests on this pillar. Miss MacIntosh's defining characteristic, the one the narrator names as the revelation that reorganizes everything, is her baldness, the fact that her red hair was a wig. But the wig is not simply a disguise. It is the primary construction by which a self becomes livable.

The narrator says: "I thought her red hair was her own, of course, and never looked at her too closely. I had not yet discovered her without her wig like the red sunset upon the waters." The wig is not the lie and the bald head the truth. Both are real. The wig is the construction that allows Miss MacIntosh to exist in social space, to teach lessons, to walk in the surf lecturing on socialism, to visit the Stock Exchange, to be a person at all. Without it, she is exposed to a kind of ontological nakedness that the text treats as catastrophic, not because the bald head is shameful in itself, but because the social world requires the construction of a self that can be seen.

Her imaginary investments at the Stock Exchange extend this logic. She makes "imaginary money", keeps her investments on "slips of brown wrapping paper, neatly cut, made with a red pencil". She knows they are imaginary. She does it anyway. The imaginary fortune is not a delusion; it is a practice, a way of inhabiting the world's structures without being destroyed by them. The line between illusion and reality is, as the philosophy states, itself a construction. Miss MacIntosh lives this truth more honestly than most.

The Arctic explorer intensifies the theme: he claims to have reached the North Pole, but Miss MacIntosh suspects both he and Captain Cook and Commander Peary of being "liars" about having reached the center, "which was surrounded by five hundred miles of mush and no solid ice to uphold any foot". The Pole (the fixed point, the center, the truth) cannot be stood upon. It is mush. There is no sunlit world outside the cave.

Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

Pillar note: Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

The chapter's emotional climate is grief, but it never announces itself as such. It accumulates in the background of every lesson, every booming question, every piece of grey knitting intended for an orphan in a cold country, who is, the narrator quietly notes, "herself, no doubt".

Miss MacIntosh grieves:

  • Her baldness, which she has carried since birth
  • Her mastectomy, her removed ovaries: the reproductive body she never had
  • The King of Sweden, who "promised much to her" and misled her
  • Mr. Bonebreaker, who fled before the honeymoon upon seeing her bald head
  • The Arctic explorer, who disappeared "without her, leaving no name"
  • Lorena, who knew "before seeing this baldness": a figure whose full story the text withholds, but whose knowing is described with the tenderness of intimacy
  • What Cheer, Iowa, the lost origin, the plain and simple place that no longer exists as she remembers it

None of this grief resolves. The text does not move Miss MacIntosh through stages toward acceptance. Instead, it accumulates: lesson upon lesson, question upon question, wig upon bald head upon recipe for walrus heart upon Eskimo cookbook upon silk nightgown. The grief is the weather of the chapter, the atmospheric pressure under which every scene is set.

The final image makes this explicit. The shore after her drowning is not a scene of resolution. It is a scene of accumulation: her corset on a rock, her watch among sand dollars, her grey socks unknitting at the tide's edge, her red wig on a horseshoe crab. These are not the remnants of a completed life. They are grief made visible as sediment.

Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

Pillar note: Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

The narrator's function in this chapter is precisely that of the Witness. She does not fix Miss MacIntosh. She does not conclude her. She watches.

"Not that she cared for the answers. But our lessons must go on in spite of the storm and the moon drowned in the sky and the carcasses on the beach."

The narrator receives Miss MacIntosh's confessions during "that last month of her life" without judgment, without interruption, without resolution. She records the Arctic explorer's long monologue, Miss MacIntosh's imaginary finances, her social welfare concerns, her loneliness in New York City, her visits to Grant's Tomb, her terror at the cafeteria for mutes: all of it held in the same attentive, non-simplifying gaze.

The ethical weight of this witnessing becomes explicit at the end:

"Yet once more, Miss MacIntosh, my darling, and once more — old Friday barking by the sea..."

The repetition of "once more" is not nostalgia. It is the act of witnessing refusing to conclude. The narrator will not arrive at a tidy grief. She will not summarize Miss MacIntosh. She will stay in the room (which is now the sea, the shore, the echo) and keep looking. The refusal to simplify is the act.

Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

Pillar note: Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

Miss MacIntosh's lessons are the clearest image of recursive construction in the chapter. She asks the same questions again and again: Who was Martin Luther? What is the altitude of Tibet? Who is John L. Sullivan?, not because she expects new answers, but because the asking is the building. The lessons are provisional, acknowledged as such by both teacher and student, and yet they continue.

"In spite of death itself, our lessons must go on."

This is the recursive structure stated plainly: you build anyway. The building is never finished. The narrator confesses she never knew the answers then, but the lessons "took on a new light in memory" after Miss MacIntosh was gone. The building continues after the builder has drowned. What was constructed in the nursery during storms is still being constructed in the act of remembering and narrating.

Miss MacIntosh's imaginary Stock Exchange fortune follows the same logic. She builds it, knowing it is imaginary, covering "her investments with her investments", hedging "herself about with paper mills". The building is provisional. That is not failure. That is how it works.

Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

Pillar note: Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

The chapter's form enacts this pillar structurally. The lessons are never completed. The Arctic explorer's proposal is never answered. The story of Lorena is never fully told. Mr. Bonebreaker's umbrella is left behind but he himself is not explained. Miss MacIntosh's body is never found.

"There being no sign of her upon the water or the sand where her old mackintosh must lose its colors."

The demand for completion (for a body, for a resolution, for an explanation of why she walked into the sea) is refused. The text treats this refusal not as a failure of narration but as its highest honesty. Miss MacIntosh herself enacts this ethic: she never finishes her grey knitting, never cooks the recipes she collects, never places her first ten cents in the actual market, never goes to the North Pole or anywhere else.

Her life, as rendered here, is a series of ongoing sentences. The concluded life, the finished woman, would be a falsification. The unfinished is not failure. It is honesty.

Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Pillar note: Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Miss MacIntosh is the Pillar 7 figure made fully explicit. She exists at the intersection of multiple marginalities:

  • Bald in a world that requires hair as femininity
  • Mastectomized and oophorectomized: her body surgically removed from the reproductive order
  • Poor in a world of the idle rich she serves
  • From What Cheer, Iowa: a place so marginal it is almost a joke, a place whose very name is an irony
  • A woman who dresses as a whaler but is not one
  • A socialist who haunts the Stock Exchange but invests nothing
  • A nursemaid who loathes children

"She had always been lonely for adult companionship and had always had a private loathing for children and orphans."

This is the marginal person as evidence. Miss MacIntosh does not fit any category cleanly, not woman, not man, not rich, not quite poor, not teacher, not explorer, not wife, not mother. At every categorical edge, the constructed nature of the category becomes visible. Her baldness is not incidental. It is the physical sign of her categorical instability: the place where the construction shows.

The Arctic explorer is a second marginal figure: a man who killed women with an arrow and has never recovered, who cannot close his eyes, who is partly wooden, who has "eaten his dead master", who lives in a cold water flat on lower Broadway. Together, Miss MacIntosh and the explorer constitute not exceptions to the human but its evidence: the places where the seams show.

Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

Pillar note: Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

The temporal structure of the chapter is entirely sedimentary. The narrator is remembering from "long years after Miss MacIntosh's disappearance", but the past does not recede; it presses upward through every sentence.

Miss MacIntosh herself is a figure of accumulated sediment. Her body carries the layers: the removed breast, the removed ovaries, the broken nose, the bald head covered by a red wig, the eye going blind. Each loss is a geological stratum. She is not moving through time toward a future. She is standing on the accumulated weight of everything that has been taken from her.

The What Cheer of her childhood is not behind her. It is beneath her: pressing up through her obsession with oil lamps over electric lights, her disdain for zippers, her belief in mended fences and honest poverty. The sectarian world of What Cheer, where women washed men's feet with their hair, is not past. It is the sediment that determines her present posture, including the specific way she cannot kneel before a man, having no hair to dry his feet with.

The Emperor Constantine who "changed the calendar" is the chapter's figure for the violence of trying to escape sedimented time. Miss MacIntosh cannot endure this. Time "must have hung heavy on his hands, or he would not have changed time." The attempt to restructure time is read as a symptom of corruption, of having too much: time, power, the luxury of tampering. Miss MacIntosh, who has too little of everything, knows that time cannot be changed. It accumulates.

Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

Pillar note: Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

The chapter's language performs its own argument. Young's prose is deliberately recursive, accumulative, refusing the clean sentence. Consider the passage about Miss MacIntosh's hair:

"...having no hair of seduction, no hair bright or dark, no illusion, not even a hair of the sunlight, moonlight, starlight, and surely she could not be attractive with her broken nose or with the breast of her amputation..."

The accumulation of "no hair of seduction, no hair bright or dark, no illusion" is not decorative. It is a demonstration that language constructs what it names: each phrase adds a new dimension to what hair means, revealing that hair was never simply hair but a whole system of constructed femininity, seduction, illusion, celestial metaphor. To name the absence is to reveal the construction.

Miss MacIntosh's own language (her booming questions, her "Faugh!" and "Phaw!" and "Oh, faugh!") is language that knows its own location. It speaks from What Cheer, Iowa. It speaks from a body that has been surgically altered. It speaks from poverty and loneliness and the specific historical moment of a woman who cannot place her ten cents. It does not pretend to speak from nowhere.

The Arctic explorer's language, by contrast, is language that claims transcendence; he speaks of the place "where nothing was known, there was nothing unknown", of a land "horizonless", of forgetting her name, of no boundary between the living and the dead. His language reaches for the beyond. Miss MacIntosh's language stays resolutely here, in the nursery, in the storm, asking what are the states adjoining Kansas.

Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

Pillar note: Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

The sacred in this chapter lives entirely within the ordinary and the marginal. It does not live in the Emperor Constantine's changed calendar, or in the King of Sweden's promises, or in the Arctic explorer's six months of darkness. It lives in:

  • The hurricane lamp in the nursery during the storm
  • The grey knitting intended for an orphan in a cold country
  • The silver-dollar watch among the sand dollars on the beach
  • Old Friday barking at the waves
  • The red wig laid over the horseshoe crab crawling in the sand

These objects are not symbols pointing upward to a transcendent meaning. They are the sacred itself, located in the immanent. The wig on the horseshoe crab is not a symbol of Miss MacIntosh's vanity or her tragedy. It is Miss MacIntosh: her constructed self, her illusion, her survival mechanism, now returned to the natural world that she walked into.

The final elegy makes this explicit:

"Yet once more, Miss MacIntosh, my darling, and once more — old Friday barking by the sea, her watery bier, great, blowing tides and storm clouds knotted which were her coffin, its lid the star-studded sky, its shores all shores..."

The coffin is the sea. The lid is the sky. The sacred is not elsewhere. It is here, in the water and the sand and the barking dog and the waves "like sheep with a thousand bells". The transcendence is immanent, pointing deeper into the world, not out of it.

Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

Pillar note: Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

The narrator is the Crossing Point made visible. She is constituted by Miss MacIntosh, by the lessons she could not answer, by the questions boomed above the storm, by the discovery of the bald head, by the last month of confessions. She did not choose this constitution. It was deposited in her before she could evaluate it.

"I took on every color except my own."

This is the Crossing Point described from the inside: the self as the place where prior depositions cross, where Miss MacIntosh's loneliness and What Cheer's sectarianism and the mother's opium dreams and the Arctic explorer's proposal all intersect in the body of a child who cannot name the author of their freedom.

Miss MacIntosh herself is a Crossing Point between What Cheer and the wider world, between the sectarian past and the socialist present, between the body she was born with and the body that was surgically altered, between the self she presents (red hair, capable nursemaid, normal woman) and the self beneath the wig.

Her drowning is not an exit from the Crossing Point. It is its completion: the moment when the accumulated sediment, the plural self, the permanent grief, the provisional constructions all return to the element from which they came. And the narrator, carrying all of it forward in language, becomes the ground the not-yet-born will stand on.

"The amputated feet, Miss MacIntosh once said, will walk by themselves, walk by themselves through sands and surfs and flowering meadows and orchards of golden apples."

The carrying continues.

Research notes: Chapter 1 · Reading guide: Guide, Chapter 1

Characters: Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Pillar 1 Not One Self

Pillar note: Pillar 1 Not One Self

The narrator Vera Cartwheel is constitutionally multiple and irresolvable. She exists simultaneously as a child in the New England house, a wanderer through harbor cities, a typist typing mortality rates, a searcher on this bus, and none of these selves supersedes the others. She tells us plainly:

"Every heart is the other heart. Every soul is the other soul. Every face is the other face. The individual is the one illusion."

This is not a philosophical position she has arrived at. It is the texture of her experience. She cannot plan a house "if there was one soul which could not live in it": her self is already too porous, too identified with the multiple, to function as a singular agent. The bus journey is itself a figure for this: she is among strangers whose inner lives she partially inhabits, the pregnant girl, the sleeping boy, the whistling driver, and she cannot stop constructing their interiorities even while knowing she is constructing them.

Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

Pillar note: Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

The chapter does not present illusion as a veil over reality. It presents illusion as the medium in which reality occurs. The landscape outside the bus window is described not as a landscape but as the failure of landscape:

"There was now no landscape but the soul's, and that is the inexactitude, the ever shifting and the distant."

The mother's opium house is not contrasted with a real world outside it: the world outside is equally constructed, equally a "conspiracy of memories and dreams floating without purpose, without limitation." Even Miss MacIntosh, the novel's avatar of plain reality and common sense, is revealed to be, from the perspective of years, "almost vague": the very figure of anti-illusion has been consumed by the illusory process of memory. The cave does not have an outside. The chapter knows this.

Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

Pillar note: Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

Grief in this chapter is not an event. It is the atmosphere through which everything is perceived. Vera's mother is "dead among her dreams"; Miss MacIntosh has disappeared or died; the search has lasted "long years"; and the grief does not resolve; it accumulates sedimentarily into the present tense of the bus ride. Note that the chapter moves associatively, not chronologically, because grief does not observe chronology:

"There were always the dead seagulls in the whirlwind, the brown leaves falling, an empty, resonant house of broken mirrors reflecting the light of the sea, my mother dead among her dreams."

The word "always" is the key. This is not a memory being visited. This is the permanent climate. The chapter's syntax enacts this: the sentences do not conclude, they accumulate, clause upon clause, like weather systems that never fully pass.

Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

Pillar note: Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

The extended description of the pregnant girl on the bus is the chapter's purest exercise in the ethics of witnessing. The description runs for nearly two full pages and refuses to simplify her into a type. She is simultaneously pathetic and defiant, gaudy and tragic, resisting sleep "as if they were the powers of oblivion and of death". The narrator does not pity her, does not judge her, does not resolve her into a lesson. She sees the rings, the charm bracelets, the stuffed canary with the moth-eaten wing, the absence of a wedding ring, the "cold and transparent look of being not satisfied, of being not filled with the light which comes from love".

This is attention as ethical practice. The narrator stays in the room. She does not rush toward meaning. The girl is not a symbol. She is a person seen fully, which in this novel is the highest act available.

Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

Pillar note: Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

Vera's entire life as narrated here is recursive. She escapes her mother's house to find Miss MacIntosh; she searches harbor cities; she drifts from employment to employment; she arrives on this bus, and she is still building the same search, returning to the same beginning with what she has learned, which is mostly the knowledge of what she has not found:

"I had drifted from place to place, holding such little jobs as I could concentrate on and yet continue my dreams, beginning to study architecture, then giving it up."

The abandoned study of architecture is a perfect recursive figure; she cannot build a house because the building is always provisional, always incomplete, always unable to contain every soul. She returns to the search. The bus is not a destination. It is another iteration of the recursive loop, another attempt to build toward something she already knows cannot be completed. The chapter itself is structured recursively; it circles back through the same images (the harbor cities, the seagulls, the whaler's hat) each time with slightly more accumulation.

Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

Pillar note: Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

The chapter's sentences are themselves the formal argument for this pillar. They do not end. Consider the description of the girl's clothing:

"...velvet butterflies like pansies hovering upon the moth-eaten fox fur collar of her green cloth coat which would not close and was too tight and did not cover her, coming only to her hips, and was of an old-fashioned style with pointed sleeves and pointed cuffs and scalloped edges and many velvet-covered buttons or marks where the buttons had been, small, tinkling bells moving when, in her sleep, she moved from side to side..."

This sentence does not conclude because the girl cannot be concluded. The demand for a period, for completion, would be a violence against her particularity. The novel's famous length is not excess. It is the formal consequence of this ethical position: the ongoing sentence is the honest one. Vera tells us she typed "mortality rates through a blur of tears": the irony being that mortality rates are the bureaucratic imposition of completion on lives that resist it.

Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Pillar note: Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Every figure in this chapter occupies a marginal position. The bus driver with his Jehovah's Witness hair and his whiskey bottle, drinking openly and calling upon God simultaneously, is a figure who cannot be categorized. The pregnant girl without a wedding ring, overdressed in a landscape of grey poverty, wearing the entire field of outdoor sports on her body while being unable to participate in any of them, is the marginal made visible. Vera herself is marginal: the daughter of an opium-dreaming mother, the searcher for a dead nursemaid, the woman who cannot finish architecture school because she is too porous to the excluded.

The marginal figures here are not exceptions to the social order. They are, as the pillar states, evidence: evidence that the categories (wife/not-wife, real/unreal, living/dead) are constructions. The pregnant girl's absent wedding ring is the chapter's most compressed symbol: the category that should organize her situation (married mother) is visibly absent, and what fills that absence is an extravagant over-compensation of other signifiers that cannot substitute for it.

Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

Pillar note: Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

This pillar is perhaps most explicitly enacted in the chapter's temporal structure. The past does not recede in Vera's narration; it presses upward:

"My life had been made up of just these disrelated, delusive images hovering only for a moment at the margin of consciousness, then passing like ships in the night, even ships manned by dead helmsmen, by ghostly crews, by one's own soul at large."

The dead helmsmen are not behind her. They are in the ship she is sailing. Miss MacIntosh's voice ("Common sense is the finest sense", "the way was very plain, quite direct") is not a memory being recalled. It is sediment that is still pressing up, shaping Vera's present journey. The mother's opium dreams are not past events; they are the ground Vera stands on, the thing she is still fleeing and still carrying. The chapter's movement is not linear but geological: layer upon layer of the same material, compressed.

Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

Pillar note: Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

The chapter is acutely aware of its own linguistic situation. Vera's extended meditation on illusion and reality is not delivered from a neutral position; it is delivered from inside a Grey Goose bus in southern Indiana, by a woman whose head is "roaring with the memory of space", who has been shaped by an opium-dreaming mother and a common-sense nursemaid and years of harbor-city wandering. The language knows its own location.

More specifically, the chapter uses language's constructive power against itself. The description of the pregnant girl is so exhaustively particular, "pairs of stuffed red valentine hearts dangling from ribbons and faces which were painted powder puffs", that it enacts the impossibility of language ever fully capturing a person. The list keeps going because no item on the list is sufficient. Language here names its own insufficiency as it proceeds.

Contrast this with Miss MacIntosh's language, always quoted in plain declarative sentences: "nothing had happened", "the way was very plain". Her language claims to speak from nowhere, from common sense itself. The novel's implicit argument is that this is also a location, a "plain, old-fashioned" Middle Western location, and that its claim to neutrality is itself a construction, however beloved.

Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

Pillar note: Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

The sacred in this chapter lives entirely inside the ordinary and the broken. The blind man at the all-night lunch counter, groping for his coffee cup, asking "When shall the light, Peter, enter my soul again?"; this is the chapter's central religious image, and it is located in a fog-shrouded waterfront diner, not a church. The transcendent question is asked by a man whose eyes "had been withered in their sockets", with a bare light bulb glaring three inches from his face, unable to see it.

The grey bus itself becomes sacred through the quality of attention brought to it:

"the world stretching out to an unseen horizon, the world flat"

The flat, grey, featureless Middle Western landscape, which Miss MacIntosh recommended as the antidote to the opium house, turns out to be not a destination but another version of the sacred ordinary. The bus groans. The mist blurs the windows. The bus driver imitates birdsong. These are not symbols pointing outward to a transcendent beyond. They are the sacred, here, in the immanent, in the grey.

Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

Pillar note: Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

This is perhaps the pillar most structurally embedded in the chapter's architecture. Vera is explicitly constituted by what was deposited before she arrived: her mother's opium dreams, Miss MacIntosh's plain ethics, the harbor cities, the dead steersman. She did not choose this constitution. It is structural:

"I had been too long half sleeping, cut off from communication with others... asking no more reasonable questions than a patient asks under the ether mask."

But she is also, on this bus, moving toward something, toward "this far place", toward the interior of America that Miss MacIntosh recommended, toward a life that might constitute ground for something not yet born. The double-headed man by the road, "a tall man with a child perched on his lean shoulders", is the chapter's most compressed image of the Crossing Point: the adult carrying the child, the past carrying the future, the two heads looking in different directions, standing at the edge of a road that "seemed to go back the way it had gone before."

Vera will never know his name. But he is "forever engraved on memory's whirling disc"; he has been deposited into her sediment, and she into his, and neither chose it. The obligation is not chosen. It is structural. The carrying continues.

Chapter 16

Research notes: Chapter 16 · Reading guide: Guide, Chapter 16

Characters: Falada · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Pillar 1 Not One Self

Pillar note: Pillar 1 Not One Self

Vera Cartwheel is never singular in this chapter. She is simultaneously a fourteen-year-old girl, a bareback circus rider "wearing a plume, a pair of pink tights," a headless rider, an orphan whispering secrets, and a child who does not know what she thinks "until I heard myself speaking the words".

This last detail is crucial. The self is not prior to its own expression. It discovers itself in the act of speaking, which means there is no unified interior self waiting to be expressed. There is only the ongoing, surprising production of selfhood through language and action.

"I often did not know what I thought until I heard myself speaking the words. I was frightened when sometimes, though whispering, I heard my voice shouting among the stars."

The fright here is the fright of plurality, of discovering that you are larger, louder, and less controlled than you believed. The self overflows its own container. This is not psychological instability presented as a problem to be solved. It is presented as the condition of being alive and conscious.

The rider and the horse further split the self. By the chapter's end, Falada "seemed to be my head, my intelligence. I was the headless rider". Vera distributes her own cognition into the animal beneath her. The self is not located in the body or the mind; it is dispersed across the relationship between them.

Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

Pillar note: Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

The entire landscape of this chapter refuses the distinction between real and constructed. The house contains "ghostly players like swans running back and forth in the moonlight" on tennis courts: are these real players in white, or apparitions? The text does not adjudicate. The moon's reflection becomes a polo ball that Falada can see before Vera can. The horse perceives a reality the human cannot access.

The most philosophically dense passage on this pillar concerns the mother:

"She might think we were phantoms, of course, and then we would be safe. If we were phantoms, she would not be afraid... But if we were real, she might die of shock."

This is a stunning inversion of the usual ontological hierarchy. Being real is the dangerous condition. Being phantom is the safe one. The mother, submerged in her dreams, has constructed a world in which the imaginary is habitable and the real is lethal. Young does not mock this. She presents it as a coherent epistemological position: one that Vera must navigate carefully and respectfully.

The house itself is the architectural embodiment of illusion as primary. It is "a water castle" on dry land, containing gondolas, dolphins, a phoenix, a gold piano upheld by cherubim. These are not decorations. They are competing realities layered on top of each other, none more authoritative than any other.

Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

Pillar note: Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

Grief in this chapter is not announced. It is the climate through which everything moves.

The pony Falada is old, wind-broken, diseased, his mane "withered," his heart rasping "like a door opening on rusted hinges". He is beautiful and dying simultaneously. Vera's love for him is inseparable from his deterioration. The joy of the ride and the approaching loss are not sequential; they are concurrent. This is grief as permanent weather: the cold and the celebration occupying the same air.

The house is similarly structured. Everything in it is a monument to what has already been lost: "old wheels and carriage bodies," "broken torsos and marble heads lying in the grass," "faded marquees and dragging nets", the tomb of a musician "who had gone to join the world of music", a marble boy whose tomb may never have had an occupant. Loss is not past tense here. It is the present tense of the environment.

Even Vera's orphanhood, "I had no mother and was an orphan, how I had never known my father", is whispered as a secret to the horse, not as a wound seeking healing but as a fact of the self, deposited like sediment, carried forward.

Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

Pillar note: Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

The narrative voice of this chapter is one of sustained, unflinching attention. Young does not rush past the dying horse toward the drama of Miss MacIntosh's revelation. She stays, for pages, with the foam on Falada's sides, the dust mop feathers of his mane, the cold of his nose against the warmth of his sweating sides.

This is the ethics of the witness made structural. The prose refuses to simplify, refuses to accelerate toward conclusion. Every object in the house receives full attention:

"We passed the empty tomb of some old musician who had gone to join the world of music, the tomb which was a gold grand piano upheld by cherubim pallbearers with folded wings wading through a musical fountain."

The sentence does not pause to evaluate whether this is beautiful or grotesque, real or symbolic. It witnesses. The cherubim are pallbearers. The fountain is musical. The tomb is a piano. These contradictions are held open, not resolved.

The chapter's final movement, toward Miss MacIntosh's room, is itself an act of witnessing. Vera chooses to go to the one person who "would know that we were real". The ethical imperative is not comfort or validation but confirmation of reality: someone willing to see what is actually there.

Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

Pillar note: Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

The ride itself is circular. They ride "around and around on a path that made a circle like an eye through the garden of the blind". The structure of the chapter mirrors this: it begins with exultant pride and returns, through the interior of the house, to the threshold of knowledge, Miss MacIntosh's door, where something will be revealed that affirms "some older shock which had been forgotten".

This is recursive construction precisely: you return to the beginning with what you have learned, and the return reveals that you already knew, at some level, what you are now discovering. The building of the self is never finished. The ride never truly ends; it becomes the chapter, becomes the novel, becomes the narrator's life.

The pony's pedigree extends this recursion across time. Falada is descended from the horse that inspired the cabriole, the Chippendale furniture, the carousel. His bloodline is a recursive loop through human aesthetic history: the horse that became furniture that became the horse again in the merry-go-round. Nothing is original. Everything returns.

Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

Pillar note: Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

The chapter ends mid-recognition:

"She had greatly changed since last I had seen her, and she was unbelievably not herself, and yet—how was it that I recognized her instantly as if she were something I had always dimly known, and the shock of this knowledge was but the affirmation of some older shock which had been forgotten and laid over by the autumn leaves, the snow falling, the first buds of spring?"

The sentence does not complete its own revelation. It opens onto the next page, the next chapter, the ongoing sentence of the novel. This is not a cliffhanger in the commercial sense. It is an ethical commitment to incompletion: a refusal to conclude what has not concluded, to resolve what is still in the process of being known.

The novel Miss MacIntosh, My Darling is famously 1,198 pages long, and this structural incompletion is not accidental. Young is making the argument, through form, that the demand for resolution is a violence against experience. The ongoing sentence is the honest one.

Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Pillar note: Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Every figure in this chapter exists at the edge of a category. Falada is barely a horse: "almost only an idea of a horse". The mother is barely present: submerged in dreams, entertaining imaginary guests, neither fully conscious nor unconscious. Miss MacIntosh, when we reach her, is "unbelievably not herself", which implies she has a self, but that self has become unstable, marginal to its own identity.

Vera herself is marginal: an orphan, a child without parents, a girl riding a horse through a house at night, occupying no stable social category. She is neither the dreaming mother nor the plain nurse. She is the figure who moves between them, which is to say she is the figure who makes the constructed nature of both categories visible.

The house's contents are similarly marginal objects: things that were once functional (gondola, piano, furniture) now existing as monuments, tombs, or decorations. They are at the edge of their own categories: the piano is a tomb, the tomb is a piano. The marginal object reveals that all categories are constructions.

Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

Pillar note: Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

This pillar is perhaps the most visually explicit in the chapter. The house is literally a sediment of historical time:

"We passed the sleeping marble lions which had once guarded the palace of a Venetian doge who long ago had joined the world of water."

Layer upon layer: Venetian doge, marble lions, American estate, moonlit night, fourteen-year-old girl. The past does not recede. It accumulates. The doge is gone but his lions are here, pressing up through the present.

The furniture pedigree (Falada's ancestor inspiring the cabriole, Queen Anne furniture, Chippendale, "whole forests" of it, still present "in the best Boston houses") is an explicit theory of sedimentary time. The horse from an Arabic fairy tale became the furniture in an English queen's court became the chairs in a Boston drawing room. The past is not behind us. It is beneath us, holding us up.

The silver comb and brush that Vera uses on Falada "tarnished by age and the dews of the grave, had belonged to a beautiful dead lady now sleeping in her marble tomb". Vera grooms the horse with the instruments of a dead woman's vanity. She is living inside someone else's past, using it as her present. The sediment is not metaphorical. It is material.

Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

Pillar note: Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

The chapter is acutely aware of the constructive power of naming. Mr. Spitzer's meditation on Falada's name is the most explicit statement of this pillar in the text:

"It seemed to him that the name of a horse was important as the name of a man, and he never had held with those who believe that a rose by any other name would smell as sweet. What was in a name? All things were in their names, Mr. Spitzer believed."

This is a direct refutation of the Shakespearean position. Language is not a neutral label applied to a pre-existing reality. The name constitutes the thing. Falada is not merely called Falada; he is Falada, the horse from the Arabic fairy tale whose severed head spoke oracles above the city gates. The name carries the mythology. The mythology shapes what the horse is and what his death will mean.

Vera's own experience of language as construction appears in the passage about not knowing what she thinks until she speaks it. Language is not the vehicle for pre-existing thought. It is the construction site where thought comes into being. And the result is sometimes terrifying: "I was frightened when sometimes, though whispering, I heard my voice shouting among the stars". Language exceeds its speaker. It speaks from somewhere the speaker did not intend.

Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

Pillar note: Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

The sacred in this chapter is entirely immanent: located in the dying pony, the cold nose, the diseased mane, the rasping heart. Not in heaven, not in an afterlife, not in a symbol pointing beyond itself, but here, in the body of an old horse in a moonlit garden.

"I lay on Falada's back with my arms around his bony, pulsing neck with its long, straining tendons and my face against his diseased, withered mane with its dust mop feathers."

The transcendence is in the contact. The bony neck, the straining tendons, the diseased mane; these are not obstacles to the sacred. They are the sacred. The deterioration is not something to be transcended. It is where the sacred lives.

The house's interior offers a similar immanent transcendence: the phoenix "rising from those cold ashes of the dream", the musical fountain, the crystal beads "each crystal gleaming with interior fire as if water were the coffin of fire". The sacred is inside the material: fire inside water, music inside stone, life inside the dying horse. It does not point outward. It points deeper in.

Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

Pillar note: Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

The chapter's final image crystallizes this pillar completely. Vera, riding Falada through the house, is not a self moving through space and time. She is the point where multiple times cross: her own childhood, her mother's dreaming, Miss MacIntosh's plain reality, Falada's dying body, the Venetian doge's marble lions, the dead lady's silver comb, the Arabic fairy tale's speaking horse head, the Chippendale forests of Queen Anne's England.

She did not choose any of this. She was born into it. The house was already there. The sediment was already laid. The pony was already old. The name Falada already carried its mythology.

And yet she is also constituting the ground for what comes next. She is riding toward the revelation of Miss MacIntosh's secret: a revelation that will, we understand, change her forever, deposit a new layer in the sediment of her self, become part of what the not-yet-known future Vera will stand on.

"the shock of this knowledge was but the affirmation of some older shock which had been forgotten and laid over by the autumn leaves, the snow falling, the first buds of spring"

The crossing point is described explicitly here: the new shock affirms the old shock. The present confirms what was already deposited in the past. The self is not moving forward in time. The self is where time crosses itself, where the old shock and the new shock meet and recognize each other.
wheel-chapter-29:
Chapter 29

← Chapter 28 · Wheel and Spokes Home · Chapter 30 →

Research notes: Chapter 29 · Reading guide: Guide, Chapter 29

Characters: Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer

Pillar 1 Not One Self

Pillar note: Pillar 1 Not One Self

Mr. Spitzer is constitutively multiple. He cannot determine where he ends and his dead brother begins:

"he was not always sure, of course, whether his present ghostly thoughts were his own or his dead brother's thoughts moving now through him"

This is not a temporary confusion awaiting resolution. The text refuses to resolve it. He asks:

"Were these two souls which moved through him, old Joachim, the dreamless one? Were these three souls or the amalgamations of many souls"

The plural self here is not psychological fragmentation as pathology. It is presented as the structural condition of being a surviving twin, but by extension, of being any self at all. Peron lives through Joachim; Joachim cannot think without Peron thinking alongside him. The self is a haunted house, not a single occupant.

He is also multiple in his social roles: attorney, mourner, butterfly collector, musician, go-between, reluctant pander for his brother's desires. Each role is a different person, and none is the "real" Joachim. The chapter never locates a core self beneath these layers. There is no core. There are only layers.

Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

Pillar note: Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

The butterfly colors are the chapter's central philosophical image of this pillar:

"Yet butterflies were colorless — the colors being the effects not of pigmentation but of the illusion of light shattered on the gleaming mirror scales as if they were so many geometric prisms"

This is not incidental natural history. It is a thesis statement. The most beautiful things are not colored; they produce the illusion of color through structural refraction. Beauty, meaning, identity: all are effects of light on surfaces, not substances residing in things themselves.

The chapter extends this outward. My mother's visitors, "purple pharaohs in their swan boats, the Irish poets wrapped in bands of fog", are illusions she insists are real. But Mr. Spitzer's butterflies are also, increasingly, illusions:

"what he sensed now was probably the perfume of his thoughts. He swore that he could smell his thoughts."

The line between the butterfly in the room and the butterfly in the mind is never drawn. The chapter does not draw it because the chapter does not believe it exists. Reality is not what we find. It is what the prism of consciousness makes.

"perhaps everything was the devious imitation of everything"

This is Pillar 2 stated with almost brutal directness.

Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

Pillar note: Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

This is perhaps the pillar most fully embodied by the entire chapter. Mr. Spitzer's grief for Peron is not a phase he passed through. It is the climate in which everything else occurs:

"Only his silent music and his memories of his recurring butterflies consoled him now for his brother's early death and for his continuing life"

Note the syntax: his brother's early death and his continuing life are presented as parallel afflictions requiring equal consolation. To continue living after the death of one's twin is itself a form of grief, an ongoing wound.

The grief has not resolved in however many years have passed since Peron's death. It has instead accumulated: accumulating butterfly knowledge, accumulating memories, accumulating the dead brother's thoughts until Joachim is a sediment of grief more than a living man:

"he had suffered this great wound of death, and yet he had suffered more, this wound of life"

The wound of life is the wound that does not close because the person who inflicted it by dying is still present, in thoughts, in memories, in the face that mirrors Joachim's own face. Grief here is not weather that passes. It is the atmosphere itself.

Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

Pillar note: Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

Mr. Spitzer is the chapter's supreme practitioner of witnessing. He does not fix, conclude, or resolve. He observes, catalogs, remembers, and stays in the room:

"he had not disturbed the sleeper"

This moment, finding the mourning cloak butterfly hibernating in a hollow tree in winter and choosing not to disturb it, is a small but perfect enactment of the witness ethic. He sees fully. He does not intervene. He does not pin it down.

The same impulse governs his relationship to his brother's mystery:

"Peron had been, Mr. Spitzer still believed, the greater mystery, and death had enhanced his mystery"

He does not claim to have solved Peron. He witnesses him: incompletely, lovingly, without conclusion. And crucially, he witnesses himself with the same refusal to conclude:

"though he had never yet gotten a total glimpse of himself"

The witness ethic here extends to the self. He does not claim self-knowledge. He observes himself as he observes butterflies, with attention, without capture.

Later, directly:

"Who was Mr. Spitzer now to impale a butterfly, as he would sometimes ask, to pin it down?"

To pin down is to kill. The witness refuses to pin. This is the ethics of the pillar made literal through the central image of the chapter.

Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

Pillar note: Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

The chapter is itself a recursive structure. Mr. Spitzer returns again and again to butterflies (from different angles, with different names, through different memories) never completing the catalog, always beginning again:

"He knew butterflies of every region and of both hemispheres... He knew Urania Sloanus, Ornithoptera Paradisea..."

The list is not a list moving toward completion. It is a list that generates more list. Each butterfly evokes another. The chapter's prose enacts this: sentences accumulate subordinate clauses, each clause opening onto another, the period always deferred.

He is also recursively constructing his understanding of his brother. Each return to Peron reveals a slightly different facet:

"He had been a being of so many volatile impressions and mad designs and fickle moods, so many sudden turns and twists, so many inexpressible ideas"

This is not the description of someone who has been understood. It is the description of someone being perpetually re-approached. The building of Peron's portrait is never finished, and Mr. Spitzer knows it, and continues anyway.

Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

Pillar note: Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

The sock meditation is the chapter's most explicit philosophical comedy of this pillar:

"as there had been so many holes, so many darns and patches, were these new socks or old he wore? The ghostly conformation of his old sock persisted, showing the ghostly shape of his leg, his foot — and yet it seemed to him that, technically, he might be considered to be wearing... new socks — or that he would be when the last original thread had disappeared."

This is the Ship of Theseus rendered in hosiery, and it is not merely comic. The question of identity, whether the patched thing is still the original thing, runs through the entire chapter. Is Joachim still Joachim after so many years of grief? Is his butterfly knowledge still his own after it has been saturated with his brother's absence? The sock is a figure for the self: perpetually repaired, never completed, never quite the same thing it was, never quite a new thing either.

The demand for completion (for a finished self, a concluded grief, a solved brother) is refused throughout. The chapter's length, its refusal to end, is itself an ethical stance. The ongoing sentence is the honest sentence.

Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Pillar note: Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

The chapter opens with the problem of the boundary between butterfly and moth:

"creatures who seemed to be at the boundary line between butterfly and moth, evasive creatures who, though they were of the dawn, were so nearly alike in their almost intangible features as to make it difficult for even a great expert like Mr. Spitzer to draw, with absolute certainty, a map or boundary line"

The marginal creature, the thing that cannot be classified, is not an anomaly. It is the evidence that the categories themselves are constructions. The butterfly/moth boundary is the same kind of construction as the happiness/sorrow boundary, which the chapter immediately invokes:

"just as it might at times be difficult to distinguish between brother and brother or between the ecstasy of happiness and that of sorrow"

Brother and brother. This is the chapter's deepest marginal figure: the identical twin, the person who exists at the boundary of selfhood itself. Joachim is not quite one person. Peron is not quite gone. They occupy the margin between self and other, between living and dead.

Mr. Spitzer himself is a marginal figure: too fat, too old, too grief-struck, too obsessed with butterflies to be a fully functional social being. He comes each evening to sit with a woman who may not be awake, in a house full of imaginary guests. He is the evidence that the category of "normal person" is a construction.

Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

Pillar note: Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

This is perhaps the pillar most structurally embedded in the chapter's form. The past does not recede for Mr. Spitzer. It accumulates:

"these butterfly memories, rather than expiring, had shown such durability, that these transitory and mutable things should seem immutable and lasting and protracted and prolonged"

The butterflies he saw decades ago are more present to him now than they were then. The dead brother is more present with each passing year. The grief deepens rather than resolves. This is not pathology in the chapter's terms; it is the honest description of how time actually works for a consciousness that does not pretend otherwise. The hibernating mourning cloak butterfly is the chapter's image of sedimentary time made literal:

"the beautiful mourning cloak butterfly hibernating in a hollow tree trunk... it was sleeping a long winter through, sleeping with folded wings, and he had not disturbed the sleeper"

The butterfly is the past, folded and sleeping inside the present, ready to emerge. When he sees a mourning cloak in spring:

"he had felt as if it were an old friend, and he had almost greeted it, had almost lifted his hat"

The past is not behind him. It wings toward him across the daisy-starred fields.

The geological metaphor becomes explicit in the discussion of original butterflies:

"They had come down through the long corridors of time"

Time is a corridor through which things travel toward us, not away from us. The ancestors are in the sediment. The butterflies of the first stars are in the wings of the butterflies of Boston Common.

Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

Pillar note: Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

The chapter is acutely aware of its own linguistic performance. The butterfly names are not neutral labels; they are constructions that carry entire mythological worlds:

"the butterfly Aphrodite... the twelve-spotted butterfly Apollo, namesake of that god who was the twin of the virgin huntress Artemis... butterflies fashioned by Morpheus, god of dreams"

To name a butterfly after Aphrodite is to construct a connection between erotic beauty and the winged psyche. To name one after Apollo is to embed the sun god's twin-ness into the creature's identity. The naming is not description. It is world-making.

The chapter is also self-aware about the limits of language:

"so many inexpressible ideas"

And about the way language shapes what can be known:

the "hieroglyphs engraved upon their gleaming wings as by their names, the nameless dead should still be known and recognized"

The dead who have names can be known. The nameless dead are lost. Language is the condition of existence, not merely its description.

The pun on "ribbing", which Mr. Spitzer both makes and apologizes for, is a moment where the chapter becomes self-conscious about language as play, as construction, as something that can mean multiple things simultaneously, like a butterfly with two souls written on its wings.

Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

Pillar note: Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

The chapter explicitly and repeatedly refuses transcendence in the conventional sense:

"Mr. Spitzer, though he had sought through the wide heavens and earth, had not found the face of God and had not found the location of immutable paradise, yet though he had visited such phantasmal places as the Happy Isles, the Fortunate Isles... Valhalla, Nirvana, the happy hunting grounds"

He has looked everywhere for the beyond. It is not there. And yet the chapter is saturated with the sacred. It is just located here, in the immanent:

"he was sure that it could hear... the thunder in the heart of the rose"

The sacred is inside the rose, not above it. The transcendence is immanent: pressing inward, not outward.

God is cataloged with the same exhaustive, accumulating energy as the butterflies:

"God, it had been said, was the True Vine, the Bread of Life, the Gate, the Door, the Wine... God was the Man of Sorrows, the Old Man, the King of Glory... God was the Narrow Way, the Rose, the Thorn"

This catalog does not affirm God. It dissolves God into multiplicity, into so many names that the name becomes meaningless as a pointer to a single transcendent being. What remains is the quality of attention that the names represent: the sacred is the act of naming with full attention, not the thing named.

The butterfly itself is the chapter's primary figure of immanent transcendence:

"they had always seemed to him the most perfect symbol of immortality, each being the image, the perfect image of himself"

Not immortality in heaven. Immortality as the image that repeats itself, the pattern that persists through metamorphosis. The sacred is the chrysalis, the emergence, the wing: all of it happening here, in the hollow tree, in the spring field, in the old man's clouded mind.

Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

Pillar note: Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

This is the pillar that gives the chapter its deepest structure. Mr. Spitzer is explicitly figured as a crossing point between the living and the dead, between past and future, between his own self and his brother's:

"he enjoyed no after-life now except through Mr. Spitzer's literal-minded and mournful memory of him, the approximate repetition of this broken life through fragmentary gleamings until it should be no more, until Mr. Spitzer himself should be dead and beyond recall"

Peron exists only because Joachim carries him. Joachim is the medium through which Peron continues. This is not metaphor; it is the chapter's literal account of how the dead persist. The carrying is structural. It is not chosen.

And the butterflies themselves are crossing points: between the first stars and the present moment, between death and life, between caterpillar and winged creature:

"They had come down through the long corridors of time"

"They had survived the deaths of stars, the cyclic whirlwinds, the ages of fire, the ages of ice"

Mr. Spitzer is where butterfly time crosses human time. He is constituted by what was deposited before him: the butterfly knowledge that grew without his conscious attention, the brother whose thoughts move through him, the grief that accumulated without his permission.

The chapter's final image of this pillar is the lamp-lighter:

"an old lamp-lighter whose face was also streaked with tears and who had said... — He will never light another lamp"

And then:

"Mr. Spitzer had been somewhat surprised by the brevity of human memory, surprised to see the lamps going on one by one down a dark street where the old lamp-lighter moved like Jacob with his ladder of dreams reaching to the clouds"

The lamps go on. The dead man will never light them. But they go on anyway, because the structure of lamp-lighting continues, because others carry it forward, because the obligation is not personal but structural. This is the crossing point: the place where what was deposited before you continues through you into what comes after.
