Chapter 56

← Chapter 55 · Wheel and Spokes Home · Chapter 57 →

Research notes: Chapter 56 · Reading guide: Guide, Chapter 56

Characters: Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer

Pillar 1 Not One Self

Pillar note: Pillar 1 Not One Self

"Like Peron, he was becoming all others, all except himself"

Mr. Spitzer's selfhood is structurally plural from the beginning. He dressed his dead brother in his own clothes, of his own dimensions, his own cut. The brothers are not merely similar; they are ontologically entangled. Peron wore the checkered suit; Mr. Spitzer wore the swallow-tails. But Mr. Spitzer asks:

"Or what if Mr. Spitzer should put on the brown derby, the checkered suit such as his brother had worn to a race-track, carry the bright cane? Would he be his brother?"

The question is not rhetorical. It is genuinely unanswerable. Not One Self here is not a metaphor for complexity of personality; it is a literal philosophical crisis about whether identity is constituted by clothing, by posture, by the rose one wears. The self is sartorial before it is essential. Mr. Spitzer exists as Mr. Spitzer only insofar as he wears the Prince Albert cutaway, the white rose, the Inverness cape:

"there was perhaps not even Mr. Spitzer in his black suit and cape"

Remove the garments and there is no remainder. Not One Self is not a richness here; it is a terror. He is simultaneously himself, his dead brother, a shadow, a copy, a counterfeit, a tailor's dummy, a puppet. All at once. Irresolvably.

Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

Pillar note: Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

This is perhaps the chapter's most explicit philosophical argument, stated with almost doctrinal directness:

"Reality was that which was unreal and was clothed with the dream of reality, dream with dream, body of this chameleon dream"

The chapter does not merely suggest that illusion is pervasive; it argues that stripping away appearance produces not reality but nothing:

"if one should strip away the appearances, there should be no reality — no visible colors, no white rose if one should strip away the rose"

This is the larger cave more carefully lit. Mr. Spitzer's nightmare about being unable to distinguish propositions from furniture is the epistemological core of the chapter: the boundary between the conceptual and the material has collapsed. Golden mountains, baroque mirrors that mirror nowhere, the furniture of the dream; these are not failures of perception. They are the accurate report of a world where illusion is constitutive rather than derivative.

The philosopher's version: there is no sunlit world outside the cave. Mr. Spitzer's version: he cannot tell whether he is awake or dreaming, and has concluded the distinction may not hold.

Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

Pillar note: Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

"his sorrows, tremulous as clouds with silver linings, were diffused and almost indefinite, vague of outline"

The chapter's great catalogue of mourning, spanning nearly two full pages, is one of the most extraordinary enactments of grief-as-climate in literary prose. Mr. Spitzer does not mourn for specific things in a sequence that moves toward resolution. He mourns everything simultaneously and permanently:

"he mourned for everything — for the dew drop trembling on the lip of the helmet flower, for the moth flying away from the flower, for the mirror of the flower"

Notice the structure: not just the dewdrop, but the moth leaving it, but also the mirror of the flower, the representation of the thing, not just the thing. Grief here has become so total it consumes not only the object but the object's reflection, its departure, its trace. This is grief that has no object because it has absorbed all objects.

The passage continues through tides, moles, bats, whales, swallows, lighthouses, whelks, dolphins, dogs, windows: an accumulation that never arrives at catharsis because catharsis is not the point. The point is that this is the climate of Mr. Spitzer's world since his brother's death. He does not move through it. He lives in it permanently.

"Since that day, he had never been the same, he verily believed"

The honest life stops pretending otherwise. Mr. Spitzer has stopped pretending.

Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

Pillar note: Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

The chapter itself, and Mr. Spitzer within it, performs the ethics of the Witness in a paradoxical way. Mr. Spitzer is simultaneously the one who sees and the one being seen, the observer and the observed, the mourner and the mourned. His practice is relentless attention to the world's dissolution:

"He was the anthropologist counting mollusks, trying to determine which had been mortal"

This is the Witness in its purest form: cataloguing without concluding, observing without fixing. The anthropologist does not solve the mollusks. He counts them. He tries to determine. The trying is the practice.

The chapter's refusal to simplify Mr. Spitzer's condition (is he alive or dead? is he himself or his brother? is he sane or mad?) is itself an act of witnessing. The narrative stays in the room with his irresolution rather than resolving it. When he asks:

"Ah, what crucible was this, he still must ask, or were there two deaths, one at either pole of life, or were there many deaths, more than even he knew?"

The answer is not provided. The question is the act. Attention without conclusion is the practice.

Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

Pillar note: Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

"he had come to the conclusion that he was not real, for reality had forsaken him... and there was no bridge but that bridge one built by walking where there was no bridge"

This is the most precise statement of Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary in the chapter: you build the bridge by walking it, knowing there is no bridge, knowing the building is provisional. Mr. Spitzer returns to the beginning constantly (to his brother's funeral, to the clothes, to the question of identity, to the question of reality) not to resolve these returns but because the returning is itself the structure of his being.

He has paid the tailor, dressed the corpse, distributed the wardrobe, asked the questions, and then he does it again, in memory, in thought, in the chapter's own recursive prose structure which spirals back on itself like the pagoda shells it describes :

great pagodas "of many spirals spiralling toward the water-reflecting heavens"

The pagoda is the formal image of Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary: each level returns to the shape of the previous level, slightly transformed, never finished, never a failure.

Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

Pillar note: Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

The chapter's prose enacts this pillar structurally. The sentences are themselves incomplete in their completion; they accumulate through dashes, through catalogues that never close, through questions that receive no answers. The famous inventory of mourning does not end with a period of resolution. It ends with more mourning.

Mr. Spitzer's coat is the material emblem of this pillar:

"this old coat which had been mended so many times... with the loosest basting stitches imaginable as life was temporary — so that he was about to lose his sleeve — or part of his being — or perhaps there had been no patch to cover the great hole — perhaps the hole was covered only with a greater hole"

The patch over the hole covered by a greater hole: this is Unfinished Is Honest made visible as textile. The demand for a final, complete repair would be violence against the coat's history, against the life it has registered. The basting stitches are honest. The finished seam would be a lie.

"he was like his brother now—like a man in his grave or in a stranger’s grave, yet though he lived on like the tattered clouds, the tattered birds"

Tattering is not failure. It is the record of duration.

Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Pillar note: Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Mr. Spitzer is the marginal figure made central, or rather, made the only figure. He is:

  • The man who dresses the dead in his own clothes
  • The man who gives away a dead man's wardrobe to homeless men in alleys
  • The man who cannot be sure whether he is alive or dead
  • The man who wears the same mourner's/bridegroom's suit for decades

But the chapter extends the marginal outward. The homeless men of Boston who receive Peron's jockeys' silks and harlequin suits; they are not background figures. They are the recipients of identity, the inheritors of selfhood's cast-offs. The dwarf's suit found in Peron's wardrobe :

"he wondered — who was the little man, as tiny as a flower, a snowflake, a moth? Should the things which were always dying die? Was the little man the one who could not die?"

The dwarf, the most marginal of marginal figures, becomes the philosophical crux. The miniature, the anomalous, the one who does not fit the standard dimensions: this is where the constructed nature of identity becomes most visible. Peron, a large man, owned a dwarf's suit. The categories do not hold.

Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

Pillar note: Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

This pillar is the chapter's geological substructure. Mr. Spitzer does not remember his brother's funeral as a past event; it presses upward through everything he does:

"He remembered that it had been his painful duty, after his lamented brother's death, to dispose of his brother's clothing"

But the remembering is not retrieval. It is eruption. The clothes distributed to homeless men years ago still surface:

"still to this day would sometimes catch a glimpse of a tattered silk or a bright rag"

The past is not behind him. It is beneath him, appearing in the streets of Boston as fragments of Peron's wardrobe worn by strangers. The earth itself is described in terms of this sedimentary pressure:

"The earth was moved by the moon like the tide in ripples and furrows — earth in an old orchard swelled, heaved like a woman in child labor. He had seen the hummocks in the soil which had moved like the moving waters"

The ground rises. What is buried pushes upward. Sedimentary time is not metaphor here; it is the literal behavior of the world Mr. Spitzer inhabits.

Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

Pillar note: Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

The chapter is acutely aware of language's constructive and ultimately unstable role. Mr. Spitzer's nightmare about propositions is precisely a nightmare about language's failure to be neutral:

"he could not, for the life of him, distinguish propositions as to reality from tables and chairs and rose-colored divans"

Propositions, the basic units of linguistic truth-claiming, have become furniture. They have weight, dimension, solidity. The statement "There is not a golden mountain" does not dissolve the golden mountain; it creates a mysterious entity of the golden mountain, a something that must be defined by its nonexistence. Language that says there is not still conjures the is.

The chapter's own language performs this: the prose constructs Mr. Spitzer through accumulation, through the list, through the catalogue, forms that name their own location as provisional and ongoing rather than claiming the authority of the concluded statement. The dashes, the qualifications, the perhaps and sometimes and it seemed; these are honest language, language that knows it is constructing rather than reporting.

Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

Pillar note: Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

"the dead musician lived, and he lived in spite of all that Mr. Spitzer could do to stop his singing, his creaking like the frozen clouds, the creaking mast-heads, the demented sea shells singing to themselves"

The sacred in this chapter is emphatically not elsewhere. It is in the horse barnacles, the wentletraps "like staircases to heaven", the luna moths on the beach, the Dog Star. These are not symbols pointing outward to a transcendent beyond; they are the sacred itself, immanent in the material world, pointing deeper into the world's own strangeness.

Mr. Spitzer's mourning catalogue is a liturgy of immanent transcendence: each item (the star-nosed mole, the flower-faced bat, the spouter whale) is treated with the reverence usually reserved for the divine, but the divinity is located in the thing, not beyond it. The empty lighthouse filled with dead moths is sacred not because it points to God but because it is, in itself, a complete image of life, death, guidance, failure, and beauty simultaneously.

The track bugler who played at Peron's grave, "former first trumpet of the Boston Symphony, former first trumpet of the Philadelphia Symphony", plays the starter music at a funeral. Racing and death and music collapse into a single immanent moment where the sacred is not separate from the ordinary but is the ordinary fully attended to.

Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

Pillar note: Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

This is the pillar that most completely describes Mr. Spitzer's ontological condition. He is explicitly described not as a person moving through time but as a crossing point:

"he, old Joachim, was his own angelic sarcophagus and a great city and the city gates — was this world"

He is the city and its gates simultaneously: the container and the threshold, the past deposited in him and the future passing through him. He is constituted by what came before:

"He was the horse barnacles forming in constantly shifting patterns like the seething foam... and the great hermits, the great kings in their shells"

And he is constituting ground for what comes after: the clothing he distributed to the homeless men of Boston will be worn, will be seen as bright rags in alleys, will carry Peron's identity forward into lives neither brother knew.

The chapter's most devastating statement of this pillar:

"He only knew that he was Peron, his dead brother"

He is not Peron's mourner. He is not Peron's survivor. He is Peron, not through confusion but through the structural logic of the Crossing Point. The ancestors are in the sediment. Mr. Spitzer is the sediment. The carrying continues in spite of everything, in spite of his not knowing whether he is alive, in spite of the cables being broken:

"when the cables were broken, danced on with many jerks and whirls, not knowing that the cables were broken"
wheel-chapter-73:
Chapter 73

← Chapter 72 · Wheel and Spokes Home · Chapter 74 →

Research notes: Chapter 73 · Reading guide: Guide, Chapter 73

Characters: Esther Longtree · Joe Goldberg

Pillar 1 Not One Self

Pillar note: Pillar 1 Not One Self

Esther is constitutively multiple. She is simultaneously:

  • A waitress serving customers
  • An eternal mother who has never successfully given birth
  • A beloved of men she cannot remember
  • The keeper of secrets she never chose to keep
  • A defendant in a trial that has not yet happened
  • A woman nursing her own thumb, her own fist, a bullfrog

"She had always been so maternal ever since she could remember, she really had, mothering everything, all the torments, and even when she was a little girl had nursed her thumb, wrapping her thumb in a silken hood with draw-strings, imagining the fingernail her other face"

The fingernail imagined as "her other face" is not metaphor; it is a structural confession. Esther does not have one face. Her self proliferates outward into objects, animals, absent children, dying men's memories of her. She is the woman Joe Goldberg remembers, who is not the woman she is. She is the mother of children she cannot locate. She is the peak of a man's existence and simultaneously cannot place him in her mind at all.

Not One Self pillar insists this is not a problem to fix. The chapter agrees completely. There is no moment where Esther strains toward unity or coherence. Her multiplicity is her mode of being. She moves slowly, she forgets, she smiles and is sad, she is "brilliant but dumb"; these are not contradictions awaiting resolution. They are the simultaneous truth of what she is.

Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

Pillar note: Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

The entire chapter is structured around the question of whether anything happened. Did Joe Goldberg meet Esther in the graveyard? Did she conceive his child? Was there a child? The text never resolves this. More radically, it suggests the question itself may be malformed.

"It might have been some other woman he had met among the angels, faceless, void beings, some other woman with immense, swinging hips, with crossed eyes, puzzled smile"

"He could have been right, and she could have been wrong, and there was no answer but time"

The dying fathers build entire architectures of meaning (apple orchards in North Dakota willed to children, requests for photographs, memories of graveyards and marble slabs) on events that may or may not have occurred. But here is the philosophical precision of the chapter: the constructed reality of the dying fathers is not more or less real than Esther's constructed reality of forgetting. Both are fabrications. Both are lived inside with full sincerity.

Old Doctor articulates the epistemological position directly:

"Supreme knowledge was always the last cruelty"

This is not cynicism. It is the honest acknowledgment that the "sunlit world outside the cave" (the true account of what happened, the real child, the verified father) does not exist. There is only the cave of Esther's clouded memory and the cave of Joe Goldberg's dying wish. Neither is more primary. The line between illusion and reality is, as the pillar states, itself a construction.

Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

Pillar note: Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

This is perhaps the pillar most viscerally embodied in the chapter. Esther does not grieve and recover. She is grief, continuously, structurally, climatically.

"She was nearly always silent, waxing, waxing, never waning, her flesh swollen with tides of memory and of forgetfulness"

The stillborn do not recede. They accumulate:

"The stillborn clapped their hands when she came by, shouted in her ear like torments"

The grief is not located at a single loss. It is the atmosphere of her existence. Every pregnancy adds to the total. Every dying father's letter adds to the total. Every silence she keeps adds to the total. The chapter's extraordinary length (its refusal to conclude, its circling and recircling of the same events from slightly different angles) formally enacts this accumulation. We are not moving through the chapter toward resolution. We are deepening into it, layer by layer.

The most devastating expression of grief-as-weather comes in the description of the birth of nothing:

"The birth of nothing was the hardest birth to bear"

This is not a single event. It is a category of experience she has lived through repeatedly. The hardest grief is not the grief of losing something. It is the grief of the thing that never arrived, the child that moved all night and was not there at dawn. This grief has no object to mourn, no grave to visit, no name to speak. It is pure weather.

Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

Pillar note: Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

Esther is, paradoxically, both the subject of witnessing and its most complex practitioner. She witnesses the dying fathers with a completeness that refuses the easy comfort of truth-telling:

"Let the dying fathers believe the utmost, that she had conceived their children, that their children were born, that their children lived! What could she have said?"

This is not deception in the morally simple sense. It is a form of radical witnessing: seeing the dying man so fully, seeing the fragility of his constructed meaning so completely, that she refuses to destroy it with a fact. Old Doctor names the ethics:

"There was no harm in deceiving the dying who would never live to find out what the matter was"

But Esther also witnesses herself, and this is where the pillar becomes most demanding. She does not flinch from her own forgetting. She does not excuse it or explain it away. She holds it:

"It did disappoint her to be so grossly forgetful"

"Her lack of any feeling was her deepest feeling now"

That last line is one of the most precise formulations of Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act in the entire chapter. She does not pretend to feel what she does not feel. She witnesses even her own numbness without rushing to replace it with performed emotion. The pillar demands refusal to simplify. Esther's silence (to the dying fathers, to the census-taker, to the detective) is the enacted form of that refusal. Every silence says: this cannot be simplified into an answer.

Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

Pillar note: Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

Esther knits:

"She was knitting a little hood in the empty hours here in the restaurant, forgetful that she had no thread, for it did not matter, she having no baby as yet to wear the little hood"

This image is the purest possible icon of Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary. She knits without thread, for a baby not yet born, in a restaurant where fewer and fewer customers come. The building is entirely provisional. It may produce nothing. She builds anyway.

The chapter itself is recursively structured; it returns again and again to Joe Goldberg, to the graveyard, to the stillborn, to the question of the child, each time from a slightly different angle, each time having accumulated slightly more. This is not poor construction. It is the formal enactment of the pillar: the building is never finished, and the return to the beginning is not failure but method.

Esther's perpetual pregnancy is itself recursive construction. She conceives, carries, loses, and conceives again. The cycle does not produce accumulating product. It produces accumulating experience: the sediment of all those pregnancies, all those silences, all those fathers. She is built by her own building.

Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

Pillar note: Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

The dying fathers demand completion. They demand to know: was the child born? Is the child alive? What is the child's age, complexion, weight? They write letters seeking the concluded sentence of their lives.

"Years, years after the child was conceived, the father would write, asking, Was the child ever born? The father might even send something, a little shoe."

The little shoe is heartbreaking precisely because it presumes completion: a child of determinable size, a foot that can be measured. Esther cannot provide this. Not because she is withholding, but because the completed version does not exist. The child is the ongoing sentence. The child is still coming, still moving under her heart, still the little shadow boxer.

The chapter's most explicit statement of this pillar:

"If not, then always."

This extraordinary sentence, placed almost alone, is Unfinished Is Honest in its most compressed form. The child that was not conceived is not simply absent. It is always: permanently in the state of not-yet, permanently in the ongoing sentence. The demand for completion (was it conceived or not?) is answered with a category that refuses the binary: always.

The trial that may come, the detective seeking proof of murder, represents the violence of the demand for completion. The law wants a concluded sentence: guilty or innocent, child born or not born, alive or dead. Esther's body refuses to provide one.

Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Pillar note: Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Esther is marginal in every possible register:

  • Physically: deformed foot, crossed eyes, bald spot, "too, too solid flesh"
  • Socially: unmarried, multiply impregnated, working-class waitress
  • Legally: potentially facing murder charges for children who may never have existed
  • Epistemically: unable to remember, unable to verify, unable to provide the accounts that social reality requires

She was "a big, dumb-headed waitress, brilliant but dumb"

The paradox, brilliant but dumb, is not ironic. It names her exact position at the margin of the categories. She exceeds the category of "dumb waitress" (she understands more than the dying fathers, more than old Doctor, more than the detective) while simultaneously being excluded from the category of "brilliant" by her body, her class, her forgetting.

But the pillar's deepest claim is that the marginal person reveals the constructed nature of the categories themselves. Esther does this constantly. Her body refuses to behave as a body should: pregnancies that produce snowflakes, labor that produces nothing, children hidden under persimmon trees and in hollow stumps. She makes visible that "child," "birth," "mother," "father" are categories with edges, and that at those edges, the construction becomes visible.

The old mule is her shadow-double in this register:

"For the mother mule had only rudimentary breasts, small stalks, and when she came into heat, as would sometimes happen because of life's vagaries and life's persistence, yet the heat was meaningless, for nothing could be born"

The mule is the pure marginal figure: biologically positioned at the edge of reproduction, structurally excluded from the category of "mother" while experiencing all its drives. The mule follows Esther everywhere. It is not accidental. It is the text's own ontological argument: Esther and the mule are the evidence that the category of "mother" is a construction, and that the construction has edges where creatures live who cannot be contained by it.

Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

Pillar note: Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

The chapter's temporal structure is explicitly sedimentary. Events do not recede into the past. They press upward:

"The stillborn clapped their hands when she came by, shouted in her ear like torments"

The stillborn are not memories. They are presences, accumulated beneath and around her, still active, still demanding. The chapter circles back through time not as nostalgia but as geology; each pass through the graveyard scene, the birth-of-nothing scene, the dying-fathers scene adds another layer of deposit.

The birth of nothing is the most powerful sedimentary event in the chapter. It happened in summer, but when morning came it was winter. Time had collapsed. The past and present had exchanged places. The landscape had moved. Only Esther remained, and she was thin: emptied of the deposit she had been carrying.

"How had time passed? It had been summer when she was taken by her labor pains, and only one night had passed, but it was winter when the morning came so clear."

This is not magical realism for its own sake. It is the phenomenology of sedimentary time made literal. The night of labor was not one night. It was all the nights. The season that ended was not just summer. It was the accumulated summers of all her pregnancies. Time does not move linearly in Esther's world because sedimentary time does not move linearly. It compresses.

Joe Goldberg, dying in the Colorado mountains, experiences the same compression:

"The stars roaring around him, he could not strike"

His entire career (all the fights, all the victories, all the women) is simultaneously present to him as he dies. The past is not behind him. It is beneath him, and it is rising.

Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

Pillar note: Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

The chapter performs a sustained meditation on the failure of language to contain Esther's experience. The words available to describe her, "mother," "pregnant," "stillborn," "father," "child", are all technically applicable and all fundamentally inadequate.

Consider the word "stillborn." It is used throughout, but the stillborn here are:

"the snowflakes, the marsh butterflies, the cobwebs, the ears without eyes, the eyes without ears, the little foot"

These are not stillborn children in any medical or legal sense. But the word "stillborn" is the only word Esther has for what she produces. The language shapes what can be seen: by using "stillborn," the text makes visible the violence of the word's inadequacy; it names her losses as deaths, as children who almost were, when they may have been something the language has no word for at all.

The dying fathers' language is explicitly constructed and explicitly located:

"He had fought when the blood streamed down his face, had never given in, had won all his battles with men"

Joe Goldberg describes himself entirely in the language of boxing: feinting, sparring, knockouts, the surprised look in the other guy's eyes. This is not neutral description. It is language speaking from a particular location: the masculine, competitive, victory-organized worldview of a professional fighter. When he applies this language to God, to death, to Esther herself ("he had taken her against her will", "he had knocked her out"), the violence of that language's location becomes fully visible.

Esther's language, by contrast, is the language of weather, seasons, accumulation:

"a powder of baby stars strewn upon the dark, glassy sky, an old sound of crying, of falling leaves as thin as air, of wind scraping"

This is language that names its own location; it speaks from inside the body, inside the season, inside the accumulation. It does not pretend to speak from nowhere.

Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

Pillar note: Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

The chapter is saturated with the language and imagery of the sacred (angels, graveyards, God, worms, resurrection, inscriptions) but every sacred reference is pulled back into the immanent. God appears only as Joe Goldberg's opponent in a boxing match. Angels appear only as crumbling stone figures in a hillside graveyard, their noses knocked off during struggles in the grass. The graveyard itself, the most sacred space in the chapter, is littered with:

"the birth control devices littering the bare ground, the paper sacks, the beer bottles, the crumbling angels, the baby angels, the crosses"

This is not desecration. This is The Sacred Is Here in its most precise form. The sacred is not elsewhere. It is here, in the graveyard where lovers meet and are separated by the night policeman, where Joe Goldberg stumbles upon Esther Longtree, where the living and the dead share the same ground.

Old Doctor is the chapter's most explicit theologian of immanent transcendence:

"Death was kindred to love. It was his love of death and not of life which had caused him to enter the medical profession in the first place"

This is not nihilism. It is the recognition that the sacred, the deepest intensity of being, is found not by transcending the mortal world but by going deeper into it, past the surface of the living body into the womb, the grave, the space where love and death are indistinguishable.

Esther herself is the sacred in the ordinary. She is described with consistent imagery of luminosity:

"illuminated from within, increasing"

"her dark eyes bright with light"

She does not transcend her ordinariness: the deformed foot, the restaurant, the slow movement, the forgetting. She is transcendent through it, as it. The sacred lives in her crossed eyes and her bald spot and her everlasting pregnancy. This is exactly where the pillar says it lives.

Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

Pillar note: Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

This is the pillar that most completely illuminates the structural meaning of Esther's perpetual pregnancy. She is not a woman waiting to give birth. She is the crossing point: the place where all the dying fathers' time crosses the not-yet-born children's time, where the accumulated past presses up through her body toward a future that has not arrived.

"She was all alone here, waiting, a big, dumb-headed waitress, brilliant but dumb, waiting on customers, waiting for the visitant, whole and complete, the child to come"

The "visitant, whole and complete" is not just a baby. It is the conclusion that time has been building toward: the crossing point made visible. But the chapter's radical insight is that the crossing point cannot be concluded. The little shadow boxer remains under her heart because the crossing point is not an event. It is a position. Esther is constitutively that position.

The pillar states: you are constituted by what was deposited before you arrived, and you are constituting the ground the not-yet-born will stand on. Esther's body is the literal enactment of this. She is constituted by:

  • All the fathers who deposited their seed and their dying wishes in her
  • Old Doctor who deposited his epistemology of silence
  • The graveyard with its inscriptions and its accumulated dead
  • The old mule with its impossible heat

And she is constituting the ground for:

  • The little shadow boxer, not yet born
  • The children of the stillborn, who clap their hands at her passing
  • The jury that will judge her
  • The reader, who stands on the ground she is making

The obligation is structural. She did not choose to be the crossing point. She was made into it by the accumulation of fathers, losses, silences, pregnancies. The carrying continues because it cannot stop. The little shadow boxer is still moving:

"A fury inhabited her womb, a shadow boxing, and might be his—so old, it might creep forth as a white-bearded child leaning on a crutch."

White-bearded, leaning on a crutch, ancient before birth; this is the child of sedimentary time, the child of the crossing point. It has been in gestation so long it has aged inside her. The ancestors are in the sediment. The carrying continues.

Chapter 35

← Chapter 34 · Wheel and Spokes Home · Chapter 36 →

Research notes: Chapter 35 · Reading guide: Guide, Chapter 35

Characters: Cousin Hannah · Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer

Pillar 1 Not One Self

Pillar note: Pillar 1 Not One Self

The mother is explicitly fragmented throughout. She is described as having

"so many selves, such as the look-out in the crow's-nest, the negress in the belfry, the human barometer moaning whenever the wind shifted, the lady in the phaeton, the figurehead in the foam"

This is not metaphor deployed for color. It is ontological statement. The self here is not a unified consciousness narrating experience; it is a collection of partial selves, each operating semi-independently, each incomplete. The text explicitly names this condition:

"these fragmentations of partial selves, of splintered mirrors and partial images, vague and illusive thoughts seeming to have a being of their own, to act outside of her even when she was sleeping"

Crucially, the mother is contrasted with Cousin Hannah, who appears to possess a unified self: "that splendid unity of character which she herself had never achieved". But the text does not valorize Hannah's unity straightforwardly. The mother's fragmentation is presented with a kind of awed, melancholy pride. Hannah's singularity is admired but also slightly suspect: too clean, too resolved, perhaps a kind of violence against complexity.

Mr. Spitzer adds a third mode of selfhood: the twin without his twin, a self defined by absence, by being the lesser reflection of another. He is "not his identical brother", perpetually haunted by the shape of what he is not.

The chapter thus presents three models of selfhood: the radically plural (the mother), the apparently unified (Hannah), and the negatively defined (Spitzer). None is stable. None is complete.

Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

Pillar note: Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

The entire chapter operates inside a system where the distinction between the living and the dead has been dissolved as an organizing principle. The mother issues formal invitations to the dead:

"how cordial she would be now if Cousin Hannah should accept her formal invitation, her announcement that she would be at home, receiving at three minutes after three"

This is not presented as madness or delusion requiring correction. It is presented as a legitimate mode of social reality. The dead are more present, more vivid, more reliably communicative than the living:

"Cousin Hannah had always answered her, sometimes achieving communication in spite of unbelievable distances"

while Mr. Spitzer, physically present, produces only

"silence roaring like the ebony waves of the sea"

The text thus inverts the conventional hierarchy of real/illusory. The living man who sits in the room is less real, less present, less communicative than the dead woman who exists only in memory and imagination. Reality is not found; it is constructed by attention and desire. The mother's attention constitutes Hannah as real. Her inattention renders Spitzer ghostly.

The line

"Cousin Hannah should remain in mind, even like Queen Maud Mountains with her trailing cape of snow reaching five hundred miles"

makes this explicit: the dead woman has become geological, more permanent than the living, precisely because she exists now only as construction, as memory, as language, as the mother's ongoing act of making.

Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

Pillar note: Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

This is perhaps the pillar most completely embodied by the chapter's texture. Grief here is not an event with a trajectory. It is climate.

The prose itself enacts this. The sentences do not resolve. They accumulate, circle, return, add new layers without concluding. The mother's grief for Hannah is not moving toward acceptance or release. It is simply the condition in which she exists:

"my mother, through all the empty years, yearned for her as one might yearn for anyone who was no more, anyone who was less than water, less than fire, less than wind, anyone who was less than a thought, less than a dream repeating itself"

The diminishing series (less than water, less than fire, less than wind, less than a thought, less than a dream) does not arrive at zero. It arrives at an ongoing sentence that cannot end because ending would mean release, and release is not available.

Even Hannah's death is described in terms that refuse finality:

"now when she was dead, cold and petrified and rigid, now when she should have passed beyond the powers of insult"

The phrase "should have passed beyond" is telling. She should have, but hasn't. Death has not resolved her. It has intensified her presence, made her "more vivid in death than she had been in life".

Grief accumulates here rather than resolving. The mother's bed, from which she never rises, is the spatial emblem of this permanent weather. She lives inside grief the way one lives inside a climate.

Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

Pillar note: Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

The narrator's stance throughout is one of sustained, non-resolving attention. The prose refuses to simplify any of its figures. Cousin Hannah is simultaneously:

  • A heroic suffrage captain of genuine courage and vision
  • A possible card cheat
  • A woman who may have secretly yearned for marriage
  • A figure who showed "no compassion to the weak"
  • Someone who died clutching a faded rose, "forgotten"

Mr. Spitzer is simultaneously:

  • Pathetically limited, unable to tell "a heart from a spade"
  • Possibly correct in his assessment of Hannah as a cheat
  • A man of genuine if unexpressed knowledge: "his pride which gave him his

knowledge of that which he did not know"

  • A figure of real compassion, sheltering "dead men, poor creatures incomplete

and helpless"

The narrator does not adjudicate between these. The ethical act is the refusal to conclude. To stay in the room with all of it. The chapter's extraordinary length and syntactic complexity is not stylistic excess; it is the formal enactment of this witnessing stance. Every qualification, every subordinate clause, every returning spiral is the text refusing to simplify what it sees.

Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

Pillar note: Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

The chapter's structure is itself recursive. It begins with card games, spirals outward through Hannah's suffrage campaigns, Antarctica, Arabia, the Arctic, and returns again and again to the same domestic scene: the mother in bed, Mr. Spitzer present and absent, Hannah dead and vivid.

Each return arrives with new sediment. We know more about Hannah each time we circle back, but the knowledge does not resolve into a portrait; it deepens the mystery. The building of Hannah as a figure is explicitly provisional:

"Cousin Hannah's life had been well known, not shrouded in mystery"

stated with confidence, immediately followed by layers of speculation, qualification, and uncertainty that reveal how unknown she actually is.

The mother's imaginative construction of Hannah (inviting her to visit, imagining her in the spare rooms, planning the conversation) is presented as ongoing creative work, never finished, never successful, never abandoned:

"A light burned at the window against which the blind moth fluttered with jewels upon its wings"

The light is kept burning. The building continues. That it will never be completed, Hannah will never arrive, is not failure. It is the structure of the work.

Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

Pillar note: Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

The prose style is the most direct embodiment of this pillar. These are sentences that refuse to end. Consider the passage describing Hannah's qualities:

"with unflinching firmness, with undiminishing vigor even when her strength diminished, with dauntless and increasing spirit when her body faded, with heroic fortitude when she was faced with only gentleness and evasiveness, with that noble rigor of manner which was and perhaps is always the outgrowth of the resistance against quavering timidity, even one's own"

This sentence does not conclude so much as exhaust one angle of approach before the next clause begins. The demand for a concluded sentence (a clean subject, verb, object, period) would be a violence against the complexity of what is being described. Hannah herself is described as "the ongoing sentence" in structural terms: her life was "seemingly only one course, grand but not simple", but the simplicity is immediately qualified, complicated, opened back up. Her apparent unity is itself shown to be a kind of ongoing construction, not a achieved resolution.

The mother's life, by contrast, is explicitly described as radically incomplete, "this fragmented ego", and this fragmentation is presented not as failure but as honesty about what a self actually is.

Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Pillar note: Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Every significant figure in this chapter occupies a marginal position:

  • The mother: bedridden, outside ordinary social time, conversing with the dead
  • Mr. Spitzer: the surviving twin, defined by his brother's absence, "amorphous", existing in the margins of his own life
  • Cousin Hannah: a woman who occupied public space in ways women were not meant to, who "crashed the gates", who rode through capitals, crossed forbidden frontiers, entered spaces guarded by "minotaurs and dragons and speaking

birds"

Hannah's marginality is the most developed. She is described as having crossed "so many boundary lines which had been forbidden during her life", and these are not only geographical. She crossed the boundary of gender performance, of acceptable female life, of domestic expectation. She is explicitly described as having "a pointed silver beard": a detail that places her outside conventional gender categories entirely.

The text presents her marginality not as exception or aberration but as evidence: evidence of what the categories are, where they are enforced, and what it costs to cross them. Her death clutching a faded rose, forgotten, in a bed, the most conventionally feminine of deaths, is the text's most devastating irony: the woman who escaped every boundary was finally contained by the ultimate one.

Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

Pillar note: Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

This pillar is perhaps the chapter's deepest structural principle. The past does not recede in this text. It presses upward.

Hannah is dead, but she is described in the present tense of active memory, more present than the living Spitzer. The mother's grief is not a memory of grief; it is current grief, still accumulating:

"his jealousy had been fed by every new disappointment"

The same is true of the mother's love for Hannah. Each new absence feeds it. Time does not move these figures away from their losses; it deposits new layers of loss on top of the original loss, making it heavier, more present, more geological.

The house itself is described as

"unchanging throughout the years because it was always changing, even through changelessness"

This is a precise description of sedimentary time: the house accumulates change without losing what was there before. The "beds of great kings who had migrated to other beds": the kings are gone but their beds remain, the impression of their bodies still somehow present in the mattresses.

The Antarctic imagery that recurs throughout, "great glacial mountains of snow and ice and lakes of ice", is also sedimentary imagery: ice as compressed time, layer upon layer of accumulated weather, the past literally frozen into the present landscape.

Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

Pillar note: Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

The prose here is self-consciously constructive. It does not pretend to transparent description. It builds Hannah through accumulation, qualification, metaphor, and revision, and in doing so, it makes visible the act of construction.

Consider how Hannah is described:

"she was still, my mother insisted, unforgettable even when she was forgotten"

This is language naming its own paradox, its own location. My mother insisted: the text marks the source, marks the subjectivity, refuses the pretense of objective description. Hannah's reality is explicitly the mother's construction: "my mother's continuing memory of her".

The passage about the mother's walk is particularly striking:

"she had walked in circles and semicircles, describing various elegant patterns in her most casual movements, measuring the distance from a blue brocade divan to a gilt and ivory chair as if this distance were a complicated problem in infinity"

The mother's movement through space is itself described as language: as "describing" patterns, as choreography, as inscription. Movement is writing. The body speaks. But it speaks in a language that "confus[es] persons with whom she had tried to carry on a polite conversation", because her language is not theirs, does not pretend to speak from nowhere, does not pretend to the neutral.

Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

Pillar note: Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

The sacred in this chapter is entirely immanent: located in the ordinary materials of the world, pointing deeper in rather than upward and out.

The house is described with a kind of reverence that is explicitly not supernatural:

"its crazy porches and balconies and chimneys and widow walks lighted like amphibian stars and intricate mother-of-pearl circular stairways, great wentletraps reaching to mother-of-pearl clouds, helmeted snails in salt pools, rain-drenched gardens and broken shells and furry buds"

The sacred is in the snails, the broken shells, the widow walks. The "wentletraps", a type of spiral shell, reaching to "mother-of-pearl clouds" is the chapter's most concentrated image of immanent transcendence: the shell (entirely earthly, biological, ordinary) reaching toward the sky, but the sky itself made of the same material as the shell. Transcendence is the ordinary world seen more deeply.

The light burning at the window, against which the moth with "jewels upon its wings" flutters, is another such image. The moth is not a symbol pointing elsewhere. It is the sacred: fragile, drawn to light it cannot reach, beautiful in its futility, entirely of this world.

Hannah's death (clutching a faded rose, forgotten) is presented with the same quality of immanent sacredness. The rose is not a symbol of eternal love. It is a faded rose, possibly imaginary, possibly brought by the mother in a dream she has forgotten. The sacred is here, in the fading, in the forgetting, in the not-knowing.

Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

Pillar note: Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

This is the pillar that gives the chapter its deepest structure. The mother, Hannah, and Spitzer are all crossing points: places where time crosses itself, where the deposited past presses up through the living present.

The mother is constituted by Hannah, by what Hannah was, what Hannah represented, what Hannah's life made possible and impossible. She is also constituted by the absent Peron (Hannah's twin's brother), by dead kings whose beds she inhabits, by all the "birds of passage" who have moved through the house.

The chapter's most explicit statement of this pillar:

"she having achieved emancipation, having escaped this wide-meshed net of years as a fish escapes from the fisherman's net or as the fisherman escapes from the boat"

Hannah has escaped, but into what? Not into a beyond. Into the sediment beneath the mother's present. She is now part of what the mother stands on. The obligation continues: the mother keeps the light burning, keeps the invitation open, keeps the memory alive, not out of choice but out of structural necessity. She is where Hannah's time crosses her time.

Spitzer embodies this pillar in its most painful form. He is the crossing point of his brother's life and his own: "not his identical brother", defined by what was deposited before he arrived (his brother's gambling debts, his brother's charisma, his brother's death), constituting nothing forward, apparently, but the "mournful, wild howling" of his continued presence.

The suffrage movement itself is described in these terms: Hannah as the crossing point of all the women who came before her and all who would come after:

"she had been this unconquerable, tumultuous suffrage captain... carrying her emblazoned suffrage message to the far corners of the earth"

She carried what was given to her and deposited it forward. The carrying continues, in the mother's memory, in this text, in the reader's encounter with it.

Research notes: Chapter 3 · Reading guide: Guide, Chapter 3

Characters: Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh

Pillar 1 Not One Self

Pillar note: Pillar 1 Not One Self

Miss MacIntosh is constructed as the anti-plural self; she insists on a single, stable, unambiguous identity. "She was neither a high brow nor a low brow but just, as she was pleased to admit, a plain middle brow, a Middle Westerner, trying to steer her middle course". She is always in her harness, her bells always tinkling so that "it might always be known where she was".

And yet the text quietly, devastatingly multiplies her. Mr. Spitzer hired her believing she was a brunette: "he had rather been under the impression that she was a brunette, that her forehead was overhung by cliffs of darkness, that her eyebrows were dark and beetling cliffs". He sees her again and finds a different woman. Her past is irrecoverable, contradictory, full of gaps: she had been connected with lighthouses for the blind, asylums for the mad, homes for old sailors, and yet "she was always, it was true, sufficiently cryptic when she mentioned what, precisely, she had done with her life". She has a lost brother consumed by the very head-hunter she despises. She is simultaneously the woman of absolute certainty and a woman whose history cannot be assembled into a coherent self.

The narrator's title, "Miss MacIntosh, my darling", is itself a plural act: it names her as both the plain nursemaid of Iowa and as an object of profound, almost mythological love, "truer than the North star". These two Miss MacIntoshes cannot be fully reconciled. The self she insists upon (singular, knowable, direct) is exactly the self the text refuses to grant her.

Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

Pillar note: Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

Miss MacIntosh's entire project is the destruction of illusion in favor of unmediated reality. She dismisses phantoms, imaginary moose, hallucinations, the head-hunter's dreams, the mother's opium visions. "She was under no influence of that hallucinatory atmosphere in which she lived, and she had never seen these phantoms thickening in the air around us".

But the chapter performs a slow, relentless argument that her "reality" is itself a construction: simply a more aggressively maintained one. Her heaven, if any existed, "should be bare and plain and unfurnished"; she constructs an afterlife in the image of her own preferences. She cannot see "the purple hairstreak moths among the evening flowers": her vision has its own selective blindness. She dismisses her mother's pearls as probably imaginary, "not real", collapsing the distinction between what is owned and what is dreamed: "it was all the same to her".

Most strikingly, the text observes that she "seeming not always to distinguish between what my mother possessed and what she thought she possessed". This is a devastating inversion: the woman who exists to enforce the real/illusory distinction cannot herself reliably make it. Her What Cheer, Iowa (plain, unadorned, the ground of all her certainties) is never seen; it exists in the novel only as her assertion of it, a constructed origin story no more verifiable than the mother's opium paradise. The line between illusion and reality is, exactly as Pillar 2 insists, itself a construction, and Miss MacIntosh's construction is simply louder and more aggressively policed than the others.

Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

Pillar note: Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

Miss MacIntosh explicitly refuses grief its proper weather. "There was never an unoccupied moment, and there was no time for the luxury of idle tears, for vague griefs". She insists that "each day's business should be finished and left behind us", that grief "was no creation" and "nothing of which one should be proud".

And yet grief saturates her. Her brother disappeared among the cannibals she despises. Her nose was "broken in a traffic accident and never correctly mended, she having gone to no doctor": a small, terrible detail of a pain deliberately left unhealed, unacknowledged, the body carrying what the will refuses to mourn. She has "no friends". She carries two pennies for closing her own eyes at death. She is "always alone, single and single-minded, accompanied by no guardian angel".

The chapter's closing movement reveals grief that has been accumulating beneath the entire narrative: the narrator's grief at Miss MacIntosh's disappearance. "Who but I had caused this terrible thing... who but I had killed her?". This grief does not resolve; it is the emotional climate of the entire novel, the reason the narrator is on the bus, the reason the chapter exists. The very length and recursiveness of the prose, its refusal to end a sentence when another clause can be added, is the formal enactment of grief that "accumulates" rather than concludes. Miss MacIntosh tried to teach the child that grief was nothing; the novel's form is the child's answer.

Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

Pillar note: Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

The narrator is the chapter's supreme ethical figure, not Miss MacIntosh. Miss MacIntosh acts; the narrator witnesses. The narrator watches Miss MacIntosh "searching through the waves at the shore's edge, searching for something she had not lost and had not found": a perception Miss MacIntosh herself would refuse, but which the witnessing child holds without resolving.

The narrator witnesses without flinching the full contradiction of Miss MacIntosh: her robustness and her mortality, her certainty and her unknowability, her practicality and her hidden grief. The narrator does not simplify her into either a saint of common sense or a figure of pathos. Both are held simultaneously.

The act of witnessing extends to the disappearance itself. The narrator catalogs the "fugitive details" (the eye-glasses rose in the sunlight, the folded handkerchief, the one remaining button) with the precision of someone who has refused to look away: "Such trivial things by which to remember her, yet now more precious than crowns of silver and crowns of gold!". This is witnessing as ethical practice: to hold the small real thing against the erasure of death, to refuse the comfort of abstraction.

Mr. Spitzer, by contrast, fails as witness. He "had never noticed precisely what Miss MacIntosh wore". He picks up things from the beach that were never hers. His memories are "baffled by his tendency to remember false memories". He is the novel's anti-witness, and his failure is explicitly moral; it is why he cannot search for her, cannot find her, cannot grieve her properly.

Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

Pillar note: Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

The chapter is itself a recursive construction. The narrator is on a bus, moving away from the world of Miss MacIntosh, reconstructing her from memory, but the reconstruction is not linear. It circles, returns, adds, qualifies. The sentence structure enacts this: clauses accumulate, loop back, modify what was just said. "Her marcelled red hair fitting close like a helmet and lighting the dark days like a second sun or moon": the description is never finished, always being revised with another "or," another "and."

Miss MacIntosh herself practices recursive construction in her activities: "We would work all day pulling nails out of an old box, straightening the nails, then driving them into another box made of old boards". This is labor that returns to its own beginning, that builds provisionally, that does not arrive at a final structure. She sweeps footprints from the sand before the tide erases them anyway. She mends the fence, caulks the boat, hammers the raft, always returning to maintenance, to the ongoing work that is never finished.

The narrator reads Pilgrim's Progress "straight to the end" and then from "the end, reading straight to the beginning, working from redemption backward": a perfect image of recursive construction, of the building that is never finished because it can always be entered from another direction.

Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

Pillar note: Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

Miss MacIntosh demands completion obsessively. "One finished task should be preferred to a hundred started". She insists that "each day's business should be finished and left behind us". She stamps out the last ember before the waves come. She folds clothes "as carefully as if we never expected to put them on again".

But the chapter itself is the argument against her. Its sentences refuse to end. Its paragraphs accumulate subordinate clauses that defer closure endlessly. The description of Miss MacIntosh walking the beach runs for pages without arriving at a conclusion about who she is. This is not stylistic excess; it is the ethics of incompletion enacted in prose form. The demand for completion that Miss MacIntosh enforces is exposed as "its own violence against experience."

Her disappearance is the ultimate incompletion: no body, no proof, no conclusion. "Without the dead body, there could be no proof of death in a legal sense". She who demanded that everything be finished is herself unfinished: her story has no ending, her death is unconfirmed, her past is irrecoverable. The novel refuses to grant her the completion she demanded of everything else.

Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Pillar note: Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Miss MacIntosh is herself a marginal figure: "this comparatively colorless person", ignored by the visitors to the house, unseen by the surf fishermen and clam-diggers as she passes, hired without inquiry, never looked at twice. She is the nursemaid, the servant, the plain woman, the woman from What Cheer, Iowa: the margins of every social category.

But she is also the evidence that the constructed nature of reality becomes most visible at the edges. In the context of the mother's opium household (where imaginary butlers, phantom moose, and head-hunters are the norm) Miss MacIntosh's radical ordinariness becomes extraordinary, "more peculiar than flower-crowned satyrs and moon-eyed minotaurs". Her marginality to the household's reality-system makes her the most visible demonstration that reality-systems are constructed: she simply refuses to participate in the household's construction, and this refusal is itself a kind of strangeness.

The head-hunter, another marginal figure, is her mirror: he comes "each afternoon in a black-curtained cab for fear of startling the simple country people", hidden at the margins of the road, just as she is hidden at the margins of the house. Both are evidence of the constructed categories they transgress.

Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

Pillar note: Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

The past does not recede in this chapter; it presses upward through everything. The house itself is sedimentary: "many rooms which had not been visited for years", coins "unearthed from graves", the garden full of "broken marble or porous statues sloping toward the edge of the wild sea", the beach strewn with "rotted masts and canvas sails", "the hull of an old fishing boat swept up".

Miss MacIntosh tries to live only in the present, but the beach she walks is composed entirely of the past's wreckage. She throws driftwood back into the sea; the sea returns it. She sweeps footprints from the sand; the tide makes new ones. The past is not behind her; it is beneath her, in the sediment of the shore she walks.

Her own past presses up through her in ways she cannot control: the brother lost to cannibals, the broken nose never set, the cryptic references to asylums and lighthouses and a "Slough of Despond". She refuses to excavate these layers, "she did not believe in delving into the past, blowing up a cold spark among the dead ashes", but the layers are there regardless. The text excavates them for her, against her will, through the accumulation of small revelations across the chapter.

The narrator's grief is itself sedimentary: "Seldom could I bring myself to think of her unless I saw a shadow moving far away in the whistling wind or the faded colors of an old plaid raincoat laid out upon the sand". The past is not behind the narrator; it is in every shadow, every plaid coat, every faded color. It is the ground the narrator stands on.

Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

Pillar note: Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

Miss MacIntosh's language is aggressively positional; it speaks from What Cheer, Iowa, from Protestant plainness, from the tradition of practical virtue, and it pretends to speak from nowhere, from simple common sense. "She was always right". "She was bare-faced and clear of vision". Her speech has no nuance, no qualification: "she would argue with the world's greatest preacher if she knew him".

The narrator's language is the counter-argument. It is explicitly located, in memory, in grief, in the child's perspective, in the retrospective reconstruction of a woman who has disappeared. It names its own uncertainty: "it would always seem", "perhaps", "as she might say", "in her opinion". The narrator's language knows where it speaks from; Miss MacIntosh's does not.

The chapter also enacts the constructive power of language in its treatment of Miss MacIntosh's origin. "She had originated, quite simply, in What Cheer, Iowa, a small town like any other, as she frequently pointed out, and no different from its neighbors. If anything, it was more like its neighbors than its neighbors were". This is language performing its own absurdity: the insistence on typicality so extreme it becomes a kind of myth-making. What Cheer, Iowa is not a neutral fact; it is a constructed origin, a language-act that grounds Miss MacIntosh's authority in a place that is itself only ever present in the text as her assertion of it.

Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

Pillar note: Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

Miss MacIntosh explicitly rejects transcendence: no heaven, no angels, no afterlife, no God who has not left "many things uncreated". And yet the sacred keeps erupting through the ordinary in her world. When she and the child are lost in darkness, "Miss MacIntosh found an old glass jar at the edge of the dark surf and made a lamp by filling it with fireflies": an image of immanent transcendence so precise it is almost unbearable: the sacred light made from the ordinary world's own creatures, carried like a lighthouse over dark waters.

She nurses a wounded seagull "carrying it against her bosom under her faded mackintosh until it had mended its wing and recovered its strength": the sacred act of care performed with no sacred language, no ritual, just the body's warmth and the faded coat. Her "idea of heaven" is simply "that no man should have a hole in his coat here on earth, that all should have enough to eat": a heaven entirely immanent, entirely within the ordinary world.

The grey feather she wears, "a seagull feather which she had found on the beach, something which had drifted through a drifting cloud. That was something which was already lost. That was something which did not cost money", is the perfect emblem of immanent transcendence: the sacred object is the found, the lost, the free, the ordinary. The transcendent is not elsewhere; it is in the feather already falling through the cloud.

Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

Pillar note: Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

This is perhaps the deepest pillar in the chapter, and it operates most powerfully through the narrator's relationship to Miss MacIntosh. The narrator is not simply remembering her; the narrator is constituted by her. "There was only then, after all, to lead the bewildered child with her own dark problems of that childhood which groped toward light, one who could be trusted". Miss MacIntosh is the sediment upon which the narrator's self was built: the one stable point in the opium paradise, the "North star" by which the child navigated.

But the narrator has also constituted Miss MacIntosh: has preserved her, has made her visible, has refused to let her disappear into the sea that took her. "Such trivial things by which to remember her, yet now more precious than crowns of silver and crowns of gold!". The narrator carries Miss MacIntosh forward in time; Miss MacIntosh deposited the narrator's capacity for witness, for grief, for attention to the real. The obligation is structural, not chosen. "Who but I had caused this terrible thing... who but I had killed her?". The narrator cannot escape the crossing point: cannot stand outside the relationship to claim innocence or distance. The ancestors are in the sediment. Miss MacIntosh is in every shadow the narrator sees. The carrying continues.

And Miss MacIntosh herself stands at a crossing point she refuses to acknowledge: between the world she came from (What Cheer, Iowa, the asylums, the Slough of Despond) and the world she inhabits (the opium house, the sea, the child who will carry her). She is "constituted by what was deposited before she arrived" (the brother lost to cannibals, the broken nose, the two pennies for closing her own eyes) and she is "constituting the ground the not-yet-born will stand on" through every lesson she gives the child. She insists she is only passing through, only doing her job; the novel insists she is a crossing point, and the crossing continues long after she has walked into the sea.

Research notes: Chapter 77 · Reading guide: Guide, Chapter 77

Characters: Esther Longtree

Pillar 1 Not One Self

Pillar note: Pillar 1 Not One Self

"The truth that she was always pregnant? The truth that she was never pregnant?"

Esther Longtree is not one person. She is simultaneously:

  • The accused murderer of children she never had
  • The grieving mother of children who died
  • The waitress scrubbing a restaurant clean
  • The pregnant woman whose pregnancy may be dream or body or both
  • The judge, jury, and body of her own trial

The chapter does not present these as contradictions to be resolved. It presents them as simultaneous and irresolvable truths. When she asks herself whether she is always pregnant or never pregnant, the text does not choose. Both are offered as her truth. The self that is Esther Longtree is not a stable center around which these identities orbit; it is the orbit, the spinning, the irresolution.

Most strikingly, she identifies herself with the landscape, the blackbirds, the wind, the starlight, and the void:

"How could she come to any conclusion, she being the judge, the jury, the bodies, the dreams, the vastness, the blackbirds, the wind, the starlight?"

This is not metaphor decorating a stable self. This is the self described as constitutively multiple, not a person who contains multitudes but a person who is multitudes, indistinguishable from the world she inhabits.

Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

Pillar note: Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

"It was all, oh, the terror of a dream. Let us kill her anyhow, said the old woman abortionist to her assistant, for she has sinned against the flesh."

The story of the mass murderess, embedded within Esther's consciousness like a newspaper clipping within a novel, turns on the discovery that a woman's pregnancy was entirely a dream, a bodily illusion with no biological content. And yet the old abortionist kills her anyway, because the dream was real enough to constitute guilt. The woman had sinned against the flesh, not in the flesh, but against it, through the sheer force of imagined pregnancy.

This is the chapter's most explicit philosophical moment: the line between illusion and reality is not just blurred but structurally irrelevant. The dreamed child produces real grief, real swelling, real accusation, real death. The question "was she really pregnant?" is answered by the text with: it doesn't matter, and the distinction is violence.

Esther herself inhabits this logic entirely:

"Perhaps it seemed to her sometimes, the grey landscape was the world unborn, hovering still at the threshold of realization."

Reality is not found. It hovers at the threshold. It is made, or it fails to be made, and in either case it produces consequences as material as any fact.

Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

Pillar note: Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

This pillar is perhaps the chapter's deepest structural principle. Grief in this text does not move. It accumulates.

"She was weighted down so by the death of a small thing! Her spinal column was curved by the weight of memory and was too slender a stem for her large head."

The physical image is precise: grief has architectural consequences. It curves the spine. The body is reshaped by what it carries. And what it carries does not lighten:

"Yet no matter how cheerful she was, there was a sadness that she remembered, and it was not hers. It was somebody else's fear and sadness."

This is grief that has become climate, not even locatable in a single loss, not even entirely personal. It is inherited weather, ambient sorrow, the atmosphere of a consciousness that has stopped pretending grief resolves. The stillborn children, the alphabet book in the grass, the little brown hand: these do not recede. They accumulate beneath her like sediment.

Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

Pillar note: Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

The prose style of this chapter is the practice of witnessing. The narrator does not editorialize, does not correct Esther's logic, does not resolve her contradictions. It stays in the room with her. Consider the extraordinary passage of alphabetical exhibits:

"Exhibit A, the agony, exhibit B, the birthday, exhibit C, the candle on the birthday cake, the empty coffin, exhibit D, a dimple, a daisy..."

This list does not conclude. It does not build toward a verdict. It accumulates evidence without arriving at judgment. The prose enacts the ethical stance of the Witness: to see fully, to name everything, to refuse the simplification of a verdict. The "jury" the text imagines would search Esther's bedroom with "high-powered telescopes and signal mirrors and bellows and tuning forks and anesthesia and dumb, fumbling fingers": an absurdist inventory of instruments that cannot find what they are looking for, because what they are looking for cannot be found by instruments. The witnessing the text models is of a different order: patient, non-conclusive, attending.

Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

Pillar note: Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

"She had worked hard with her hands in order to be happy. She had scrubbed this restaurant clean."

Esther builds. She cleans. She works. She is always pregnant, always in the process of creating, of carrying toward a future. And yet the building is always provisional. The children do not arrive, or arrive dead, or arrive as dreams. The restaurant is clean but the bedroom is a chaos of evidence. She writes to the detective, then regrets it, then tries to unsend the letter through the force of her own anxiety.

The recursive structure of the chapter itself (circling back to the detective, to the murders, to the alphabet, to the pregnancy) enacts this pillar formally. We are not moving forward toward a conclusion. We are returning to the beginning with what we have learned, which is that the beginning is still there, unchanged, pressing.

"Old, forgotten murders, innumerable as the warped autumn leaves falling in a wintry gale, old murders which might be held against her in the very hour of her deliverance!"

The very hour of deliverance is threatened by the past. The new is always already entangled with the accumulated. You build anyway. The building is never finished.

Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

Pillar note: Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

The chapter refuses to conclude. It refuses to tell us whether Esther murdered children, whether she was ever truly pregnant, whether the detective is real, whether her guilt is real. This refusal is not evasion. It is the chapter's ethical core.

"Who could find the heart of a mystery that had no heart?"

The demand for resolution (the detective's project, the jury's project, the reader's instinct) is repeatedly identified in the text as a form of violence:

"No strange man should crawl inside her womb to find out what the answer was."

The womb as the site of mystery, as the place where the demand for completion becomes literal violation: this is the chapter's most visceral statement of Unfinished Is Honest. To force a conclusion, to open the mystery and extract an answer, is assault. Integrity, the chapter insists, looks like the ongoing sentence:

"She was always pregnant, and that was the answer."

Not she gave birth or she never gave birth. She was always pregnant. The ongoing condition, not the concluded event. The answer is the process, not the product.

Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Pillar note: Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Esther Longtree is the marginal figure rendered as philosophical evidence. She is:

  • A woman in a patriarchal legal system that defines her by her reproductive capacity
  • A waitress: service worker, invisible
  • A woman whose pregnancy may be psychosomatic, at the margin of the real/unreal distinction
  • A "stillborn mother": a category that should not exist, a person defined by what failed to happen

She being "the stillborn mother, stifling her cries with her hands, long and loose."

The phrase "stillborn mother" is itself an ontological paradox: a person constituted by a negation, existing at the edge of a category. You cannot be a mother of what was never born. And yet she is exactly this. The text does not resolve the paradox. It insists on it.

The detective's racism, his refusal to investigate the deaths of Black children, is presented not as an aberration but as the structural logic of his entire enterprise:

"He only dealt with the deaths of little white children, for the deaths of the little black children were not his business, there being so many and so unimportant."

This passage is devastating in its flat, reported tone. The detective's white supremacy is not editorialized; it is simply shown as the organizing principle of his epistemology. What counts as a mystery worth solving, what counts as a death worth investigating, is racially constructed. The marginal person (the Black child, Esther herself) is not the exception. They are the evidence of how the center constructs itself.

Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

Pillar note: Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

This pillar is perhaps most visible in the chapter's treatment of the dead children:

"The dead brain had learned what the living brain had never learned, some old, old mystery that was bigger than hers or anybody's. It had learned to read, to write. It had gone to school."

The dead child is not behind Esther. It is beneath her, still developing, still accumulating knowledge, still pressing upward through the ground. The alphabet book found in the grass (rain-stained, buried) is the sediment of a life that never fully lived, still generating meaning.

The newspaper clippings the detective sends are themselves sedimentary objects: "yellowed," "faded," "soft, falling apart". Old murders pressing upward into the present. Old horrors that "might be held against her in the very hour of her deliverance". The past is not past. It is the ground she stands on.

"The longer the days, the shorter the nights of torment, furious cries, misgivings, of all that now made her tired, the swellings, the heavings, the small brown hand of the other child, brown as a driven leaf, laid upon the marble door, laid upon her womb."

The small brown hand laid upon the womb: the dead child touching the place where new life might form. Sedimentary time made physical. What was lost is not behind her. It is touching her from below.

Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

Pillar note: Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

The chapter is acutely aware of language as a system that constructs what it describes. The alphabet book is the chapter's central symbol of this pillar:

"The A, the B, the C that kept asking her, Mother, why did you kill me? Mother, why did you not kill me? Mother, where am I?"

The alphabet, the most basic structure of linguistic construction, becomes the instrument of accusation. Language does not neutrally report Esther's guilt or innocence. It constitutes the accusation. The letters stand for things:

"All the letters in the alphabet book stood for something—the A, the B, the C—the eye, the ear, the head, the heart, the hand, the eternal doubt and question."

This is language described as a system of exhibits, of evidence, not a transparent window onto truth but a constructed grid that determines what can be seen and named. Esther's resistance to the detective is partly a resistance to being named, categorized, concluded:

"She would prefer an everlasting silence to stare at them rather than answer one solitary question which the wind and stars had already asked her."

The wind and stars have asked her questions that language cannot answer. The detective's language (newspaper clippings, legal categories, murder verdicts) is identified as a language that "speaks from somewhere in particular": from whiteness, from patriarchy, from the demand for resolution.

Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

Pillar note: Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here
