"Hers was this song, the Song of Songs of the sterility which is the creation."

The biblical allusion (the Song of Songs, the most immanently sacred text in the Western canon, a poem of bodily love) is redirected here toward sterility. The sacred is not in fertility, not in successful creation, not in the living child. It is in the ongoing condition of creative longing itself. Sterility that is creation. Pregnancy that may never deliver. This is the sacred located entirely within the immanent, the ordinary, the failed.

"Her body was pregnant with death which moved its little hand inside of her."

Death moving inside her like a child. The sacred and the terrible occupying the same space, the same body. No transcendence outward to a beyond, only deeper into the immanent, into the body, into the grey fields, into the ordinary grief of a woman scrubbing a restaurant clean.

"The child was the cold starlight, the wind, the blackness, the void, and, oh, her sense of pity, of remorse, of loneliness. Her big, aching heart!"

The child is not a person. The child is everything that is present and cannot be held. The sacred lives here, in the aching heart, in the cold starlight, in the void. This is The Sacred Is Here at its most precise.

Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

Pillar note: Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

Esther Longtree is constituted by what was deposited before she arrived: her mother she had not slapped "for several years", the old Doctor who told her her children were formations, the flour miller whose epilepsy is inherited from a father who could not pass down his thumb print, the mass murderess whose crimes echo through yellowed newspaper. She did not choose these inheritances. They are structural.

And she is constituting the ground the not-yet-born will stand on: the children she carries or dreams she carries, the alphabet book that the dead child left for her to find, the mystery she will leave unsolved for whoever comes after.

"Parts of us, she had learned, must die even as we are conceived — must die in the still waters of the womb, where already the icy hand of old age is laid upon the mouth."

This is the Crossing Point stated with almost unbearable precision. At the moment of conception, the very beginning, the end is already present. Old age laid upon the mouth of the newborn. The ancestors in the sediment. The carrying continues. Esther does not choose this obligation. She is made of it.

The flour miller's tragedy encapsulates this pillar perfectly:

"He had been told by his father that his father would give him the secret of his exact thumb print upon the flour... but when the old man died, it was not so — for no one could pass a thumb print down."

The promise of transmission, of the ancestor's mark continuing into the future, is revealed as impossible. You cannot pass a thumb print down. And yet the son labored his whole life in the expectation of it, shaped entirely by the promise of what could not be transmitted. He is constituted by the deposit of that promise. The carrying continues even when what is carried cannot arrive.
wheel-chapter-68:
Chapter 68

← Chapter 67 · Wheel and Spokes Home · Chapter 69 →

Research notes: Chapter 68 · Reading guide: Guide, Chapter 68

Characters: Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Mr. Weed

Pillar 1 Not One Self

Pillar note: Pillar 1 Not One Self

"Who was I?"

The narrator does not ask this rhetorically. She asks it with genuine ontological uncertainty, sitting in a rocking chair in a tavern lobby, watching her face change while seeming changeless, feeling herself pass "from my youth to my age without so much as a sigh." She is simultaneously the child who loved Miss MacIntosh, the woman who has journeyed through the night, the widow with no husband, the mother with no children, the old woman tottering at the edge of a grave: all at once, in the same body, in the same chair.

Not One Self is not a metaphor here. It is the literal condition of the narrator's experience. She inhabits multiple temporal selves simultaneously: the nine-year-old watching sleigh bells in a cherry tree, the woman screaming that Miss MacIntosh is drowned, the ancient figure with brown spots on her arms, and none of these selves cancels the others. They are all present, layered, irresolvable.

The hangman, Mr. Weed, enacts the same plurality in a darker register. He is simultaneously the humanitarian missionary, the man who stopped to put on his galoshes while his wife hanged, the dreamer who boils his children in a pot, the father who nearly beats his children with the branch from their mother's death-tree. He insists: "I am a good father,’ he said. ‘I always was." This insistence is not hypocrisy; it is the desperate attempt to resolve the plural self into a single, manageable identity. The chapter refuses to let him.

Even the landlord is multiple: the married man who ties lovers' knots, the sailor who drowned four times and survived, the man who is "unofficially alive", the innkeeper who has seen everything and feigns deafness to manage what he cannot stop hearing.

Not One Self is the chapter's population principle. Every character is irresolvable. That is not their flaw. That is what they are.

Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

Pillar note: Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

"For there was only one definition of reality, that it was real, real as my mother's opium dreams of scallop boats and the feet of satyrs and sails upon the waves, real as Mr. Spitzer's brother who might be the musician or the gambler, real as Miss MacIntosh's sand-colored face which had no hair-line, real as a sea which had no surf line, and real as that rock which was perched upon an angel's wing."

This is the chapter's philosophical thesis statement, delivered at its opening. The narrator does not distinguish between opium dreams and waking perception. She places them in a list of equivalences. The only definition of reality is that it is real, and everything experienced is, by that definition, real.

The second pillar states that "the line between illusion and reality is itself a construction." The narrator goes further: she dissolves the line entirely. The unreal things are real. "Even the unreal things were real, even those who were ignored, rejected, despised, abandoned, unloved, perhaps even unknown, never of fruit or flower."

This is not relativism. It is a more radical claim: that the hierarchy between the real and the illusory is itself an ideological construction, and that the honest mind refuses it. Miss MacIntosh, with her sand-colored face and her insistence that sleigh bells belong only in snow, represented the attempt to maintain that hierarchy: to put everything in its proper place, to keep the cave well-lit and orderly. And then she walked into the sea, leaving her galoshes on the shore, leaving everything in "such a wild confusion." The woman who most insisted on the boundary between real and unreal destroyed herself on it.

The tavern itself operates as a space where illusion has become primary. The sign reads "Bride Ahead" when it means "Bridge Ahead." The miner sits with his headlight out, mining only his dreams. The lobby contains bald men studying what may or may not be a map. Nothing is confirmed. Everything is possible. The larger cave is more carefully lit, but it is still a cave.

Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

Pillar note: Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

"Perhaps even before a river is seen, its invisible presence distends all things, much like a bellows blowing up many fires of many dreams, dead dreamers and their dreams."

Grief in this chapter does not arrive as an event. It is the atmosphere: the distending pressure of the river not yet seen, the accumulated weight of every lost thing pressing outward into the present.

The narrator's grief for Miss MacIntosh is not a past event she is processing. It is the condition of her perception. She sees everything through it. The sleigh bells in the cherry tree, the galoshes on the shore, the swollen copy of Pilgrim's Progress; these are not memories she visits. They are the medium through which she sees the tavern, the signboards, the hangman, the landlord.

The hangman's grief operates the same way. His first wife Marie hanged herself years ago, and yet she is present in every scene he describes: in the peach tree that still stands, in the children who play at hanging, in the second wife who wears the first wife's clothes, in the dream where he boils his children alive. Marie has not receded. She has accumulated. She is the weather of his domestic life.

Most devastatingly, the narrator confesses:

"I was frightened, frightened, frightened by my own defective character which had loved imperfections and distortions and mad dreams more than it had loved that reality which I did not know, the flesh and blood, perhaps might never know, for I had loved only the dead. I had loved only the departed."

Grief as permanent weather means that the beloved dead are not behind you. They are the climate you live in. The narrator does not grieve Miss MacIntosh. She is grief for Miss MacIntosh. The distinction between the griever and the grief has collapsed.

Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

Pillar note: Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

"I sat with my face glued against the bus window, studying a not unusual wilderness architecture."

The narrator's primary activity throughout this chapter is watching. She watches the tavern from the bus before she enters it. She watches the boy and girl walk up the street. She watches the hangman and the landlord from her rocking chair at the edge of the circle of light. She does not intervene. She does not conclude. She does not rush to judgment.

This is the ethical stance of the Witness: to stay in the room, to see fully, without flinching, without rushing toward resolution.

The hangman's stories are grotesque: a woman's severed head in a wheat field wearing rose-colored sunglasses, children hanged like dolls from a peach tree, a man who boils his children in dreams. The narrator does not recoil from these. She does not editorialize. She presents them with the same flat, accumulating attention she gives to the signboards and the weeds growing between broken pavements.

The landlord models a cruder version of witnessing: he listens, plucks at his deaf ear, occasionally interjects, but mostly allows the hangman to speak. He has heard these stories before, "You tell the same damned stories every time you come here, Weed", and he has not resolved them. He simply keeps the room open.

The refusal to simplify is the act. The chapter's extraordinary length, its refusal to summarize the hangman's monologue, its insistence on following every digression about poker chips and peach trees and the race-horse tout who kept crying "Casho!"; this is not self-indulgence. It is the formal enactment of the Witness. Attention is the practice. The chapter will not look away.

Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

Pillar note: Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

"All might have been like the extension of one of my mother's opium dreams."

The narrator has been journeying. She is arriving. But the arrival does not end the journey; it reveals that the journey was always already the destination, and that the destination is simply a new point from which the journey continues.

The hangman's procedure is explicitly recursive: he rehearses every hanging, practices with a sandbag dummy weighted to the condemned man's exact measurements, corrects his form letter "over a period of years", returns again and again to the same peach tree, the same orchard, the same stories. He is building, knowing the building is provisional. The peach tree still stands. He has always intended to cut it down. He never does.

The landlord's hotel "sinks every night", and yet it stands each morning. The recursive construction is not a metaphor for the hotel. It is the hotel. The building is never finished. That is how it works.

The narrator's own construction (this novel, this journey, this search for Miss MacIntosh) is recursive by definition. She is returning to a beginning she never left. The journey toward the real was always already a journey through the constructed. She builds anyway.

Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

Pillar note: Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

"The bus, in the middle of the street now, was as motionless as the old ghost buggy. Nobody made a move to get out of the bus. We three might have been corpses in an undertaker's hearse, it seemed to me as we waited, perhaps waited for the journey to begin when it had ended."

The journey has ended. The journey has not ended. Both are true simultaneously, and the chapter refuses to resolve them. This is Unfinished Is Honest in its purest form: the journey does not conclude because conclusion is a violence against the experience of journeying.

The hangman's memoirs, which he announces he is writing, will be "quite sketchy, an outline". He cannot include everything. "Every leaf that falls" cannot be included. The memoirs are incomplete by necessity, and the hangman's acknowledgment of this is, paradoxically, the most honest thing he says.

The narrator's account of herself is similarly incomplete. She does not know if the woman whose black hat hangs on the rocking chair exists or is a phantom. She does not know if her stone foetus is real or imagined. She does not know who she is. The unfinished self is not a failure of self-knowledge. It is the only honest self-knowledge available.

The demand for completion (Miss MacIntosh's insistence that there is "a place for everything", that sleigh bells belong in snow and not in cherry trees) is revealed as its own violence. Miss MacIntosh walked into the sea rather than live with incompletion. The chapter suggests this was the wrong choice, or at least an unnecessary one.

Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Pillar note: Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

"Even the unreal things were real, even those who were ignored, rejected, despised, abandoned, unloved, perhaps even unknown, never of fruit or flower."

The chapter is populated entirely by marginal figures. The narrator herself (the daughter of an opium addict, the lover of a vanished woman, the widow with no husband, the mother with no children) is marginal by every social category. The hangman is marginal in the most literal sense: he operates at the edge of the law, the edge of life, the edge of the community's ability to acknowledge what it requires. The landlord has been officially dead in multiple shipwrecks and continues to exist as a kind of ontological surplus.

The chapter's most sustained marginal figure is the unnamed Negro who was cut down from the rope a split second too soon and then seen pushing a baby buggy across a field. He is "unofficially alive": existing in a category that the social order cannot accommodate. He is the chapter's most devastating figure, because his marginality is not chosen or accidental. It is imposed, and it is the direct product of a society that hanged him for "sleeping with a white woman as he surely never did." He is the evidence that the categories are constructed, that the margins are where the construction becomes most visible, and that the cost of that construction is borne by specific bodies.

The hangman's humanitarian self-narrative cannot survive contact with this figure. He entered the profession because of the unnecessary pain of that inefficient hanging. But the unnecessary pain was not primarily the pain of an unskillful knot. It was the pain of a man hanged for a crime that "never happened and yet happened, happened every day in America." The hangman sees the technical problem. He cannot see, or will not see, the structural one. His marginality to his own moral narrative is the chapter's quiet indictment.

Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

Pillar note: Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

"The streets were splotched as if with rain or a disease."

The village the narrator enters is not a present place. It is a sedimentary accumulation of every past that has happened in it. The Tavern was built in 1827. The signboards are tattered. The chassis are rusted. The mattresses are sodden. The bed-springs are "like old musical instruments never to be played on again." The past has not receded. It has deposited itself as the physical substance of the present.

The hangman carries the past literally in his pocket. The black poker chip from an old unsolved case has been in the lining of his coat for years, forgotten, and then recovered. He carries, in the same coat, the Parker fountain pen given to him by a condemned man's relatives, the Jew's harp, the stopped watch from the family driven off a cliff. He is a walking sedimentary deposit of other people's catastrophes.

The narrator's own sedimentary time is organized around Miss MacIntosh's galoshes:

"Her galoshes, thrown up by the tide, were water-logged. Seaweed, the color of coral, adhered to them. On the sole of one, there was plastered a green leaf."

This image has been deposited in the narrator so deeply that it surfaces here, in a landlocked tavern, far from any shore. The past is not behind her. It is beneath her, pressing up. The green leaf on the sole of the galosh is still wet.

Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

Pillar note: Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

"Far up the street, which climbed uncertainly toward the indistinct sky, Josh's Place, a wreath of fuzzy blue neon lights, was like a funeral wreath both for Josh and the world. Beyond this, another sign read Gentle Incline — Bride Ahead — but obviously what was meant was Bridge Ahead, a warning of the river which must be crossed — surely no aromatic river with clouds of bridal lace hanging over it and the white skull moon like the face of the bride, dead bride."

Language fails, and in its failure, it reveals. The misspelled sign, Bride for Bridge, opens a space where the literal and the figurative collapse into each other. The bridge that must be crossed becomes the bride, the dead bride, the marriage with death that the hangman will later name explicitly. The misprint is not corrected. It is followed: the narrator pursues the error into its implications, and finds there a deeper truth than the intended meaning would have provided.

The hangman's language is a sustained exercise in this dynamic. He speaks in euphemisms (helping "a fellow creature out of his misery", "the painless knot", "I come in toward the end and tie the knot") that simultaneously reveal and conceal. His language shapes what can be seen: by calling himself a humanitarian, he makes it possible not to see the violence. By calling his procedure efficient, he makes it possible not to see the bodies.

The narrator's language, by contrast, is language that names its own location. It says: I am speaking from grief, from fear, from a defective character that loved imperfections. It says: I do not know if what I see is real. It says: the journey may have ended or may not have ended. This is language that refuses to pretend to speak from nowhere.

The Tavern's sign, "built in 1827 by God's servants who were believers in the lamb", is language that claims the authority of the universal while speaking from a very particular location. The narrator's question, "Who, I wondered, were God's servants, and why should they advertise themselves?", is the exact question the ninth pillar demands we ask of all language that claims to speak from nowhere.

Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

Pillar note: Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

"My mother's face would never be old, I thought even now when surely I knew that my mother had grown old. Hair, hair, that was the great deception, hair, a woman's crowning glory, hair which keeps growing in the grave. The bald woman was the woman I loved."

The sacred in this chapter does not point outward to a beyond. It points inward and downward, into the ordinary, the broken, the mortal. The bald woman (Miss MacIntosh, stripped of every conventional sign of femininity and beauty) is the object of the narrator's deepest love. The sacred is located precisely in what social convention marks as deficiency.

The hangman's Jew's harp is a sacred object of this kind. He takes it out, plays a soundless tune, puts it back. It is a child's instrument, associated with no tradition of seriousness, and yet it is the thing he reaches for in moments of difficulty. It is the thing that cannot console him and yet he keeps reaching for it. The sacred is here, in the inadequate instrument, in the gesture that knows it will not work and makes it anyway.

The Tavern itself, "built in 1827 by God's servants who were believers in the lamb", is now a commercial establishment that sinks every night and rises every morning, full of tattered streamers and rusted signboards and a landlord with ships tattooed on his arms. The transcendence has not departed. It has become immanent. It lives in the creaking chain and the scraping sign and the hobnailed boots of the sleeping miner whose headlight has no light in it.

The chapter's most explicit statement of immanent transcendence is the narrator's vision of herself as simultaneously young and old, living and dying, in the rocking chair:

"Now in a split second, in the flicker of an eyelid, here as I sat rocking in a chair which creaked, I seemed to myself to be passing from my youth to my age without so much as a sigh."

The sacred is this: the flicker of an eyelid in which all of time is present. Not heaven. Not resolution. The grey bus, the permanent grief, the plural self in all its unresolved reality. This is where the sacred lives.

Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

Pillar note: Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

This pillar finds its most complete expression in the chapter's final image, or rather, in the chapter's refusal of a final image:

"The landlord and the hangman climbed the stairs together — while I, rocking back and forth, waited for service. A clock should have struck somewhere, telling the hour. No clock struck."

The narrator waits. Time does not mark itself. The clock that should have struck does not strike. She is not moving through time toward a destination. She is the place where time has stopped marking itself, where the accumulated past and the unbegun future press against each other without resolution.

The chapter's opening establishes this structural position explicitly:

"To come into a village by night may mean perhaps never to know it in the same way as if one came in the incandescence of sunlight. Perhaps never would the darkness lift, I thought then — that the shadows of the night might always remain."

She arrived in darkness. The darkness is constitutive. She is constituted by what was deposited before she arrived (her mother's opium dreams, Miss MacIntosh's galoshes, the Negro pushing the baby buggy, the peach tree where Marie hanged herself) and she is constituting the ground the not-yet-born will stand on. The chapter she narrates will become sediment.

The hangman's stopped watch makes this explicit. It stopped at the exact moment the car went over the cliff. The crystal was not broken. The watch preserves the crossing point, the instant when one thing ended and another began, and the hangman carries it in his pocket, wound down, refusing to wind it again. He is carrying the crossing point with him. He does not know what to do with it. None of them do.

The obligation is not chosen. It is structural. The ancestors are in the sediment. The carrying continues.
wheel-chapter-09:
Chapter 9

← Chapter 8 · Wheel and Spokes Home · Chapter 10 →

Research notes: Chapter 9 · Reading guide: Guide, Chapter 9

Characters: Miss MacIntosh · Solomon the Turtle · Vera Cartwheel

Pillar 1 Not One Self

Pillar note: Pillar 1 Not One Self

The narrative voice is constitutively fractured. Vera cannot stabilize her own identity because she exists simultaneously as obedient student, secret rebel, dreaming visionary, and retrospective mourner. These are not phases; they coexist.

The most explicit articulation comes in the circus fantasy, where Vera imagines herself as "a bareback rider wearing pink tights and jumping through her exaggerated ivory embroidery hoops" while simultaneously sitting at her sewing. The same body performs obedience and transgression at once. She notes: "I was, back of my dreaming eyes...a bareback rider", the self is layered, not sequential.

Miss MacIntosh herself is a plural figure: the authoritative nurse, the secret bald woman, the self-deceived, the deceiver. The narrative explicitly names this duality: "In seven years, I had lived with a stranger, someone I thought I knew. In one month, I had lived with a dearly cherished friend, someone I would never know". Two Miss MacIntoshes, irreconcilable.

Even the question of guilt is plural and unresolvable: "What terrible deed was this which I had done...that I, even as a little child, had killed Miss MacIntosh, that I had done so only perhaps by opening my eyes". The self that may have killed, the self that mourns, the self that doubts: all present simultaneously, none conclusive.

Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

Pillar note: Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

The chapter is structured around the systematic collapse of the distinction between illusion and reality, and crucially, it does not resolve in favor of either.

Miss MacIntosh's entire project is the enforcement of the real against the imaginary: "there were no fifty white horses struck by lightning in the garden, no sail-boats moored in the lily ponds...and I was simply lying, and there were no wooden eagles. The dream was always the lie". Her epistemology is militantly anti-illusory.

But the chapter systematically undermines her authority to make this distinction. Her red marcelled hair is a wig. Her eyebrows are absent. Her ovaries, asked for directly, are apparently stored "in the bottom drawer...next to the spare corset": an answer so absurd it reveals that Miss MacIntosh herself inhabits a constructed reality, one of performed normality over an absent body.

The deepest irony is structural: Miss MacIntosh, the enforcer of the real, is herself the greatest illusion in the text. Her "What Cheer, Iowa" (the supposed ground of authentic, undeceived life) is itself a mythologized construction, a pastoral of frozen feet and flour-bag underwear that Vera suspects but cannot confirm.

The "larger cave more carefully lit" is precisely What Cheer: not the absence of illusion, but illusion with better lighting.

Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

Pillar note: Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

The chapter opens not with narrative but with grief already in progress, grief that cannot locate its own cause or object: "What terrible deed was this which I had done and which I never should forget, not until all the seas are emptied, until the waves fall away from the sea, not even then?".

This is grief as climate. It does not arrive after loss; it precedes understanding of the loss. It cannot be discharged because its object is uncertain: "Did she kill herself...Did she kill me?". When the object of grief is indeterminate, grief cannot complete its work. It simply continues.

The seagull passage performs this structurally: Miss MacIntosh nurses the wounded seagull "beneath her shawl, against the coldness of her breast", and "the seagull died when its wound was healed". Recovery and death are simultaneous. This is not irony; it is the chapter's meteorological law: healing does not precede loss. They are the same event.

Even Vera's birthday, which should mark the beginning, is saturated with anticipated ending: "that day was the beginning of the end". Joy arrives already grieving itself.

Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

Pillar note: Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

The narrator's primary ethical act is sustained, unflinching attention: to Miss MacIntosh's body, her contradictions, her self-deceptions, without resolving them into judgment.

The question of Miss MacIntosh's eyebrows is paradigmatic. Vera asks, and Miss MacIntosh deflects into a lecture on the Chicago fire. Vera notes: "I did not realize, until long years afterward, that she had never answered mine, that she had evaded the issue". The narrator does not press, does not conclude. She witnesses the evasion and holds it.

Similarly with the ovaries: Vera looks, does not find them, did not "mention the subject again, for I soon forgot it or put it away in the back of my mind as something of no conceivable importance to anyone". This apparent forgetting is actually a form of witnessing: the detail is preserved precisely by being held lightly, without forcing resolution.

The most sustained act of witness is the description of Miss MacIntosh's body: "Her fingers were knotted and yellow-stained...her fingernails were always dirty and cracked". No judgment. No explanation. Pure attention. The body is seen without being interpreted away.

The narrator refuses to simplify the question of Miss MacIntosh's death across the entire opening passage (murder, suicide, disappearance, God's hand, nobody's hand) all held open simultaneously. This refusal is not indecision. It is the ethical stance of the witness.

Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

Pillar note: Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

The chapter enacts recursion formally. It begins with the adult narrator looking back, then moves into childhood memory, then within that memory constructs fantasy (the circus), then within the birthday scene constructs the imagined husband: layer within layer, each built on the previous, none canceling the others.

Miss MacIntosh's housekeeping project is itself recursive: "Everything had to be as it had been in What Cheer, Iowa". She is perpetually rebuilding a lost original, knowing (at some level) it cannot be recovered. The sewing, the hemming, the embroidery hoops that "would roll under the bed as if they were trying to get away from her": the work undoes itself and must be redone.

Vera's birthday reverie is the most explicit recursive construction: she builds an entire marriage, an entire life, an entire geography of adventure, "foreign countries, the European capitals, the Asiatic temples", from within a room where no guests came, where she danced alone with her shadow. She builds knowing it is provisional. That is not pathology. That is how it works.

The chapter's final image, "Were not true marriages made in heaven, and could they ever be dissolved by mortal law or circumstance", is itself a recursive question, returning to the beginning: what is real, what is constructed, what persists?

Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

Pillar note: Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

The chapter's syntax is its ethics. Sentences accumulate without concluding. Questions proliferate without answering. The opening paragraph alone contains seven consecutive rhetorical questions, none answered, all held open.

Miss MacIntosh's speech is structured as incompletion: "Run, fetch my needle and thread, for we must hem a handkerchief before the sun sets...When, Vera Cartwheel, did the first Viking land upon this bleak New England shore?...Where are my scissors, and what's become of my darning egg?". Tasks and questions pile up. Nothing is finished. The demand for completion, Miss MacIntosh's central demand, is itself revealed as the violence: it produces anxiety, not order.

The embroidery hoops that roll away are the perfect image: the instrument of completion, fleeing completion.

The ethics of incompletion is most explicit in the marriage fantasy: Vera does not conclude her imagined husband's identity, does not fix his complexion, does not resolve whether she will find him. "He must not be ordinary": the definition proceeds by negation, by what he is not, preserving the openness. The unfinished portrait is the honest portrait.

Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Pillar note: Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Miss MacIntosh is the chapter's central marginal figure, and her marginality is precisely what makes the constructed nature of normality visible.

She is unmarried in a chapter obsessed with marriage as natural law: "All the creatures of the earth, all the creatures of the air and of the water were married". Her unmarried state is framed as misfortune, "No man was ever tempted by her", but this framing itself reveals the violence of the norm. She is the evidence that the universal is not universal.

Her body is the most radical site of marginality. The absent eyebrows, the probable wig, the missing ovaries: her body does not conform to the female body that marriage discourse requires. She is, in the most literal sense, a woman whose body refuses the categories assigned to it.

Her anti-British oxfords, British shoes worn by an anti-British woman, perform the same logic: she cannot exist outside the categories she rejects. The marginal person is constituted by the categories they exceed.

The blind violinist and the deaf dancer who miss the train extend this: figures defined by the absence of the sense their art requires, who cannot arrive because one "hearing its whistle but not seeing it, one seeing it but not hearing its whistle", marginality as the structural condition of the world, not the exception to it.

Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

Pillar note: Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

The past does not recede in this chapter. It accumulates as pressure.

What Cheer, Iowa is the deepest sediment: "Everything had to be as it had been in What Cheer". Miss MacIntosh's childhood (frozen feet, flour-bag underwear, the broken nose from the bus accident) is not past. It is the ground on which every present action stands. She reproduces it compulsively.

The schoolroom is the chapter's most explicit image of sedimentary time: "The same cracked blackboards lined the walls. There were maps of sunken continents...The same proverbs were framed in frames of peeling gold". Sunken continents on the walls. The past is not behind them; it is beneath them, mapped and present.

The turtle Solomon, "quite ancient, one who might have carried, as in some legendary preadamite time, the whole world on his back", is the image of sedimentary time made flesh: the preadamite past, still moving, still carrying its flower pot, still scraping against Miss MacIntosh's nerves.

The genealogies Vera must memorize, "the sons of Levi, Judah, Er, Onan, Issachar, the sons of Tola, Phuvah, Zebulun", are pure sedimentation: names deposited layer upon layer, required to be carried forward without understanding, pressing up through the present as obligation.

Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

Pillar note: Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

Miss MacIntosh's language is the chapter's most sustained demonstration that language shapes what can exist.

Her speech is a continuous act of world-construction through naming and categorizing: "Locate my scissors, and locate the Grand Canyon, and don't point to the map of Africa, for that's not where it is". Geography is language. To name correctly is to constitute reality. To point wrongly is to be wrong about the world.

Her nautical metaphors, "trimming her sails," "scudding along," "never becalmed", construct her as a sailor who has never been to sea. The language performs a self that her circumstances cannot support. She is "the land-locked sailor": language building what reality denies.

The word "What Cheer" is the chapter's most loaded linguistic construction. It names a real Iowa town, but in the text it functions as a signifier for undeceived normalcy, cheerful practicality, the real. Vera notes: "Cheerful, I supposed she had been in What Cheer, and always skipping a rope", the name generates the fantasy. Language creates the place that justifies the discipline.

Most precisely: Miss MacIntosh insists that "the dream was always the lie", but this is itself a linguistic act, a declaration that one category (dream) maps onto another (lie). Language is not reporting a pre-existing distinction. It is making one.

Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

Pillar note: Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

The sacred in this chapter is entirely immanent (located in the specific, the bodily, the ordinary) and it is most present in the moments of greatest apparent ordinariness.

The turtle Solomon carrying a clay flower pot with a red geranium "which smelled like tobacco"; this is the sacred in its precise, unglamorous, immanent form. Ancient enough to have carried the world, now carrying a pot that smells wrong. The transcendent is here, in this specific, slightly comic, entirely present object.

The seagull nursed "beneath her shawl, against the coldness of her breast": the sacred is in the coldness of the breast, the specific texture of the shawl, the wounded leg. Not in the symbolism of the bird but in the body of the woman holding it.

Vera's birthday dance is the chapter's central immanent transcendence: "I danced alone. I danced with my shadow. My hair unbraided, whirling, my cheek shadowed, I could imagine any partner I pleased, for no one else would ever see him, and he was entirely mine". No guests, no music, no partner, and yet this is the most alive moment in the chapter. The transcendent is here, in the empty room, in the shadow, in the entirely private imagination.

When Vera says "I am dancing with Death", Miss MacIntosh replies that Death is not yet. But the sacred is precisely in this anticipation, not in death as metaphysical category but in the fourteen-year-old girl alone in a party dress, already in conversation with it.

Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

Pillar note: Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

The chapter's deepest structure is the crossing of times: Vera is constituted by what was deposited before her, and she is constituting the ground for what comes after, and she exists at the crossing point of these two movements.

She is constituted by: her mother's opium dreams, Miss MacIntosh's What Cheer childhood, the genealogies she memorizes without understanding, the turtle given by a dead guest, the Roman coin from excavators, all of these are deposits she did not choose and cannot refuse.

She is constituting: the imagined husband, the imagined marriage, the imagined voyage on "uncharted seas, the crossbeams crackling like frozen twigs above our heads, sea birds screaming in the many winds, and no shore imaginable". This is the ground she is laying for a future she cannot yet inhabit.

The chapter's opening question, "What terrible deed was this which I had done...not until all the seas are emptied, until the waves fall away from the sea, not even then?", is the crossing point made explicit. The adult narrator is constituted by the child's act (opening her eyes, or failing to keep them closed), and that act reaches forward to the end of the seas. The obligation is not chosen. It runs in both directions through time.

Miss MacIntosh's final words in the chapter, "When thou diest, I shall die with you, the flowers of the fields", name this structural entanglement directly. They will cross together. The carrying continues.
wheel-chapter-70:
Chapter 70

← Chapter 69 · Wheel and Spokes Home · Chapter 71 →

Research notes: Chapter 70 · Reading guide: Guide, Chapter 70

Characters: Joachim Spitzer · Lisa Lunde · Miss MacIntosh · Mr. Res Tacamah · Mrs. Hogden

Pillar 1 Not One Self

Pillar note: Pillar 1 Not One Self

The narrator is never singular. She is simultaneously the child raised by Miss MacIntosh, the absent adult on a bus miles away, the dreamer reconstructing Mrs. Hogden from secondhand reports, and the consciousness that confesses it cannot separate these selves. She openly admits the substitution:

"It was a trick of my imagination, this substituting of the one for the other."

But the plural self extends beyond the narrator. Mrs. Hogden herself refuses singular identity (she is Mrs. Hogden, Mrs. Logden, Mrs. Fogden, Mrs. Hogden-Fogden, Mrs. Logden-Hogden-Dogden) the text proliferates her name as if to demonstrate that naming is itself unstable. She is simultaneously:

  • An arithmetic teacher
  • A possible shoplifter
  • A descendant of Daniel Boone, William the Conqueror, and Alexander Graham Bell
  • A ghost of Miss MacIntosh
  • A gargoyle in progress
  • The mistress of the house she does not own

"Mrs. Hogden or Mrs. Logden? Nobody knew which it was, as nobody thought to ask."

The mother is equally plural; she is present and absent, dead and alive, the person who wrote the letter and the person who denies writing it. Even Mr. Spitzer is doubled: Mrs. Hogden entertains two Mr. Spitzers, alike as peas in a pod. The self in this chapter is not a stable unit but a field of overlapping projections, each claiming primacy, none achieving it.

Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

Pillar note: Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

The entire architecture of this chapter is built on the impossibility of distinguishing the real from the constructed. The central question (did the mother write the letter inviting Mrs. Hogden?) is never resolved. It cannot be resolved, because:

"From nobody else could Mrs. Hogden have learned so much of my mother's most private life."

And yet the mother denies it absolutely. Both things are simultaneously true within the text's logic. The letter exists and does not exist. Mrs. Hogden was invited and was not invited.

The mother's bedroom is protected by a door that plays music when opened: reality is mediated by an aesthetic threshold. Mr. Res Tacamah, believed by Mrs. Hogden to be a shy gentleman caller, is a drug bottle. James the chauffeur, promised to Mrs. Hogden as help, has been in Alaska for a quarter century. The house itself is described as a place where:

"Shadowy figures stepped out of the walls. There were moths with human faces."

This is not presented as pathology. It is presented as the operating condition of the household, and by extension, of consciousness itself. The cave is not outside; it is the house. The house is not outside; it is the mind. The text offers no sunlit exterior.

Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

Pillar note: Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

The chapter is saturated with a grief that never announces itself as grief, which is precisely how the pillar describes it, not as event but as climate.

Miss MacIntosh's absence haunts every sentence about Mrs. Hogden. The narrator is not mourning Miss MacIntosh in this chapter; she has been mourning her continuously, and Mrs. Hogden is the latest weather formation produced by that permanent grief:

"Miss MacIntosh, with a firm hand and a resolute mind and the unswerving ideal of common sense, brought me up to understand..."

"and then it was of her I dreamed the most when she was dead, in fact, of her only."

The grief does not resolve. It recruits new objects. Mrs. Hogden becomes a vessel for the grief about Miss MacIntosh, who was herself perhaps a vessel for something prior. The narrator confesses this directly:

"Perhaps it is wrong to imply companionship where it does not exist or to be betrayed by the apparent similarity of persons who differed so much from each other."

But she cannot stop the substitution. Grief is the mechanism of substitution. The playroom (the physical site of the lost childhood, of Miss MacIntosh) becomes Mrs. Hogden's room, and then becomes empty again, and the narrator stands in it at the end asking:

"Who came here during my absence?"

The question is not really about Mrs. Hogden. It is about Miss MacIntosh. It is about the self that existed before the loss. Grief, here, is the permanent weather of the house, of the narrative, of the prose itself, which never stops circling.

Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

Pillar note: Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

The narrator never meets Mrs. Hogden. This is the chapter's most radical formal choice, and it is a direct enactment of the Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act pillar, but inverted and complicated. The narrator cannot be in the room, and yet she witnesses anyway, through Lisa Lunde, through inference, through imagination, through the evidence left behind. She constructs a complete portrait of a woman she never saw:

"Yes, just by closing my eyes, by concentrating, I could see her now."

This is witnessing as an act of sustained attention across absence. The narrator refuses the easy conclusion that because she did not see Mrs. Hogden, Mrs. Hogden does not matter:

"After all, however, how can we confine our life to our actual life? Mrs. Hogden is important to me for her own sake."

This sentence is a manifesto of the Witness stance. The ethical obligation to see fully is not contingent on physical presence. It is an obligation of consciousness. The narrator stays in the room, the imaginative room, without flinching from Mrs. Hogden's grotesquerie, her smell, her drinking, her delusion, her loneliness, her dignity, her absurdity. She does not simplify her into villain, victim, or comic figure. She holds all of it.

Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

Pillar note: Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

The chapter is itself a recursive structure. The narrator begins by describing a dream-state in a hotel room, moves into memory of Miss MacIntosh, slides into the story of Mrs. Hogden told to her by Lisa Lunde, circles back to Miss MacIntosh, returns to Mrs. Hogden, and ends in the playroom, which is both the physical site of the story and the mental site of the narrator's construction of it.

The blackboard Mrs. Hogden leaves behind is the emblem of recursive construction:

"She would write with a piece of red or yellow chalk on the child's blackboard, four marks crossed by a fifth — as if she were counting off the days, however, not as if she were solving a problem."

She is not solving. She is marking time, building a record of her own presence, knowing it will be chalked over. And indeed the final message on the blackboard is:

"All a’s are b’s, it read—all b’s are c’s—and therefore, dear heart, all a’s are c’s. You know me."

This is a syllogism, the form of logical construction, but it is also a declaration that all substitutions are valid, that the building is made of replaceable parts, that the construction continues regardless. Mrs. Hogden builds her life in the playroom, her island of order amid boxes she never opens, knowing it is temporary, knowing she is unwanted, building anyway.

Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

Pillar note: Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

The chapter refuses every form of conclusion. Mrs. Hogden never teaches arithmetic. The mother never learns it. The narrator never meets Mrs. Hogden. The letter's authorship is never established. Mrs. Hogden's real name is never confirmed. Her past is never disclosed:

"Talking out loud to herself, yet Mrs. Hogden never betrayed who she was or exactly why she had come to my mother's house."

"She was one of those persons who, disappearing from the earth, would have been missed by nobody at all."

Even her departure is shrouded:

"Mrs. Hogden rode away in the mist one day and was never seen again in that district."

The text does not apologize for these non-resolutions. It accumulates them as a form of structural honesty. The demand that Mrs. Hogden be explained, classified, concluded, represented by Lisa Lunde's attempts to fix her as shoplifter or madwoman, is shown to be a failure of perception:

"She was hard to classify. It would be like trying to pick up all her packages from the floor. It would take a life time."

The incompletion is not laziness. It is the text's refusal to commit the violence of false closure against a human being who exceeds every category offered to contain her.

Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Pillar note: Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Mrs. Hogden is a catalog of marginality. She is:

  • Too old to be employable, too present to be dismissed
  • Too poor to be respectable, too confident to be pitied
  • Too real to be a ghost, too strange to be ordinary
  • A teacher who never teaches, a companion who is never companioned
  • A woman wearing four coats, carrying an empty birdcage and birdseed for a bird she does not have

She lives at the edge of every category. The text uses her marginality not to pathologize her but to reveal the constructed nature of the categories themselves. When the servants cannot classify her:

"She was hard to classify... there was something so evasive about her, something that evaded definition."

This is not Mrs. Hogden's failure. It is the failure of classification. She is the evidence that the categories are insufficient. Similarly, Miss MacIntosh, described at the chapter's end as "neither man nor woman, neither dark nor fair", occupies the same ontological position. Both women live at the margins, and both are where the text's deepest meaning accumulates.

The old man who stole egg-beaters because they brought him closer to his dead wife belongs to the same ontology. His behavior is irrational by any utilitarian standard, and yet the narrator treats it with complete seriousness. The marginal act reveals the marginal truth: that grief and love operate outside the logic of use.

Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

Pillar note: Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

The playroom is the chapter's central spatial emblem of sedimentary time. It is described as:

"a catch-all for useless or forgotten objects"

containing "my father's most useless collection, the dolls exhumed from children's graves". The room holds the layered past of the household: Miss MacIntosh's physical exercises, the narrator's childhood basting stitches "to hold together surf and shore", the father's European travels, the mother's dreams. Mrs. Hogden moves into this sediment and adds her own layer.

When the narrator stands in the empty playroom at the end:

"The white dust was streaked with wheeling footprints as if someone had walked around and around, slapping her hands — Miss MacIntosh, doing her physical exercise."

Miss MacIntosh's footprints are still in the dust. She left years ago. She is still pressing up through the ground. The sediment is literal (dust, footprints, whiskey bottles, apple cores, broken egg shells, the artificial eyelash) each layer deposited by a different inhabitant, none of them gone.

Time in this chapter does not move forward. It accumulates downward. The mother's dreams contain the past; the playroom contains the past; the narrator's consciousness contains the past. The present moment is always already composed of everything that preceded it.

Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

Pillar note: Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

The chapter's language is relentlessly self-aware about its own constructedness. The narrator constantly marks the limits of her knowledge:

"Perhaps I slept for a while, or perhaps I dreamed. Perhaps I was awake and dreaming of the past..."

"Who could tell?"

"Is it possible that any life can be the surface impression only, just no more than it seems to others?"

The proliferation of Mrs. Hogden's names (Hogden, Logden, Fogden, Bogden, Dogden) is a linguistic enactment of the pillar's claim. The name is not a stable referent. It is a sound that shifts. The text uses this not as error but as philosophical demonstration: if the name is unstable, the person named is constructed, and if the person is constructed, so is the reality in which she lives.

The final blackboard message is the chapter's most explicit statement about language as construction:

"All a’s are b’s, it read—all b’s are c’s—and therefore, dear heart, all a’s are c’s. You know me."

This is a logical syllogism, the most formal structure of language, used to say something that exceeds logic: that substitution is valid, that one person can stand for another, that the narrator knows Mrs. Hogden despite never having seen her. Language here names its own location: it speaks from the position of radical uncertainty and calls that uncertainty knowledge.

Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

Pillar note: Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

The chapter's most striking formal feature is its treatment of Mrs. Hogden's grotesque body and chaotic possessions as sacred material. The description of her arrival (four coats, Javanese temple bells, empty birdcage, tape measure around her neck, lemon-colored gloves with twisted strings) is rendered with the same reverence and attention as a liturgical procession.

The text explicitly reaches toward transcendence through the ordinary:

"God, if there is a God, cannot know everything, any more than Mrs. Hogden-Fogden could, poor soul. There must be at least one small, warped flower growing, I believe, contrary to the ideal of unity, outside the consciousness of God, outside His field — and that would be the crucial flower, of course, the important one."

The sacred is not in the transcendent unity. It is in the warped flower outside the field: the exception, the marginal, the overlooked. Mrs. Hogden herself is that warped flower. Her temple bells whisper as she speaks. Her radio, running down, produces voices that she hears as company. Her chess games, played alone, produce genuine tears. These are not parodies of the sacred. They are the sacred in its immanent form: found in the creaturely, the lonely, the absurd.

The Arctic tern that visited her every year at the Dutch windmill, "compelled by his own nature to circle the earth from pole to pole as if he were some kind of minor planet on its course in the starry endless heavens", is another figure of immanent transcendence. The cosmic and the domestic are not separate registers. The tern is both a bird and a cosmological force, and Mrs. Hogden is both a fat old woman and the person the cosmos singles out for its annual attention.

Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

Pillar note: Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

The chapter's final movement enacts the Crossing Point with extraordinary precision. The narrator stands in the playroom (physically absent from the house during the events described, now returned) and finds herself at the intersection of multiple temporal streams:

  • Miss MacIntosh's footprints in the dust
  • Mrs. Hogden's derelict whiskey bottles and apple cores
  • The narrator's own childhood, embedded in the room's objects
  • The blackboard message addressed to someone who is not quite her

"As if Mrs. Hogden, whoever she was, had guessed who it was I would be looking for — but I was Lisa Lunde, she had mistakenly supposed — she had written a message on the little three-legged blackboard..."

The message was meant for Lisa Lunde. It reaches the narrator. The substitution, the very substitution the chapter has been about, is enacted one final time. The narrator receives a message not addressed to her, from a woman she never met, about a woman (Miss MacIntosh) who left before Mrs. Hogden arrived. She is the crossing point of these temporal and personal streams.

"All a’s are b’s, it read—all b’s are c’s—and therefore, dear heart, all a’s are c’s. You know me."

This is the Crossing Point articulated as logic. The narrator is constituted by what was deposited before she arrived: Miss MacIntosh's lessons, her mother's dreams, Mrs. Hogden's brief habitation of the room. She is also constituting the ground for whoever reads this text. The "dear heart" addressed on the blackboard is not Lisa Lunde. It is the reader. The carrying continues.
wheel-chapter-53:
Chapter 53

← Chapter 52 · Wheel and Spokes Home · Chapter 54 →

Research notes: Chapter 53 · Reading guide: Guide, Chapter 53

Characters: Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer

Pillar 1 Not One Self

Pillar note: Pillar 1 Not One Self

"if other people...did not always know which brother he was, how should he know, with absolute certainty, that he was Joachim"

The novel does not treat Mr. Spitzer's identity confusion as psychological pathology. It treats it as ontological truth. He is simultaneously:

  • Joachim the composer
  • Peron the gambler (in others' eyes)
  • The mourner
  • The lawyer
  • The ghost
  • The survivor who suspects he is the one who died

"he lived in two worlds at once, though in neither world was he at home, and he was only his sad visitor"

The phrase "sad visitor" is crucial. He does not inhabit himself; he visits himself. The self is not a home but a transit point. This is Not One Self not as philosophical abstraction but as lived, daily, exhausting experience. He cannot even change his clothing without risking becoming someone else entirely:

"he would be afraid to wear any other clothing — for fear he should put on a different body and lead an altogether different life"

Clothing, here, is not metaphor. It is ontological infrastructure. The self is assembled from external materials. Change the materials, change the self. This is Radical Immanence's Not One Self at its most literal.

Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

Pillar note: Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

"what a pity it would be for all of us...if we had not lived also through a mistaken dream"

This single sentence is perhaps the most direct statement of Pillar 2 in the entire chapter. Young argues not merely that illusion is unavoidable but that it is constitutive: that a life lived only through verified experience would be an impoverished, diminished life. The mistaken dream is not the enemy of the real. It is the real.

The chapter multiplies illusions deliberately:

  • People mistake Joachim for Peron
  • Joachim mistakes himself for Peron
  • The city of Boston contains ships "he had supposed were sunken in far seas"
  • Hobble-skirted ladies and Victorian carriages appear in what should be contemporary streets
  • He crosses from Boston to Boston and finds "wild regions of purple mountains"

These are not hallucinations to be corrected. They are the primary texture of experience. The "sunlit world outside the cave" (the fixed, verifiable real) never appears. What appears instead is an endlessly larger cave, more elaborately lit, in which the dead walk alongside the living and the past refuses to become past.

Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

Pillar note: Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

This pillar is perhaps most completely embodied in this chapter. The text never describes grief as a process with an arc. Instead:

"His grief had settled over everything, spreading like an ink blot over a page of his unwritten, most beautiful music"

The ink blot is not a wound that heals. It is a climate condition; it has "settled," it spreads, it takes different shapes (ace of spades, ace of clubs, ace of hearts) but it never lifts. The grief is not for a specific loss at a specific time. It is for:

  • His brother
  • His unwritten music
  • His unlived life
  • His lost youth
  • The love that never answered
  • Himself, whom he may have already buried

"his grief had been diffused, no doubt, having outlived its reason and its object"

This is the most devastating formulation: grief that has outlived its object. It no longer even has a specific referent. It has become the atmosphere itself. Pillar 3 says "the honest life stops pretending otherwise", and Spitzer, for all his evasions, never pretends. He does not claim to be recovering. He claims to be weather.

Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

Pillar note: Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

The narrative stance of this chapter enacts Pillar 4 structurally. The prose does not rush toward resolution. It accumulates, circles, returns, digresses through billiards and boxing and kite-fighting and chess, not to arrive anywhere but to stay in the room with Spitzer's condition.

Spitzer himself is a witness in the most radical sense:

"For he should walk the earth, and he should knock upon all doors, all ivory doors. He should stare through every window. He should stand upon every street corner"

He watches. He searches. He does not fix. He cannot fix. His entire existence is an act of sustained, unresolved attention: to his brother's absence, to the city's layered times, to the faces of strangers who may or may not be Peron.

The chapter's catalogue of sports knowledge (boxers, billiard players, wrestlers, golfers) is itself an act of witnessing. Spitzer accumulates these figures not to judge them or resolve their stories but simply to hold them:

"Poor fellows — all! And who would not pity them? Mr. Spitzer did — in his own sad, empty way — though yet his sympathy was one and the same as his indifference"

This is the Witness in its most honest form: sympathy that does not pretend to rescue, attention that does not pretend to change. "Sympathy...one and the same as his indifference"; this is not coldness. It is the recognition that true witnessing does not alter what it sees.

Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

Pillar note: Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

"There were only these poor notes, marked by many segnos, many signs like his S which concealed other signs"

The segno in musical notation literally means "sign"; it marks a point to which the player returns. The music is structurally recursive: you build forward, you return, you build again. Spitzer's entire compositional and existential method is recursive:

  • He wanders the city and returns to the same corners
  • He thinks through the same problems of identity and never resolves them
  • He builds toward "crescendos of unbelievable climax" that are "saved for finales" that never arrive
  • He sets the breakfast table for two every morning, knowing Peron will not come

"he had achieved perhaps more than he had wished to achieve"

The building continues even when the builder doesn't intend it. The recursive construction is not chosen; it is structural. He returns to the beginning because there is no other movement available. This is Pillar 5's "you build anyway, knowing the building is provisional", except here, the builder is barely aware he is building. The building happens through him.

Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

Pillar note: Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

The unfinished music is the central symbol of the entire chapter:

"this lost musician with his unfinished song"

"too timid a composer to write a music which could be heard"

"the music not written for the ears of living men — and perhaps...not even for the dead, who were equally indifferent"

The incompletion here operates on multiple levels simultaneously:

  1. The music is unfinished because life interrupted it 2. The music is unfinished because it was always already beyond the reach of any keyboard that exists 3. The music is unfinished because completion would be a kind of death: the chess player who refuses to move his knight because "having moved his man, he would never move again" 4. The self is unfinished because identity is never resolved 5. The grief is unfinished because it has no terminus

The chapter explicitly frames the demand for completion as violence:

"like that mad man who had waited all his life to make one move toward final victory because it would be his absolute, final defeat, his death"

Completion = death. The unfinished is not failure; it is the condition of continued existence. Pillar 6's "integrity looks like the ongoing sentence, not the concluded one" is here made literal: the chapter itself is one enormous ongoing sentence, grammatically and philosophically refusing to conclude.

Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Pillar note: Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

The chapter is populated almost entirely by marginal figures, not as local color but as epistemological evidence:

  • The old billiard-hall king who miscued and drowned himself
  • The politician who died in a shelter house, discovered post-mortem to have been a woman
  • The featherweight who killed a man by touching him lightly, then retired forever
  • The fighter who thought he was battling his father's ghost
  • Old fighters on Skid Row, "babbling like old infants in the storm"
  • The baseball player who thought he was a football player carrying the moon

These figures are not exceptions to the social order. They are, as Pillar 7 states, the evidence: the places where the constructed nature of identity, gender, victory, and selfhood becomes most visible. The politician-woman is the most explicit case:

"His political cronies did not know whether he should be buried as a woman or as a man"

The categories fail at the margin. And Spitzer himself (twin, ghost, musician-lawyer, living-dead) is the supreme marginal figure, the one whose existence makes the constructed nature of every category visible.

Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

Pillar note: Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

This pillar may be most perfectly illustrated in the chapter's treatment of Boston:

"he was crossing strange frontiers — that this was not New England as he knew it — that these were wild regions of purple mountains...castles perched upon inaccessible peaks"

The city is not one time. It is all its times simultaneously, pressing upward through the present. Victorian carriages share streets with modern traffic. Ships "supposed were sunken in far seas" sail the harbor. Ladies in hobble skirts pass alongside "old gentlemen with faces the color of pumice stone".

The sedimentary metaphor becomes explicit in the treatment of Spitzer's knowledge:

"a knowledge seeming to spurt up from some underground, hidden source — perhaps his dead sportsman brother's realm"

The dead brother's knowledge literally rises through the living brother. Peron is in the sediment beneath Joachim. His gambling world, his sporting contacts, his shady acquaintances: all of it presses up through Joachim's consciousness unbidden. The past is not behind him. It is beneath him, and it erupts.

"Whole centuries might be a baby’s cry in the darkness"

Time is not linear progression but compression: centuries collapsed into a cry, a moment expanded into eternity. This is sedimentary time: not a river flowing past but layers accumulating, each one still present, still pressing.

Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

Pillar note: Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

The prose style itself enacts Pillar 9. Young's sentences are extraordinarily long, recursive, hedged, qualified; they perform the instability of language rather than pretending to transparent description:

"Sometimes it seemed to old Joachim that only one piano key was missing...sometimes that he had no keyboard, not even the pale, foaming, starlighted surf rolling on a distant shore"

"Sometimes...sometimes": the language refuses to fix. It names its own uncertainty, its own location in a consciousness that cannot stabilize its perceptions.

The chapter also contains a remarkable meditation on the way language categories fail:

he "knew that tallyho was a term in hunting and not in golf—that archery was employed originally only in hunting...that fistmele, which he might at one time have supposed was a term in boxing, was a term in archery"

This is not trivia. This is a sustained demonstration that words do not naturally belong to their referents; they are assigned, reassigned, confused, mistaken. Language is a system of provisional placements, not a map of fixed truths. Spitzer's entire knowledge-base is a comedy of misapplied categories, words that have wandered from their domains.

Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

Pillar note: Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

The chapter reaches repeatedly for transcendence (the music of the spheres, the singing stars, immortal love, the vast overture of finality) and locates it consistently inside the ordinary world, not beyond it:

"the logical music which should be played in empty halls"

Not in heaven. In empty halls. The transcendent music is immanent; it belongs to this world's spaces, even if no living ears can hear it.

"the slow city lamps went on one by one like the slow stars of a returning consciousness"

The city lamps are the stars. The transcendent is not elsewhere; it is the ordinary seen with full attention. The swan boats on the Public Gardens, the black swans quarreling with white swans, the purple balloon vendor, the coin for the ferryman; these are the sacred objects of this chapter. Not symbols pointing beyond themselves, but things dense with immanent significance.

"the sacred is here, inside the ordinary world, pointing deeper into the immanent"

Spitzer's entire life is this pointing (his music, his grief, his love for his brother, his walks through Boston) all of it pointing deeper into the world rather than out of it. The opium lady's face appears "in every cloud conformation or rippling shadow": the beloved is not in heaven but in the weather, in the water, in the light.

Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

Pillar note: Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

This is perhaps the pillar that most completely describes Spitzer's metaphysical situation:

"as if his brother's train should pull out just as Mr. Spitzer's train pulled in...he would always miss connections"

Spitzer is the crossing point: the place where his brother's life and his own intersect without meeting, where the living and the dead share the same streets without touching, where past Boston and present Boston occupy the same geography.

"he was constituted by what was deposited before you arrived, and you are constituting the ground the not-yet-born will stand on"

This is enacted in Spitzer's relationship to his brother's debts, his brother's acquaintances, his brother's knowledge: all of it deposited in Joachim by Peron's life and death:

"He was simply amazed that he seemed to know, perhaps because of his dead brother whose circle had been a good deal larger than his own"

He did not choose to carry this knowledge. It was structurally deposited in him by the fact of being Peron's twin. And he carries it forward (paying Peron's debts, tipping his hat at Cockerel Church in memory of him, setting the table for two) constituting the ground on which Peron's memory continues to exist.

"the individual should not die so long as one remembered him"

This is the Crossing Point's ethics made explicit: the obligation to carry is not chosen. It is structural. Joachim is the place where Peron crosses from death back into the world. Without Joachim's memory, his grief, his daily acts of commemoration, Peron ceases entirely. The carrying continues.
wheel-chapter-05:
Chapter 5

← Chapter 4 · Wheel and Spokes Home · Chapter 6 →

Research notes: Chapter 5 · Reading guide: Guide, Chapter 5

Pillar 1 Not One Self

Pillar note: Pillar 1 Not One Self

The bus-driver is irreducibly multiple. He is simultaneously:

  • The driver of an actual bus through flooding roads
  • A man lying in a four-posted bed at the old hotel
  • His mother's baby, still crying in her arms
  • Penelope, weaving rather than wandering
  • A potential Arctic whaler
  • A corpse who "died in his sleep two or three years ago"

The text does not resolve these into one. It insists on their simultaneity: "perhaps he only thought he was the bus-driver...and he was just turning and tossing upon his feather mattress". The narrator never adjudicates. The self here is not fragmented: fragmentation implies an original wholeness that broke. This self was always already plural, always already irresolvable.

The bus-driver himself names this multiplicity when he says he is "only thinking he was the bus-driver", not that he is confused about who he is, but that identity is itself a provisional act of thinking, subject to revision, never settled.

Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

Pillar note: Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

The chapter is architecturally committed to the undecidability of reality. The old doctor's patients may or may not exist. The pregnant woman on the bus may or may not be real. The bus itself may or may not be moving:

"perhaps he only thought he was the bus-driver...steering his old bus through the roaring floods while all the time he was at home in his four-postered bed"

But crucially, the text does not offer the bed as the real answer and the bus as the illusion. Both are held with equal ontological weight. The doctor's "imaginary birth" and the bus-driver's "crazy dreams" are not contrasted with a stable reality; they are the only reality available.

The cave metaphor from the pillar is literalized here: the bus moves through permanent darkness, rain, and mist, past "vanished orchards" and "places which were no more but only in his imagination". There is no sunlit destination. There is only the larger cave of the journey itself, "more carefully lit" by the bus-driver's burning hair and the occasional "far light [that] twinkled like a tired star".

Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

Pillar note: Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

The chapter's weather is not metaphorical. It is ontological. The rain does not stop:

"though now the rain seemed only to hover, pebbling the grey sky as with pebbles in a brook"

And later:

"'It ain't going to rain no more, no more,' the bus-driver sang in the midst of the driving rain, now pouring like a deluge."

This is grief as permanent weather made explicit: the song denying rain is sung inside the rain. The denial is not delusion; it is the human gesture of continuing to speak inside the grief that never resolves.

The losses accumulate without resolution: the mother who thinks her son is still a baby, the old doctor's patients who are dead and cannot pay, the "vanished orchards", the "filling station that was always closed", the barber shop covered in spiders' webs. Nothing is recovered. Nothing is mourned and then set aside. The text holds every loss simultaneously, layered, present.

The bus-driver's political grief, his refusal to cut his hair until Roosevelt leaves office, is formally identical to every other grief in the chapter: it does not move toward resolution. It accumulates as hair accumulates, as snow accumulates on branches, as the dead accumulate beneath the living.

Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

Pillar note: Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

The narrator of this chapter occupies the position of pure witness. They ask "How much longer?" and "Why don't you cut your hair?": minimal interventions that function not as attempts to change anything but as invitations for the monologue to continue. The narrator does not judge, does not conclude, does not flinch from the bus-driver's drunkenness, his political rants, his terror, his grief.

This is the ethics of witness enacted structurally. The prose itself refuses to simplify. When the bus-driver describes people buried alive:

"Sometimes only their hands reached out from their graves, their hands holding great clumps of human hair which they had torn out of their heads"

The narrator does not soften this. Does not contextualize it as mere drunken rambling. Does not reassure the reader. The attention stays fully in the room with the image.

The witness position is also morally costly here: staying in the room with this bus-driver means staying with his misogyny, his political rage, his contempt for the pregnant woman, his aggression toward the doctor. The text does not resolve these into acceptable form. The witness holds them as they are.

Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

Pillar note: Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

The chapter's formal structure is recursive construction. The bus-driver circles back repeatedly:

  • To his hair
  • To the doctor
  • To his mother
  • To the Democrats
  • To the same broken landmarks: "the same rail fences broken down and horse

fountains...the filling station that was always closed, the same old barber poles"

Each return brings slightly different freight. The hair that begins as political statement becomes angel, becomes dead mother, becomes Penelope's web, becomes the thing that will keep growing in the grave. The building is never finished; each return adds a layer without resolving the previous ones.

The bus itself enacts recursive construction:

"we must detour a thousand miles, it seemed, to advance one, and we must always go back"

This is not failure of navigation. It is the structural condition of the journey. You build anyway. You return with what you learned. The detour is the road.

Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

Pillar note: Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

The chapter's sentences formally embody incompletion. They accumulate clauses, pile image upon image, refuse to conclude:

"his hair drifting always around him, soft as a cloud, as a feather mattress and a soft pillow, as a bride in a bridal chamber, and his hair would not molt as would this mortal hair, and his hair would grow when nothing else grew"

The "and...and...and" construction is not stylistic excess; it is the honest form for a reality that does not conclude. To end the sentence cleanly would be to lie about what the sentence is describing.

The bus-driver's political oath is also formally incomplete; he swore not to cut his hair until a condition is met that cannot be met from within the journey. The oath has no completion point available. He knows this. He keeps the oath anyway. This is the ethics of incompletion: "keeping also even those promises he had not made".

The unborn passenger, "one as yet unborn", is the figure of structural incompletion itself: present, counted, real, but not yet arrived.

Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Pillar note: Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Every figure in this chapter exists at the edge of categories:

  • The bus-driver: alive or dead? sleeping or driving? sane or mad?
  • The old doctor: practicing or not? his patients real or imaginary?
  • The pregnant woman: her condition real, "everything about her artificial,

everything but the one thing that mattered"

  • The unborn passenger: present but not yet born
  • The mother: dreaming she is young while her son drives a bus

The bus-driver names this explicitly regarding himself: "had died in his sleep two or three years ago and now only thought he was driving this bus". He is the marginal person in the most literal sense, on the margin between living and dead, and it is precisely this marginal position that makes the constructed nature of both categories visible.

The barber (bald, sharpening his razor on pumice stone) is the figure who enforces categorical norms (cut hair = normal man) and is himself the most extreme case of what he would impose. The marginal person reveals the arbitrariness of the center.

Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

Pillar note: Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

This pillar is perhaps most richly developed in the chapter. The past does not recede; it presses upward:

"The past does not recede. It accumulates beneath us, layer on layer."

The text gives us this literally in the image of the buried-alive:

"Sometimes, their graves opening in the spring floods and rains, they were washed up, years afterward...and then it could be seen that they who had been buried alive had torn out their hair"

The past erupts through the ground in the spring floods. The dead return not as ghosts but as geological evidence: their torn hair in their hands, their bald heads testifying to what happened beneath the surface.

The bus-driver's hair is itself sedimentary time; it has been growing since before the Democrats took power, accumulating political history, personal history, maternal history on his body. It is "already longer than it seemed": the past is always deeper than it appears.

The road itself is sedimentary: the bus passes "the places which were no more but only in his imagination, of course, the cherry trees bending and breaking under their weight of snow".
