The vanished orchards are still there, pressing up through the present landscape. The bus-driver navigates by them even as he acknowledges they are gone.

Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

Pillar note: Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

The bus-driver's language is aggressively self-locating. He speaks from a specific position (Republican, motherless, drunken, long-haired, driving) and he knows it:

"I'm no Democrat but just the same old bus-driver I always was, my mother's son"

His political rants are not digressions from the philosophical content; they are the philosophical content. Language that pretends to speak from nowhere is exposed here by a speaker who cannot stop announcing where he speaks from. His location is his obsession.

The doctor's language is equally constructed but from a different position; he speaks the language of medical authority (stethoscope, forceps, prescriptions) from an empty office, to patients who may not exist. His language constructs a practice. The bus-driver's language constructs a self.

The text's own language is self-conscious about its constructedness: the similes pile up and contradict each other ("soft as a cloud, as a feather mattress and a soft pillow, as a bride in a bridal chamber") in a way that draws attention to the act of comparison itself. Language here is not finding the right metaphor. It is accumulating metaphors until the act of metaphor-making becomes visible.

Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

Pillar note: Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

This pillar is the chapter's spiritual center. The sacred is located precisely in the grey bus, the drunken driver, the flooding roads:

"the elegiac music of the spheres or with those heavenly harmonies no mortal ears could hear, the angels accompanying those spheres down the accustomed road, the great dolphins uplifting the stone boats of the dead upon the turbulent waves"

But this transcendence is immediately grounded: "for he was only, somewhat erratic, this wild-eyed bus-driver, driving his stuttering and wheezing bus through the roaring spring floods". The angels and dolphins and music of the spheres are not elsewhere. They are in the bus. They are the bus.

The bus-driver's hair is his angel. His dead mother lives in him. The sacred is not above the grey miles; it is in the grey miles, in the permanent rain, in the drunken singing, in the burning eyes in the matted hair.

The chapter's most explicit statement of immanent transcendence comes in the bus-driver's prayer-like address:

"Giddy up, giddy up, little cherub dogs...Giddy up, little rabbits, little stars, for we are coming home...and Papa is very drunk."

The cherubs are addressed as if they are horses. The sacred is harnessed to the mundane. This is not blasphemy. It is the correct theological position of the chapter: the sacred lives here, in the harness, in the drunk voice, in the coming home.

Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

Pillar note: Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

The bus-driver is explicitly constituted by what was deposited before he arrived and is constituting the ground for what comes after. His mother deposited his hair: "His hair, of course, had come from the distaff side". The dead doctor brought him into the world: "You brought me into this world, and now would you take me out of it?". He carries the promises he made before he could understand them: "those promises he had made when he was too young to know what the promises were".

And he is constituting the ground for the unborn passenger: the "one as yet unborn" who is already being carried, already counted among the four passengers, already present in the bus that may or may not be moving.

The crossing point is literalized in the rear-view mirror:

"I can see what's coming from before, behind, having this rear mirror view"

This is the structural position of the crossing point exactly: you see what is coming by looking at what is behind. You are where time crosses itself. The bus-driver sees forward through the windshield and backward through the mirror simultaneously, not as a metaphor for time, but as the literal form of his navigation.

The chapter closes with the sky "suddenly reddened as if with a sudden but hallucinatory dawn": a dawn that is immediately "fading", that illuminates bare branches and distant hills before disappearing. This is the crossing point as image: the moment of illumination that is already passing, that shows us the sediment and the structure and the distance, and then withdraws, leaving us still on the road, still in the bus, still carrying the passengers, the living and the unborn alike.

Chapter 61: Radical Immanence in the World of Mr. Spitzer: A Philosophical Analysis

← Chapter 60 · Wheel and Spokes Home · Chapter 62 →

Research notes: Chapter 61 · Reading guide: Guide, Chapter 61

Characters: Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer

Preface: The Chapter as Philosophical Object

This chapter from what appears to be Marguerite Young's Miss MacIntosh, My Darling is not merely a narrative about an eccentric mourner and a deaf-mute burying a frog. It is a sustained philosophical performance: a prose enactment of precisely the conditions described by the Eleven Pillars of Radical Immanence. The chapter does not illustrate these ideas from outside; it is them, structurally and linguistically. To analyze it through this philosophy is to discover that the philosophy was already living inside the prose, unnamed.

Pillar 1 Not One Self; You are not one person

Pillar note: Pillar 1 Not One Self

Mr. Spitzer is constitutionally multiple. His night is his day, his day his night, his beginning his end, his end his beginning. This is not poetic paradox deployed for ornament. It is the ontological condition of his selfhood. He cannot be located at a single coordinate.

He is simultaneously:

  • A mourner at a frog's funeral
  • A lawyer who has presented his last case and cannot remember the decision
  • A musician whose music no one has heard
  • A brother to a dead twin, himself arguably already dead
  • A dreamer who may be dreaming this entire episode

The chapter makes the plurality explicit when it describes him as uncertain whether he is "the creator or the creation which should perilously endure". This is not a rhetorical question. It is the genuine condition of a self that cannot stabilize into singularity. He forgets "from moment to mortal moment the music he had immortalized": meaning that even his own interiority is not continuous, not retrievable, not one.

Most strikingly, his dead brother Peron haunts the chapter as a kind of shadow-self, a second person who was always already part of him. The twin structure is described as "two born at a birth or so closely related that they were the same in death". Mr. Spitzer is the living brother who remained: "even like the body without the soul or the soul without the body". He is literally half a self, the remainder of a plural entity that death has not resolved but only redistributed.

Even his physical presence is described as a "mere facade of a dead musician, pointing his dead fingers to which a starfish clung". The facade is not a mask over a real self. The facade is the self. There is no interior solid person behind the flowing cape and the rustling musical manuscripts. He is surfaces, accumulations, echoes.

Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed: Reality is what we make

Pillar note: Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

The chapter is saturated with the deliberate confusion of reflection and original, image and thing. Mr. Spitzer consistently cannot distinguish between the real and its shadow:

"perhaps all were reflections, and there was no other image"

This is not described as a failure of perception or a symptom of his grief. It is offered as a genuine epistemological position. The chapter asks whether there is any image that is not a reflection of a reflection. The answer it gives is: probably not.

The meadow where the frog is buried is described with extraordinary hallucinatory precision (hundreds of named plants, birds, streams, insects) and yet the whole landscape has a dreamlike quality, an excess of detail that paradoxically makes it less real rather than more. This is the logic of the constructed real: the more elaborately you build it, the more visible the building becomes.

The cave metaphor from the Eleven Pillars appears almost literally:

"hallucinatory spires painted upon the fog, hallucinatory carriages and carriage wheels"

The city is explicitly hallucinatory. Its spires are painted; that is, constructed representations, not solid architecture. And yet Mr. Spitzer lives in this city, navigates it, mourns in it. The hallucinatory is not contrasted with the real. It is the real, more carefully lit.

The frog itself, the instrument of the mute's voice, is the chapter's central figure for constructed reality. The frog speaks the Lord's Prayer, asks for a light, gives racing tips, requests coins. Each of these is a real communication that is simultaneously an illusion: a frog's croak shaped by labial and laryngeal manipulation into the appearance of human speech. The chapter never resolves whether this is miracle or mechanism. It holds both.

Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End: The climate of a world where everything is always already changing

Pillar note: Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

This pillar is perhaps the most completely enacted of all eleven. Grief in this chapter is not a response to a specific loss. It is the atmospheric condition of existence.

Mr. Spitzer mourns:

  • The frog
  • His dead brother Peron
  • His own youth
  • The brevity of life generally
  • The mute's voicelessness
  • His own unheard music
  • The death of all things, frogs and men alike

These griefs do not compete with each other or take turns. They are simultaneous, layered, climatological. The chapter says explicitly:

"Such was mortality that all must die, of course, both frogs and men, and all must go through death's great metamorphosis"

But this is not consolation. The universality of death does not diminish the grief; it expands it to encompass everything. Mr. Spitzer is described as one who "if only a frog had died in all the world, if no one else had ever died...would still have been the universal mourner". He is constitutionally a mourner. Grief is not his reaction to events. It is his mode of being.

The chapter also refuses the stages of grief entirely. There is no movement toward acceptance, no arc of healing. The frog died "long ago under the blind moon", yet the mourning is as present as ever, as immediate as the rain. The past does not recede. It accumulates.

Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act: Stay in the room. See fully. Refuse to simplify.

Pillar note: Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

Mr. Spitzer is the chapter's witness figure, but he is a witness of a very particular and philosophically precise kind. He does not interpret what he sees. He does not resolve it. He attends to it with an almost unbearable thoroughness.

The catalogue of plants at the frog's burial ground is the most extreme example. The list: milkwort, cockscomb, moonwort, Dutchman's pipes, Dutchman's breeches, jack-in-the-pulpit, coneflowers, fringed orchis, hedge hyssop, nightshade, heliotrope, cattails, oxlip, bladder campion, frog lilies, snakeroot, crowfoot, couch grass, crab grass, pectoral grass, mouse-ear, snakemouth, yellow marsh mallows, large periwinkle, pennyroyal, marsh flags, star grass, starflowers: goes on for a full paragraph. This is not decoration. This is the practice of witness. Every plant is named. Nothing is generalized into "wildflowers" or "vegetation." The world is attended to in its full particularity.

The same witnessing is applied to the mute's sign language at the graveside, where Mr. Spitzer watches and catalogs every gesture: sign of the cross, sign of man, signs of North and South and East and West, sign of the hour hand, sign of the minute hand, sign of the quick and the dead, sign of prayer, sign of meeting, sign of parting, sign of flight, without claiming to fully understand them. He witnesses without concluding. He sees without resolving. The ethical weight of this witnessing is made explicit when Mr. Spitzer accompanies the mute on the long journey to the burial ground, not because he is obligated to, not because he knows the mute well, but because:

he "had been ruled by his sympathies which had made him offer himself as mourner in the first place. For who else would express the mute’s grief?"

The Witness does not fix. The Witness stays. Mr. Spitzer stays, even when his Congress gaiter breaks and drags, even when his trousers are splattered with mud, even when he is slightly irritated by the long route. He stays because attention is the practice.

Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary; You build anyway, knowing the building is provisional

Pillar note: Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

Mr. Spitzer builds music. He builds it constantly, compulsively, on every available surface:

"his starched white shirt front or the white cuff of his sleeve or his black-bordered handkerchief...or his crumpled calling cards or marble table tops in public restaurants or paper lace napkins...or crumbling city walls or the sands of the sea before the tides came in"

The building is explicitly provisional. The tide comes in. The napkins crumple. The calling cards are lost. He scatters his manuscripts "all over Boston and sometimes Philadelphia and sometimes Trenton, Camden, Asbury Park", forgotten by him and noticed only by janitors and street-cleaners and beachcombers.

Yet he continues. He builds not despite the provisionality but within it. The chapter describes him composing an elegy for the mute while the mute is still alive, "feeling quite disloyal, as if he anticipated an event which might never take place." He builds the memorial before the death. He begins again before the ending. This is recursive construction in its purest form: the return to the beginning with what was learned, the building that is never finished.

The chapter also performs recursive construction formally, in its prose. Sentences return to their beginnings, clauses loop back through earlier clauses, images recur in slightly altered form. The opening paradox, "his night was his day, and his day was his night", is itself a recursive structure, a sentence that builds and then returns to its starting point transformed.

Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest: The unfinished is not failure

Pillar note: Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

The chapter is built around incompletions. Mr. Spitzer's music is never performed. His elegy for the frog is improvised, half-croaked, lost in the wind. His legal career has ended with a case whose decision he cannot remember. His twin brother is dead, leaving the self permanently incomplete.

The chapter explicitly philosophizes this incompletion:

"Half should always be omitted, Mr. Spitzer thought — perhaps less than half, perhaps more than half. As to which there should be, he was never quite clear"

This is not resignation. It is a principled position about the nature of honest expression. The demand for completion (the concluded sentence, the resolved grief, the finished symphony) is itself named as a kind of violence, or at least as a falsification. The ongoing sentence is the honest one.

The mute's sign language enacts this formally. His signs are "signs which Mr. Spitzer had not understood", signs that exceed interpretation, signs for which there is no grammar. The communication is real, something is being expressed, but it is never completed into meaning. The ethical response is not to demand completion but to witness the expression in its incompleteness.

Even Mr. Spitzer's eulogy for the frog trails off:

"Indeed, Mr. Spitzer must have said much else which he had forgotten now"

The elegy is incomplete. The forgetting is not a failure. It is the condition of all elegies, all memorials, all attempts to hold what is already dissolving.

Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth: The edges of categories are where the constructed nature of reality becomes most visible

Pillar note: Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

The chapter is populated almost exclusively by marginal figures, and each one is marginal in a way that illuminates the constructed nature of the categories they fall outside:

The frog-musician: Not human, not merely animal. A frog trained to speak human language, to ask for a match, to give racing tips, to recite the Lord's Prayer. The frog occupies the margin between animal and human, between nature and culture, between the sacred (Lord's Prayer) and the mundane (a racing tip). At this margin, the categories themselves become visible as constructions.

The mute: Neither fully in the world of sound nor fully outside it. He communicates through signs, through a frog's voice, through the trembling of his throat cords. He is marginal to language, and his marginality reveals that language is not a natural fact but a constructed system from which some are structurally excluded.

Mr. Spitzer himself: A musician whose music is never heard, a lawyer who no longer practices, a living man who is arguably already dead, a twin who is half of a self. He occupies the margin between life and death, between sound and silence, between existence and non-existence. The chapter describes him as "a mere facade of a dead musician": a person at the margin of personhood.

The frog's funeral: A funeral for an animal, conducted with the full seriousness of human burial ritual, silver spoon, cigar box coffin with silver foil and black cross, a red rose dropped into the grave, a eulogy. The ceremony occupies the margin between the sacred and the absurd, and at that margin reveals that all funeral ceremony is constructed, that the distinction between a meaningful death and a meaningless one is a human imposition.

The chapter makes this explicit in Mr. Spitzer's meditation on burial rites (Etruscans, Eskimos, Indians, Egyptians) which demonstrates that every culture constructs its own version of the sacred passage, and that none has priority.

Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away: The past accumulates beneath us, still pressing up

Pillar note: Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

This pillar is enacted in the chapter's very prose texture. The past does not recede in this chapter. It presses up through every paragraph.

Mr. Spitzer's dead brother is present throughout, not as a memory that is visited and then set aside, but as a continuous pressure on the present. When he hears the bull frog croaking "too deep, too deep", he immediately thinks of his brother, and the chapter spirals into a meditation on whether "too, to, two" (adverb, preposition, or noun) and whether the two brothers were "the same in death, going together". The brother is not behind him. He is beneath him, pressing up.

The chapter also figures sedimentary time through its geological and oceanic imagery. Sea shells are described as having traveled from the Arctic to the Antarctic, from China beaches to Atlantic shores, "sometimes pulverized by friction of waves and wind before they reached their journey's end". The sea shell carries its entire journey in its form. It is made of its accumulated passage.

Mr. Spitzer himself is described in these terms. His coat lining is "lined with music, the great symphony", his hat stuffed with musical movements and notes. He is literally a sedimentary figure, layered with accumulated composition, carrying his entire history in his person.

The chapter also figures this through the Etruscan burial meditation, where the dead are described as sleeping in their houses with mirrors in their hands and stone ferrets at their feet and "submarine memories painted on the walls." The dead carry their memories into death. The past does not stop when the person stops. It continues, deposited, pressing up.

Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible: Honest language names its own location

Pillar note: Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

The chapter is acutely conscious of the constructedness of language. This consciousness is most concentrated in the meditation on the bull frog's croaking:

"For it would make a great difference in the meaning, Mr. Spitzer believed, as to whether it was too, to, two — adverb or preposition or noun"

This is not wordplay. It is a genuine philosophical claim: that the same sound carries entirely different meanings depending on which grammatical construction you impose on it, and that there is no neutral, pre-linguistic reality that determines which construction is correct. Language shapes what can be seen.

The chapter extends this to the mute's sign language, which is described as:

"silence being filled with ambiguities like the sign language of God Who created heaven and earth, these hieroglyphic birds and beasts and flowers and men walking on stilts"

God's creation is itself a sign language: a constructed system of meaning that is filled with ambiguities. The natural world is not a transparent reality but a text, and like all texts, it is subject to misreading, over-reading, under-reading.

The chapter also demonstrates that language excludes as much as it includes. The mute is excluded from the English-speaking world, but the chapter imagines this exclusion multiplied:

"what more pitiful than to be a Spanish deaf mute lip-reader in Boston or a Persian deaf mute in this grey city of the moving lips"

The person who cannot access the dominant language is not simply inconvenienced. They are, in a real sense, unable to exist in the social world that language constructs. The mute's silence is not merely personal. It is structural.

Mr. Spitzer's own musical language participates in this construction. His scores are described as "sometimes unintelligible even to him"; he has constructed a language that even he cannot fully read. The language has exceeded its author.

Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here: The sacred lives inside the ordinary world

Pillar note: Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

The chapter is saturated with the sacred, but the sacred never points outward to a beyond. It points inward, deeper into the immanent.

The frog's funeral is the chapter's central sacred event, and it is conducted with complete seriousness: silver spoon, cigar box coffin, red rose, eulogy, the mute's elaborate sign-language prayers. The sacred is not diminished by being applied to a frog. The frog is not a symbol of something larger. The frog is the thing. The sacred lives in the frog's actual death, the mute's actual grief, the muddy walk through actual marshland.

The chapter's most explicit statement of immanent transcendence comes in Mr. Spitzer's eulogy:

"for thou shalt be a man, little frog, in the next world — and thou shalt have thy musical memories, thy rain music like the water gurgling in the water pipes"

Even the promised afterlife is described in terms of immanent experience: rain music, water gurgling in pipes. The transcendent is imagined as a continuation of the immanent, not an escape from it.

The stars throughout the chapter are described not as a transcendent beyond but as part of the same fabric as the earth: "stars like flying sparks or fireflies reflecting on whirling pools", meadows "moored not upon this earth but were islands floating above his head", "the long-stemmed lilies of light, trumpet lilies, silent trumpets gleaming through the clouds". The sacred is not up there, separate. It is woven into the same cloth as the fog, the mud, the broken Congress gaiter.

The mute's sign language at the graveside is the chapter's most sustained sacred ritual, and it is performed in a muddy meadow, by a man with spotted skin and frog's eyes, using a silver spoon borrowed from his breast pocket. The sacred does not require a church or a priest. It requires only full attention to the actual.

Pillar 11 The Crossing Point; You are where time crosses itself

Pillar note: Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

This is perhaps the deepest pillar, and the chapter enacts it most completely in its treatment of Mr. Spitzer's relationship to his dead brother, to the mute, and to time itself.

Mr. Spitzer is explicitly described as a crossing point. He is the living twin, the remainder, the one who stayed: "the living brother who had remained, even like the body without the soul or the soul without the body". He is constituted by what was deposited before him (his brother's existence, his own musical inheritance, the long history of burial rites from Etruscans to Eskimos) and he is constituting the ground others will stand on (his scattered musical manuscripts, his witness to the mute's grief, the elegy he composes for the still-living mute).

The chapter makes the structural nature of this obligation explicit:

"He was the hub, the central part of the wheel — but his brother was the blurred, the singing spokes of that great wheel turning with its periphery lost among the clouds"

Mr. Spitzer is where time crosses itself. He is the hub through which past and future pass. He did not choose this position. It is structural.

The sea shell meditation is the chapter's most extended figure for the Crossing Point. The sea shell carries within its form the entire history of its journey: every sea it crossed, every shore it touched, every current that shaped it. It is constituted by what was deposited before it arrived at this shore, and it will constitute the shore it rests on, its calcium eventually becoming part of the sand. The obligation is not chosen. It is structural. The ancestors are in the sediment.

Mr. Spitzer's musical manuscripts scattered across multiple cities are his version of the sea shell's journey: deposits left in the sediment of the world, to be found by janitors and beachcombers and street-sweepers, constituting a ground that the not-yet-born will stand on without knowing it. The carrying continues, even in forgetting, even in loss.
wheel-chapter-47:
Chapter 47

← Chapter 46 · Wheel and Spokes Home · Chapter 48 →

Research notes: Chapter 47 · Reading guide: Guide, Chapter 47

Characters: Cousin Hannah · Joachim Spitzer

Pillar 1 Not One Self

Pillar note: Pillar 1 Not One Self

"Sometimes he wondered...Did he really know, after all, which brother he was, for had he not lived on both sides, died on both sides"

The chapter opens with an identity crisis that never resolves. Mr. Spitzer cannot determine whether he is himself or his dead twin Joachim. This is not presented as pathology but as ontological condition. He has lived on both sides (of life and death, of self and other) and the boundary has dissolved entirely.

The snowflakes whispering "I am the king...I am the clown in the peaked hood—I am the queen...I am the Ethiope" enact the plural self as cosmic principle: every particle of consciousness contains multiple, simultaneous identities, none primary, none conclusive. The self is not one person moving through time but a chorus of positions that cannot be reconciled.

Most strikingly, Mr. Spitzer cannot even locate the boundary between himself and his dead brother:

"for his brother, by his dying...had robbed death of much of its power"

His brother's death has become constitutive of his own consciousness. He is not one person. He is the living twin plus the dead twin plus the space between them: a self that is structurally multiple and irresolvable. Not One Self is not a philosophical position Mr. Spitzer holds. It is what he is, and the chapter is its demonstration.

Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

Pillar note: Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

"illusion was the world, each man being clothed but by a dream"

This is stated almost baldly, but the entire chapter enacts it with far greater complexity. The fat-bellied coachman who "mistook a firefly for the moon and followed a firefly into a sea burning like the moon" is the chapter's central parable of illusion: the substitution is not a mistake that could have been avoided. The firefly was the moon, functionally, in that darkness. There is no corrective sunlit world outside the cave.

Mr. Spitzer's perceptions are systematically untrustworthy:

"He did not know whether he was inside or outside. There were moon halos where there were no moons, fireflies where there were no fireflies"

But crucially, the chapter does not treat this as a deficiency. His "pristine vision had faded, perhaps before he had ever opened his blurred infant eyes": suggesting that clarity was never available, that illusion is not a fallen state but the original and only condition. Reality is not what we find; it is what the fog, the wave, the grief, and the body make together. The line between illusion and reality is itself dissolved in the salt water of his perception.

Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

Pillar note: Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

This pillar may be the chapter's most fully realized theme. Grief here is not a response to a single death. It is the climate in which every thought occurs.

"Death was ever this dying love. If it were not dying, it would not be love"

Grief and love are not sequential: grief does not follow love's ending. They are simultaneous. Love is already grief in the act of loving, because transience is constitutive of beauty:

"transience was this beauty breaking like foam upon a star"

Mr. Spitzer does not grieve Cousin Hannah's death as an event. He grieves continuously, for his dead brother, for his unlived love, for the music never written, for the child never born, for the image that fades even as he watches it. Grief accumulates rather than resolves:

"Only the mourner lived longer than love, lived only to mourn, to reproach, to sorrow"

The chapter refuses every consolation. The brother's death on the other shore, the possibility of reunion, the harmony of death: all are offered and then immediately qualified, doubted, dissolved. The honest life, as Radical Immanence demands, stops pretending otherwise. Mr. Spitzer cannot pretend. The grief is the weather he lives inside, and the chapter is its atmosphere.

Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

Pillar note: Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

Mr. Spitzer's entire function in this chapter is to witness, and to witness without resolving. He is Cousin Hannah's attorney closing her estate the one who says good-night as she dies the one who lays a skirt over her body. But he refuses, or is constitutionally unable, to draw conclusions:

"He had scarcely known what to do for her"

"he was still at some loss to understand what the answers might be"

This is not incompetence. It is the ethical stance of the Witness: to stay in the room, to see fully, without flinching, without rushing toward resolution. When he is afraid to look at the dying suffragette's face it is precisely because he fears what resolution (beauty returning, or not returning) might demand of him. The refusal to simplify is his act of integrity.

Most powerfully, he witnesses his own uncertainty as an object of attention:

"should one be held accountable for one's entire life or for one moment of unforeseen and unforeseeable transmutation"

He does not answer this. He cannot. The Witness does not answer. The Witness holds the question open, which is itself the practice.

Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

Pillar note: Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

"He had sought for answers and had found only questions. He had asked of every dead heart and had found only whispers"

Mr. Spitzer is perpetually building: music never finished, elegies written too soon, portfolios stuffed with papers he is always losing legal cases for dead clients mathematical equations that never balance because "there being always some factor missing".

He returns constantly to the beginning (the shore, the wave, the question of which brother he is, the question of what he could have done for her) with what he has learned, which is never enough:

"He was always trying to translate...these notes into a component music, always trying to compose"

The building is never finished. The music is never written. The equation never balances. But he does not stop. The recursive construction is not failure; it is the only available mode of being for a consciousness this honest about incompletion. He builds anyway, knowing the building is provisional, because the alternative, stopping, would be a lie about the nature of things.

Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

Pillar note: Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

The chapter's most explicit philosophical statement may be this:

"music which should include, if it were complete as no music ever was — for if music was complete, then it was not music, not even the dirge"

Completion is here defined as ontological impossibility. A complete music would not be music. A concluded sentence would not be honest. The demand for completion is its own violence against experience, and Mr. Spitzer feels this violence acutely when he contemplates what elegy he could write for Cousin Hannah:

"What could he do for that old bloomer girl when she was dead — what elegy could he write or in what way commemorate that which surpassed not only his memory but his intuitional life?"

He cannot write the elegy because the elegy would conclude her, and she resists conclusion. His elegies, written too soon, are acts of premature completion he immediately regrets and qualifies. Unfinished Is Honest demands that he keep the sentence going, and the chapter's own extraordinary, never-ending sentences, running for pages without full stops, are that ongoing sentence. The form enacts the philosophy.

Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Pillar note: Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Cousin Hannah is the chapter's central marginal figure: a suffragette, a woman who wore bloomers and rode horses in storms, who was "ambiguous and never easily defined in spirit or in body or in soul". Her ambiguity is not incidental. It is evidential:

"doubted that the grave should contain one who had been ambiguous and never easily defined in spirit or in body or in soul, in divisible dreams or indivisible death"

She cannot be categorized, not as bride or bridegroom not as masculine or feminine, not as living or dead in any clean sense. She is the figure at the edge of every category, and at those edges the constructed nature of the categories becomes visible.

Mr. Spitzer himself is marginal: the twin who is not quite the living one, not quite the dead one, the attorney with no court the king of no realm, the emperor of no crown. He walks "simultaneously on many roads" which is not metaphor but description of his actual ontological condition. The marginal person is not the exception. In this chapter, the marginal person is everyone, and the edges of categories are where the only honest seeing happens.

Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

Pillar note: Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

No pillar is more fully embodied in this chapter than this one. The chapter's entire temporal structure is sedimentary. Mr. Spitzer cannot locate himself in time:

"Mr. Spitzer had forgotten at what hour his necessity had ceased, all clocks tolling together with inaccurate accuracy in distant clouds, and after that had been no time"

The dead brother is not behind him; he is beneath him, pressing up through everything:

"his brother's laughter rippling all day long. His brother whispered in his conch ear. His brother's music of discord interfered with his music"

The dead love, the unborn child, the unwritten music, the lost cities: all are described not as past but as submerged, still present beneath the surface:

"Perhaps this world was the Lost Atlantis with bells ringing under water...this sunken continent for which we mourned, not knowing that we were what we mourned, that we were on the ocean's floor"

This is The Past Doesn't Go Away rendered as cosmology. The past is literally the ocean floor beneath the present. The bells still ring. The cities are still there. What was lost is not behind us; it is beneath us, still pressing up through the water, still audible to those who listen with a conch ear.

Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

Pillar note: Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

The chapter is acutely self-aware about language's constructive, and destructive, power. Mr. Spitzer's music, his legal documents, his elegies, his whispered good-nights are all language acts that shape reality rather than describe it:

"Good-night and good-morning — simply to imply that she would live beyond the night"

The implication is the act. The word makes the reality it names. But language also fails, constantly:

"music so intricate that many notes should fly away like blackbirds from windy boughs and many tones were lost and many chords were blurred and many keys were melted"

The chapter's own language performs this failure: sentences that accumulate qualifications, that circle back, that lose their grammatical thread in waves of subordinate clauses, that cannot arrive at full stops. This is not stylistic excess. It is honest language naming its own location: inside a consciousness that knows language cannot contain what it is trying to say, and says so, in language, endlessly.

The legal language (torts, leases, mortgages, promissory notes) is particularly pointed. It is the language that claims to fix reality, to make it binding, to give it permanent form. And it is applied entirely to properties "which were no more of earth, perhaps had never been of earth". The language of certainty is applied to the most uncertain things. Language that pretends to speak from nowhere (legal language, the language of finality) is revealed to speak from somewhere very particular: from the human need to stop the flood.

Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

Pillar note: Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

The chapter is saturated with the sacred, but it is never located elsewhere. The transcendent is always folded back into the immanent:

"Perhaps death had come at the moment of creation. Perhaps there had been no time between the love and the death"

The sacred is not in an afterlife Mr. Spitzer believes in. It is in simultaneity, in the moment where love and death, creation and destruction, the living and the dead, occupy the same instant. The brother's death has made death "seem, after all...slightly ridiculous", not because there is a heaven beyond it, but because the boundary between life and death has dissolved here, in this world, in this consciousness.

The grey, fog-bound, wave-eroded shore is the site of the sacred. The dead pigeon that made him burst into tears. The sand grain scraped by starlight. The firefly mistaken for the moon. These are not symbols of transcendence pointing elsewhere. They are the transcendence, pointing deeper into the immanent world, into its grief, its beauty, its irresolvable plurality. The sacred lives in the permanent weather of grief, in the plural self that cannot be unified, in the music that can never be completed.

Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

Pillar note: Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

This final pillar may be the most structurally important for understanding the chapter's deepest movement.

Mr. Spitzer is explicitly figured as a crossing point throughout the chapter. He stands between his living and dead brother, between this shore and the other, between the suffragette's life and death, between the music written and the music never written. He is not moving through time; he is the place where time folds:

"Perhaps he was forever between two shores as between two worlds, each ephemeral, each receding from the other"

He is constituted by what was deposited before he arrived (his brother's suicide, his unlived love, the dead suffragette's cause, the music of composers he has absorbed) and he is, through his elegies and his witnessing, constituting the ground the not-yet-born will stand on. His papers, his musical notations scattered in his wake his elegies written before the deaths they mourn; these are deposits in the sediment.

The obligation is structural, not chosen:

"he owed much, far more than the promissory notes he was always meeting out of his own pocket"

He did not choose to be the surviving twin. He did not choose to be Cousin Hannah's attorney. He did not choose to love a beauty who would grow old, or to fear age, or to be constituted by his brother's death. The carrying continues not because he elected it but because he is the crossing point. The ancestors (his brother, his dead love, the suffragette, the drowned cities) are in the sediment. He walks above them, carrying their weight, depositing his own.
wheel-chapter-42:
Chapter 42

← Chapter 41 · Wheel and Spokes Home · Chapter 43 →

Research notes: Chapter 42 · Reading guide: Guide, Chapter 42

Characters: Cousin Hannah · Joachim Spitzer

Pillar 1 Not One Self

Pillar note: Pillar 1 Not One Self

Mr. Spitzer is constitutionally, irresolvably multiple. The text makes this not a psychological observation but an ontological one. He cannot determine whether he is himself or his dead brother:

"there was certainly no way for him then or later to know whether she thought he was himself or his dead brother, he who had played his last spade"

This is not confusion or madness. The text presents it as a structural condition. The self here is not a unified subject moving through events but a site where multiple selves (the living and the dead, the present and the absent) occupy the same body simultaneously. Mr. Spitzer does not have an identity crisis. He is the crisis, permanently. The brother is not a memory he carries. The brother is a layer of him that cannot be separated from the surface layer others see.

Similarly, Cousin Hannah is revealed to be plural across the chapter. She is Hannah in Boston, Hamid in the East, Al Hamid in the desert cities, the Great Moor in the mountains of snow. These are not disguises or roles. They are simultaneous selves, each fully real within their geography and cultural moment. The chapter refuses to resolve these into a single coherent identity. The great suffrage captain, the secret woman, the abandoned bride, the dying patriarch; these are all present at once in that final room.

The plural self is also enacted grammatically. The prose refuses to stabilize its subject. Sentences accumulate subordinate clauses that keep modifying who is doing what, so that by the end of a long sentence the subject has become uncertain. The reader shares Mr. Spitzer's condition.

Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

Pillar note: Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

The chapter opens with an act that is explicitly impossible and treats it as simply true:

"My mother rode in the carriage with the black coachman and the four alabaster horses through the sleeping house"

This visit, the opium lady's farewell journey to Cousin Hannah, could not have occurred. Both women were bedridden. Mr. Spitzer knows this. He reminds himself of it. And yet:

"My mother's farewell visit was only in the realm of imagination — and in what other realm could a farewell visit ever be, Mr. Spitzer asked"

This is not a rhetorical question. It is a philosophical proposition. The text argues that the imagined visit is more real than any visit that could have been physically arranged, because it contains the full emotional and spiritual truth of the relationship. The cave is all there is. But this cave (the cave of imagination, of dream, of hallucination) is not a lesser reality. It is the primary one.

The chapter then performs a remarkable move: Cousin Hannah also remembers the visit. She describes it from her side: the purple feathers, the trailing skirts, the request to arise and cast off mortal chains. Two people share an impossible memory. The illusion has become intersubjective. It has achieved the social confirmation we normally reserve for "real" events. The line between illusion and reality has not merely blurred. It has been shown to be a construction from the beginning.

Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

Pillar note: Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

Grief in this chapter does not move. It accumulates. It is the atmosphere through which every sentence breathes.

Mr. Spitzer's grief for his brother is not a past event. It is his present condition, indistinguishable from his consciousness:

"his brother whose memory was now the only life to him — sustaining him through many weary hours"

The grief for Cousin Hannah's forgotten career is not resolved by her death. It deepens:

"she had outlived her fame, and no one remembered that war in which she had fought"

The grief for the abandoned bridegroom, whoever he was, is not resolved by time. It persists in rumors still circulating, in flowers still clutched in a dead hand.

Most powerfully, the text presents grief as the medium through which Mr. Spitzer perceives everything:

"His grief was so diffused through clouds, winds, waters that it was this grief which gave him sympathy, no doubt, for all living things, and identified him with all others"

This is grief as epistemology. It is not an emotion he experiences. It is the lens through which experience becomes possible. The chapter does not offer resolution. The final image, Cousin Hannah crying out for a pavilion to hide her from the storm, is pure unresolved grief, weather that has no end.

Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

Pillar note: Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

Mr. Spitzer's entire existence in this chapter is an act of witnessing. He goes back and forth between two dying women. He arrives. He sits. He watches. He does not fix anything. He cannot fix anything. The chapter is explicit about this:

"Of what necessity, he asked, to arrange a visit which she imagined had already taken place?"

He understands that his role is not intervention. It is presence. He comes to Cousin Hannah's deathbed and simply stays:

"He had sat by that rickety bedside, drawing out his black handkerchief"

He does not speak. He does not announce himself. He does not demand recognition. He witnesses her dying without requiring that it mean something he can articulate. When she does not acknowledge him, he does not leave. When she cries out in hallucination, he stays.

The ethical weight of this is enormous. The chapter presents witnessing as the highest available act in a world where nothing can be fixed, where death comes anyway, where recognition is not guaranteed. To stay in the room (to see fully without flinching, without rushing toward resolution) is what Mr. Spitzer does, and the text presents this as his great, unrecognized virtue.

His refusal to simplify is equally important. He resists every temptation to conclude about Cousin Hannah's life. Every time he forms a judgment, the text immediately qualifies it, reverses it, opens it again:

"Surely...she had suffered no great breakage or scattering of her powers...But he had been wrong, as he knew now in retrospect"

The ongoing revision is the witnessing.

Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

Pillar note: Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

The chapter is formally recursive. It circles back. The opening image of the carriage journey returns. The question of the visit recurs. Mr. Spitzer's uncertainty about his own identity recurs. The ships lost at sea recur. Each return brings new sediment, new qualification, new depth, but no resolution.

Mr. Spitzer's list-making is a perfect image of recursive construction:

"He had been making then as now a list of ships which had gone down"

He builds lists. He compiles registers. He searches for lost heirs. He composes epitaphs. None of these projects ever completes. He adds another note to the music when the iceberg melts. The building is never finished. The text presents this not as failure but as the only honest form of work available to a consciousness that knows the provisional nature of all construction.

The great suffrage captain's life is also recursively constructed. She begins campaigns, returns from them, begins again. She organizes a blacksmiths' union when there are almost no blacksmiths. She pickets a clock. These are not failures of judgment. They are the recursive return to the beginning with what was learned, even when what was learned is that the beginning has already ended.

Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

Pillar note: Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

The chapter is saturated with incompletion presented as integrity. The ships that left no wreckage. The bridegroom whose identity was never found. The visit that never physically occurred. The brother who never said farewell. The letter dropped into a slot thousands of years ago.

Most powerfully:

"she had not found the Holy Grail or any object of her quest. She was that Jason who had not found the golden fleece"

The text does not present this as tragedy in the conventional sense. It presents it as the condition of every life honestly examined. The demand for completion (the golden fleece, the Holy Grail, the resolved identity) is itself the violence. Cousin Hannah's greatness lies precisely in having pursued the quest fully without the consolation of completion.

Mr. Spitzer's legal and musical projects are similarly incomplete by design:

"epitaphs in dozens like bargains...Epithalamiums sadder still, dirges for the drowning or the drowned"

He composes for occasions that are themselves incomplete: marriages that are also deaths, deaths that are also marriages. The ongoing sentence is his entire existence.

Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Pillar note: Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Cousin Hannah is the chapter's central figure of the marginal. She is:

  • A woman who fought against the conventions governing women
  • A figure who was Hannah in Boston and Hamid in the East
  • A suffrage captain forgotten by those she rescued
  • A woman who may have had a secret female beloved
  • A figure described alternately as masculine and feminine, warrior and bride

"she was perhaps not too different from himself in his oblivion"

The marginal person is not the exception. Mr. Spitzer and Cousin Hannah are both figures who exist at the edges of every category: living/dead, male/female, present/absent, self/other. Their marginality is not incidental to the chapter's meaning. It is the meaning. They are the evidence that the categories themselves are constructed.

The chapter's treatment of Cousin Hannah's possible secret life is particularly important here:

he had been "surprised to find at the last moment a secret woman, a bride"

This revelation, the final sentence of a long passage about expected secret men, is delivered without drama, without resolution, without explanation. It simply stands. The marginal truth is offered and left uncontained.

Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

Pillar note: Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

The chapter's entire temporal structure is sedimentary. The past does not recede. It accumulates beneath every present moment, pressing upward.

The ships lost at sea are not in the past. They are in Mr. Spitzer's present consciousness with full weight and presence:

"Racehorse, lost in the China Sea...mail boats, vanished far out at sea...Oceanus which sank with the evening star"

These ships exist in the text with the same ontological status as the living characters. They are not memories. They are sediment pressing up through the present.

The graveyard registers, the census reports, the population rolls; these are Mr. Spitzer's obsessions because they are the material form of sedimentary time. The person always missing from the census is himself; neither living nor dead, present in the sediment but absent from the official record.

Most explicitly:

"Time had never advanced for her, it seemed to him — and, indeed, in many hysterical and nervous persons he had observed that all of time is but the crystalization of one sad, wild moment. They go not beyond that time though time may pass."

This is the philosophy of sedimentary time stated directly. The one moment (the wedding that did not happen, the brother's death, the great campaign) does not recede. It crystallizes. Everything subsequent is deposited around it, but it remains the structural core.

Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

Pillar note: Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

The chapter's prose style is itself an argument about language. The sentences are extraordinarily long, accumulative, self-qualifying. They refuse the authority of the concluded statement. Every assertion immediately generates its own qualification:

"perhaps he had already taken his last step"

"He was almost certain though she gave him no reassurance"

"He was almost certainly himself according to his definition of that changing moment"

The repeated perhaps, doubtless, it seemed to him, he believed; these are not hedges. They are honest language naming its own location. The text refuses to speak from nowhere. It speaks from Mr. Spitzer's partial, blurred, uncertain position, and it marks that position constantly.

The lists of ship names (Racehorse, Arcturus, Ptarmigan, Nautilus, Oceanus) are language performing a different function. These names are incantatory. They do not describe. They summon. They make the lost ships present through the act of naming. Language here is not a vehicle for pre-existing truth. It is the act of construction by which the lost become briefly real.

Cousin Hannah's multiple names across cultures demonstrate that language does not describe an identity. It constitutes one. She is a different person in each language, each geography. There is no original self beneath the names.

Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

Pillar note: Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

The chapter is full of images that reach toward transcendence (golden towers, resurrection, eternal life, the morning star) but every one of them is immediately pulled back into the immanent, the ordinary, the bodily, the specific.

The most explicit statement:

"Ah, yes — might there be resurrection and eternal life"

This follows immediately from the detail of Cousin Hannah lifting her hood and the light flashing in her eyes. The transcendent possibility is generated by a specific physical gesture in a specific room. It does not point outward to a beyond. It points deeper into this moment, this body, this dying woman.

The carriage journey through the sleeping city is the chapter's central image of immanent transcendence. It is not a journey to heaven. It is a journey through Boston, through traffic lights, through jogs in roads, past milestones and gate posts. The sacred geography is the ordinary geography, made luminous by the quality of attention brought to it.

Mr. Spitzer's relationship to his brother is similarly immanent. The brother is not in heaven. He is in Mr. Spitzer, in his face, his uncertainty about his own identity, his grief that is also life:

"the great lamp-lighter going his rounds through darkened heavens light that lamp which had gone out and was himself shining through clouds"

The sacred is here, in the lamp that was a man, in the clouds that are grief, in the shining that is memory.

Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

Pillar note: Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

Mr. Spitzer is the chapter's most complete embodiment of the Crossing Point. He is explicitly constituted by what was deposited before him:

"he had been preoccupied at that time as usual by his quasi-legal interests such as his unflagging search for lost heirs to lost estates"

He searches for those who are constituted by the dead: heirs, inheritors, those who stand on ground deposited by ancestors. He is himself such a figure. His brother's death constitutes him. His mother's opium dreams constitute him. Cousin Hannah's rescue of his mother constitutes the entire web of obligation that brings him back, again and again, to these dying women.

The structural obligation is named directly:

he had "spent all his life saying farewell to my mother—as she to him"

This is not chosen. It is structural. The obligation to witness, to return, to carry the memory forward; these are not decisions Mr. Spitzer makes. They are what he is.

And he is constituting ground for those who come after. The narrator, the "I" whose mother this is, exists because Mr. Spitzer went back and forth. The chapter is being written from that ground. The crossing point is not metaphor. It is the literal structure of the text: the narrator stands on sediment deposited by Mr. Spitzer's faithfulness, which itself stands on sediment deposited by Cousin Hannah's rescue, which stands on the opium lady's dreams, which stand on the carriage journey through the sleeping city.

"for no dream dies except into another dream"

This is the Crossing Point as cosmology. The ancestors are in the sediment. The carrying continues. The obligation is not chosen. It is structural.
wheel-chapter-18:
Chapter 18

← Chapter 17 · Wheel and Spokes Home · Chapter 19 →

Research notes: Chapter 18 · Reading guide: Guide, Chapter 18

Characters: Miss MacIntosh

Pillar 1 Not One Self

Pillar note: Pillar 1 Not One Self

Miss MacIntosh is simultaneously and irresolvably multiple throughout these pages. She is nursemaid and rapist, woman and man, the familiar and the terrifying stranger. The narrator explicitly names this:

"It was neither man nor woman but some angelic demon, the flesh and blood with features missing, with senses missing, and yet with something more than sense had provided."

This is not metaphor for confusion. It is ontological statement. Miss MacIntosh does not have a hidden true self that the night reveals. Rather, the night reveals that selfhood was always this: plural, simultaneous, irresolvable. The red-headed nursemaid of the daytime was not a lie concealing the bald figure of the night. Both are equally real, equally constructed, equally partial.

The narrator's own self is equally multiple. She is the child who trusted, the witness who sees, the lover who grieves, the guilty one who stumbled on a secret. These selves do not reconcile:

"I am not sure now that Miss MacIntosh did say all I remember her as saying in that night's passage when nothing seemed certain."

Memory itself produces a plural narrator: the one who experienced and the one who reconstructs, and neither can claim priority.

Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

Pillar note: Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

This pillar is perhaps the chapter's most explicit preoccupation. The text does not simply say that illusion was present and is now stripped away. It says something more radical: that the stripping away is itself another illusion, that there is no bedrock beneath.

"That night, the curtain of illusion had been stripped away, it seemed, even as if the illusion were the only reality, and our self-deception was the only rose."

The phrase "it seemed" is doing enormous work here. The revelation is not stable. And the formulation (the illusion were the only reality, and our self-deception was the only rose) does not mourn this. The rose does not become less beautiful because it is made of self-deception. It becomes differently beautiful. More honestly beautiful.

Miss MacIntosh herself insists on this from within the encounter:

"Nothing that you think is happening is happening! Nothing that you think is true is true. Nothing that you see is real!"

But this is not a reassurance. It is a philosophical position delivered in extremis, by a bald woman who has just committed violence, which makes it simultaneously more and less credible. The text refuses to arbitrate. The cave has no outside. There is only, as the text says, "a larger cave more carefully lit."

Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

Pillar note: Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

The chapter is saturated with a grief that has no object and no resolution; it is simply the atmosphere in which everything occurs. Miss MacIntosh's litany of losses is not organized toward catharsis:

"Oh, where's my old heart? Oh, where's my hair?"

"Oh, how ephemeral are we! Oh, how transient were we, my child! The earth has known us not. Our mothers and our fathers never knew us."

These are not cries that expect answers. They are the accumulation of grief as weather: the permanent condition of existing in time, of loving things that change, of being a body that loses its hair, its breast, its youth, its certainty. The missing left breast is not a dramatic revelation but one more item in the inventory of what is gone. It joins the hair, the heart, the Iowa of her childhood, the red wig on the chair post.

The narrator's grief is equally structureless:

"I knew even then, as she held me in her arms, that our proximity was doomed, that we must part, that she must always leave me."

The grief is already present before the parting. It is not produced by loss. It is the climate of attachment itself.

Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

Pillar note: Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

The narrator's fundamental stance throughout this chapter is that of the witness who stays in the room. She does not flee, does not rationalize, does not rush toward resolution. She continues to look at the bald head even as Miss MacIntosh insists there is nothing to see:

"I am not sure now that Miss MacIntosh did say all I remember her as saying... Perhaps, in retrospection, every lost event must be changed by the illumination larger than that of any instant."

This is the ethics of witnessing made explicit: the witness knows their own perception is imperfect, knows memory distorts, and continues to witness anyway. The refusal to simplify is the act.

The chapter's extraordinary length (its refusal to summarize the night, its insistence on rendering every turn of Miss MacIntosh's voice, every sensation of the encounter) is itself a formal enactment of this pillar. Young does not write: "That night I discovered Miss MacIntosh was bald and something terrible and tender happened." She stays in the room for pages, refusing the shortcut.

The narrator also witnesses her own cruelty:

"For I had been cruel to her, and I had discovered her essential baldness."

The witness does not exempt herself. Seeing fully includes seeing one's own participation in what is seen.

Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

Pillar note: Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

The chapter begins and ends in uncertainty, but it is not the same uncertainty. The narrator at the opening says she cannot be sure what happened; the narrator at the close is still uncertain but has built something from the uncertainty: a way of being charitable, a mark on her forehead, a commitment to remembering.

Miss MacIntosh herself enacts recursive construction in her monologue. She returns again and again to the same proverbs, the same geographical questions, the same invocations of Iowa, but each return is slightly altered by what has accumulated:

"Where, oh, where’s Miss MacIntosh, that old fool we used to see here?"

She asks after herself in the third person. She is building a version of herself even as she loses the materials. The building is never finished. The proverbs keep starting over.

The promise of the morning (that everything will return to normal, that the schedule will resume) is explicitly a recursive gesture:

"In the morning, everything would be all right, shipshape... two simple wayfarers in a thorny way, two grey pilgrims climbing the naked rock."

This is not delusion presented for mockery. It is the human necessity of returning to the beginning with what one has learned, of building again knowing the building is provisional.

Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

Pillar note: Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

The chapter's formal structure is itself an argument for this pillar. Sentences extend for half a page. Qualifications multiply. The narrator explicitly refuses to conclude:

"I am not sure now that Miss MacIntosh did say all I remember her as saying."

This phrase appears twice, bracketing the central encounter. It is not a disclaimer. It is an ethical position: the experience is too large for the sentence that would contain it. To conclude would be to do violence to what actually occurred.

Miss MacIntosh's monologue is structurally incomplete; it circles, interrupts itself, asks questions it cannot answer, shifts register from the cosmic to the domestic without warning. This is not presented as her failure. It is presented as the honest shape of a consciousness confronting its own limits:

"Stuff, fiddle, and balderdash—she suddenly exclaimed... what was she saying?"

She loses the thread of her own argument. The unfinished sentence is the honest one.

Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Pillar note: Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Miss MacIntosh is the chapter's central evidence for this pillar. She exists at the edge of every category: woman/man, familiar/terrifying, sane/mad, alive/dead ("Long ago, I died and was not buried"), clothed/unclothed, haired/bald. Her marginality is not incidental to her meaning; it is her meaning.

"Who was that old rapist if not Miss MacIntosh, she who had warned me against him."

This sentence performs the ontology of the marginal: the category of rapist and the category of nursemaid who warned against rapists collapse into the same person. The categories themselves are revealed as constructions. Miss MacIntosh is not the exception to the rule. She is the evidence that the rule was always a construction.

The missing breast is another marginal marker: the body that does not conform to what a woman's body is supposed to be, the body that has been altered by forces the text does not explain, the body that is "that knob where the breast was missing". This is not presented as tragedy or as medical fact. It is presented as one more way in which Miss MacIntosh exists at the edge of the categories we use to organize persons.

Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

Pillar note: Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

The chapter's treatment of memory and the past is precisely sedimentary. The past does not recede. It accumulates beneath the narrator and continues to press upward:

"There is no new experience which shall not have emerged from the old. There is no surprise but of our own slow-wittedness, our own failures in understanding that the thing was always present."

The bald head was always there beneath the red wig. The violence was always there beneath the lessons. The grief was always there beneath the routine. The night does not introduce something new. It reveals what was already deposited in the sediment.

Miss MacIntosh's own monologue is sedimentary: layer upon layer of proverb, geography, scripture, folk wisdom, personal lament, all pressing against each other without hierarchy:

"Dead men tell no tales... God pity us. God pity the small fishes and the great whales beached on this beach."

These are not random. They are the accumulated layers of a consciousness formed by a particular culture, a particular time, a particular body of losses. The proverbs are not wisdom. They are sediment: the compressed residue of everything that was handed down to her.

The mark left on the narrator's forehead is the chapter's most precise image of sedimentary time:

"There, that will teach you to remember me."

The past is not behind. It is inscribed on the body, pressed into the skin, carried forward as physical fact.

Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

Pillar note: Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

The chapter is acutely self-conscious about what language can and cannot do. The opening meditation is essentially a treatise on language's failure:

"Memory is surrounded by the unknown, the void, and there is so much that we have not heard, much that we have not seen... Memory sometimes provides the one flower more than ever blossomed. Memory sometimes omits the only flower there really was."

Language here is not a neutral vehicle. It adds flowers that were not there and removes the ones that were. The narrator's language knows its own location; it speaks from the position of retrospection, of uncertainty, of someone who was young and is no longer, of someone who was there and cannot fully recover what being there meant.

Miss MacIntosh's language is equally self-aware of its own constructedness. Her proverbs are explicitly marked as borrowed, as received, as coming from "the World Almanac or farmers' journals". She speaks in a language that was handed to her, and she knows it:

"Stuff, fiddle, and balderdash—she suddenly exclaimed... what was she saying?"

She catches herself speaking in received language and rejects it, then has nothing to replace it with. The honest language names its own location. The location here is: a woman who has lost her hair and her breast and her certainty, speaking in the only language available to her, which is not adequate to what she is.

Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

Pillar note: Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

The sacred in this chapter lives entirely within the immanent: within the bald head, the false teeth clicking, the missing breast, the cold hands, the wet kiss on the eyelids. There is no gesture toward a beyond. The transcendence, when it appears, points deeper into the ordinary:

"Our nakedness is God's nakedness."

This is not a metaphor for spiritual elevation. It is a statement of immanent transcendence: the naked, bald, one-breasted body of an old nursemaid is the sacred. God is not above this scene. God is bald in this scene.

The chapter's repeated invocations of God are not prayers directed outward. They are recognitions of the sacred within the wreckage:

"God pity poor sailors with their faces upturned on the leaden waters at dawn. God pity the poor streetwalker whose heart is virginal... and pity us all, for we are all alike in our being mortal and lost."

The pity is not divine condescension from above. It is the quality of attention that the immanent sacred requires: the willingness to see the streetwalker, the sailor, the bald nursemaid, and not look away. The sacred is here, in the grey light, in the spotted head, in the false teeth clacking.

Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

Pillar note: Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

This pillar finds its most concentrated expression in the chapter's final image and in Miss MacIntosh's last speech. The narrator is constituted by what was deposited before she arrived, by Miss MacIntosh's lessons, her proverbs, her violence, her tenderness, her baldness. And she is constituting the ground that comes after:

"Ever since, in a moment of extreme revelation when I have seen that people are not exactly what they have seemed to be, I have tried to be charitable."

The mark on her forehead is the crossing point made visible: the place where Miss MacIntosh's time crossed the narrator's time and left a physical trace that carries forward.

Miss MacIntosh's final words make the structural obligation explicit:

"I have lost my hair in your service. When I came here, I had all my own hair, a thick mane of it, pale gold hanging down my back... I am no older than the day I was born. Age is the most difficult thing to achieve."

She is simultaneously the ancestor depositing into the sediment and the child who has not yet grown old. She is where time crosses itself. The carrying continues: the narrator will carry the mark, the charitable habit, the memory of the bald head, the knowledge that nothing is what it seems, forward into a future Miss MacIntosh will not see.

The chapter ends not with resolution but with this structural obligation intact and unresolved. The ancestors are in the sediment. The carrying continues.
wheel-chapter-22:
Chapter 22

← Chapter 21 · Wheel and Spokes Home · Chapter 23 →

Research notes: Chapter 22 · Reading guide: Guide, Chapter 22

Characters: Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Peron Spitzer · Vera Cartwheel

Pillar 1 Not One Self

Pillar note: Pillar 1 Not One Self

The chapter opens with Vera in a state of bodily fragmentation that she cannot explain: "There were scratches on my arms and legs as if I had walked in my sleep through patches of spiked brambles... My breasts ached. My knees were black and blue. My lips were dry, cracked and scaling". She is a self that has been somewhere she has no memory of. The body has acted independently of consciousness. This is not metaphor; it is a structural demonstration that the self is not unified, not sovereign over its own history.

Miss MacIntosh, meanwhile, presents as aggressively singular: the most insistently one-person character imaginable, with her flat Middle Western certainty, her routines, her umbrella. Yet the chapter quietly dismantles this. Her voice is described as "haunted by another's sad, imploring voice which I could almost recognize". The woman who insists most loudly on the singularity and reliability of the self is herself inhabited by another voice she cannot name or suppress. The pillar holds: the self is multiple even when, especially when, it performs unity.

Mr. Spitzer further fractures the chapter's selfhood. He exists as twin, as double, as sometimes "seen double, standing in two places at once". His dead brother Peron haunts every reference to him, so that it becomes genuinely impossible to determine which Mr. Spitzer is meant at any given moment. The chapter does not resolve this. It lets the doubling stand as ontological fact.

Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

Pillar note: Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

Miss MacIntosh's entire philosophical project is the defense of the real against the illusory. She is "far from self-pity... who lived not by illusions or memories or dreams and who never would". She insists the phantom is only "a spar or an empty fish barrel or a shad-bush moving with the leeward tide". She is the novel's designated realist.

But the chapter systematically shows that her realism is itself a construction, and a fragile one. The breakfast table, which she does not notice, is laid with "vermilion and silver and gold... a hammered silver bowl of white roses glistening with coarse water-drops": luxury she refuses to perceive because she has already decided she lives in What Cheer, Iowa, with broken crockery and smoky lamps. She sees "only the old place at What Cheer... She could not get used to anything else". Her "reality" is a remembered image imposed on the present. Her realism is revealed as nostalgia performing itself as fact.

Vera's mother represents the opposite extreme: a woman for whom "a dish of apples" becomes "the portrait of a lady" and "a golden harp" becomes "a fan". But crucially, the chapter does not privilege Miss MacIntosh's perception over the mother's. Both are constructions. The line between illusion and reality is, as the pillar states, itself a construction. Young places the two women as poles of the same problem, not as error and correction.

Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

Pillar note: Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

This is perhaps the pillar most deeply embedded in the chapter's texture. Vera's grief is not named, not located, not caused by any identifiable event. It is simply the climate of the morning: "my spirits were drooping with a nameless disappointment". It does not arrive; it is already there. It does not move toward resolution; it accumulates through the chapter's long, winding sentences.

Miss MacIntosh's grief is more buried but more devastating when it surfaces. Her speech about knitting hoods for orphans breaks open suddenly: "we shall have no baby of our own, none to lay its head on this cold and empty breast. How handsome it might be with its curls, its three-inch hair, its closed eyes and long eyelashes. We shall save ourselves this trouble. We are not married, my dear. No man has asked for my hand". This erupts from a woman who has spent the entire chapter performing cheerful practicality. The grief has not been processed or resolved. It has been sealed beneath the surface, and it presses up through the cracks of her own discourse.

The chapter's final extended passage about sunken ships ("so many ships going down in sight of shore", bells ringing through water, the captain's table still set) is grief rendered as landscape. The coast itself is a graveyard. The weather of loss is literal weather here.

Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

Pillar note: Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

Vera is the chapter's witness. She does not intervene, does not fix, does not conclude. She watches Miss MacIntosh with an attention that is simultaneously irritated and profound. She notices the "brick red top of her head, the redness as of the rooster's comb", the "ivory castanets, her false teeth", the knife and fork crossed accidentally in the sign of the cross. These details are not offered as symbols to be decoded. They are offered as things seen, fully, without flinching.

The witnessing is most acute when Vera observes Miss MacIntosh's face losing its individuality: "Her face, it seemed to me then, was hardly personal and almost featureless, drained of all color, a face which might be anybody's or nobody's". This is not a failure of attention but its deepest achievement: the witness sees through the surface of the performed self to the void beneath it, without rushing to fill that void with meaning.

Vera's refusal to simply answer Miss MacIntosh's relentless questions is also a form of witnessing. She holds the space of not-knowing open. Her question, "Did you throw away my party dress for a punishment?", is an act of witness against evasion, forcing the unsaid into the room.

Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

Pillar note: Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

The chapter's structure is itself recursive. Miss MacIntosh reads the newspaper, which contains the same news as yesterday's newspaper. She asks the same questions she has always asked. The creation narrative (what God made on Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday) is rehearsed again, as it has been rehearsed every morning. "There is no news today that was not yesterday", she finally says, and this is not cynicism but ontological description.

Young's sentences enact recursion formally. The long catalog of newspaper items, "a Brazilian rebellion or a needle-workers' strike or a new garment union or the obsolescence of schooners... the tonnage of water falling each day over Niagara Falls... a great drouth in the sheep-raising lands of Western Alberta, a fall in sea island cotton", circles back through similar catalogs later in the chapter. The reader is returned, again and again, to the same material, but each return carries more sediment. We are building, as the pillar says, knowing the building is provisional. The chapter does not progress in a linear sense. It deepens.

Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

Pillar note: Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

Miss MacIntosh's theology of God's failure is a direct articulation of this pillar: "The first was to have begun what He could not finish. The second was not to have finished what He had begun". God's incompletion is not condemned; it is simply stated as the condition of existence. And the response to it is not to demand completion but to work on both Sunday and Saturday, "observing no period of rest", not because completion is achievable but because the ongoing work is what there is.

The chapter itself formally enacts incompletion. Young's sentences do not conclude so much as they accumulate and pause. The chapter does not arrive at a revelation. It ends mid-process, as all the chapters do, the sentence still running. The demand for a conclusion, for the chapter to mean something resolvable, is, as the pillar states, a violence against the experience the prose is tracking.
