Chapter 28

← Chapter 27 · Wheel and Spokes Home · Chapter 29 →

Research notes: Chapter 28 · Reading guide: Guide, Chapter 28

Characters: Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer

Pillar 1 Not One Self

Pillar note: Pillar 1 Not One Self

Mr. Spitzer is perhaps the most literal embodiment of Not One Self possible in fiction; he is a twin whose identity has become permanently entangled with his dead brother Peron. The text makes this explicit when it describes how his brother's death "had divided and sub-divided his own rational soul almost to the point of lunacy". He cannot answer the most basic ontological question: "How should he know the actual man he was?". He is not one person. He is the living remainder of a divided unit, haunting himself. His selfhood is structurally incomplete because it was always constituted by its double. Not One Self here is not metaphor; it is the literal architecture of the character.

Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

Pillar note: Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

The chapter exists inside a layered hall of mirrors. Mr. Spitzer visits a woman, the narrator's mother, who lives entirely inside narcotic hallucinations: "a bearded Russian bishop or an iridescent lighthouse keeper, perhaps the Antarctic Queen Maud Mountains with her snow-capped mountain peaks and white umbrellas". What is remarkable is that the text does not position her visions as inferior to Mr. Spitzer's perception. He himself wonders whether he might be "among my mother's irresponsible hallucinations, only another of the luminous and metamorphic dead she entertained". The text refuses to establish a stable ground of the real. The mother sees things invisible made visible. Mr. Spitzer sees butterflies that are "almost incorporeal". Neither perception is privileged. There is no sunlit world outside this drugged room, only a larger, more elaborately furnished cave.

Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

Pillar note: Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

This is perhaps the chapter's most sustained philosophical commitment. Grief here is not an event but a climate. Mr. Spitzer stopped collecting butterflies "on the day of Peron's devastating funeral", and that cessation was total: "many other things had come to an end on the day of Peron's devastating funeral, including, of course, his own capacious heart, the living heart, his way of life or most of it, the important part". Years have passed. Nothing has resolved. He still comes to this room. He still remembers the butterflies "though for years quiescent in his mind". The grief does not move through stages. It accumulates beneath everything he does. His evenings here are not healing; they are the ongoing weather of loss, the only climate he now inhabits.

Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

Pillar note: Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

Mr. Spitzer's entire existence in this chapter is an act of witnessing. He comes each evening "as to a brilliant star" to sit by the bedside of a woman lost in hallucination, a woman who denies and turns him away, and yet he returns. He does not fix her. He does not conclude anything about her. He simply stays in the room. The text describes his renewal coming "perhaps by my mother's obtuse faith that he would always return": his faithfulness is not productive, not therapeutic, not goal-directed. It is pure attendance. Attention as practice. The refusal to simplify is enacted structurally: the prose itself refuses to resolve, piling image upon image, clause upon clause, never arriving at a summary judgment about what any of this means.

Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

Pillar note: Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

Mr. Spitzer returns every evening to the same room where "no chair had changed its place for years". This is recursive construction made spatial. He rebuilds the same evening, provisionally, knowing it will not hold, knowing he will be "denied and turned away", and yet returning to begin again. His butterfly memories follow the same pattern: "quiescent in his mind" for years, then suddenly returning, rebuilt from the same materials. He does not add to the collection. He simply remembers it. The building is never finished. The return is the practice.

Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

Pillar note: Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

The prose style itself enacts this pillar. These are among the longest, most syntactically unresolved sentences in literary fiction: subordinate clauses breeding subordinate clauses, lists that do not conclude, images that transform into other images mid-sentence. The chapter never arrives. It is the ongoing sentence, not the concluded one. And thematically, Mr. Spitzer's life is explicitly described as "problematical": his living, his dying, his identity, all of it unresolved: "it was also problematical, that spindle of creative flame which is said to sleep in the eternal darkness, weaving our bodies, weaving our separate souls". The demand for completion is refused at every level: stylistic, thematic, ontological.

Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Pillar note: Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Every figure in this chapter occupies the margins of legible categories. Mr. Spitzer is a twin without a twin: a category that has lost its defining term. His mother exists at the border of consciousness and unconsciousness, reality and hallucination. The dead brother Peron haunts the living without being present. The butterflies Mr. Spitzer collected exist at the border of flower and insect, life and death: "the butterfly perching upon the flower had seemed as identical to the flower as twin to twin, and the flower had seemed to fly away, and the winged petals had remained". These are not exceptions to the order of things. They are the evidence that the order of things is constructed. The marginal is the site of revelation.

Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

Pillar note: Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

This pillar is perhaps most explicitly theorized in the chapter's own language. The past does not recede for Mr. Spitzer; it accumulates. His dead brother is remembered "with an increasing vivacity when he had forgotten himself": the brother grows more present as the self grows dimmer. The room itself is sedimentary: unchanged chairs, old mirrors, candle flames, bellropes, all of it "ethereal gleamings of gold and silver and watered silk" preserved from another era. The mother's hallucinations are themselves sedimentary: old waltzes, old bishops, old landscapes pressing up through her drugged consciousness. The past is not behind Mr. Spitzer. It is beneath him, constituting the ground he stands on, pressing upward through every evening he spends in this room.

Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

Pillar note: Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

The language of this chapter is conspicuously, almost aggressively, constructed. It does not pretend to transparency. The lists of the mother's hallucinations ("the headless horseman fording a brook, the flowers turning into serpents", "the pagodas moving on the waves, the swan weathercocks lifting their wings") are not descriptions of a reality but constructions of an interior. The prose announces its own artifice. The butterfly descriptions, "brimstone-colored butterflies burning like torpid flames in the wind, bejeweled butterflies as precious to him as the most precious jewels", are language making reality, not reporting it. The chapter's style is itself an argument: that what we call experience is always already shaped by the language we use to hold it.

Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

Pillar note: Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

There is no beyond in this chapter. No afterlife is affirmed. Mr. Spitzer knows "the dead did not return except in our thoughts". His brother "would not be born again". And yet the sacred is absolutely present, in the candle flames reflected in dark Venetian mirrors, in the gossamer wings of butterflies reflecting prismatic lights, in the booming bells like the loud sea bittern, in the moment of the butterfly's birth and death which are indistinguishable. The transcendence is entirely immanent; it lives inside the drugged room, inside the ephemeral wings, inside the ambiguous moment when you cannot tell if what you are witnessing is beginning or end. "The manifestations of birth and death were the same in this realm". The sacred does not point outward. It points deeper in.

Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

Pillar note: Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

Mr. Spitzer is, structurally, a crossing point. He is where his dead brother's time and his own living time intersect. He carries Peron forward, not by choice but by constitution. "His faithfulness drew him each evening here", not will, not decision, but structural obligation. He is made of what was deposited before him: his twin's life, his mother's faith, the unchanged room, the accumulated butterfly memories. And he is, without knowing it, constituting the ground the narrator stands on; this chapter is being narrated by the child of the woman he visits, meaning his faithful presence has shaped the consciousness that is now telling his story. The ancestors are in the sediment. He is both the ancestor and the sediment. The carrying continues, whether or not he understands himself to be carrying anything.

Chapter 17

Research notes: Chapter 17 · Reading guide: Guide, Chapter 17

Characters: Miss MacIntosh

Pillar 1 Not One Self

Pillar note: Pillar 1 Not One Self

The chapter refuses to locate the narrator in a single, stable subject position. She is simultaneously the terrified child, the laughing victor, the fading consciousness, and the future old woman looking back:

"my body seemed divided as if now there were two of us, one who fought, one who lay still and watched it all"

This is not metaphor for psychological stress. It is a structural claim about selfhood. The self that fights and the self that witnesses cannot be reconciled into one person. They coexist without resolution. The narrator also projects herself forward in time:

"ask no questions of this night until long years afterward, perhaps when I was old and grey and had no other occupation but to search through memory, asking the why, the wherefore, composing, recomposing, finding perhaps no answer"

The self is therefore plural across time as well as within the moment: the fourteen-year-old girl, the future old woman, the witness, the combatant, all present simultaneously. The chapter does not resolve these into a unified "I." It holds them open.

Miss MacIntosh herself enacts the plural self from the outside. She is the reliable nursemaid and the bald stranger and the male wrestler and the phantom, not sequentially but all at once:

"She was other than herself, and she had deceived me"

The deception is not a lie told at one moment. It is the revelation that she was always already multiple, that the singular "Miss MacIntosh" was a construction the narrator had imposed.

Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

Pillar note: Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

This pillar is perhaps the chapter's most explicit philosophical preoccupation. The narrator does not simply discover that Miss MacIntosh was not what she seemed. She discovers that the very distinction between appearance and reality is unstable:

"What shall we do when, fleeing from illusion, we are confronted by illusion? When falling from illusion, we fall into illusion? Have we not deceived ourselves? Where was the real world?"

This is not a rhetorical question. The chapter provides no answer because no answer exists within its ontology. The "real" Miss MacIntosh (sensible, red-haired, knitting her stitches) turns out to have been the illusion. But the bald, violent figure who replaces her is equally phantasmagoric:

"determined to vanquish this phantom, this bald pretender who had no business in Miss MacIntosh's bedroom"

The word "pretender" is applied to both versions. The nursemaid with hair was a pretender. The bald figure is a pretender. There is no original beneath the masks, only successive layers of construction. The cave, to use the framework's language, goes all the way down.

Even the physical evidence of the encounter dissolves:

"the next morning, of course, my long braids were exactly braided down my back, and there were no scratches upon my cheeks but those which might have been made by leafless branches"

The morning light does not confirm the night's events. It neither validates nor refutes them. It simply offers another surface, another constructed reality, equally provisional.

Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

Pillar note: Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

The grief in this chapter is not the grief of a single loss. It is the accumulated grief of a foundational relationship revealed as something other than what it was, and the grief is amplified precisely because it cannot be dated. When did Miss MacIntosh become this? The answer is: she always was this. The loss is therefore not located in the present moment but distributed across all the years of the narrator's childhood:

"she had been pulling the wool over my eyes, and she was the bald pretender"

The phrase "all during the years" makes the grief retrospective and total. Every memory of the reliable nursemaid is now contaminated. The grief cannot be assigned to a moment of loss because the loss was always already happening. This is precisely what Pillar 3 describes: grief that accumulates rather than resolves, that is the climate of a world where everything is always already changing.

The narrator's cry for her mother mid-combat deepens this:

"made me cry out even now for my mother? Where was my mother that she did not rescue me"

The mother is the other absent anchor: the opium-addicted, absent mother established elsewhere in the novel. The narrator reaches for both of her primary figures of stability in the same moment and finds neither. The grief is not singular; it is structural. It is the permanent weather of a world without reliable ground.

Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

Pillar note: Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

The chapter stages a radical tension between the witness function and the participant function. The narrator is split, as noted above, into one who fights and one who watches. The watching self is described with particular precision:

"my body seemed divided as if now there were two of us, one who fought, one who lay still and watched it all"

The witness does not intervene. The witness does not resolve. The witness simply sees. This is the ethical stance of Pillar 4: to stay in the room, to see fully, without rushing toward resolution. But the chapter also tests the limits of this stance. The narrator does intervene (she laughs, she screams, she strikes) and each intervention produces not clarity but further complexity. The witness self is the more honest self. The acting self generates only more illusion.

The narrative voice itself performs the witness function at the level of prose. The long, recursive sentences do not summarize or conclude. They accumulate detail, qualify every claim, refuse to simplify:

"her eyes standing out like striped marbles as she moved through beams of broken moonlight, her head cold and sweating, a great mirror where one should see one's self if one looked closely and did not lose one's mind and fade into unconsciousness"

This is prose that refuses to look away. It is the practice of attention enacted at the level of syntax.

Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

Pillar note: Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

The narrator explicitly describes the process of returning to the beginning with what she has learned, composing and recomposing, finding no final answer:

"asking the why, the wherefore, composing, recomposing, finding perhaps no answer"

This is Pillar 5 stated almost directly. The building is never finished. The narrator will return to this night for the rest of her life, constructing and reconstructing its meaning. The chapter itself performs this recursion: the prose circles back repeatedly to the same images (the bald head, the moonlight, the curtains, the breathing) without ever arriving at a stable interpretation.

The physical encounter also has this recursive quality. Blow follows blow, each one building on the last, but the structure never resolves into victory or defeat; it simply continues until consciousness fades:

"blow after blow was still delivered — the rabbit punch which cracks against the base of the skull, the upward punch which thrusts upward to the heart, the Sunday punch"

The enumeration of blows is itself recursive: each named punch is another attempt to land on something definitive, and each one fails to end the encounter.

Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

Pillar note: Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

The chapter ends without resolution. The morning after is described in a single subordinate clause that refuses to confirm or deny what happened:

"even though, the next morning, of course, my long braids were exactly braided down my back, and there were no scratches upon my cheeks but those which might have been made by leafless branches"

The "of course" is doing enormous work here. It performs normalcy while simultaneously undermining it: the qualification "those which might have been made by leafless branches" refuses to close the question. The sentence is structured to deny completion even as it appears to offer it.

The narrator's consciousness does not recover. It "fades into consciousness": a paradox that refuses the clean arc of unconsciousness followed by recovery:

"my consciousness faded into my consciousness"

This is the ethics of incompletion enacted at the level of grammar. The sentence cannot conclude because experience cannot conclude. The demand for a finished sentence (a resolved encounter, a confirmed identity, a clear answer about who Miss MacIntosh was) is itself identified as a kind of violence.

Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Pillar note: Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Miss MacIntosh's baldness is the chapter's central symbol, and it functions precisely as Pillar 7 describes: the marginal body as evidence of the constructed nature of all categories. Hair, specifically Miss MacIntosh's "red, shining hair, tawny as an August sunset", had been the marker of her femininity, her reliability, her legibility as a woman and a nursemaid. Its absence does not simply make her less feminine. It dissolves the category:

"She was bald as the egg or as the rock where nothing grows. She had no hair on her head, no hair at all, not one hair to cast its shadow, and her face was as absolutely impersonal and expressionless as a face may be and still be human"

"Still be human" is the key phrase. Baldness pushes Miss MacIntosh to the edge of the human category itself. She becomes the evidence that "human," "woman," "nursemaid," "reliable" are all constructions that depend on surface markers, and that when those markers are removed, the categories collapse.

The narrator's cry, "Miss MacIntosh, you are a man!", is not simply a discovery. It is a recognition that gender is itself a constructed category, and that Miss MacIntosh has been living at its margins all along. The marginal person is not the exception; she is the evidence. Miss MacIntosh's body, bald and one-breasted, is the place where the constructed nature of gender becomes most visible.

Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

Pillar note: Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

The chapter is saturated with the past pressing up through the present. The narrator's recognition of Miss MacIntosh in her altered state is achieved not through present perception but through accumulated sediment:

"I knew her by her broken nose and something that was definite in her manner, something suggesting the intimacies forgotten"

The "intimacies forgotten" are not gone. They are beneath the surface of the present encounter, pressing up through it, making recognition possible even in the face of radical transformation. This is sedimentary time: the past does not recede, it accumulates.

The historical references function similarly. The narrator's mind, even in the midst of physical combat, drifts to pharaohs, Sumerian wrestlers, Roman gladiators, Jacob at Peniel:

"perhaps even that holy angel with whom Jacob struggled at Peniel. Perhaps it was a reindeer"

These are not random associations. They are the sediment of human history pressing up through a bedroom fight in an American coastal house. The encounter is simultaneously this specific event and every struggle between humans and the forces that define them. The past (mythological, biblical, historical) is not behind the narrator. It is beneath her, constituting the ground she stands on.

Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

Pillar note: Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

The chapter is acutely self-aware about the inadequacy of language to capture what is happening, and yet it proceeds anyway: generating simile after simile, qualification after qualification, in a performance of language's simultaneous necessity and failure.

The prose is structured around the word "perhaps" and its equivalents. The narrator cannot assert; she can only propose:

"Perhaps it was a reindeer. Perhaps, I reasoned, my consciousness slipping like a train through an airless mountain tunnel, it was no one, after all"

Language here names its own location: it is the language of a consciousness that cannot achieve certainty, that is always constructing rather than discovering. The similes are equally self-conscious: "like a train through an airless mountain tunnel" is a simile about the failure of consciousness to move through its own experience, and it is itself a labored, imperfect vehicle. The language knows it is not transparent.

The narrator's scream, "Miss MacIntosh, you are a man!", is the moment when language attempts to fix identity, to nail down a truth. And it is immediately undermined. The laughter that follows it, the acknowledgment that "it was a horse ballet, a Spanish carousel with many mirrors", dissolves the assertion. Language that claims to speak from certainty is exposed as speaking from a particular, limited, constructed position.

Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

Pillar note: Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

The sacred in this chapter is not elsewhere. It is in the bald head, the moonlight, the corset stays, the breathing. The chapter is full of imagery that reaches toward transcendence (pharaohs, angels, Jacob at Peniel, the Arctic Circle, the moon) but every transcendent reference is immediately pulled back into the immanent:

"the moon, dimly radiant but distant, invulnerable to our assault, the moon which draws the waves in its wake and has no life of its own"

The moon is not a symbol of higher truth. It is a cold, dented disc with no life of its own. It is physically present and metaphysically empty. The sacred, if it exists, is here, in this bedroom, in this bald woman, in this confused fourteen-year-old girl, in this violent and inconclusive encounter.

The description of Miss MacIntosh's bald head as a "great mirror where one should see one's self" is the chapter's most concentrated statement of immanent transcendence. The sacred is not in a beyond. It is in the reflective surface of another person's skull. To look at it fully is to see yourself, and potentially to lose your mind. The ordinary (a woman's baldness) becomes the site of the most profound and destabilizing revelation.

Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

Pillar note: Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

The narrator is explicitly constituted by what was deposited before her arrival. Miss MacIntosh has been her primary reality-anchor throughout her childhood. The revelation of Miss MacIntosh's constructed identity is simultaneously a revelation about the narrator's own constitution:

"that she had never been herself at all but someone else, this appalling apparition clothed with flesh and blood which should fade"

If Miss MacIntosh was always someone else, then the narrator who was raised by her, shaped by her, oriented by her, was shaped by a fiction. The narrator is the ground on which Miss MacIntosh's sediment was deposited, and that sediment is now revealed as unstable. This is the crossing point: the narrator is where Miss MacIntosh's constructed identity crosses with her own not-yet-formed identity.

The forward projection, the old woman who will spend her life "composing, recomposing, finding perhaps no answer", confirms the structural obligation of Pillar 11. The narrator is not moving through time toward a destination. She is the place where this night will continue to cross with every subsequent night. She is constituting, through this encounter, the ground on which her future self will stand. The carrying continues, even though, perhaps especially because, what is being carried is irresolvable.

Chapter 69

Research notes: Chapter 69 · Reading guide: Guide, Chapter 69

Pillar 1 Not One Self

Pillar note: Pillar 1 Not One Self

"Only my eyes were reflected in its depths, as if they had swam out of my face like two silver fishes detaching themselves from a porous underwater flower."

The narrator cannot see her own face in the mirror, only her eyes, swimming free of her. This is not a gothic flourish. It is a precise ontological statement: the self does not cohere into a single visible image. The self detaches from itself, observes itself from a distance, and cannot be reassembled.

Dr. O'Leary enacts the plural self even more dramatically. He is simultaneously:

  • A practicing physician making professional appointments
  • A man wrestling with a ghost or hallucination
  • A child mourning a dead sister
  • A drunk raving in a hotel room
  • A sailor, a soldier, a farmer: identities the landlord narrates as if they belong to different men

The landlord himself is explicitly plural: candy merchant, ventriloquist, sailor, soldier, hunter, Intelligence officer, circus husband. His body is a palimpsest of selves: tattoos layering over skin, a battleship behind chest hair, a woman's face in his palm that winks when he closes his fist. He is not one person. He is a walking archive.

The hangman is split from his own shadow, and the shadow is described as more interesting, more loquacious, more real than the hangman himself. The shadow says what the hangman will not. This is the plural self made architectural: one person occupies two ontological positions simultaneously.

Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

Pillar note: Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

"Tillie," he had said, with an air of finality. Who was Tillie? "A young girl," he had answered, "a very young girl."

The landlord describes the same person as simultaneously an old woman with turkey buzzards and a young girl who will knit baby hoods. When the narrator presses him, he does not correct himself; he holds both descriptions as equally valid. There is no authoritative version. Reality is not discovered; it is asserted, and different assertions coexist without resolution.

The turkey buzzards become canaries, or the canaries are as big as turkey buzzards. The landlord's correction is casual, smiling, as if the distinction is minor. The line between the monstrous and the domestic is itself a construction, casually reversible.

Dr. O'Leary is described as having been killed in a traffic accident earlier in the evening, "he who even now if the bus-driver had been right should be pinned under a steering wheel in a flooded meadow", yet he is loudly, riotously alive in the next room. His death is simultaneously true and false. The text does not resolve this. It presents both realities and moves on. There is no sunlit world outside the cave. There is only the hotel corridor, where the dead practice medicine and the living cannot see their own faces.

Sarah herself is the supreme illustration: she died at age one and was buried in the vegetable garden, yet she is also an old woman with grey hair crawling on the floor, also a young beautiful woman with a wide forehead, also a ghost, also perhaps no one at all,,. She is all of these simultaneously, and the text refuses to adjudicate.

Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

Pillar note: Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

"God damn it, Sarah, God damn it, Sarah!" That was the old refrain, I had heard even in my sleep.

This is grief as climate, not event. The doctor does not grieve Sarah in a moment of crisis; he has apparently been grieving her for decades, and the grief has not moved. It has accumulated into a permanent atmospheric condition that fills every room he occupies. The narrator herself carries a "small, faded pillow upon which I had always rested my head, pillow which had received my childhood tears". She has brought her grief with her, physically, as luggage. It is not behind her. It is under her head.

The hotel itself is a structure of accumulated grief: old people with hardening of the arteries, a legless newspaper man reporting news from ten, fifteen, twenty years ago, a doctor who cannot stop delivering a dead woman's baby. The building does not move forward. It sediments. Every room holds a grief that never resolved, only deepened.

The doctor's mourning is described as "like that of a wind rising and falling": weather language, precisely. Not a storm that passes. A wind that rises and falls and rises again. The honest life stops pretending otherwise, and O'Leary, drunk and raving, is perhaps the most honest character in the chapter precisely because he has stopped pretending.

Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

Pillar note: Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

The narrator's position throughout this chapter is almost purely that of witness. She lies in her bed, unable to sleep, and she listens. She does not intervene in O'Leary's monologue. She does not go to him. She does not call the management. She does not explain or conclude. She receives.

"I was drifting toward sleep, but I was jerked back to consciousness by a quarrel between two persons in the bedroom next to mine."

She is jerked back: consciousness is not chosen here, it is imposed. The witnessing is not voluntary. It is structural. She cannot not hear. She cannot not receive what the hotel delivers to her.

The one moment she breaks this stance is devastating in its brevity:

"Go, Sarah!" I screamed.

This single intrusion, the only direct speech the narrator makes in the entire chapter, is immediately swallowed back into O'Leary's monologue. The witness screams once and returns to witnessing. The scream changes nothing. Sarah does not go. The doctor does not stop. The walls continue shaking. The ethical act was not the scream but the sustained attention before and after it.

The text itself performs the ethics of the witness: it does not summarize O'Leary, does not diagnose him, does not resolve whether Sarah is real or imagined. It stays in the room, recording the full texture of the experience without flinching from its grotesquerie: the stink of the dead, the cold legs, the toothless mouth, the sores.

Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

Pillar note: Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

The landlord's monologue is the structural embodiment of recursive construction. He begins to tell a story, loops back, corrects himself, adds a new layer, forgets his original point, arrives somewhere unexpected, and begins again. His account of the hangman is never completed; it is perpetually revised as he climbs the stairs,.

"The landlord had corrected himself, casually, smiling..."

The correction is not embarrassment. It is method. He builds, revises, rebuilds. The building is never finished. The landlord's entire biography, candy merchant to ventriloquist to sailor to soldier, is a recursive construction of identity, each version not replacing but layering over the previous one.

O'Leary's argument with Sarah follows the same recursive logic. He dismisses her, then addresses her again. He says she is the wrong woman, then continues speaking to her as Sarah. He says he has forgotten her, then demonstrates that he has forgotten nothing. He returns to the beginning with what he learned, which is that he has learned nothing, which is itself a form of knowledge.

Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

Pillar note: Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

The chapter does not end with resolution. It ends mid-sentence, mid-disease list, mid-question:

"Was she her mother's only daughter?"

This is not a cliffhanger in the commercial sense. It is a philosophical commitment to the ongoing sentence. The demand for completion (for Sarah to be definitively dead or alive, for O'Leary to be definitively sane or mad, for the narrator to arrive somewhere) would be its own violence against the experience the text is rendering.

The legless newspaper man is perhaps the purest emblem of this pillar: he reports "all the news of what happened here ten, fifteen, twenty years ago". He has no legs, he cannot move forward, and so he reports backward, indefinitely. His room is "big enough for a man's head but not big enough for a man's body". He exists in a state of permanent incompletion, and the text treats this not as tragedy but as a form of integrity. He has an excellent head on his shoulders. He does his work.

The hangman's watch "was never wound": time is suspended, unmeasured, incomplete. The clock that should strike the hour does not strike. Completion is refused at the structural level. The chapter exists in a time that does not tick forward.

Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Pillar note: Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Every character in this chapter occupies the edge of a category:

  • The hangman is a prosperous farmer and model citizen who ties knots for pay; he is both executioner and agrarian, the violence of the state hidden inside the pastoral
  • The landlord is simultaneously a man of the world and a man who has never seen America: cosmopolitan and provincial at once
  • The legless man is a journalist without mobility, a reporter who can only report the past
  • Tillie is simultaneously old and young
  • Sarah is simultaneously dead and present, infant and crone, sister and lover,
  • The narrator occupies the Fire Escape: literally the marginal space, the emergency exit, the room that exists only in case of catastrophe

"I thought that if there should be a fire, all people would stream past me in their long nightgowns, their long hair burning like meteors as I lay still, unable to move."

The narrator imagines herself as the still center while the marginal becomes the main event: fire turning everyone into meteors, the emergency becoming the norm. The marginal person is not the exception. They are the evidence. The Fire Escape room is where the truth of the building lives: in the exit, in the emergency, in the space that exists only because the main structure might fail.

Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

Pillar note: Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

"He reports all the news of what happened here ten, fifteen, twenty years ago."

The legless man is sedimentary time made flesh. He cannot move forward, so he reports backward. The past does not recede; it is actively reported, continuously present, delivered on a sled made of a child's toy and roller skates, announced by rusted sleigh bells.

The doctor's relationship with Sarah is the deepest expression of sedimentary time in the chapter. Sarah died, possibly, at age one. She was buried in the vegetable garden. Yet she presses up through the ground, through decades of the doctor's professional life, through the hotel floor, into his bed. The past is not behind him. It is beneath him, and it has broken through.

"I am aware that, if I started digging in the vegetable garden, I would come upon, not the skeleton of a dust-small infant but of an old, old woman."

This is sedimentary time made explicit: dig down through the layers and you find not what you expected but what time has made of what was buried, the infant has become the old woman, the past has aged in the ground. The sediment transforms what it holds.

The hotel itself is sedimentary: "this old Tavern which was going to wrack and ruin", filled with people whose stories are decades old, whose bodies carry the marks of previous lives, tattoos, bullet wounds, old hair in wire baskets, lipstick covered with tobacco flakes. Everything in the building is a deposit from a previous time.

Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

Pillar note: Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

The landlord's speech is the most explicit demonstration of language as construction. He does not describe reality; he builds it as he speaks, correcting himself, revising, asserting, withdrawing. When he says "They are canaries" after having implied turkey buzzards, he is not correcting a factual error. He is choosing which reality to construct in this moment, for this listener.

O'Leary's language is similarly self-aware of its constructive function. He addresses Sarah in a medical register ("When was the last time she had enjoyed sexual communion with her husband?"), then in a familial register ("my little sister"), then in a legal register, then in a theological register ("Jerusalem, Jerusalem"). Each register constructs a different Sarah and a different O'Leary. The language does not reveal the relationship; it constitutes it, differently each time.

The picture over the bed, "Forget me not", is language performing its most naked constructive function: an imperative directed at time itself, an attempt to use words to hold what time dissolves. It fails, of course. The room is full of forgotten things: blonde hair in a waste basket, lipstick under tobacco, sodden toilet paper. Language that pretends to speak from nowhere, the universal imperative of "Forget me not", speaks from the very particular somewhere of a narrow room in a failing hotel where everything is already forgotten.

Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

Pillar note: Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

The hangman's feet "were beating a light tattoo on the ceiling above my head."

The sacred does not descend from above in this chapter. It beats on the ceiling from the floor above. The transcendent is always just one story up, making noise, scraping like matches on wet tinder. It is immanent (present, nearby, embodied) but never fully accessible.

The picture of the silver church steeple "piercing a pink cloud and garlanded with blue flowers" hangs over the narrator's bed, but it hangs crooked when O'Leary's raving shakes the walls. The sacred image cannot maintain its vertical orientation in this building. It tilts. It participates in the disorder of the immanent world rather than presiding over it from above.

The doctor's invocations ("Oh, God, God damn it", "Jerusalem, Jerusalem", "Jesus Christ, my God") are not prayers directed outward to a transcendent God. They are eruptions of the sacred within the immanent, blasphemous and reverent simultaneously, the sacred living inside the profanity, inside the drunk old man's grief, inside the shaking hotel room. The sacred is here. It is the grey bus, the permanent grief, the plural self. It is O'Leary on his knees washing out dirty slop jars, which is simultaneously degradation and a kind of terrible devotion.

Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

Pillar note: Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

"The bed having lived to the ripe old age of sixty in the city of St. Louis, you did, indeed, die of pneumonia at the tender age of one."

This extraordinary sentence (addressed to Sarah, or to the bed, or to both) collapses the distinction between object and person, between the narrator's present and Sarah's past, between the age of one and the age of sixty. The narrator is where time crosses itself. She lies in a bed that has accumulated sixty years of other bodies, in a room that holds other people's hair and lipstick and toilet paper, listening to a doctor mourn a woman dead for decades.

She did not choose this position. She was put in the Fire Escape room because there was a couple in the bridal suite. The obligation is structural, not chosen. She is constituted by what was deposited before she arrived: the hair combings, the sediment in the slop jar, the creaking rocking chair that moves as if a heavy body were in it.

And she is constituting the ground for what comes after: her witness, her screaming "Go, Sarah!", her carrying of the old pillow and its childhood tears; these become deposits in the sediment. The ancestors are in the room. The carrying continues. She cannot leave the Fire Escape room without having been changed by what pressed up through its floor.

"I am the only man in this town who remembers you."

O'Leary says this (man, though he is speaking to the narrator's consciousness as much as to Sarah) and it is the central statement of Pillar 11. Memory is not personal sentiment. It is structural obligation. To be the one who remembers is to be the crossing point, the place where the past and the present intersect, where the dead continue to press their claim on the living, where the infant Sarah and the old woman Sarah are the same sedimentary deposit pressing up through the vegetable garden into the doctor's bed into the narrator's sleepless night.
wheel-chapter-82:
Chapter 82

← Chapter 81 · Wheel and Spokes Home

Research notes: Chapter 82 · Reading guide: Guide, Chapter 82

Characters: Esther Longtree · Joachim Spitzer · Lucie Bell · Miss MacIntosh · Peron Spitzer · The Stone Deaf Man

Pillar 1 Not One Self

Pillar note: Pillar 1 Not One Self

The chapter opens with the narrator cataloguing what she could have told Esther Longtree but did not, and this act of withheld speech is itself a portrait of a self that is never singular or present. The narrator exists simultaneously as:

  • The daughter mourning her mother
  • The woman in love with a man she has not yet met
  • The child who was cared for by Miss MacIntosh
  • The observer of Mr. Spitzer's grief
  • The dreamer who may be dreaming all of it

Mr. Spitzer is the chapter's most explicit embodiment of the plural self. He is Peron and Joachim, the living and the dead, the lover and the mourner. The revelation that he is Peron, "never a musician at all, knew not one note of music from another note", does not resolve his identity. It multiplies it. He has spent decades performing a self that was not his, and now that he confesses the truth, his audience is dead. The confession changes nothing and everything simultaneously.

Even the stone deaf man at the chapter's end is plural: he is the man who shouts in the corridor, the man who loved Lucie Bell, the man who sleeps in the narrator's arms, the painter, the child who lost his hearing, the dreamer who hears "the cryings of little foxes" in a world of silence. He is all of these at once, and none of them resolves into the others.

The self here is not a stable container. It is a site of accumulation, of identities, losses, performances, and dreams that cannot be separated from one another.

Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

Pillar note: Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

This pillar is perhaps the chapter's central obsession. Young returns to it again and again with the insistence of a tide.

The narrator reflects:

"perhaps into reality, perhaps into a dream if nothing was real. Perhaps there is always a sense missing, that sense which would make the world real"

This is not a passing observation. It is the novel's epistemological foundation. Reality is always partial, always constructed through the senses available to us, and since those senses are always incomplete, reality is always already a version of illusion.

The mother's opium paradise is the chapter's most sustained image of constructed reality. Her house with its "golden turrets and towers", her imaginary guests, her drugged dreams; these are not presented as pathological departures from reality but as one valid mode of world-making among others. When the house is swept out to sea, the narrator does not mourn the loss of illusion. She mourns the loss of a particular construction:

"the divan upheld by dolphins was dreaming now under the flood"

The mother's death and the storm that follows collapse the distinction between the real house and the dreamed house. Both are gone. Both were real while they lasted.

Mr. Spitzer's entire life has been an illusion, or rather, a construction he maintained so long it became its own reality. He played Joachim for decades, and the question the chapter refuses to answer is: was he lying, or was he genuinely becoming? The novel does not distinguish between performance and being. This is not a flaw. It is the philosophy.

Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

Pillar note: Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

The chapter is saturated with grief, but Young is careful never to let it resolve. Each loss generates another loss, which generates another:

  • The mother's death
  • The house swept away by the storm
  • The old clam-digger drowned
  • Mr. Spitzer's lifelong unspoken love, confessed to a woman already dead
  • The narrator's pearls lost in the grass
  • Miss MacIntosh gone under the waves
  • Lucie Bell already gone before the narrator arrives

What is remarkable is the grammar of this grief. It is written in the past perfect and conditional, "I could have told," "might have told," "had waited," "had hoped", tenses that refuse to locate grief in a single moment. The grief is structural, embedded in the syntax itself.

Mr. Spitzer's loss of the old clam-digger is described with an almost comic excess of grief that Young uses to make a serious point:

"his grief had amounted to rage as he had stamped furiously with his cane upon the Boston sidewalks"

This grief is disproportionate to the apparent relationship. But that is precisely the point. Grief does not observe proportion. It accumulates: the clam-digger's death carries within it the death of Joachim, the death of the mother, the death of all the years of waiting. You do not grieve one thing. You grieve everything at once, always.

The chapter ends not with resolution but with continuation: the narrator conceives a child in the grass, loses her pearls, and the stone deaf man sleeps in her arms. The grief does not end. The weather continues. Life moves into it.

Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

Pillar note: Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

The narrator's primary mode throughout this chapter is witnessing. She does not intervene in Mr. Spitzer's grief. She does not rescue him. She does not offer conclusions about her mother's life. She listens: to Mr. Spitzer in the car after the funeral, to the stone deaf man through the wall at night, to Esther Longtree's stories, to her own interior voice.

The ethical weight of this witnessing is made explicit in the chapter's opening:

"I spoke not, for I listened as one might listen for one lonely heartbeat in the midst of the great silence."

This is not passivity. It is the hardest kind of attention: to hold the full weight of another's reality without converting it into something manageable. The narrator imagines what Esther Longtree would have said if she had confessed:

"So what if my mother was dead? So what difference did that make? So why did I mourn?"

Esther Longtree's imagined response is the voice of false witnessing: the rush to contextualize, to relativize, to conclude. The narrator refuses this. She chooses instead to hold the grief unresolved, to stay in the room with it.

The extended meditation on deafness and blindness is itself an act of witnessing: an attempt to imaginatively inhabit experiences of perceptual loss without claiming to resolve them, without converting them into metaphor too quickly. Young stays with the phenomenology: "the deaf man sees the rose but does not hear the voice, the whir of wings". She does not rush to the lesson.

Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

Pillar note: Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

The chapter's structure is itself recursive. It begins with what the narrator could have said, moves through Mr. Spitzer's confession, the storm, the mother's death, the clam-digger's habits, Miss MacIntosh's songs, and arrives finally at the stone deaf man and the narrator's conception of a child, only to loop back through the imagery of pearls, clouds, rivers, and silence that opened the chapter.

Mr. Spitzer is the chapter's great builder. He has constructed an entire life (a musical career, a legal practice, a decades-long vigil at a dying woman's bedside) on the foundation of a borrowed identity. When that identity collapses, he does not stop building:

"just as he had picked up a little music, enough to make a little ode, he had picked up enough law to close an estate, to bring this long affair to its just close"

He builds the urn burial. He preaches the funeral. He continues. The construction is provisional, it always was, but the building continues anyway.

The narrator's own construction is the most recursive of all. She is building this narrative (this long, looping, accumulating sentence that is the novel itself) out of losses and fragments and half-remembered things. She builds it knowing it will never be complete. She builds it because that is what building is.

Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

Pillar note: Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

Mr. Spitzer's tragedy is precisely a tragedy of forced completion. He waited his entire life for the moment when he could speak his love fully, when the conditions would be right, when the moon would come out from behind the cloud:

"He had waited for the moon to come out from behind the cloud."

And when he finally speaks (in the surrey at the sea's edge, the broken moonlight dashing against her withered face) she is already dead:

"my mother had not answered, for she was dead, had died at the beginning of his whispers"

The demand for completion (for the perfect moment of declaration, for the full revelation) is the violence that destroys him. He waited for completion and received only silence. The chapter implicitly argues that he should have spoken sooner, imperfectly, incompletely. The ongoing sentence, not the concluded one.

The stone deaf man at the chapter's end embodies the ethics of incompletion in his very speech. His monologue through the wall is a cascade of unfinished thoughts, interrupted declarations, sentences that trail into other sentences:

"This be the silent world, so cold and dark. Thou art not my imaginary love."

He does not conclude. He continues. And this continuation, this refusal to arrive, is what the narrator falls in love with. She loves him for his incompletion, not despite it.

Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Pillar note: Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Every significant figure in this chapter exists at the edges of categories:

  • The mother: between life and death, between dreaming and waking, between beauty and decay
  • Mr. Spitzer: between Peron and Joachim, between the living and the dead, between love and mourning
  • The old clam-digger: between the city and the sea, between servant and companion, between the living and the drowned
  • Miss MacIntosh: between sanity and madness, between the average and the phantasmagoric, between presence and absence
  • The stone deaf man: between sound and silence, between the world and his interior
  • The narrator herself: between childhood and adulthood, between the opium house and the ordinary world, between grief and love

Young makes the philosophical point explicit in the meditation on deafness:

"And what if one should be both deaf and blind? One would be closer to death than now"

The deaf, the blind, the deaf-blind; these are not pitied as deficient. They are examined as evidence of the constructed, partial nature of all perception. The marginal person reveals what the centered person conceals: that everyone is missing a sense, that everyone's reality is incomplete, that the average is itself a construction.

Miss MacIntosh's praise of the average is treated with deep irony:

"The individual, long ago, Miss MacIntosh had denied in favor of, as she had always said, what was average"

But Miss MacIntosh herself was the most extraordinary person the narrator knew. Her averageness was a performance, a construction, and when it crumbled, it revealed "the most phantasmagoric dream that man has dreamed". The marginal is always already inside the average, pressing outward.

Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

Pillar note: Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

This is perhaps the pillar most visibly embedded in the chapter's prose style itself. Young does not write in a linear past tense. She writes in layers: the past perfect accumulating beneath the simple past, the conditional accumulating beneath the actual, the dreamed accumulating beneath the remembered.

The image of the sunken house is the chapter's central sedimentary image:

"the divan upheld by dolphins was dreaming now under the flood"

The house is not gone. It is under. It continues to exist in the sediment of the sea, in the narrator's memory, in the structure of the novel itself. The past does not recede. It sinks.

The extended description of the mother's aging makes this explicit:

"as if through all of timelessness time had run with a secret logic of its own and must assert itself at the end like a dark river coming to light"

All those years of suspended time (the opium years, the dreaming years) did not disappear. They accumulated beneath her, and at the end they all surfaced at once:

"Suddenly then the years roared—all trains coming in at once"

The years were never gone. They were sediment. They pressed up through the ground.

The stone deaf man carries his own sedimentary time. He can still remember "the clatter of the moon vines upon an old, rotted porch": the last sounds he heard before his deafness. Those sounds are not behind him. They are beneath his silence, still audible in memory, still shaping the world he inhabits.

Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

Pillar note: Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

The chapter is acutely self-conscious about language as construction. The narrator's opening move is to catalogue the speech she did not make: to make visible the gap between experience and utterance:

"I could have confessed much to Esther Longtree if she had been as much interested in my confessions as I had been in hers"

This is language naming its own failure, its own conditionality. The novel is built out of sentences that begin with "I could have," "I might have," "perhaps": constructions that foreground their own provisionality.

The stone deaf man's speech is the chapter's most radical example of language naming its own location. He speaks from silence, into silence, about silence:

"I am a stone deaf man"

His language is not a neutral vehicle. It is generated from a specific, marginal location: a world where sound is interior, where words are felt rather than heard, where the human voice is something remembered rather than present. His speech sounds different from ordinary speech because it is different; it is language constructed from a position where the usual relationship between word and world has been severed.

Miss MacIntosh's songs are another example of language naming its own location: old psalms, old faiths, "fragments of the old songs of the old faiths of her childhood", sung over an ironing board by a woman who doubted their truth but could not abandon their form. The language carries its history. It cannot speak from nowhere.

Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

Pillar note: Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

The chapter is full of what might be called failed transcendence: moments where the sacred seems to promise a beyond that it then refuses to deliver. Mr. Spitzer waits for "one moment of blinding light in which all should be revealed". The light never comes. Or rather, it comes, but it illuminates only the ordinary: an old woman dying in a surrey, a horse at the sea's edge, a broken moon.

But Young does not treat this as tragedy. She treats it as the right answer to the wrong question. The transcendent was never going to be found outside. It was always here:

"Perhaps there was no storm but the stars emptying themselves."

The urn burial, the sandpipers running "back and forth like little urns themselves", the narrator sleeping in the grass under the stars while the stone deaf man whispers of clouds and rivers; these are not symbols pointing toward a beyond. They are the sacred itself, located precisely in the immanent, in the ordinary, in the grief-saturated present.

Miss MacIntosh's songs enact this most clearly. She sings of a transcendent God, "Thou hast led me to the still waters", but she sings them while ironing a shirt, her broken nose turning red, her face "smiling and dented with light". The sacred does not live in the words. It lives in the woman ironing, the voice breaking, the ordinary morning.

The old Negro woman's speech to the young stone deaf boy is the chapter's most explicit statement of immanent transcendence:

"life is imaginary, and this be an imaginary world"

This is not nihilism. It is the opposite. If life is imaginary, then imagination is life. The sacred is not above the imaginary world. It is the imaginary world, made with full attention and full love.

Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

Pillar note: Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

The chapter's final movement, the narrator's conception of a child in the grass, is the most explicit enactment of this pillar. The narrator does not know the night of conception, just as she does not know the night of her own conception:

"I do not know the night in which I conceived as I do not know the night in which I was conceived."

She is the crossing point. She carries within her the mother's dreams, Mr. Spitzer's grief, Miss MacIntosh's songs, the stone deaf man's silences, and she is constituting the ground on which her unborn child will stand. The child will inherit all of this sediment. The carrying continues.

The stone deaf man's wedding fantasy makes this structural obligation explicit:

we "would invite everybody to our wedding, little Johnny-jump-up and little jack-in-the-pulpit and the snapdragon... and Esther Longtree, for she was also our love, all her loves"

The wedding is not a private event. It is a gathering of everything: the living and the dead, the flowering and the fading, the human and the natural. The child to be born will stand on ground made of all of this. The obligation is not chosen. It is structural.

The chapter's final image, Esther Longtree's misspelled sign in the window: "Owt to luntsch. bee bak in a whale", is Young's most tender statement of the crossing point. Esther Longtree cannot spell. She will be back. She is always coming back. The misspelling is the human mark on the world: imperfect, provisional, continuing. The not-yet-born will read it. The ancestors are in the sediment. The carrying continues.

The Novel as Philosophical Practice

What Chapter 82 demonstrates, read through the Eleven Pillars, is that Miss MacIntosh, My Darling is not a novel that contains a philosophy. It is a philosophy: enacted in prose, in syntax, in the accumulation of images that refuse to resolve.

Young's great formal achievement is that she found a language adequate to radical immanence: a language that is itself plural, recursive, sedimentary, incomplete, and self-aware. The chapter does not argue for these pillars. It performs them, in the long, looping sentences that carry the past inside the present, in the characters who are always more than one person, in the grief that never arrives at resolution, in the love that comes through silence rather than speech.

The stone deaf man who hears everything and the narrator who speaks to him in the dark, spelling her name on his hand when darkness crosses the moon, are perhaps the novel's perfect image of what radical immanence looks like in practice: two imperfect, plural, grief-carrying selves, meeting at the crossing point of time, building something provisional and beautiful in the grass.
wheel-chapter-54:
Chapter 54

← Chapter 53 · Wheel and Spokes Home · Chapter 55 →

Research notes: Chapter 54 · Reading guide: Guide, Chapter 54

Characters: Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer

Pillar 1 Not One Self

Pillar note: Pillar 1 Not One Self

The chapter's central dramatic tension is not between Mr. Spitzer and the world, but between Mr. Spitzer and himself, or rather, between the multiple selves that occupy his single body.

"On one street, he was Peron. On another street, he was Joachim, the unchanging one."

This is not metaphor. The text presents it as ontological fact. Mr. Spitzer does not remember his brother or miss his brother; he becomes his brother, involuntarily, at street corners, in restaurants, when someone greets him with recognition. The plurality is not psychological disorder in the clinical sense; it is the structural condition of a self that has been constituted partly by another self.

The passport image crystallizes this:

He would "look at the passport picture which was taken in his youth but was Peron’s picture and was not his own, though serving equally well for him—he had never had his picture taken."

The document that certifies identity, the passport, already belongs to someone else. Identity as legal fiction, as administrative construction, collapses here. The plural self is not a problem to fix; it is what Mr. Spitzer is. He carries Peron's ticket stubs, Peron's pawn tickets, Peron's coin purse. He is haunted not by a ghost but by a co-tenant of his own body.

The text also presents the plurality as irresolvable. When a great physician offers to test his heart:

"Perhaps he would have found that Mr. Spitzer's was the beating heart, and perhaps he would have found that his was the resting heart... or perhaps, and this was what Mr. Spitzer had so greatly feared, he would have heard the beatings of two hearts."

Two hearts. The plural self, confirmed medically, refused medically. He declines the test precisely because resolution, knowing which heart beats, would destroy the ambiguity that constitutes him.

Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

Pillar note: Pillar 2 Reality Is Constructed

The chapter does not present a real Boston against which Mr. Spitzer's hallucinations are measured. It presents only the hallucination, with no stable referent outside it.

"For all was so much like my mother's wilderness of opium dreams that Mr. Spitzer... was less and less able to distinguish between what my mother imagined and a great city where he walked through constantly changing streets, here in this world where everything which was not was and everything which was was not."

This is the Pillar's core claim: reality is not what we find; it is what we make. The city Mr. Spitzer walks through is assembled from sediment, from Peron's world, from the opium lady's dreams, from historical Boston, from the Boston of the dead. The Flatiron Building appears in the Boston fog. The old Mather's hill coexists with President Wilson's death announcement. St. Sophia's Dome rises over a blind alley.

The chapter refuses to mark these as errors. They are presented in the same syntactic register as the grasshopper weathervane on Faneuil Hall, which is a real landmark. The text will not tell you which is real because the distinction is itself the illusion.

The penny arcade moment is particularly precise:

"Often, he had done nothing but stop to inquire into the unfamiliar pleasures of a penny arcade — when suddenly, sometimes without his knowledge, he had changed, imperceptibly changed, another personality taking over his life."

The trigger for ontological shift is trivial: a penny arcade, a gramophone honking, a wind against his face. This is not dramatic transformation. It is the ordinary porousness of the constructed self, leaking into adjacent constructions without warning.

Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

Pillar note: Pillar 3 Grief Doesn't End

This is perhaps the Pillar most completely embodied by the chapter. Grief here is not a response to a specific loss. It is the climate.

"His sorrow was great enough to admit a city gate, great as a city with this long traffic roar. Nothing should diminish it. All things should increase it, even as it diminished."

Note the paradox: all things increase it, even as it diminishes. This is not the arc of mourning toward resolution. This is grief as self-sustaining atmospheric condition: the weather of a world where everything is always already changing.

The chapter makes this explicit through the structure of Mr. Spitzer's daily life. Every morning he searches through Peron's belongings (ticket stubs, pawn tickets, gate receipts) not to find anything, but because the search is the condition of being alive:

"Sorrowfully each morning when he awakened, putting aside those concerns which were not immediate, he would look over old horse scores, track figures, unintelligible turf accounts."

He carries a mourning band. He carries black-bordered handkerchiefs. He wears a white rose. These are not performances of grief; they are the costume of a man for whom grief has become identity. And crucially, the chapter acknowledges what the Pillar names: that the honest life stops pretending otherwise:

"And yet there was ineffable beauty in this grief, more precious than crown jewels or lost empires or ruined dynasties, this precious grief without which he could not live, could not die, for it illuminated him."

Grief is not something to pass through. It is the light source.

Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

Pillar note: Pillar 4 Witnessing Is The Core Ethical Act

Mr. Spitzer is, structurally, a witness. He does not fix. He does not conclude. He watches, records, attends.

His legal practice has become this: not advocacy, not judgment, but the patient observation of the marginal:

"Never once, he believed, had he challenged another person's illusions or pretenses as his were so often challenged... For each man was a deposed king, surrounded by his own fallen glory — living by his own mistaken light or darkness."

This is the Witness ethic made explicit. He will not tell the man with the soap flake certificate that he is not the soap flake king. He will not tell the man with the Ivory stock that he does not own gold mines. He takes the matter under advisement. He says he will return. This is not cowardice or evasion; it is the refusal to simplify another person's reality, the refusal to impose resolution on an experience that has not resolved.

The witness stance extends to his own condition. He does not diagnose himself. He does not seek the physician's verdict. He refuses the heart test. He stays in the room of his own ambiguity, attending to it without rushing toward the conclusion that would end the attending.

His musical composition practice is also witnessing: catching inspiration on the wing, writing on shirt cuffs and handkerchiefs, not organizing, not concluding:

"He was waiting for perfect leisure, a moment which would be undisturbed by another moment, an interruption which would not be interrupted."

The moment of perfect witness never arrives, and he knows it will not. He composes anyway.

Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

Pillar note: Pillar 5 Build Anyway, Knowing It's Temporary

Mr. Spitzer builds. He composes music no one will hear, on scraps of paper that blow away. He searches streets for lost heirs he cannot find. He returns, again and again, to the same corners, the same searches, knowing they will yield the same non-results.

"He would seek out the rude, crude, bearded men... searching for him, that one brother he knew he would not find, either among the living or the dead, though he searched through all the avenues of time, all the avenues of space."

He knows he will not find Peron. The search continues. This is not delusion: the text is clear that he knows. It is recursive construction: returning to the beginning with what you learned, building anyway, knowing the building is provisional.

The musical composition is the purest instance:

"He had scarcely the time now to indulge himself in long hours of isolated concentration as to his echoic elegy — and it was written in so many fragments, he could scarcely imagine what the comprehensive thematic patterns of his music would be when the music was completed."

He cannot imagine the completed form because completion is not the point. The composition is the returning. The fragments are the structure, not the failure of structure.

The moment when the scraps blow out of his hat is devastating precisely because it is recursive: the music is lost, but he will write more music, on more scraps, which will also blow away. This is not tragedy in the classical sense. It is the honest description of how building works.

Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

Pillar note: Pillar 6 Unfinished Is Honest

The chapter is formally incomplete; it does not resolve. Mr. Spitzer does not find his brother, does not complete his elegy, does not discover whether the rajah's jewel was found, does not establish his identity. The chapter's final image is of his music blowing down an unending street:

"Saw his elegy blowing, winging down a long, dark, unending street — passing the omniscient angel of the meridian, passing the last street lamp which gave off a dim radiance outside itself? Passing all human knowledge?"

The question mark at the end of the chapter is Unfinished Is Honest made typographic. The text will not close. It passes beyond human knowledge and stops there, in the open.

The rajah's jewel subplot is a perfect structural emblem of this ethic:

"Suddenly, it had been forgotten — and there were other headlines... Only gradually, however, had Mr. Spitzer been able to dismiss from his mind the great mystery... everything was anticlimactic now, though there had been no climax."

No climax. The demand for resolution (who stole the jewel?) is quietly, ruthlessly denied. Life does not provide climaxes. The demand for them is its own violence against experience. The chapter enacts this formally: it raises mysteries and lets them dissolve, not into answers, but into other mysteries.

Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

Pillar note: Pillar 7 The Margins Reveal the Truth

The chapter is populated almost entirely by marginal figures: derelicts, exiled grand dukes working as doormen, old Lady Macbeths wandering hobo camps, cancer specialists dying anonymously among criminals, kings of Cracow living in city dumps.

"He had found a banker who had not known he was a banker, a lawyer who had not known he was a lawyer, a judge who had not known he was a judge, a Wall Street broker who had not known he was a Wall Street broker, an Arctic explorer who had not known he was an explorer until Mr. Spitzer came."

This list is not comic. It is ontological evidence. The marginal person (the deposed, the dispossessed, the unrecognized) reveals what the centered, recognized, socially legible person conceals: that identity is not inherent but assigned, constructed, and revocable. The banker does not know he is a banker because being a banker is not a property of his soul but a social construction that can be stripped away by circumstance.

Mr. Spitzer himself is the supreme marginal figure: a dead man still walking, a musician no one has heard, a lawyer with no clients, a twin who is simultaneously himself and his dead brother. He is not the exception to the social order. He is, as the Pillar states, the evidence of what the social order is made of.

Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

Pillar note: Pillar 8 The Past Doesn't Go Away

The chapter's treatment of time is its most philosophically radical feature. Time does not move forward here. It accumulates.

He would "look at the passport picture which was taken in his youth but was Peron’s picture... see how many times his passport had been stamped, how many frontiers he had crossed, how far he had travelled."

The passport shows journeys he never took: to Siam, to Cracow, to Bangkok. The sediment of Peron's life has deposited itself into his documents, his pockets, his memories. The past is not behind him. It is in him, pressing up.

The newspaper scene is the Pillar's clearest illustration:

"He had realized that the newspapers he was reading with baited breath... were dated ten years ago, no matter which year he was counting from — that the crown jewel had been stolen in the same year as Peron's death."

He has been reading ten-year-old newspapers as if they were current. The past has not receded; it has remained at the surface, indistinguishable from the present. The sedimentary layers have not separated. They press together.

The Boston geography enacts this too: Paul Revere's lantern-bearer asks for horse racing tips. President Wilson dies in the streets. The British Red Coats are coming, and the last trolley has already passed,. All historical moments coexist in the same fog. The past is not behind Mr. Spitzer. It is the ground he walks on, and it is still moving.

Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

Pillar note: Pillar 9 Language Shapes What's Possible

The chapter is written in a style that performs the instability it describes. The long, recursive, clause-within-clause sentences do not move toward conclusions; they accumulate qualifications, reversals, parenthetical doubts. The syntax enacts the plural self, the sedimentary time, the grief as weather.

Consider this construction:

"He was not always aware of them until he had passed beyond them — or be aware of them, yet their significance was better seen in retrospect. Also, there were not always, as the years seemed to increase, those indications which should have warned him whether he was himself or his dead brother."

The language here is doing what it is describing: it is not sure of itself, it qualifies, it opens possibilities it does not close. This is language that names its own location: the location of a consciousness that cannot achieve stable perspective on itself.

The chapter also plays with the language of legal and financial documents (pawn tickets, certificates, passports, stock shares) showing how the language of official reality construction (law, finance, identity documents) is just as unstable as the language of dreams. The soap flake certificate and the Grand Union Pacific Railway stock are presented with the same syntactic weight as the grasshopper weathervane. Official language does not confer reality. It constructs a particular kind of claim to reality, which can dissolve as easily as any other.

Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

Pillar note: Pillar 10 The Sacred Is Here

The sacred in this chapter lives entirely within the ordinary: within fog, snow, street lamps, cigarettes handed to the dead, scraps of paper blowing down dark streets.

"And yet there was ineffable beauty in this grief, more precious than crown jewels or lost empires or ruined dynasties, this precious grief without which he could not live, could not die, for it illuminated him."

The illumination is grief itself, not a transcendence of grief, not a consolation beyond grief, but grief as the immanent sacred. The light source is the wound.

The two packs of cigarettes (one perfumed for himself, one cheap cheroot for the dead) are a small liturgy of immanent transcendence. He carries offerings for the dead as a matter of practical habit, the way one carries subway tokens. The sacred is not elevated above the ordinary. It is continuous with it, indistinguishable from it, practiced in the same gesture as buying a newspaper or checking a watch.

The music scattered in the wind is the chapter's final image of immanent transcendence: the elegy passes beyond human knowledge, not upward into a heaven, but deeper into the immanent, into the fog, the dark street, the unending. The sacred does not transcend the world. It goes further in.

Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

Pillar note: Pillar 11 The Crossing Point

This is the Pillar that most completely describes what Mr. Spitzer is in this chapter. He is not a self moving through time. He is where time crosses itself.

"For years collapsed into a moment of sighing. Or a moment of sighing was extended to many years. At one moment, Mr. Spitzer was living — at the next moment, was translated among the dead — simply because he had paused for a moment to sigh."

He is constituted by what was deposited before he arrived, by Peron's life, by the opium lady's dreams, by the dead clients, by the drowned cities, by the historical Boston layered beneath the present Boston. And he is constituting ground: his wanderings, his music on scraps of paper, his legal advice to the grand duke doorman, his gifts of false teeth and wooden legs and second-hand overcoats, all of this is deposited into the sediment that the not-yet-born will stand on.

The chapter makes this structural obligation explicit:

"He would try to lose himself by helping others who were lost to find themselves."

This is not charity. It is the carrying forward that the Crossing Point demands. He cannot not do it. It is structural, not chosen. He carries Peron's errands because Peron is in the sediment of him. He carries music because music was deposited in him by dead composers whose buzzings live in his deaf ear.

The most devastating instance of the Crossing Point is the phone call to himself:

"He had even telephoned himself, though well knowing his phone had long ago been disconnected... and the phone had rung and rung, and he had waited with considerable trepidation, but no one had answered."

He is calling across the crossing point, from the living side to the dead side of himself, or from the present to the past, or from Joachim to Peron. No one answers because the crossing point is not a place where conversation is possible. It is a place where constitutions happen silently, below the level of speech, in the sediment, in the carrying.
